Welcome
This is an interactive book. You will not only read it: you will fill in tables, answer quick questions, move sliders, and run and edit real R and Python code without installing anything. title: AI and Machine Learning for Health Sciences
section: The idea that runs through the book
text:
The idea that runs through the book

A model is only as good as the decision it improves.

Health care is full of decisions taken under uncertainty: whether to start a treatment tonight, which batch of a cell therapy to release, which patient to call first. Data describe what has happened; models turn data into information; people use that information to decide; and their decisions create new data. We call this the decision loop, and every chapter ends by asking where its method sits in the loop, what can go wrong, and who stays in control.

title: AI and Machine Learning for Health Sciences
text:
How to use this book

Read it your way. The chapters tell one story, from data to decisions to language models, and reading them in order is the smoothest route. But each chapter also stands on its own: it opens with a Starting here? box that recaps, in a few lines, everything it borrows from earlier chapters and reintroduces the running examples, and every technical term links back to its definition (hover over the link to see it without leaving the page).
Do the gate. Each chapter opens with a short task that checks you are ready. You can skip it.
Answer the quick checks. One question, a few options, and an explanation for every option — including the wrong ones. Wrong answers are part of learning; they cost you nothing.
Play with the “Try it” widgets. Change a number, watch a figure react.
Complete the missions. Short coding tasks, graded instantly in your browser. Each one has a hint and a solution. Choose R or Python with the tabs; your choice is remembered across the book.
Run the Lab. A longer piece of code at the end of each chapter, also downloadable as .R and .py scripts so you can run it on your own computer.







The code runs in your browser — what if it does not load?





The R and Python engines (webR and Pyodide) download the first time you press Run code, which can take 10–30 seconds on a slow connection. If they cannot load (for example on a locked-down network), the text, quick checks, gates and widgets still work, and every Lab can be downloaded and run in RStudio, Positron, VS Code or Jupyter.

title: AI and Machine Learning for Health Sciences
text:
Who this book is for
Any health professional or student — in medicine, nursing, pharmacy, biomedical sciences, public health, therapeutic technologies and beyond — who wants to understand, use and question AI and machine learning with rigour. You need some basic statistics; you do not need to know how to program, and no prior knowledge of AI is assumed. The mathematics is there when it matters, introduced step by step: every term is defined the first time it is used, and the glossary is never more than a click away.

title: AI and Machine Learning for Health Sciences
text:
The data in this book
All datasets in this book are simulated: they look like real clinical data but describe no real person. That makes them safe to share — every dataset can be downloaded from the data appendix, together with the code that generated it — and it gives us a superpower real data never have: we know the truth, so we can check whether a method finds it.

title: 1  Data, models and decisions
text:
1.1 Four running examples
Throughout the book we return to the same four situations. They come from different corners of health care, so that you see the same idea working in different places, and they grow with the book: the table you meet today becomes a prediction problem, then a risk with uncertainty, then a dataset with holes, a cloud of points in many dimensions, groups of patients, an explained model, a causal question, a stream of clinical text and, finally, a decision supported by a language model. All four datasets are simulated (they describe no real person) and can be downloaded, with the code that generated them, from the data appendix.

Example 1 — Ward 7 ICU is our primary example. Acute kidney injury (AKI) is a sudden loss of kidney function that is common in critically ill patients; a rise in serum creatinine of at least 0.3 mg/dL within 48 hours is one of the internationally agreed criteria for it (Kidney Disease: Improving Global Outcomes (KDIGO) Acute Kidney Injury Work Group 2012). Example 2 — ONCO-1 is a randomised trial in which patients with solid tumours were allocated, by chance, to chemotherapy or no chemotherapy. Tumour size was measured before and after treatment, and the expression of 2 000 genes was recorded. Example 3 — HomeBeat follows 500 people at home who wear a smartwatch as part of a decentralised trial (one run largely outside the clinic). Example 4 — CellWorks records 420 production batches of a cell therapy; each batch must pass a potency test before it can be given to a patient.
Images are data too. When we reach neural networks (Chapter 7) a fifth source joins the four examples: paediatric chest X-rays labelled normal or pneumonia, taken from the public PneumoniaMNIST collection (Yang et al. 2023; Kermany et al. 2018). They are described in the data appendix.

In which running example was the assignment of the main exposure decided by the investigators rather than by circumstances?

Ward 7 ICU The ICU team decided how fully the protocol was delivered, but nobody assigned it at random for study purposes. This is routine care, recorded as it happened.
ONCO-1 trial Yes. Patients were randomised to chemotherapy or no chemotherapy; the investigators, not the patients’ circumstances, decided who received what. We return to why this matters in Section 1.3.
HomeBeat HomeBeat is a trial in name, but the wearable signals simply record what happens in daily life; no exposure is assigned.
CellWorks Process deviations happen during production; they were not deliberately assigned as in a designed experiment.

title: 1  Data, models and decisions
text:
1.2 Living in the data era

Definition 1.1 (Data) Data are recorded representations of facts, observations or measurements about objects, events or phenomena: numbers from a sensor, entries in a medical record, pixels in an image, words in a discharge letter, the sequence of bases in a strand of DNA. On their own they are symbols; they become information when interpreted in a context.

We live in an era of abundant data. Over recent decades the cost of computing and storage has fallen while the capacity to collect, transmit and analyse information has grown by orders of magnitude (Hilbert and López 2011). The life sciences are a striking case: genomics, transcriptomics, proteomics and metabolomics produce massive, high-resolution descriptions of biological systems (Stephens et al. 2015; Hasin, Seldin, and Lusis 2017). In health care, electronic health records (EHR), laboratory results, imaging, wearable sensors and omics profiles together give a multidimensional view of each patient (Jensen, Jensen, and Brunak 2012; Hripcsak and Albers 2013).
The challenge is no longer only to collect data but to integrate heterogeneous sources into coherent, trustworthy evidence for prediction, personalised treatment and clinical decision support (Raghupathi and Raghupathi 2014; Karczewski and Snyder 2018) — while keeping care safe, fair and transparent (Topol 2019). On Ward 7, for instance, Aoife’s record already combines a severity score, a blood-gas analyser reading, a blood-pressure monitor and laboratory results, each produced by a different system.

title: 1  Data, models and decisions
section: 1.3 Where data come from: observation and experiment
text:
1.3 Where data come from: observation and experiment
AI and machine-learning methods depend on the quality and nature of the data used to train them. Most health data come from one of two kinds of process.

Definition 1.2 (Observational and experimental data) Observational data are recorded as things happen, without the investigator intervening: health records, registries, wearable streams, imaging archives, manufacturing logs. Experimental data are generated when the investigator assigns treatments, conditions or exposures according to a design — from in-vitro experiments and animal studies to randomised controlled trials.

Observational data offer breadth and realism: they show how treatments perform in routine practice, across the full variety of patients, and over long periods — which is why they are essential for monitoring the safety of new therapies after approval (Sherman et al. 2016). Experimental data offer rigour: because the investigator controls who receives what (ideally by randomisation), they are the strongest basis for claims that a treatment causes an effect (Hernán and Robins 2020), and they form the backbone of regulatory assessments of new advanced therapies.
The two are complementary. A risk model may be developed from observational data and later tested in a trial; a trial may suggest which patients benefit, and observational data then show whether that holds in practice. In our examples, Ward 7, HomeBeat and CellWorks are observational; ONCO-1 is experimental. Keep this distinction in mind: in Section 1.10 we will see that it decides which questions a model can answer.

A hospital pharmacist extracts from the records all patients who received vancomycin last year, with their kidney function before and after. What kind of data is this?

Observational Correct. Nobody assigned vancomycin for research purposes; the records simply document routine care. Patients who received it may differ systematically from those who did not — a point we return to in Section 1.10.
Experimental An experiment requires the investigator to assign the exposure according to a design. Here the prescribers chose, for clinical reasons.
Neither: it is a model It is a set of recorded facts — data. A model would be a representation of how vancomycin and kidney function are related.

title: 1  Data, models and decisions
text:
1.4 Models: representations of reality
Look at Figure 1.1. On the left is a cylinder cut at a slant. Seen from different points of view it appears as an ellipse (from below), a triangle (from the side) or a rounded arch (from the front). Each of these flat shapes represents the same solid object, each keeps some of its features and loses others, and each rests on assumptions — for instance, that a three-dimensional object can be summarised by a two-dimensional shadow. Another word for representation is model.






Figure 1.1: One reality, several representations. A slanted cut of a cylinder (left) projects to an ellipse, a triangle and an arch, depending on the point of view.




Definition 1.3 (Model) A model is a simplified representation of a part of reality, built for a purpose, resting on assumptions. Several models can represent the same reality; they can be compared by how well they serve the purpose.

Models can be drawings, flowcharts or physical replicas. In this book they are mostly mathematical. Start with the smallest dataset we can imagine (Table 1.3): five people for whom we recorded whether they have a heart condition, their level of activity and their age, together with their heart rate and their blood oxygen saturation (SpO2). This table is factual evidence about a small piece of reality, the equivalent of the cut cylinder in Figure 1.1.

From this one reality we could build many representations, depending on our goal. Suppose we want to explain heart rate and SpO2 using the rest of the information. We can write
\[
(\text{heart rate},\ \text{SpO}_2) = f(\text{condition},\ \text{activity},\ \text{age}) ,
\qquad(1.1)\]
which says that the two outcomes are some function \(f\) of condition, activity and age. As it stands, Equation 1.1 is a mathematical function: it assumes there is no error. But two people with the same condition, activity and age rarely have exactly the same heart rate: biology, unmeasured factors and measurement error all play a part. Adding an error term turns it into a statistical model,
\[
(\text{heart rate},\ \text{SpO}_2) = f(\text{condition},\ \text{activity},\ \text{age}) + \text{error} ,
\qquad(1.2)\]
which in the general notation of the book is written
\[
y = f(\mathbf{x}) + \varepsilon ,
\qquad(1.3)\]
where \(y\) is the outcome, \(\mathbf{x}\) collects the characteristics used to explain it, \(f\) is the systematic part and \(\varepsilon\) (epsilon) is the part the characteristics do not explain (James et al. 2021, ch. 2). The true \(f\) is unknown. Most of the rest of this book is about different ways of defining the function that connects what we want to explain with what we use to explain it, that is, of estimating \(f\) from data. An estimate is written with a hat, \(\hat f\), and its prediction for a person is \(\hat y = \hat f(\mathbf{x})\). On Ward 7 the same idea reads \(\text{change in creatinine} = f(\text{SOFA}, \text{lactate}, \text{blood pressure}, \dots) + \varepsilon\), and you can build one such \(f\) yourself.

Build your own model of Ward 7. Each dot is one of the 1 250 past patients: their SOFA score on admission and the change in their creatinine over 48 hours. Your model is a straight line, \(\hat y = a + b \times \text{SOFA}\). Move the sliders to choose \(a\) and \(b\). The mean absolute error (MAE) is the average distance, in mg/dL, between your line and the dots: smaller is better. Here every line is scored on all 1 250 patients, the same dots it is drawn through: there is no train/test split yet (Section 1.8 adds one). On these patients the simplest possible model — ignore SOFA and predict the average change for everyone — has an MAE of about 0.24. Target: get your MAE below 0.20.

icu = FileAttachment("data/icu_aki.csv").csv({typed: true})
icuJ = icu.map((d, i) => ({...d, sx: d.sofa + (((i * 7919) % 101) / 101 - 0.5) * 0.6}))
viewof a = Inputs.range([-0.5, 0.8], {value: 0.37, step: 0.01, label: "Intercept a"})
viewof b = Inputs.range([-0.05, 0.15], {value: 0, step: 0.002, label: "Slope b (per SOFA point)"})
mae = d3.mean(icu, d => Math.abs(d.delta_creatinine_48h - (a + b * d.sofa)))
baseline = d3.mean(icu, d => Math.abs(d.delta_creatinine_48h - d3.mean(icu, e => e.delta_creatinine_48h)))
{
  const hit = mae < 0.20;
  if (hit && window.aihs) window.aihs.complete("ch01-tryit-line");
  return html`<p style="font-size:1.1rem">Your MAE (all 1 250 patients): <strong>${mae.toFixed(3)}</strong> mg/dL
   ·  average-only model, same patients: ${baseline.toFixed(3)} mg/dL
   ${hit ? "✓ target reached — your line uses SOFA to beat the average." : ""}</p>`;
}

















































Plot.plot({
  height: 320, grid: true,
  x: {label: "SOFA score on admission"},
  y: {label: "Change in creatinine over 48 h (mg/dL)"},
  marks: [
    Plot.dot(icuJ, {x: "sx", y: "delta_creatinine_48h", r: 2, fillOpacity: 0.35, fill: "currentColor"}),
    Plot.line([[0, a], [18, a + 18 * b]], {stroke: "#1f6f8b", strokeWidth: 3}),
    Plot.ruleY([0.3], {strokeDasharray: "4,4"}),
    Plot.text([[17.5, 0.33]], {text: ["AKI threshold 0.3"], textAnchor: "end", fontSize: 11})
  ]
})










Notice three things. First, many different lines are plausible representations of the same data: models are comparable, and we need a criterion — here the MAE — to compare them. Second, even the best line leaves most dots off the line: that scatter is \(\varepsilon\). Third, your line rests on an assumption — that the relationship is a straight line, and that SOFA alone is enough. Later chapters relax both.

In \(y = f(\mathbf{x}) + \varepsilon\) for Ward 7, which of the following does \(\varepsilon\) not include?

Biological variation between patients with the same measurements This is part of \(\varepsilon\): two patients with identical SOFA, lactate and blood pressure can still respond differently.
Factors that affect kidney function but were not recorded Unmeasured factors (for example a contrast-dye scan) end up in \(\varepsilon\) because the model cannot see them.
The effect of SOFA on the change in creatinine Right. SOFA is one of the features in \(\mathbf{x}\), so its systematic effect belongs to \(f\), not to the error.
Errors in measuring creatinine Measurement error in the outcome also lands in \(\varepsilon\).

title: 1  Data, models and decisions
text:
1.5 Decisions
Look at the crossroads in Figure 1.2. A traveller who stops at the sign can turn left, turn right, go straight on or turn back. Only one route can be taken at a time; each leads somewhere different; and the traveller may know the consequences of each route well, poorly or not at all.






Figure 1.2: A crossroads: one moment, several alternatives, uncertain consequences.



White (1969) turned this intuition into a definition. A decision is a clearly identifiable process that resolves a state of ambiguity — several alternatives, only one of which can be chosen — within a state of knowledge about their consequences. Writing \(\mathcal{A}\) for the set of alternatives and \(\mathcal{K}\) for the decision-maker’s knowledge,1 a decision is the passage
1 White writes \(Q\) and \(K\). We use \(\mathcal{A}\) and \(\mathcal{K}\) because \(Q\), \(K\) and \(k\) will have other meanings later in the book (queries and keys in a transformer, the number of clusters, the number of folds).\[
(\mathcal{A}, \mathcal{K}) \longrightarrow a \in \mathcal{A},
\]
that is, from a set of alternatives and what we know about them, to one chosen alternative \(a\).

Definition 1.4 (Decision) A decision is the choice of one alternative \(a\) from a set of mutually exclusive alternatives \(\mathcal{A}\), made on the basis of the decision-maker’s state of knowledge \(\mathcal{K}\) about their consequences, which is usually uncertain.

On Ward 7 tonight, \(\mathcal{A} = \{\text{start the bundle},\ \text{standard care}\}\). The knowledge \(\mathcal{K}\) includes Aoife’s measurements, Emma’s clinical experience, the guidelines — and, if we can build one, a model’s estimate of Aoife’s risk. Health care and advanced therapeutic technologies are full of such decisions: selecting a treatment strategy; designing a trial (who is eligible, which dose, which endpoint); choosing between a gene therapy, a cell therapy and a drug; continuing or stopping therapy as biomarkers change; allocating ICU beds or organs; releasing or rejecting a manufactured batch; assessing whether a new technology is worth its cost; and evaluating whether an AI decision-support system is safe enough to use.
Theories of decision-making fall into three broad families (Bell, Raiffa, and Tversky 1988), summarised in Table 1.4.



Table 1.4: Three families of decision theories (adapted from Bell, Raiffa, and Tversky 1988).












Normative
Descriptive
Prescriptive




Question
How should an ideally rational agent decide?
How do people actually decide?
How can real people decide better?


Basis
Axioms of rationality, expected utility
Observation; heuristics, biases, bounded rationality
Normative principles adapted to real constraints


Typical fields
Economics, decision theory
Cognitive psychology
Engineering, operations research, risk management, medicine






This book takes the prescriptive view, and in particular that of decision analysis: the discipline that applies decision theory to practical problems so that real decision-makers, with their limited time and attention, can construct sound decisions (Howard 1966a, 1988). It is sometimes called decision engineering (Sarti 2013, 2015).

1.5.1 The decision basis
Decision analysis organises a problem into a decision basis: an explicit statement of the alternatives, their consequences, the decision-maker’s preferences among those consequences, and the uncertainties that link them (Howard 1988; Sarti 2013). The basis can be written as a table, drawn as a decision tree or an influence diagram (Howard and Matheson 2005), and is built iteratively: technical experts, an analyst and the decision-makers exchange knowledge, starting from an obscure problem, until the basis is clear enough to act on (Figure 1.3).






Figure 1.3: Building a decision basis: experts, analyst and decision-makers iterate from an obscure problem to a solution by making alternatives, consequences, preferences and uncertainties explicit.



Spetzler, Winter, and Meyer (2016) describe six elements of decision quality: (1) an appropriate frame, (2) creative alternatives, (3) relevant and reliable information, (4) clear values and trade-offs, (5) sound reasoning, and (6) commitment to action. A decision is only as strong as its weakest element. Element 3 is where models enter: their job is to provide relevant, reliable information about the uncertainties. That is the practical motivation for everything that follows.

  Six interlocking links form a closed chain around the words elements of decision quality: 1 appropriate frame, 2 creative, doable alternatives, 3 meaningful, reliable information, 4 clear values and trade-offs, 5 logically correct reasoning, 6 commitment to action. Link 3, information, is shaded because it is where models contribute. A decision is only as strong as its weakest link.

Looking ahead: AI as a player in the whole chain



Today, a reasonable division of labour is this: AI can strengthen link 3 (information) and link 5 (reasoning, by checking calculations and consistency), it can support link 2 (by suggesting alternatives), while framing the problem, weighing values with the patient and committing to action stay human. In this book models mostly serve link 3. But AI is starting to do more than that and to act as a meta-player across the whole decision-quality chain. A language model can help frame a problem by asking which decision is really being made (link 1), propose alternatives a team had not considered (link 2), help patients and clinicians state their values and trade-offs explicitly (link 4), check an argument for gaps and common biases (link 5), and follow whether the chosen action is carried out and monitored (link 6). Each of these roles brings its own risks: a confident but wrong frame, alternatives that sound plausible but are not feasible, values suggested by the system instead of elicited from the people concerned. None of them removes the need for people to own the values and to answer for the decision. Chapter 18 returns to this role.



Aoife’s decision basis. Suppose the only uncertainty that matters tonight is whether Aoife develops acute kidney injury (AKI) in the next 48 hours, with probability \(p_{\text{AKI}}\). The team scores each of the four possible consequences from 0 (worst) to 100 (best), all things considered. The expected value of an alternative is its average score, weighting each consequence by its probability. Move \(p_{\text{AKI}}\) and watch which alternative is better; open the panel to change the scores.

viewof pAKI = Inputs.range([0, 1], {value: 0.5, step: 0.01, label: "Probability of AKI, p"})

viewof uBN = Inputs.range([0, 100], {value: 90, step: 1, label: "Bundle, no AKI"})
viewof uSA = Inputs.range([0, 100], {value: 30, step: 1, label: "Standard care, AKI happens"})
viewof uSN = Inputs.range([0, 100], {value: 100, step: 1, label: "Standard care, no AKI"})































evB = pAKI * uBA + (1 - pAKI) * uBN
evS = pAKI * uSA + (1 - pAKI) * uSN
pStar = {
  const num = uSN - uBN, den = (uSN - uBN) + (uBA - uSA);
  return den > 0 ? num / den : NaN;
}
html`<p>Expected value — <strong>bundle: ${evB.toFixed(1)}</strong> · <strong>standard care: ${evS.toFixed(1)}</strong>.
Best choice at p = ${pAKI.toFixed(2)}: <strong>${evB > evS ? "start the bundle" : evB < evS ? "standard care" : "either (tie)"}</strong>.<br>
The two alternatives are equally good when p = <strong>${isNaN(pStar) ? "—" : pStar.toFixed(2)}</strong>: this is the <em>decision threshold</em>.</p>`






























Plot.plot({
  height: 260, grid: true,
  x: {label: "Probability of AKI, p", domain: [0, 1]},
  y: {label: "Expected value (0–100)", domain: [0, 100]},
  color: {legend: true, domain: ["Bundle", "Standard care"], range: ["#1f6f8b", "#b35c00"]},
  marks: [
    Plot.line([[0, uBN], [1, uBA]], {stroke: "#1f6f8b", strokeWidth: 3}),
    Plot.line([[0, uSN], [1, uSA]], {stroke: "#b35c00", strokeWidth: 3}),
    Plot.dot([{p: 0, v: uBN, s: "Bundle"}, {p: 0, v: uSN, s: "Standard care"}], {x: "p", y: "v", fill: "s", r: 0}),
    Plot.ruleX([pAKI], {strokeDasharray: "3,3"}),
    isNaN(pStar) ? null : Plot.ruleX([pStar], {stroke: "currentColor", strokeOpacity: 0.5}),
    Plot.text([[pAKI, 96]], {text: [`p = ${pAKI.toFixed(2)}`], dx: 4, textAnchor: "start", fontSize: 11})
  ]
})







With the default scores the threshold is \(p = 0.25\) (Pauker and Kassirer 1980): if Aoife’s chance of AKI is above one in four, the bundle is the better bet. Two lessons follow, and both run through the whole book.

A decision needs both probabilities and values. The model can estimate \(p_{\text{AKI}}\); it cannot tell the team how bad dialysis is compared with an under-dosed antibiotic. Values come from patients, clinicians and society.
Information is valuable only if it can change the decision. Without any model, the team might use the average: 58 % of past Ward 7 patients had a creatinine rise of 0.3 mg/dL or more, which is above the threshold, so everyone would get the bundle. The model we will build in Chapter 5 gives Tomás a risk of 7 %, Aoife 49 % and Priya 99 %. Aoife and Priya stay above the threshold, but Tomás falls below it: the model changes Tomás’s management — and that change is where the model earns its keep. Decision analysts call this the value of information (Howard 1966a, 1966b). We make it precise in Chapters 2 and 5.


The team decides that, for Aoife, AKI under standard care would be even worse than they first thought (they lower that score from 30 to 10). What happens to the decision threshold?

It goes down: the bundle becomes worthwhile at lower risks Correct. The worse the consequence the bundle protects against, the smaller the probability needed to justify it. Try it in the widget: set “Standard care, AKI happens” to 10 and the threshold drops from 0.25 to about 0.17.
It goes up: the bundle needs higher risks to be worthwhile The opposite: a worse outcome without protection makes protection attractive sooner.
It does not change, because the threshold depends only on the model The threshold depends only on the values, not on the model. The model supplies \(p\); the values fix where the line is drawn.

title: 1  Data, models and decisions
section: 1.6 What do we mean by AI and machine learning?
text:
1.6 What do we mean by AI and machine learning?

1.6.1 Intelligence, human and artificial
Before defining artificial intelligence, it is worth asking what intelligence is. Three lenses help, and each tells us something different about what machines can and cannot do.

Philosophy. The word comes from the Latin intelligere, “to understand”, formed from inter (“between”) and legere (“to read” or “to choose”): reading between things, choosing among them. Philosophically, intelligence has long been tied to the capacity to grasp truth, understood as a correspondence between thought and reality (David 2015). That is more than thinking (we can think freely without judging whether something is true) and more than skill (we can execute a procedure well without understanding it).
Biology. For a living system, intelligence is close to the capacity to regulate itself and adapt to its environment: to keep its internal state in balance (homeostasis) (Cannon 1929) and to sense and respond to what happens around it. The range is enormous, from a bacterium swimming towards a source of food to a human brain weighing a diagnosis.
Computing. Here the word is a metaphor. We call a system intelligent when it performs tasks that, if done by a person, would require cognitive effort: recognising a pattern, making a prediction, producing a sentence. The system manipulates symbols according to rules and learned patterns; no understanding is required, and none is claimed (Russell and Norvig 2021, ch. 1).

The third lens matters most for this book. A computer can check whether a statement is consistent with its rules, or likely given its training data; it cannot check whether the statement is true of the world. Artificial intelligence therefore describes what a system does, not what it understands. Keep this in mind whenever a system sounds sure of itself: it is the root of the “hallucinations” of language models that we study in Part V (Ji et al. 2023).






Are you a millionaire?



Your brain is a remarkably cheap and efficient computer. Estimates of how many operations per second it performs are uncertain by several orders of magnitude, from about 1013 to 1017, with a best guess around 1015 (Carlsmith 2020); it runs on about 20 watts. One modern data-centre GPU (an NVIDIA H100) performs roughly 1015 low-precision operations per second, draws about 700 watts and costs in the order of US$30 000 (NVIDIA Corporation 2023; Leswing 2024). At the best-guess estimate one GPU matches the raw arithmetic of your brain; at the upper estimate you would need about a hundred of them, some three million dollars of chips and around 70 kilowatts, thousands of times the power your brain uses. Raw arithmetic is not intelligence, of course, but the comparison is a useful reminder of two things: modern AI is expensive in energy and hardware, and the most capable “neural network” in any clinical decision is still the one inside a human head.



A large language model writes a fluent, confident paragraph explaining a drug interaction. Does it understand what it wrote?

Yes: fluent, correct text requires understanding Fluency shows that the model has learned the patterns of language extremely well. It does not show that the model checked its words against reality.
No, and so its output is useless Plausible text is often correct and can be very useful. The point is not that the output is worthless, but that it has to be checked.
Not in the philosophical sense: it produces plausible text, and plausible is not the same as true Correct. The model predicts the most plausible next words from patterns in its training data; it has no way of testing whether they correspond to the world. That tells you what to do with its answer: verify it, as you would a colleague’s suggestion you cannot yet trust.



Definition 1.5 (Artificial intelligence) Artificial intelligence (AI) is the field that builds systems able to perform tasks that would require cognitive processes if carried out by humans — perception, reasoning, learning, language, decision-making (Russell and Norvig 2021). European law defines an AI system as a machine-based system that, for explicit or implicit objectives, infers from the input it receives how to generate outputs such as predictions, content, recommendations or decisions that can influence physical or virtual environments (European Parliament and Council of the European Union 2024, Article 3(1)).

AI is a family of technologies drawing on computer science, mathematics, statistics, linguistics, cognitive psychology and philosophy. Classic examples include expert systems that encode clinicians’ rules, speech and image recognition, autonomous robots and vehicles, and natural language processing such as translation and summarisation.

Definition 1.6 (Machine learning) Machine learning (ML) is the part of AI in which a system learns from data instead of being programmed with explicit rules. Following Mitchell (1997), a program learns from experience \(E\) with respect to a task \(T\) and a performance measure \(P\) if its performance on \(T\), measured by \(P\), improves with \(E\). The term goes back to Arthur Samuel’s checkers-playing programs (Samuel 1959).

For Ward 7: the task \(T\) is to predict the change in creatinine; the experience \(E\) is the records of past patients; the performance \(P\) is, for example, the mean absolute error you minimised in the widget above. An expert system would instead encode a clinician’s rules (“if SOFA ≥ 10 and MAP < 60, flag”); a machine-learning system would learn its rule from the 1 250 records.
The difference can be put in one line. In traditional programming, people write the rules and the computer applies them to data to produce answers: rules + data → answers. The CURB-65 score for pneumonia is a good example: clinicians chose five items (confusion, urea, respiratory rate, blood pressure, age 65 or over) and how to add them up (Lim et al. 2003). In machine learning, the computer is given data and the answers, and finds the rules: data + answers → rules. An algorithm studies thousands of past pneumonia admissions and their outcomes and learns its own score. The learned score may capture patterns that no one wrote down, but it may also memorise the quirks of the hospital it learned from, the overfitting we meet in Section 1.9. The hand-written score is crude but transparent and widely validated; the learned one has to earn that trust.
How does a machine “find the rules”? Every method in this book runs a version of the same learning loop: guess with the current settings of the model, mark the guess by measuring how wrong it is, adjust the settings in the direction that makes it less wrong, and repeat until it stops improving. You did exactly this by hand with the sliders in Section 1.4; Chapters 3, 4 and 7 show how computers do it automatically.

Figure 1.4: Machine learning is one part of artificial intelligence; its applications are often grouped into predictive and generative AI.



Figure 1.4 places machine learning inside artificial intelligence and shows the two broad uses discussed below, predictive and generative AI. Inside machine learning, deep learning (LeCun, Bengio, and Hinton 2015) uses neural networks with many layers, which learn their own features directly from raw data (pixels, ECG signals, text) instead of relying on features chosen by people; it needs large amounts of data and computing power, and it is behind most of today’s headlines, from retinal screening (Gulshan et al. 2016) to chatbots (Chapter 7).


1.6.2 Four kinds of learning
Machine-learning methods are usually grouped by the kind of task they perform. Figure 1.5 shows the three classic families; generative modelling is often added as a fourth.






Machine learning methods






Supervised
trained with
labelled outcomes

Unsupervised

e.g. clustering

Reinforcement

trial and reward




Figure 1.5: The three classic families of machine-learning methods.




Supervised learning uses labelled data — examples for which the outcome is known — to learn a mapping from features to the outcome. Ward 7: predict the change in creatinine (a number: regression) or whether AKI occurs (a category: classification) from admission data (James et al. 2021). Chapters 3–9.
Unsupervised learning uses unlabelled data to find structure: groups, directions, low-dimensional summaries. HomeBeat: group participants into activity and stress profiles without being told what the profiles are (Hastie, Tibshirani, and Friedman 2009, ch. 14). Chapters 10–11.
Reinforcement learning learns a policy — a rule for acting — by interacting with an environment and receiving rewards or penalties over time. Ward 7: learn when to adjust a drug dose as creatinine changes from day to day (Sutton and Barto 2018). Chapter 14.
Generative modelling learns the distribution of the data so that it can create new, realistic examples: synthetic patient records, images, molecules, text (Goodfellow, Bengio, and Courville 2016, ch. 20). Chapters 15–19.

Labels are often the expensive part. Imagine labelling one million chest X-rays as normal or abnormal: at one minute per image that is about 16 700 hours, some eight years of a radiologist’s full-time work. Two strategies reduce the burden. Semi-supervised learning trains on the few labelled examples, lets the model label the unlabelled ones it is most confident about, and retrains on the larger set, with the risk that the model teaches itself its own mistakes (Chapelle, Schölkopf, and Zien 2006). Transfer learning starts from a model already trained on a large, different dataset (millions of everyday photographs, say) and fine-tunes it on a few thousand medical images, just as a doctor moving into cardiology does not relearn anatomy; the price is that the original data bring their own biases with them (Pan and Yang 2010). Both ideas return in Chapters 7 and 18.

Which kind of learning fits each question?

Draft a discharge letter for Tomás from his ICU notes. Generative




1.6.3 Predictive and generative AI
Recent AI is often described through two paradigms. Predictive AI estimates outcomes or probabilities from existing data: “What is likely to happen?”, “Which class is this?” — risk of readmission, tumour response, batch failure. In this book predictive AI and (supervised) machine learning are used almost interchangeably. Generative AI creates new content that resembles its training data: large language models that write text (Brown et al. 2020), generative adversarial networks (Goodfellow et al. 2014) and diffusion models (Ho, Jain, and Abbeel 2020) that create images, variational autoencoders (Kingma and Welling 2014) that synthesise records or molecules.
The two are complementary rather than rivals. Generative models can simulate scenarios, propose candidate molecules or draft documents; predictive models can then estimate the likely effect or quality of what was generated — and a human decides. In advanced therapeutic technologies this combination is already used to design molecules (Zhavoronkov et al. 2019) and optimise protocols; Chapter 18 examines a drug that went from a generative-AI design to a clinical trial.

A hospital installs software that flags any patient whose creatinine rises by 0.3 mg/dL or more, exactly as the KDIGO guideline states. Is this machine learning?

Yes, because it is software that supports a clinical decision Supporting decisions is not enough: the question is how the rule was obtained.
No, it applies a rule written by people; nothing is learned from data Correct. This is a rule-based system — arguably a simple form of AI, but not machine learning. It would become ML if the threshold or the rule were estimated from past patients’ data.
Yes, because the KDIGO threshold came from data originally The guideline committee learned from evidence; the software does not. In Mitchell’s terms, the software’s performance does not improve with experience.

Definition 1.7 (Instance, feature, outcome) Each row of a dataset is an instance (here, a patient) and each column a feature or variable. Features used to make a prediction are predictors (inputs, explanatory variables), written \(\mathbf{x}_i = (x_{i1}, \dots, x_{ip})\) for instance \(i\); the feature we want to predict is the outcome (response, target), written \(y_i\). When the outcome is known for an instance, it is called its label. A dataset has \(n\) instances and \(p\) predictors (James et al. 2021, ch. 2).

In Table 1.5, \(n = 1\,250\); patient_id is an identifier (never a predictor: it carries no information about the patient, only a label for the row); site and the nine clinical measurements are the \(p = 10\) predictors; delta_creatinine_48h is the outcome. 1.8 The predictive pipeline: train, test, deploy
Most supervised-learning projects follow the same pipeline (figure below).


  The predictive pipeline
  The 1 250 past patients are split at random into a training set of 1 000 and a test set of 250. The model is fitted on the training set, its error is measured on the test set, and only then is it deployed to predict for tonight's patients Aoife, Tomás and Priya, whose outcomes are unknown.
  
  
  Past patients
  n = 1 250
  outcome known
  
  Training set (80%)
  fit the model

  kept aside, never seen
  
  Evaluate
  error on test set

  Aoife, Tomás, Priya
  outcome unknown
  
  
  
  
  
  fitted model

The predictive pipeline on Ward 7: split, fit, evaluate, and only then deploy.


Training. The past data are split at random into a training set, used to fit the model — to choose its internal parameters, like the intercept \(a\) and slope \(b\) of your line — and a test set, kept aside. On Ward 7 the book makes this split once, at random with a fixed seed, and stores it in data/splits/ward7_split.csv: 1 000 training and 250 test patients. Every model in the book is fitted on the same 1 000 and judged on the same 250, so that models built in different chapters can be compared fairly (Chapter 3 explains how the split was made).
Testing. The fitted model predicts the outcomes of the test set, which it has never seen, and the predictions are compared with the true outcomes. This estimates how the model will do on new patients. Evaluating a model on the data it was trained on is overly optimistic, like marking a student’s exam with the answers they memorised (Hastie, Tibshirani, and Friedman 2009, ch. 7; Steyerberg 2019).
Deployment. If the performance is good enough for the decision at hand, the model is used for new cases — Aoife, Tomás and Priya tonight — whose outcomes nobody knows yet. A model that performs well on new data is said to generalise.

Figure 1.8 shows the same three steps on the five-person table: fit on three people, check on the other two, then predict for new people P06, P07, … P100 whose heart rate nobody has measured yet.






Figure 1.8: The pipeline sketched by hand on the five-person table: a training set, a test set, and deployment to completely new, unseen people.




A team fits a model to all 1 250 Ward 7 patients and reports its error on those same 1 250 patients as the error to expect tonight. What is the problem?

None — more data always gives a better estimate of the error More data helps fit the model, but the error measured on the training data says how well it memorised, not how well it generalises.
The reported error is likely to be too optimistic Correct. The model has already “seen the answers” for these patients. An honest estimate needs patients the model did not see: a test set, or cross-validation (below).
The error will be too pessimistic, because 1 250 patients include outliers Outliers affect both training and test error; the systematic problem here is optimism, not pessimism.

section: 1.10 Prediction is not causation: a first look
text:
1.10 Prediction is not causation: a first look
Models can be grouped by how they treat the process that generated the data — the data-generating process.

Associational (non-causal) machine learning looks for stable statistical patterns that predict an outcome \(y\) from features \(\mathbf{x}\), \(\hat y = \hat f(\mathbf{x})\), without representing why the pattern exists. Linear regression, random forests and neural networks used for prediction are of this kind. Such models can fail when the world changes — for instance after a new treatment policy — a problem known as distribution shift (Finlayson et al. 2021).
Causal machine learning represents the mechanism that produced the data and asks what would happen to \(y\) if we intervened on a feature, holding everything else fixed. It needs assumptions about the mechanism, usually drawn as a causal graph (Pearl 2009; Hernán and Robins 2020).

Ward 7 gives a concrete warning. Does delivering more of the care protocol protect the kidneys? Because the data are simulated, we know the truth: in the code that generated them, each additional 10 percentage points of protocol adherence lowers the 48-hour rise in creatinine by 0.028 mg/dL (a coefficient of −0.28 per unit of adherence). But adherence was not assigned at random: the sickest patients — high SOFA — are the hardest to treat by the book, and they are the most likely to have rising creatinine anyway. Severity is a confounder: it influences both the exposure and the outcome (figure below).


  Severity confounds the effect of protocol adherence
  A causal diagram. Severity (SOFA) points to protocol adherence and to the change in creatinine. Protocol adherence also points to the change in creatinine.
  
  Severity (SOFA)
  
  Protocol adherence
  
  Change in creatinine
  
  
  
  effect of interest

A confounder: severity affects both how fully the protocol is delivered and how the kidneys fare.

Run the code below. The first model looks only at adherence; the second also accounts for severity.

RPython























The naive model says adherence is almost twice as protective as it really is (about −0.53 instead of −0.28), because it credits adherence with the better kidneys that come from simply being less sick. Accounting for severity brings the estimate close to the truth (about −0.30). Both models predict reasonably well; only one would give the hospital a correct answer to the question “how much will improving adherence help?”. You do not need to understand the code yet — Chapter 4 explains these models and Chapter 13 is devoted to causal questions.

A model trained on Ward 7 predicts creatinine changes accurately. A manager proposes to use its coefficients to decide how much to invest in raising protocol adherence. What is the main risk?

None: an accurate model has accurate coefficients Accuracy of prediction does not guarantee that each coefficient measures a causal effect. The naive model above predicts quite well and still doubles the effect of adherence.
The coefficients may mix the effect of adherence with that of confounders such as severity Correct. Predictive accuracy and causal validity are different properties. Answering “what if we change adherence?” needs causal reasoning (Chapter 13) — or a randomised experiment like ONCO-1.
The model has too few patients to be used 1 250 patients is plenty for this model; the issue is confounding, which more data of the same kind does not fix.

title: 1  Data, models and decisions
text:
1.11 Reproducibility
Data are our evidence; models turn evidence into information for decisions. Across every step — collecting and organising data, building a model, evaluating it, communicating results — one principle matters above all: reproducibility, the ability of someone else to rerun the same analysis on the same data and obtain the same results (Peng 2011; Sandve et al. 2013). It is achieved with a transparent workflow: code that runs from raw data to final numbers, fixed random seeds, recorded software versions, and version control (for example Git), which keeps the full history of every file (Blischak, Davenport, and Wilson 2016). Whenever data governance, intellectual property and the law allow, data and code should be shared.
In health, reproducibility is also a regulatory matter. Agencies that approve drugs, devices and advanced therapies base their decisions on documented evidence, and the European AI Act requires providers of high-risk AI systems, including many medical ones, to keep technical documentation and logs that allow their systems to be traced (European Parliament and Council of the European Union 2024). Every dataset in this book is produced by a script with a fixed seed for exactly this reason. The data appendix lists them, and Appendix A shows how to install R, Python, Git and GitHub and put your own work under version control.

text:
1.12 Where this fits in the decision loop


  The decision loop
  A cycle of five boxes: data feed a model; the model produces information; people combine the information with values to make a decision; the decision leads to actions and outcomes, which are recorded as new data. A person is shown at the decision step: the human in the loop.
  
  Data
  
  Model
  
  Information
  
  Decision
  + values, human in the loop
  
  Action and outcome
  recorded as new data
  
  
  
  
  

The decision loop. This book is about the Model → Information step, always seen from the Decision.

This chapter built the frame for everything that follows. Data (Section 1.2, Section 1.3) are evidence; a model (Section 1.4) is a representation that turns evidence into information; a decision (Section 1.5) combines that information with values, under uncertainty; and its consequences become new data. Machine learning (Section 1.6) is a way of building the model step from data. What can go wrong? A model evaluated on its own training data looks better than it is (Section 1.8); a flexible model can memorise noise (Section 1.9); a predictive model can be mistaken for a causal one (Section 1.10). Who stays in control? The people who own the values — patients and clinicians — because no model can supply those.

Selected answers





2. Observational: nobody assigned the protocol at random, and the comparison is before–after. A drop could be due to other changes over time (new staff, a different case mix, seasonal infections, better creatinine monitoring changing how AKI is recorded).
4. Without a model everyone is treated as 58 % risk, above the threshold of 0.25, so all three receive the bundle. With the model, Aoife (0.49) and Priya (0.99) still receive it, but Tomás (0.07) does not: the model changes Tomás’s management, sparing him the costs of the bundle. That change is the model’s value.
6. With the seed used in the widget the test error is smallest at degree 4 (0.382), with degree 3 practically tied (0.383). The training error keeps falling because a more flexible polynomial can always pass closer to the 30 training points — including their noise — even when this makes it worse on new points.
8. In the simulation, adherence depends on SOFA only, so SOFA is the confounder. Variables that depend on SOFA (map_min, bun, crp, albumin) are associated with adherence through SOFA; adjusting for them is not wrong here, but it does not remove additional confounding.

title: 1  Data, models and decisions
text:
1.15 Summary

Data are recorded evidence about the world; they come from observation or experiment, and the difference matters for causal questions.
A model is a simplified, purpose-built representation of reality; a statistical model writes \(y = f(\mathbf{x}) + \varepsilon\), and learning means estimating \(f\).
A decision chooses one alternative from \(\mathcal{A}\) given knowledge \(\mathcal{K}\); decision analysis makes alternatives, consequences, preferences and uncertainties explicit. Models supply information about uncertainties; values come from people.
AI builds systems that perform tasks requiring cognition; machine learning is AI that learns from data. Learning can be supervised, unsupervised, reinforcement or generative.
Honest evaluation needs unseen data: a test set, and cross-validation for choices made during training. Too-simple models have high bias; too-flexible ones overfit.
A model that predicts well need not reveal causes: beware of confounders.

How to use this chapter






Starting here?





This chapter borrows four ideas from Chapter 1.

A model (Definition 1.3) is a simplified representation of reality built for a purpose; its output is information, here a patient’s risk of an outcome.
Each row of a dataset is an instance with features and an outcome (Definition 1.7). On Ward 7 the outcome is the rise in creatinine over 48 hours; a rise of at least 0.3 mg/dL counts as acute kidney injury (AKI) (Kidney Disease: Improving Global Outcomes (KDIGO) Acute Kidney Injury Work Group 2012).
A decision (Definition 1.4) chooses one alternative from a set \(\mathcal{A}\) given what we know. Tonight \(\mathcal{A} = \{\text{start the bundle}, \text{standard care}\}\).
The decision threshold (Section 1.5): with the scores used in Chapter 1, the bundle is the better choice whenever the probability of AKI is above 0.25.

title: 2  Uncertainty and probability for decision-makers
text:
2.1 Why decision-makers need probability
At the end of Chapter 1 a straight line predicted that Aoife’s creatinine would rise by about 0.3 mg/dL: right on the AKI threshold. A single number like that hides the question Emma actually needs answered: how likely is AKI? Two patients with the same predicted rise can carry very different risks, depending on how much the outcome varies around the prediction.
Uncertainty in health care has two sources (Spiegelhalter 2019). Some of it is variability: even patients with identical measurements respond differently, as the scatter around your line in Section 1.4 showed. Some of it is lack of knowledge: we have seen only 1 250 past patients, so even the average risk is known only approximately. Probability describes both. It can be read as a long-run frequency (“of 100 patients like Aoife, about 49 develop AKI”) or as a degree of belief (“I am 49 % sure Aoife will develop AKI”); the rules of calculation are the same either way (Blitzstein and Hwang 2019). In this chapter we lean on the frequency reading, because counting people is the most reliable way to reason about chance, and we return to beliefs when we meet Bayes’ theorem.
Probability is the currency of the decision basis of Chapter 1: the model supplies probabilities, people supply values, and the decision combines the two (Section 1.5). Before we can spend that currency, we need to know what it buys.
crumbs: 2  Uncertainty and probability for decision-makers

title: 2  Uncertainty and probability for decision-makers
text:
2.2 Random variables and their distributions

Definition 2.1 (Random variable) A random variable is a quantity whose value is not known in advance and is described by probabilities: whether a patient develops AKI, how many patients on a ward do, a participant’s resting heart rate tomorrow. It is written with a capital letter, \(X\); a value it can take is written in lower case, \(x\). \(P(X = x)\) reads “the probability that \(X\) takes the value \(x\)”.


Definition 2.2 (Probability distribution) The probability distribution of a random variable lists the values it can take and how probable each one is. A discrete variable (a count, a yes/no) has a probability for each value, and these add up to 1. A continuous variable (a heart rate, a concentration) has a density: a curve whose area over an interval is the probability of falling in that interval, and whose total area is 1 (Blitzstein and Hwang 2019).


2.2.1 Yes or no: the Bernoulli distribution
On Ward 7 the simplest random variable is whether a patient develops AKI. Write \(X = 1\) if they do and \(X = 0\) if they do not. If the probability of AKI is \(\theta\), then
\[
P(X = 1) = \theta, \qquad P(X = 0) = 1 - \theta .
\qquad(2.1)\]
This is the Bernoulli distribution, the distribution of every yes/no outcome in medicine: AKI or not, response or not, a batch that passes or fails its release test. Of the 1 250 past Ward 7 patients, 725 met the AKI criterion, a proportion of 0.58. Treating every patient as if they had the same \(\theta\) is crude — the point of building models is to give each patient their own \(\theta_i\) — but it is the natural starting point.


2.2.2 Counting yes’s: the binomial distribution
Suppose the ward has 20 patients and each, independently, has the same probability \(\theta =\) 0.58 of AKI. The number \(Y\) who develop AKI is a count between 0 and 20, with a binomial distribution:
\[
P(Y = k) = \binom{n}{k}\, \theta^{k} (1 - \theta)^{n - k}, \qquad k = 0, 1, \dots, n ,
\qquad(2.2)\]
where \(\theta^{k}(1-\theta)^{n-k}\) is the probability of one particular sequence with \(k\) cases and \(n-k\) non-cases, and \(\binom{n}{k}\) (“\(n\) choose \(k\)”) counts how many such sequences there are. Seán plans renal dose reviews for the next two days: if he can handle 14 patients with AKI, the probability that 15 or more of the 20 patients develop it is \(P(Y \geq 15) =\) 0.092. Not negligible: roughly one time in 11.

Definition 2.3 (Expectation and variance) The expectation (or expected value, mean) of a random variable, \(\mathbb{E}[X]\), is its long-run average: the sum of each value times its probability (for a continuous variable, an integral). The variance, \(\operatorname{Var}(X) = \mathbb{E}\big[(X - \mathbb{E}[X])^2\big]\), measures how far values typically fall from that average; its square root is the standard deviation. For a Bernoulli variable \(\mathbb{E}[X] = \theta\) and \(\operatorname{Var}(X) = \theta(1-\theta)\); for a binomial count \(\mathbb{E}[Y] = n\theta\) and \(\operatorname{Var}(Y) = n\theta(1-\theta)\) (Blitzstein and Hwang 2019, ch. 4).

On a ward of 20, Seán should therefore expect about 11.6 cases of AKI, with a standard deviation of about 2.2. Notice that \(\theta(1-\theta)\) is largest at \(\theta = 0.5\): a yes/no outcome is most unpredictable when both answers are equally likely — an idea we turn into a measure of uncertainty in Section 2.6.

Which of these is best described by a binomial distribution?

Whether Aoife develops AKI in the next 48 hours A single yes/no outcome is a Bernoulli variable. The binomial counts yes’s over several such outcomes.
The number of patients, out of tonight’s 20 on Ward 7, who develop AKI Correct, provided each patient has the same probability and outcomes are independent: a count of yes’s out of a fixed number of trials.
Lena’s resting heart rate tomorrow morning A heart rate is a continuous measurement, often modelled with a normal distribution, not a count.
The rise in Aoife’s creatinine over 48 hours, in mg/dL Also a continuous measurement. Only when we dichotomise it (≥ 0.3 mg/dL or not) does it become a Bernoulli outcome.




2.2.3 Measurements on a scale: the normal distribution
Many measurements are continuous. In the HomeBeat digital trial — 500 people wearing a smartwatch at home (Table 1.1) — the resting heart rate has mean 69.9 bpm and standard deviation 12.9 bpm. A common model for such a variable is the normal (Gaussian) distribution, with density
\[
f(x \mid \mu, \sigma) = \frac{1}{\sigma\sqrt{2\pi}} \exp\!\left( -\frac{(x - \mu)^2}{2\sigma^2} \right),
\qquad(2.3)\]
the familiar symmetric bell, centred at the mean \(\mu\) with spread given by the standard deviation \(\sigma\) (Figure 2.1). About 95 % of the area lies within two standard deviations of the mean: for HomeBeat the normal model puts 95 % of participants in that band, and the data actually contain 97 %.




hb = FileAttachment("data/homebeat.csv").csv({typed: true})
hrMu = d3.mean(hb, d => d.resting_hr)
hrSd = d3.deviation(hb, d => d.resting_hr)
Plot.plot({
  height: 260, grid: true,
  x: {label: "Resting heart rate (bpm)", domain: [35, 105]},
  y: {label: "Density"},
  marks: [
    Plot.rectY(hb, Plot.binX({y: (a, bin) => a.length / (hb.length * (bin.x2 - bin.x1))}, {x: "resting_hr", thresholds: d3.range(35, 106, 2.5), fill: "currentColor", fillOpacity: 0.25})),
    Plot.line(d3.range(35, 105.01, 0.5).map(x => [x, Math.exp(-((x - hrMu) ** 2) / (2 * hrSd ** 2)) / (hrSd * Math.sqrt(2 * Math.PI))]), {stroke: "#1f6f8b", strokeWidth: 3}),
    Plot.ruleX([88], {stroke: "#b35c00", strokeDasharray: "4,3"}),
    Plot.text([[88.5, 0.029]], {text: ["Lena, 88 bpm"], textAnchor: "start", fontSize: 11})
  ]
})































Figure 2.1: Resting heart rate of the 500 HomeBeat participants (bars) and the normal distribution with the same mean and standard deviation (line). The dashed line marks Lena’s reading.



A density is not a probability. The probability of a resting heart rate of exactly 75.000… bpm is zero; what has a probability is an interval, such as “above 80 bpm”, and it equals the area under the curve. Under the normal model, \(P(\text{HR} > 80) =\) 0.218; in the data, 24.2 % of participants are above 80 bpm. The model is good, not perfect — like every model in Chapter 1’s sense, it keeps some features of reality and loses others.
Lena, a HomeBeat participant, records a resting heart rate of 88 bpm. Is that unusual? It lies \(z = (88 - 69.9)/12.9 =\) 1.40 standard deviations above the mean, and the normal model says that about 8 % of participants are at least that high. Unusual, but hardly alarming on its own: whether it should trigger a call depends on what else we know about Lena, which is exactly what Bayes’ theorem will handle.

Under the normal model for HomeBeat, the density at 75 bpm is about 0.03. What is the probability that a participant’s resting heart rate is exactly 75 bpm?

About 0.03 This confuses a density with a probability. The density is the height of the curve; a probability is an area under it, and a single point has no width.
Zero, because a single value has no width; only intervals have probabilities Correct. For a continuous variable we ask about intervals, such as “between 74.5 and 75.5 bpm”, whose probability is approximately the density times the width: about 0.03 × 1 = 0.03.
It cannot be computed without more data The model gives the answer directly. The issue is not missing data but what kind of question a density can answer.



How unusual is Lena’s heart rate? The HomeBeat data are loaded as hb. Using a normal model with the mean and standard deviation of the data, compute the probability that a participant’s resting heart rate is above 88 bpm. Fill in the blank with the function that gives the area to the left of a value (the cumulative distribution function).

RPython

















R names its distribution functions with a prefix: d for density, p for probability (area to the left), q for quantiles, r for random draws. The normal is norm.


1 - pnorm(88, mean = mu, sd = s)


















NormalDist objects have a .pdf() method (density) and a .cdf() method (cumulative distribution function: the area to the left).


1 - NormalDist(mu, s).cdf(88)

title: 2  Uncertainty and probability for decision-makers
section: 2.3 Likelihood: which value best explains the data?
text:
2.3 Likelihood: which value best explains the data?
So far we have assumed that we know \(\theta\), \(\mu\) or \(\sigma\) and asked what data to expect. Real problems run the other way: we have data and want to learn about the unknown values that produced them. This reverse direction is statistical inference. For Ward 7 the questions are: what is the probability of AKI in this population? How sure can we be, given 1 250 patients? Would we be just as sure with 20?
There are two broad schools of inference (Gelman et al. 2013; Spiegelhalter 2019). In frequentist inference the parameter is a fixed but unknown constant, and randomness comes only from which data happened to be collected; the aim is a good single estimate and a statement of how much it would vary from sample to sample. In Bayesian inference the parameter itself is uncertain and is described by a probability distribution, which is updated as data arrive. The two schools disagree about interpretation, but they share one building block: the likelihood.

Definition 2.4 (Likelihood) Given a probability model and observed data, the likelihood \(L(\theta)\) is the probability (or density) of the observed data, viewed as a function of the parameter \(\theta\) with the data held fixed. It measures how well each candidate value of \(\theta\) explains the data; it is not the probability that \(\theta\) is true. Its logarithm, \(\ell(\theta) = \log L(\theta)\), is the log-likelihood (Fisher 1922).

Take the first 20 Ward 7 patients in a random order, of whom 12 developed AKI. If each patient has probability \(\theta\) of AKI, independently, the probability of exactly this sequence of outcomes is
\[
L(\theta) = \prod_{i=1}^{n} \theta^{x_i} (1-\theta)^{1 - x_i} = \theta^{k} (1-\theta)^{n-k}
= \theta^{12} (1-\theta)^{8},
\qquad(2.4)\]
where \(x_i\) is 1 or 0 for patient \(i\) and \(k = \sum x_i\) is the number of cases. At \(\theta = 0.3\) this is about \(3.1 \times 10^{-8}\); at \(\theta = 0.6\) it is about \(1.4 \times 10^{-6}\), some 47 times larger. Both numbers are tiny — any particular sequence of 20 outcomes is improbable — but their ratio says that \(\theta = 0.6\) explains these patients far better than \(\theta = 0.3\). Because products of many small numbers become unmanageably small, we usually work with the log-likelihood, which turns the product into a sum:
\[
\ell(\theta) = k \log\theta + (n-k)\log(1-\theta) .
\qquad(2.5)\]

Definition 2.5 (Maximum likelihood estimate) The maximum likelihood estimate (MLE) \(\hat\theta\) is the parameter value with the highest likelihood (equivalently, the highest log-likelihood): \(\hat\theta = \arg\max_\theta L(\theta)\) (Fisher 1922). For a yes/no outcome it is the observed proportion, \(\hat\theta = k/n\); for the mean of a normal distribution with known \(\sigma\) it is the sample mean, \(\hat\mu = \bar y\).







For the curious: why the MLE of a proportion is \(k/n\)





At the top of the curve the slope of \(\ell(\theta)\) is zero. Differentiating Equation 2.5,
\[
\frac{d\ell}{d\theta} = \frac{k}{\theta} - \frac{n-k}{1-\theta} = 0
\quad\Longrightarrow\quad k(1-\theta) = (n-k)\theta
\quad\Longrightarrow\quad \hat\theta = \frac{k}{n}.
\]
For a normal model with known \(\sigma\), the log-likelihood of the mean is \(\ell(\mu) = -\tfrac{n}{2}\log(2\pi\sigma^2) - \tfrac{1}{2\sigma^2}\sum_i (y_i - \mu)^2\), which is largest when the sum of squared distances \(\sum_i (y_i-\mu)^2\) is smallest, that is, at \(\hat\mu = \bar y\). Minimising squared distances is the least squares idea of Chapter 4: least squares is maximum likelihood under a normal model (Hastie, Tibshirani, and Friedman 2009, ch. 2).




Find the most likely value. Each Ward 7 patient either develops AKI or not. Choose how many patients you have observed (taken in a fixed random order) and move the candidate value of \(\theta\). The curve is the likelihood, rescaled so that its peak is 1. Target: with at least 20 patients, put \(\theta\) within 0.01 of the maximum. Then watch what happens to the width of the curve as you observe more patients.

icuL = FileAttachment("data/icu_aki.csv").csv({typed: true})
akiOrdered = d3.range(icuL.length).map(i => icuL[(i * 389) % icuL.length].delta_creatinine_48h >= 0.3 ? 1 : 0)
viewof nObs = Inputs.select([5, 10, 20, 50, 200, 1250], {value: 20, label: "Patients observed, n"})
viewof thetaCand = Inputs.range([0.01, 0.99], {value: 0.30, step: 0.01, label: "Candidate θ"})






























kObs = d3.sum(akiOrdered.slice(0, nObs))
mleObs = kObs / nObs
llF = th => (kObs > 0 ? kObs * Math.log(th) : 0) + (nObs - kObs > 0 ? (nObs - kObs) * Math.log(1 - th) : 0)
llMax = llF(Math.min(Math.max(mleObs, 1e-9), 1 - 1e-9))
likCurve = d3.range(0.005, 0.9951, 0.0025).map(th => ({th, rel: Math.exp(llF(th) - llMax)}))
{
  const hit = nObs >= 20 && Math.abs(thetaCand - mleObs) <= 0.0101;
  if (hit && window.aihs) window.aihs.complete("ch02-tryit-likelihood");
  const rel = Math.exp(llF(thetaCand) - llMax);
  return html`<p>${kObs} of ${nObs} patients developed AKI. At θ = ${thetaCand.toFixed(2)}: log-likelihood
  <strong>${llF(thetaCand).toFixed(2)}</strong>, likelihood ${rel < 0.001 ? "less than 0.1 %" : (100 * rel).toFixed(1) + " %"} of the maximum.
  ${hit ? html`<br>✓ Target reached: the maximum likelihood estimate is k/n = ${kObs}/${nObs} = <strong>${mleObs.toFixed(3)}</strong>.` : ""}</p>`;
}












































Plot.plot({
  height: 260, grid: true,
  x: {label: "Candidate probability of AKI, θ", domain: [0, 1]},
  y: {label: "Likelihood (peak = 1)", domain: [0, 1.05]},
  marks: [
    Plot.areaY(likCurve, {x: "th", y: "rel", fill: "#1f6f8b", fillOpacity: 0.15}),
    Plot.line(likCurve, {x: "th", y: "rel", stroke: "#1f6f8b", strokeWidth: 2.5}),
    Plot.ruleX([thetaCand], {stroke: "#b35c00", strokeWidth: 2}),
    Plot.dot([[thetaCand, Math.exp(llF(thetaCand) - llMax)]], {r: 5, fill: "#b35c00"})
  ]
})








Two lessons come out of the widget. First, the most likely value is the observed proportion: with all 1 250 patients it is 0.580. Second, the curve narrows as data accumulate. With 5 patients (1 case) every value from near 0 to above 0.5 explains the data reasonably well; with 1 250 only a narrow band around 0.58 does. The width of the likelihood is a picture of how much we still do not know: the second kind of uncertainty from Section 2.1. Chapter 8 turns this picture into intervals that a decision-maker can read.
For more complex models — the logistic regression of Chapter 5 or the neural networks of Chapter 7 — there is no formula like \(k/n\), and the maximum is found by numerical search. The principle does not change: fitting a model by maximum likelihood means choosing the parameter values under which the observed data are least surprising. Keep the word surprising; it returns in Section 2.6.

With the first 20 patients, \(L(0.6)\) is about 47 times \(L(0.3)\). Which statement is correct?

\(\theta = 0.6\) is 47 times more probable than \(\theta = 0.3\) The likelihood is the probability of the data given \(\theta\), not the probability of \(\theta\). Turning it into a probability for \(\theta\) needs a prior, as Bayes’ theorem will show.
The observed outcomes are 47 times more probable if \(\theta = 0.6\) than if \(\theta = 0.3\) Correct. The likelihood compares how well candidate values explain the data that were actually observed.
Neither value can be right, because both likelihoods are tiny Every particular sequence of 20 outcomes has a tiny probability. What matters is the comparison between candidate values, not the absolute size.



Maximum likelihood by search. The code below takes the patients of hospital ICU_D, computes the Bernoulli log-likelihood for a fine grid of candidate values of \(\theta\), and should return the candidate with the highest log-likelihood. Fill in the blank with the function that returns the position of the largest value.

RPython

















The function is which.max(); its opposite is which.min().


theta_grid[which.max(loglik)]


















The function is np.argmax(); its opposite is np.argmin().


theta_grid[np.argmax(loglik)]
