age          -0.0001     0.0004 -0.2057   0.8371
sofa          0.0415     0.0022 18.7489   0.0000
albumin      -0.0750     0.0110 -6.8279   0.0000



Residual standard error: 0.181 on 1237 degrees of freedom
Multiple R-squared: 0.641,  Adjusted R-squared: 0.638
F-statistic: 184.4 on 12 and 1237 DF,  p-value < 2.2e-16


Each row gives the estimate, its standard error (how much the estimate would vary from sample to sample), the t value (estimate divided by standard error) and a p-value. Below the table: the residual standard error, about 0.18 mg/dL, is the typical size of a residual; \(R^2 = 0.64\) says the model accounts for about 64% of the variation in the outcome (in the training data, so it is optimistic; Chapter 3); adjusted \(R^2\) applies a small penalty for the number of predictors; and the F test asks whether the predictors, taken together, explain anything at all.

Definition 4.5 (Confidence interval and p-value (brief)) A 95% confidence interval for \(\beta_j\) is a range computed so that, over many repetitions of the study, 95% of such ranges would contain the true value. The p-value for \(\beta_j\) is the probability of an estimate at least as far from zero as the one observed, if the true coefficient were zero and the model’s assumptions held.

A p-value is easy to misread (Wasserstein and Lazar 2016). It is not the probability that the predictor has no effect, and it does not measure how large or important an association is. With 1 250 patients, a tiny association can have a minute p-value; with 30 patients, a large and clinically important one may not. The confidence interval is usually more informative, because it shows both the size of the association and its uncertainty in the outcome’s own units. When a model has thousands of predictors, a few will have small p-values by chance alone; procedures that control the false discovery rate exist for that situation (Benjamini and Hochberg 1995), and regularisation, later in this chapter, offers another route.

4.3.1 ANOVA: the order of the questions matters
An analysis of variance (ANOVA) table splits the variation explained by the model into the contributions of each predictor, with an F test for each. R’s anova() does this sequentially: each predictor is credited with what it explains after the predictors listed before it, and before those listed after it. The order of the formula therefore changes the answer.
On Ward 7 the effect is striking. With age listed second, as in Equation 4.3, the sequential ANOVA gives age a p-value of 0.00014. Testing age last, after all the other predictors, with drop1(fit, test = "F"), gives 0.84. Both are correct answers to different questions. The first asks “does age explain anything, ignoring everything that comes after it in the formula?”, and it does, because older patients have higher baseline creatinine. The second asks “does age add anything once baseline creatinine and the rest are known?”, and it does not. When there is no natural order among the predictors, use the “each term last” tests (drop1() in base R, or Anova() from the car package (Fox and Weisberg 2019)), which match the t tests of the summary table for numerical predictors.

For albumin, the summary table reports \(p < 0.001\). Which interpretation is correct?

There is less than a 0.1% chance that albumin has no association with the outcome This is the most common misreading. The p-value is computed assuming the coefficient is zero; it is not the probability that the coefficient is zero.
Albumin is one of the most important predictors of AKI A small p-value says the association is unlikely to be exactly zero given this much data; it says nothing about its size or clinical importance.
If albumin had no association with the outcome (given the other predictors), an estimate this far from zero would be very unusual Correct. That is all a p-value says. The confidence interval, -0.097 to -0.053 mg/dL per g/dL, tells you the plausible size.
Raising albumin will reduce the rise in creatinine That is a causal claim, which no p-value from observational data can support on its own.

title: 4  Linear models and regularisation
text:
4.4 Six assumptions
The numbers in Table 4.1 are trustworthy only if the model is a reasonable representation of the data. Linear regression rests on six assumptions; Figure 4.2 shows what each looks like when it holds and when it fails.








Figure 4.2: The six assumptions of linear regression, each shown when it holds (left of each pair) and when it fails (right). Simulated data.






Linearity. The average outcome changes linearly with each predictor (on the scale used in the model). If the true relationship is curved, the model is systematically wrong in places. Check: residuals against fitted values, or against each predictor, should show no curve. Remedy: transform a predictor (log, square), add a spline, or use a more flexible model (Chapters 6 and 7).
Independence of errors. The residual of one patient tells you nothing about the residual of another. This fails with repeated measurements of the same patient, with patients clustered in hospitals, or with data collected over time. Consequence: standard errors are too small and p-values too optimistic. Check: plot residuals in time order or by cluster. Remedy: models for clustered or longitudinal data.
Constant variance (homoscedasticity). The spread of the residuals is the same across the range of fitted values. A funnel shape is heteroscedasticity. Check: residuals or scale–location plot; a formal test exists (Breusch and Pagan 1979). Remedy: transform the outcome, use weighted least squares, or robust (“sandwich”) standard errors (White 1980).
Normality of errors. The errors follow a normal distribution. This matters for exact p-values and intervals in small samples, and for prediction intervals; it matters little for the estimates themselves or, with large samples, for confidence intervals. Check: a Q–Q plot, where the points should follow the line.
No (severe) collinearity. Predictors are not too strongly related to one another. With highly correlated predictors the model cannot tell their contributions apart, so individual coefficients become unstable and their standard errors large, even though predictions may remain good. Check: correlations and the variance inflation factor (Section 4.5). Remedy: drop or combine predictors, or regularise (Section 4.7). Collinearity returns in Chapter 10.
No unduly influential points. No single patient determines the fit. Check: leverage and Cook’s distance (Section 4.5). Remedy: check the record for errors first; never delete a patient simply because they are inconvenient.

Not every assumption matters for every purpose (Table 4.3). Under the first three assumptions, plus no exact collinearity, the least-squares estimates are unbiased and have the smallest variance among linear unbiased estimators, a result known as the Gauss–Markov theorem; normality is the extra assumption behind exact small-sample p-values and intervals (James et al. 2021, ch. 3; Hastie, Tibshirani, and Friedman 2009, ch. 3).



Table 4.3: What each assumption protects. A purely predictive model, judged on a test set, can tolerate more than a model whose coefficients and p-values will be reported.

A team builds a linear model on 1 250 patients only to predict the change in creatinine, and will judge it by its error on a separate test set. Which assumption can they worry about least?

Linearity If the relationship is curved, predictions are systematically off in some patients, whatever the purpose.
Normality of the errors Correct. Normality underpins exact p-values and intervals, especially in small samples. For point predictions judged on a test set, and with 1 250 patients, mild non-normality hardly matters. They would need it for prediction intervals, though.
No influential points One extreme patient can pull the whole line, and with it every prediction.
Independence Independence matters less for point predictions, but if patients are clustered by hospital, a test set drawn from the same hospitals overstates how the model will do elsewhere. It is not the safest one to ignore.

title: 4  Linear models and regularisation
4  Linear models and regularisation
text:
4.6 When predictors crowd in: ONCO-1
Now turn to the ONCO-1 trial. The trial randomised patients with solid tumours to chemotherapy or no chemotherapy and measured, for each, tumour shrinkage (response_percent), a few clinical variables and the expression of 2 000 genes. The browser version of the data has 1 000 patients and the first 50 genes. Written with the names in the dataset, the linear model for the full trial is
\[
\begin{aligned}
&\mathtt{response\_percent} \\
&\quad = \beta_0 + \beta_1\,\mathtt{treatment\_chemo} + \beta_2\,\mathtt{dose\_intensity} \\
&\quad + \beta_3\,\mathtt{patient\_age} + \beta_4\,\mathtt{tumor\_grade\_G2} \\
&\quad + \beta_5\,\mathtt{tumor\_grade\_G3} + \beta_6\,\mathtt{performance\_score} \\
&\quad + \beta_7\,\mathtt{gene\_01} + \beta_8\,\mathtt{gene\_02} + \dots + \beta_{2006}\,\mathtt{gene\_2000} + \varepsilon .
\end{aligned}
\qquad(4.5)\]
Four kinds of columns stay out: patient_id (an identifier), high_response (the outcome in yes/no form), baseline_tumor_mm and post_tumor_mm (from which the outcome is calculated), and genes 08, 14 and 19 (noisy copies of the outcome, the leakage you met in Chapter 3). In the browser data that leaves 53 predictors: six clinical columns and 47 genes.
Three features of this problem push ordinary least squares to its limits.
Too many columns. In the full trial, \(p = 2\,006\) coefficients. Whenever \(p\) is at least \(n\), Equation 4.4 has no unique solution: infinitely many coefficient vectors fit the training data perfectly, with zero residuals, and they disagree wildly about new patients. Even when \(p\) is somewhat smaller than \(n\), OLS uses every column to chase noise (Hastie, Tibshirani, and Friedman 2009, ch. 18).
Correlated columns. Genes are co-expressed. In ONCO-1, gene_01 and gene_12 have a correlation of -0.84, because both follow the same underlying biological programme. Treatment and dose are even more entangled: dose intensity is zero for every no_chemo patient and between 0.8 and 1.1 for every chemo patient, so the two columns carry almost the same information. Their VIFs in the OLS fit are 67 and 67. The model can predict well and still be unable to say how to split the credit between them (Belsley, Kuh, and Welsch 1980).
Marginal and adjusted associations differ. On its own, gene_01 is almost unrelated to shrinkage (correlation 0.03). Yet in the simulation it is one of the three genes that truly affect the response. Its effect is masked because it moves together with gene_12, whose effect it offsets in the raw correlation. Only a model that includes both, adjusting for each, can uncover them; screening genes one at a time would miss gene_01 completely.
There is also a warning sign in the outcome itself: 25% of patients have a shrinkage of exactly 0%, because a tumour that grows is recorded as 0 (Figure 4.6). No straight line respects that floor; the residuals of these patients line up in a diagonal streak, a clear failure of linearity and constant variance at the bottom of the range. We keep the linear model here because it is the subject of the chapter; Chapter 5 models the yes/no version of the outcome, and Chapter 6 uses trees, which handle such floors naturally.








Figure 4.6: Residuals against fitted values for OLS on ONCO-1. The diagonal streak at the lower left comes from patients whose shrinkage is recorded as 0%: the line predicts some shrinkage, or even negative shrinkage, for them.





What does chasing noise cost? Fit OLS to just 80 training patients, with the same 53 predictors, and test it on the 200 test patients of the shared split. Its training RMSE is 2.14 percentage points; on the test patients it is 6.06. The model has memorised its 80 patients. With all 800 training patients the gap is much smaller (3.89 against 4.40). The trouble lies in the ratio of predictors to patients, and it is worst exactly where the biology is most interesting: thousands of genes, hundreds of patients.

title: 4  Linear models and regularisation
section: 4.7 Regularisation: ridge, lasso and elastic net
text:
4.7 Regularisation: ridge, lasso and elastic net
The remedy is to change what “best” means. Instead of asking only for small residuals, we ask for small residuals and small coefficients, and let a single number set the balance.

Definition 4.7 (Regularisation and penalty strength) Regularisation (or shrinkage) estimates the coefficients by minimising the residual sum of squares plus a penalty that grows with the size of the coefficients: \[
\text{RSS}(\mathbf{\beta}) + \lambda\, P(\mathbf{\beta}).
\] The penalty strength \(\lambda \ge 0\) (lambda) is a hyperparameter. With \(\lambda = 0\) we are back to OLS; as \(\lambda\) grows, the coefficients are pulled towards zero. The intercept is not penalised, and the predictors are standardised first so that the penalty treats them all alike.

Standardising matters: without it, a gene measured on a scale ten times larger would need a coefficient ten times smaller for the same effect, and would be penalised less for it. Software such as glmnet standardises internally by default (Friedman, Hastie, and Tibshirani 2010).

4.7.1 Ridge: shrink everything a little

Definition 4.8 (Ridge regression) Ridge regression uses the sum of squared coefficients as the penalty (an L2 penalty) (Hoerl and Kennard 1970): \[
\hat{\mathbf{\beta}}^{\text{ridge}} = \arg\min_{\mathbf{\beta}}
\ \sum_{i=1}^{n}\bigl(y_i - \beta_0 - \textstyle\sum_{j} x_{ij}\beta_j\bigr)^2
+ \lambda \sum_{j=1}^{p} \beta_j^2 .
\]

(“arg min” means “the values of \(\mathbf{\beta}\) that make this expression smallest”.) Ridge shrinks all coefficients towards zero but, except in special cases, sets none of them exactly to zero. It has a closed form, \(\hat{\mathbf{\beta}}^{\text{ridge}} =
(\mathbf{X}^\top\mathbf{X} + \lambda\mathbf{I})^{-1}\mathbf{X}^\top\mathbf{y}\) for standardised predictors and a centred outcome, where \(\mathbf{I}\) is the identity matrix. Adding \(\lambda\) to the diagonal makes the matrix invertible even when \(p > n\) or the columns are collinear, which is why ridge was invented. With correlated predictors, ridge tends to share the credit among them rather than give it all to one: gene_01 and gene_12 both stay in, each shrunk.


4.7.2 Lasso: shrink some all the way to zero

Definition 4.9 (Lasso) The lasso (least absolute shrinkage and selection operator) uses the sum of absolute values of the coefficients (an L1 penalty) (Tibshirani 1996): \[
\hat{\mathbf{\beta}}^{\text{lasso}} = \arg\min_{\mathbf{\beta}}
\ \sum_{i=1}^{n}\bigl(y_i - \beta_0 - \textstyle\sum_{j} x_{ij}\beta_j\bigr)^2
+ \lambda \sum_{j=1}^{p} \lvert\beta_j\rvert .
\] Because of the corners of the absolute value, the lasso sets some coefficients exactly to zero: it estimates and selects predictors at the same time.

Figure 4.7 shows why the corners matter. Each penalty can be seen as a budget: the coefficients must stay inside a region, a circle for ridge and a diamond for the lasso, and within that region we look for the smallest RSS, whose contours are ellipses around the OLS estimate. The first contact between an ellipse and a diamond very often happens at a corner, where one coefficient is exactly zero; a circle has no corners (James et al. 2021, ch. 6).







  Lasso (L1)
  
  
  β₁β₂
  
  
  OLS estimate
  β₁ = 0


  Ridge (L2)

  both ≠ 0





Figure 4.7: Why the lasso selects and ridge does not. The shaded regions are the coefficient values allowed by each penalty; the ellipses are contours of equal RSS around the OLS estimate. The red dot is the regularised estimate, where the smallest ellipse first touches the region.





4.7.3 Elastic net: a blend
The lasso has a weakness with groups of correlated predictors: it tends to keep one and drop the others somewhat arbitrarily, and with \(p > n\) it can select at most \(n\) of them. The elastic net mixes the two penalties (Zou and Hastie 2005).

Definition 4.10 (Elastic net and the mixing parameter) The elastic net penalty is \(\lambda\bigl[\alpha \sum_j \lvert\beta_j\rvert + \tfrac{1-\alpha}{2} \sum_j \beta_j^2\bigr]\), where the mixing parameter \(\alpha\) runs from 0 (ridge) to 1 (lasso). Both \(\lambda\) and \(\alpha\) are hyperparameters.

A word on software. glmnet, the R package used here, minimises \(\frac{1}{2n}\text{RSS} + \lambda\bigl[\alpha\sum_j\lvert\beta_j\rvert +
\frac{1-\alpha}{2}\sum_j\beta_j^2\bigr]\) (Friedman, Hastie, and Tibshirani 2010): the RSS is divided by \(2n\), so its \(\lambda\) values are on a different scale from the textbook formulas above, though the idea is identical. scikit-learn (Pedregosa et al. 2011), in Python, uses the same objective but calls the penalty strength alpha and the mixing parameter l1_ratio, so its alpha is our \(\lambda\). Always check which is which.

4.7.4 What shrinkage buys: bias for variance
Shrinking coefficients towards zero makes them systematically too small: regularisation adds bias. It never reduces it. What it buys is a reduction in variance: the coefficients, and the predictions, change much less from one training sample to another. When the variance saved is larger than the bias added, the error on new patients falls (Hastie, Tibshirani, and Friedman 2009, ch. 3). That is the bias–variance trade-off of Chapter 1, now with a dial: small \(\lambda\), low bias and high variance; large \(\lambda\), high bias and low variance. It is also why regularised models are recommended for clinical prediction models developed on modest samples, where OLS predictions tend to be too extreme for new patients (Steyerberg 2019; Harrell 2015).

You increase \(\lambda\) in a ridge regression from a very small to a very large value. What happens?

Bias and variance both fall, so the model always improves Shrinkage can lower the total error, but it does so by trading: bias goes up while variance goes down. Bias never falls as λ grows.
Bias rises and variance falls; the test error typically falls and then rises again Correct. At very large λ every coefficient is close to zero and the model predicts roughly the average for everyone: high bias, very low variance. The best λ lies in between, and cross-validation finds it.
Coefficients one by one become exactly zero That is the lasso. Ridge coefficients shrink towards zero but, in general, never reach it.
Nothing, because ridge only changes the intercept The intercept is the one coefficient that is not penalised.



In ONCO-1, gene_01 and gene_12 are strongly correlated and both truly affect shrinkage. What do you expect from ridge and from the lasso?

Ridge keeps both with shrunken coefficients; the lasso tends to keep fewer correlated genes, and may drop one if the penalty is strong Correct. The L2 penalty prefers to spread credit across correlated predictors; the L1 penalty prefers sparse solutions. In this dataset both genes are strong enough to survive the lasso at the λ chosen by cross-validation, as Table 4.6 shows; at larger λ they shrink, and the elastic net was designed for such groups.
Both methods set both genes to zero, because correlated predictors cancel out Correlated predictors make individual coefficients harder to estimate, not zero. Here both genes carry real signal.
The lasso keeps both and ridge removes both The other way round: only the lasso can remove predictors.

title: 4  Linear models and regularisation
section: 4.8 Choosing λ: the coefficient path and the 1-SE rule
text:
4.8 Choosing λ: the coefficient path and the 1-SE rule
\(\lambda\) is a hyperparameter, so it is chosen by \(V\)-fold cross-validation on the training data, never on the test set (Chapter 3). The usual recipe has four steps:

Fit the model for a whole grid of \(\lambda\) values, from one so large that every coefficient is zero down to one so small that the fit is close to OLS. The sequence of fitted coefficients is the coefficient path.
Estimate the cross-validated error at every \(\lambda\), using the same folds for every \(\lambda\), and for every model you intend to compare.
Pick \(\lambda\) (and, for the elastic net, \(\alpha\)) by one of the rules below.
Refit on the whole training set with that \(\lambda\), and evaluate once on the test set.


Definition 4.11 (Coefficient path) The coefficient path shows each coefficient of a regularised model as a function of \(\lambda\). For the lasso, coefficients enter the model one at a time as \(\lambda\) decreases; for ridge, all are non-zero and grow smoothly (James et al. 2021, ch. 6).


Definition 4.12 (λ min and the 1-SE rule) lambda.min is the \(\lambda\) with the smallest cross-validated error. The one-standard-error rule picks instead the largest \(\lambda\) whose cross-validated error is within one standard error of that minimum (lambda.1se): a simpler, more strongly regularised model whose error is statistically indistinguishable from the best (Breiman et al. 1984; Hastie, Tibshirani, and Friedman 2009, ch. 7).

The 1-SE rule reflects a sensible scepticism: the minimum of a noisy cross-validation curve is itself uncertain, so among models that perform about equally well, prefer the simplest. The widget below lets you walk along the paths for ONCO-1.

Walk the λ path. The model predicts tumour shrinkage in ONCO-1 from 53 standardised predictors, using the 800 training patients of the shared split; all numbers were computed in advance with glmnet. Choose a penalty and move along the path from a very strong penalty (left) to a very weak one (right). The top plot shows every coefficient; the middle one the 5-fold cross-validated RMSE with a band of ± one standard error; the bottom one the coefficients that are non-zero at the current \(\lambda\). Target: for the lasso, find the λ chosen by the 1-SE rule: the strongest penalty whose cross-validated error lies below the dashed line.

lpath = FileAttachment("data/precomputed/ch04/lambda_path.json").json()
viewof pen = Inputs.radio(new Map([["Ridge (α = 0)", "ridge"], ["Elastic net (α = 0.5)", "enet"], ["Lasso (α = 1)", "lasso"]]), {value: "lasso", label: "Penalty"})
















viewof kStep = Inputs.range([0, lpath[pen].lambda.length - 1], {value: Math.round(0.25 * (lpath[pen].lambda.length - 1)), step: 1, label: "Step along the path (0 = strongest penalty)"})







lp = lpath[pen]
lpCur = ({lam: lp.lambda[kStep], nz: lp.nzero[kStep], cv: lp.cvm[kStep], te: lp.test_rmse[kStep]})
lpLong = lp.lambda.flatMap((lam, i) => lp.beta[i].map((b, j) => ({ll: Math.log10(lam), b, name: lpath.predictors[j], role: lpath.role[j]})))
lpCV = lp.lambda.map((lam, i) => ({ll: Math.log10(lam), cv: lp.cvm[i], lo: lp.cvlo[i], hi: lp.cvhi[i]}))
{
  const hit = pen === "lasso" && kStep === lp.idx_1se;
  if (hit && window.aihs) window.aihs.complete("ch04-tryit-lambda");
  const where = kStep === lp.idx_1se ? " — this is λ 1-SE" : kStep === lp.idx_min ? " — this is λ min" : "";
  return html`<p>λ = <strong>${lpCur.lam.toPrecision(3)}</strong>${where} · non-zero coefficients: <strong>${lpCur.nz}</strong> of ${lpath.predictors.length}
  · cross-validated RMSE: <strong>${lpCur.cv.toFixed(2)}</strong> · test RMSE (for teaching only): ${lpCur.te.toFixed(2)} percentage points
  ${hit ? "<br>✓ target reached: the 1-SE rule keeps a simpler model whose error is within one standard error of the best." : ""}</p>`;
}

  ]

  y: {label: "Cross-validated RMSE (zoomed near the minimum)", domain: [lp.cvlo[lp.idx_min] * 0.97, lp.cvm[lp.idx_min] * 1.35]},
  clip: true,

    Plot.areaY(lpCV, {x: "ll", y1: "lo", y2: "hi", fillOpacity: 0.18, fill: "#1f6f8b"}),
    Plot.line(lpCV, {x: "ll", y: "cv", stroke: "#1f6f8b", strokeWidth: 2}),
    Plot.ruleX([Math.log10(lp.lambda[lp.idx_min])], {stroke: "#1f6f8b"}),
    Plot.ruleY([lp.cvhi[lp.idx_min]], {strokeDasharray: "6,4"}),
    Plot.text([[Math.log10(lp.lambda[lp.idx_min]), lp.cvhi[lp.idx_min]]], {text: ["min + 1 SE"], dy: -7, dx: 4, textAnchor: "start", fontSize: 11}),
    Plot.ruleX([Math.log10(lpCur.lam)], {strokeDasharray: "4,3"}),
    Plot.dot([[Math.log10(lpCur.lam), lpCur.cv]], {r: 5, fill: "currentColor"})
  ]
})







{
  const cur = lp.beta[kStep].map((b, j) => ({name: lpath.predictors[j], role: lpath.role[j], b}))
    .filter(d => d.b !== 0).sort((a, b) => Math.abs(b.b) - Math.abs(a.b)).slice(0, 15);
  if (cur.length === 0) return html`<p><em>All coefficients are zero: the model predicts the average shrinkage for everyone.</em></p>`;
  return Plot.plot({
    height: 26 * cur.length + 40, marginLeft: 120, grid: true,
    x: {label: "Coefficient at the current λ (largest 15 shown)"}, y: {label: null, domain: cur.map(d => d.name)},
    color: {domain: ["clinical", "causal gene", "noise gene"], range: ["#1f6f8b", "#b35c00", "#9a9a9a"]},

Things to notice as you walk. With the lasso, the first predictors to enter are treatment, dose and gene_05, the strongest signals. Some genes that have no effect in the simulation, such as gene_27, enter before gene_01 and gene_12: they are correlated with the causal genes and borrow part of their signal. gene_01 and gene_12 enter later, because each is useful mainly once the other is in, and most noise genes enter only when the penalty is already weak. Ridge never sets anything to zero, so its count of non-zero coefficients is always 53. The CV curve is flat over a wide range of \(\lambda\): many models are about equally good, which is why the 1-SE rule can afford to choose a simpler one.

Ridge by hand. For standardised predictors and a centred outcome, ridge has the closed form \((\mathbf{X}^\top\mathbf{X} + \lambda\mathbf{I})^{-1}\mathbf{X}^\top\mathbf{y}\). Compute it for the first seven ONCO-1 genes with \(\lambda = 200\) and compare with OLS. Fill the blank with the penalty strength.

RPython

















The blank is the penalty strength, already stored in the variable lambda.


b_ridge <- solve(crossprod(X) + lambda * diag(ncol(X)), crossprod(X, y))


















The blank is the penalty strength, already stored in the variable lam.


b_ridge = np.linalg.solve(X.T @ X + lam * np.eye(p), X.T @ y)

Three conclusions.

With 800 training patients and 53 predictors, the four models predict about equally well. The lasso at λ min has a test RMSE of 4.30 against 4.40 for OLS, using 28 predictors instead of 53. When \(n\) is large relative to \(p\), regularisation buys simplicity more than accuracy.
With 80 training patients, regularisation is what makes the model usable. OLS reaches a test RMSE of 6.06; ridge 5.06; the lasso 4.95. OLS has the smallest training error of all and the largest test error: overfitting in one line.
The elastic net chose α = 0.8, close to the lasso, and its rows are almost identical to the lasso rows. The cross-validated error hardly changes for α between 0.3 and 1 (cross-validated RMSE 4.113 at α = 0.3 against 4.108 at the best α), so the exact α matters little here: the blend helps most when correlated groups carry many small effects, and ONCO-1 has a few strong ones.

Patients #0042 and #0917 from the opening are two of the 200 test patients (P5440 and P9541 in onco1.csv). The lasso at λ min predicts 32.1% and 26.3% shrinkage for them, against the observed 36.6% and 20.4%. It puts them in the right order but predicts a gap of about 6 percentage points where the real gap is 16: two patients with the same clinical profile differ in ways that the 53 predictors capture only in part. Chapter 5 returns to them with probabilities.

The lasso with the 1-SE rule keeps 10 of 53 predictors (Table 4.6): 5 of the 6 clinical columns, the three causal genes (01, 05 and 12) and 2 genes with small coefficients that have no effect in the simulation but are correlated with the causal ones. In real data you would not know which is which. A lasso gene list is therefore a set of hypotheses for laboratory follow-up, not a list of discovered causes; it can also change noticeably from one sample to another when genes are correlated (Meinshausen and Bühlmann 2010). Chapters 6 and 12 compare this list with what trees and explanation methods report.

4.9.1 Back to the study questions
The v1 analysis of ONCO-1 set out four questions. Here is what this chapter can and cannot say about each.

Does chemotherapy shrink tumours more than no chemotherapy? This is a causal question, and ONCO-1 is randomised, so the simplest answer is the best: compare the arms. Average shrinkage was 37.8% with chemotherapy and 4.9% without, a difference of 32.9 percentage points. Do not read the effect off the treatment_chemo coefficient of the big model: because dose is zero for every untreated patient, the effect of chemotherapy is split between the treatment and dose coefficients, and penalised coefficients are biased towards zero by design.
Are age, grade and performance status associated with shrinkage? OLS with confidence intervals answers this, provided the assumptions of Section 4.4 are checked; the coefficients are adjusted associations.
Which genes are associated with the response? The lasso narrows 47 genes to a short list, which here contains the three causal genes and a few passengers.
How well can we predict a patient’s shrinkage? With a test RMSE of about 4 percentage points; whether that is good enough depends on the decision the prediction should support.







Too good to be true



Had we kept genes 08, 14 and 19, every model in Table 4.5 would have looked spectacular, with test errors close to zero, because those columns are noisy copies of the outcome. Penalisation does not protect against leakage (Kapoor and Narayanan 2023); it would have selected the leaky genes first. Check what each predictor is before asking how well it predicts (Chapter 3).




4.9.2 Ward 7: the comparison so far

section: 4.10 Where this fits in the decision loop
text:
4.10 Where this fits in the decision loop


  The decision loop
  A cycle of five boxes: data feed a model; the model produces information; people combine the information with values to make a decision; the decision leads to actions and outcomes, which are recorded as new data. In this chapter the model box is a linear or regularised regression and the information box holds coefficients, predictions with intervals and a short list of genes.
  
  
  Data
  
  Model
  OLS, ridge, lasso,
  elastic net
  
  Information
  predictions with intervals,
  coefficients, gene list
  
  Decision
  + values, human in the loop
  
  Action and outcome
  recorded as new data
  
  
  
  
  

The decision loop. Linear models turn data into three kinds of information: predictions, adjusted associations and, with the lasso, a short list of candidate predictors.

A linear model gives Emma and Seán three kinds of information. A prediction for each patient, best read with its interval: for Aoife it straddles the AKI threshold, which is itself useful, because it says that the model cannot settle her case and clinical judgement, or more frequent creatinine checks, must. Adjusted associations, which tell the team how patients who differ in one respect differ in outcome, and which become claims about what an intervention would do only with the causal reasoning of Chapter 13. And, with the lasso, a short list of candidate predictors, which in ONCO-1 is a list of hypotheses for the laboratory rather than a decision rule.
What can go wrong? A single influential patient can steer a small study (Section 4.5); collinear predictors make individual coefficients unstable; a coefficient can be mistaken for an effect; a p-value can be mistaken for importance; and \(\lambda\) chosen on the test set would make the reported error too optimistic. Who stays in control? The people who decide what the prediction is for, which error matters, and what a coefficient may and may not be used to claim.

4.11 Lab: linear and regularised models
The Lab gathers the chapter’s code in one place. Run it here, or download it and run it on your computer: ch04_lab.R · ch04_lab.py. The R version installs glmnet if it is missing.

RPython























Two observations to take forward. On Ward 7 the linear model clearly beats the “average” baseline of Chapter 1, and its prediction for Aoife still sits near the AKI threshold. On ONCO-1 the four models predict similarly with 800 training patients, and the lasso keeps a short list that contains the three causal genes. The R version reproduces the test errors of Table 4.5 exactly. R and Python use the same shared split and folds, but glmnet and scikit-learn differ in their λ grids and conventions, so the Python numbers differ a little. scikit-learn’s LassoCV also has no built-in 1-SE rule: it uses the λ with the smallest cross-validated error, so its lasso keeps more genes, among them the same three causal ones.

title: 4  Linear models and regularisation
text:
4.12 Exercises

A sentence for Seán. Write one sentence, for a pharmacist, that reports the albumin coefficient of Table 4.1 with its confidence interval and contains no causal language.
Log lactate. Refit the Ward 7 model with log(lactate) instead of lactate. Compare the coefficient table, the adjusted \(R^2\) and the component-plus-residual plot. How would you explain the new lactate coefficient?
Change the reference. Make ICU_D the reference site (in R, relevel(icu$site, ref = "ICU_D")). Which numbers in the coefficient table change? Do the predictions for tonight’s patients change?
Leverage without influence. In the drag widget, find a position with a large standardised residual (above 2) but Cook’s distance below 0.1, and another with leverage above the flag but Cook’s distance below 0.1. Explain both in a sentence each.
Order in ANOVA. Move age to the end of the Ward 7 formula and run anova() again. What happens to its p-value, and why?
The λ path. In the λ widget, at roughly which step does gene_12 enter the lasso? With ridge, is any coefficient ever exactly zero? With the elastic net, are there more or fewer non-zero coefficients than with the lasso at a similar CV error?
Small samples. Using Table 4.5, explain why OLS with 80 training patients has the smallest training error and the largest test error of all models.
Treatment and dose. Using the coefficients of an OLS fit of response_percent on treatment and dose_intensity only, compute the predicted difference between an untreated patient and a treated patient with dose intensity 1.0. Compare with the difference in arm means. Why is the treatment coefficient alone not the effect of chemotherapy?
Code. In the Lab, replace lambda.1se by lambda.min for the lasso. How many predictors are kept, and how does the test RMSE change?







Selected answers





1. For example: “Among Ward 7 patients who were similar in the other recorded measurements, each additional g/dL of albumin was associated with a 48-hour creatinine rise about 0.07 mg/dL smaller (95% CI 0.05 to 0.10 mg/dL smaller).”
3. The intercept and the three site coefficients change, because they are now comparisons with ICU_D. All other coefficients, the residuals, \(R^2\) and every prediction stay the same: the model is the same, only its parametrisation changes.
5. Placed last, age is tested after baseline creatinine and the other predictors, so its sequential p-value becomes the same as the “each term last” one, about 0.84. Placed early, it was credited with variation it shares with baseline creatinine.
7. With 53 predictors and 80 patients, OLS has enough freedom to follow the noise of its 80 patients closely, so the training error is small; that noise does not repeat in new patients, so the test error is large. Penalties remove some of that freedom: the training error goes up and the test error goes down.
8. In the model response_percent ~ treatment + dose_intensity, the treated-minus-untreated difference at dose 1.0 is \(\hat\beta_{\text{treatment}} + 1.0 \times \hat\beta_{\text{dose}}\), which is close to the difference in arm means. Because dose is 0 for all untreated patients and between 0.8 and 1.1 for all treated ones, the two columns share the effect of chemotherapy, and neither coefficient on its own is the effect.

title: 4  Linear models and regularisation
text:
4.13 Summary

Least squares chooses the coefficients that minimise the sum of squared residuals; a linear regression is linear in its coefficients, not necessarily in its predictors.
With several predictors, categorical variables enter through dummy coding in a design matrix; each coefficient is an adjusted association, in the units of its predictor, not a causal effect.
Confidence intervals convey size and uncertainty; p-values do neither on their own. Sequential ANOVA depends on the order of the predictors.
Six assumptions (linearity, independence, constant variance, normality, no severe collinearity, no influential points) are checked with diagnostic plots, leverage, Cook’s distance and the VIF; which ones matter depends on the purpose.
With many or correlated predictors OLS overfits. Regularisation adds a penalty with strength \(\lambda\): ridge (L2) shrinks all coefficients, the lasso (L1) sets some to zero, the elastic net mixes them with \(\alpha\). Penalties add bias and remove variance.
\(\lambda\) is chosen by cross-validation along the coefficient path, with lambda.min or the 1-SE rule; the test set is used once, at the end.

text: References

title: 5  Classification, thresholds and calibration
text:
How to use this chapter






Starting here?





This chapter borrows a few ideas from earlier chapters. In brief:

Decision threshold (Section 1.5). In Chapter 1 the Ward 7 team compared the expected value of starting a kidney-protective bundle with that of standard care. With their scores, the bundle was the better choice whenever the probability of AKI was above 0.25: the threshold.
Train and test sets (Section 1.8, Definition 1.9). A model is judged on patients who were not used to build it; choices made while building it are judged by cross-validation. Chapter 3 turns this into a routine and warns about leakage, information about the outcome sneaking into the predictors.
Sensitivity, specificity, PPV and NPV (Chapter 2). For a yes/no test, sensitivity is the proportion of people with the condition who test positive, specificity the proportion without it who test negative, and the positive (negative) predictive value the proportion of positive (negative) results that are correct. Predictive values depend on prevalence; sensitivity and specificity do not.
Likelihood and expected loss (Chapter 2). The likelihood measures how probable the observed data are under given parameter values; maximum likelihood picks the values that make the data most probable. Expected loss weighs each possible error by its probability.
Linear regression, coefficients, ridge and lasso (Chapter 4). A linear model predicts \(\hat y = \beta_0 + \beta_1 x_1 + \dots + \beta_p x_p\); penalties shrink the coefficients to fight overfitting.

title: 5  Classification, thresholds and calibration
section: 5.1 From numbers to yes or no
text:
5.1 From numbers to yes or no
In Chapters 1 and 4 the Ward 7 outcome was a number: the change in creatinine over 48 hours. But Emma does not act on a number; she acts on a question with two answers. Will Aoife develop AKI? By the KDIGO criterion, AKI means a rise of at least 0.3 mg/dL within 48 hours (Kidney Disease: Improving Global Outcomes (KDIGO) Acute Kidney Injury Work Group 2012), so we can turn each past patient’s record into a binary outcome: \(y_i = 1\) if patient \(i\) developed AKI and \(y_i = 0\) otherwise. Of the 1 250 past patients, 58 % did.
Predicting a category rather than a number is called classification. A classifier can return a label (“AKI” or “no AKI”), but the useful ones return a probability, \(\hat p\), and leave the label to a later step. This chapter is about both steps: how to estimate \(\hat p\), and how to turn it into a decision.
Why not simply use the linear regression of Chapter 4, with \(y\) coded 0 and 1? This is called the linear probability model, and Figure 5.1 shows its problem. The straight line fitted to AKI (0/1) against SOFA happily predicts “probabilities” above 1 for the sickest patients: 1.37 at a SOFA score of 18. With a feature that pushed risk the other way it would just as happily go below 0. A probability cannot leave the interval from 0 to 1; we need a curve that cannot either.








Figure 5.1: AKI (1) or no AKI (0) against the SOFA score for the 1 250 Ward 7 patients (dots, jittered so they do not overlap). A straight line (dashed) leaves the 0–1 range at both ends; the logistic curve (solid) cannot. Squares: observed proportion with AKI at each SOFA score.






The straight line in Figure 5.1 predicts a value of about 1.5 for a patient with a SOFA score of 20. What is the best reading of this?

The patient is certain to develop AKI, and then some A probability cannot exceed 1. The number is an artefact of forcing a straight line onto a 0/1 outcome.
The model is wrong at the extremes: a probability must stay between 0 and 1 Correct. The linear probability model can be a rough guide in the middle of the data, but it produces impossible values at the edges. The logistic curve fixes this by construction.
The patient’s creatinine will rise by 1.5 mg/dL The outcome here is AKI yes/no, not the change in creatinine. The line was fitted to zeros and ones.

title: 5  Classification, thresholds and calibration
text:
5.2 Probability, odds and log-odds
To build a curve that stays between 0 and 1 we take a detour through a scale that gamblers have used for centuries: the odds.

Definition 5.1 (Odds and log-odds) The odds of an event with probability \(p\) are \(\dfrac{p}{1-p}\): how many times more likely the event is to happen than not. The log-odds (or logit) are the natural logarithm of the odds, \(\operatorname{logit}(p) = \log\dfrac{p}{1-p}\). Probabilities live between 0 and 1, odds between 0 and infinity, and log-odds anywhere on the number line.

A probability of 0.75 means odds of \(0.75/0.25 = 3\), “three to one”: the event is three times as likely to happen as not. Even odds (1) correspond to a probability of 0.5 and to log-odds of 0. Table 5.1 shows a few more values; notice the symmetry of the last column.

Why bother? Because the log-odds scale has no walls. A straight line can wander from \(-\infty\) to \(+\infty\) without ever producing an impossible value, and every log-odds value maps back to exactly one probability between 0 and 1.

On Ward 7, 58 % of past patients developed AKI. What are the odds of AKI for a patient picked at random?

0.58 That is the probability. Odds divide the probability of the event by the probability of no event.
About 1.4 Correct: 0.58 / 0.42 ≈ 1.38. AKI is about 1.4 times as likely as no AKI, a bit better than even odds.
About 0.72 That is 0.42 / 0.58, the odds of no AKI.
About 0.32 That is the log-odds, log(1.38) ≈ 0.32.

title: 5  Classification, thresholds and calibration
text:
5.3 The logistic model
Logistic regression puts the straight line of Chapter 4 on the log-odds scale (Cox 1958; Hosmer, Lemeshow, and Sturdivant 2013):
\[
\log\frac{p}{1-p} \;=\; z \;=\; \beta_0 + \beta_1 x_1 + \beta_2 x_2 + \dots + \beta_p x_p .
\qquad(5.1)\]
The right-hand side, \(z\), is called the linear predictor. Solving Equation 5.1 for \(p\) gives the probability:
\[
p \;=\; \sigma(z) \;=\; \frac{1}{1 + e^{-z}} .
\qquad(5.2)\]

Definition 5.2 (Logistic function and logistic regression) The logistic (or sigmoid) function \(\sigma(z) = 1/(1+e^{-z})\) turns any number \(z\) into a probability between 0 and 1, following an S-shaped curve. Logistic regression models the probability of a binary outcome as \(p = \sigma(\beta_0 + \beta_1 x_1 + \dots + \beta_p x_p)\): linear on the log-odds scale, S-shaped on the probability scale.

Figure 5.2 shows the curve. Take Mrs K, 68, who arrives at the emergency department with a suspected infection, a lactate of 5.2 mmol/L and a weakened immune system. Suppose a sepsis model adds up her features into a linear predictor of \(z = +1.1\). Then \(p = 1/(1+e^{-1.1}) = 0.75\). The model is saying that, among many patients like Mrs K, about three in four develop sepsis. It is a probability, not a diagnosis: Mrs K herself either will or will not develop sepsis, and what to do about a 75 % risk is a separate question, the subject of Section 5.9.








Figure 5.2: The logistic function turns log-odds \(z\) (horizontal axis) into a probability (vertical axis). Grey points: the values of Table 5.1. Mrs K’s linear predictor of \(z = +1.1\) becomes a probability of 0.75.





How are the coefficients \(\beta\) found? Not by least squares. Logistic regression uses maximum likelihood (see Chapter 2): among all possible values of \(\beta\), it picks those that make the outcomes we actually observed most probable. For a patient who developed AKI the model should give a high \(\hat p_i\); for one who did not, a high \(1-\hat p_i\). Maximising the likelihood is the same as minimising the log-loss, the average surprise of the model at what really happened:
\[
\text{log-loss} = -\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\Big[\,y_i \log \hat p_i + (1-y_i)\log(1-\hat p_i)\Big].
\qquad(5.3)\]
A model that says 0.99 to a patient who then does not develop AKI pays a heavy price, \(-\log(0.01) \approx 4.6\); one that says 0.6 to a patient who does pays only \(-\log(0.6) \approx
0.5\). This is the “mark” step of the learning loop of Chapter 1 (guess, mark, adjust, repeat): squared error marks a guess about a number, log-loss marks a guess about yes or no. Unlike least squares, there is no formula that gives the best \(\beta\) in one step; the computer adjusts them iteratively until the log-loss stops falling (Hastie, Tibshirani, and Friedman 2009, ch. 4). You can do it by hand.

Fit the S-curve by hand. The dots are the 1 250 Ward 7 patients (AKI = 1 at the top, no AKI = 0 at the bottom) and the squares show the observed proportion with AKI at each SOFA score. Your model is \(\hat p = \sigma(\beta_0 + \beta_1 \times \text{SOFA})\). Move the sliders and watch the log-loss. A model that ignores SOFA and gives everyone the average risk has a log-loss of about 0.68. Target: bring the log-loss below 0.58.

icu5 = FileAttachment("data/icu_aki.csv").csv({typed: true})
icu5b = icu5.map((d, i) => ({sofa: d.sofa, aki: d.delta_creatinine_48h >= 0.3 ? 1 : 0,
  sx: d.sofa + (((i * 7919) % 101) / 101 - 0.5) * 0.6,
  sy: (d.delta_creatinine_48h >= 0.3 ? 1 : 0) + (((i * 104729) % 97) / 97 - 0.5) * 0.08}))
icu5obs = d3.rollups(icu5b, v => ({p: d3.mean(v, d => d.aki), n: v.length}), d => d.sofa)
  .map(([s, o]) => ({sofa: s, ...o})).filter(d => d.n >= 10)
viewof b0 = Inputs.range([-5, 2], {value: 0, step: 0.05, label: "Intercept β₀"})
viewof b1 = Inputs.range([-0.3, 0.9], {value: 0, step: 0.01, label: "Slope β₁ (per SOFA point)"})
sig = z => 1 / (1 + Math.exp(-z))
ll5 = d3.mean(icu5b, d => { const p = Math.min(Math.max(sig(b0 + b1 * d.sofa), 1e-9), 1 - 1e-9);
  return -(d.aki * Math.log(p) + (1 - d.aki) * Math.log(1 - p)); })
ll5base = { const m = d3.mean(icu5b, d => d.aki); return -(m * Math.log(m) + (1 - m) * Math.log(1 - m)); }
{
  const hit = ll5 < 0.58;
  if (hit && window.aihs) window.aihs.complete("ch05-tryit-sigmoid");
  return html`<p style="font-size:1.1rem">Your log-loss: <strong>${ll5.toFixed(3)}</strong>
   ·  average-risk model: ${ll5base.toFixed(3)}
   ${hit ? "✓ target reached — your curve uses SOFA to sharpen the predictions." : ""}</p>`;
}































































Plot.plot({
  height: 320, grid: true,
  x: {label: "SOFA score on admission", domain: [-0.5, 18.5]},
  y: {label: "AKI (1) / no AKI (0), and probability", domain: [-0.1, 1.1]},
  marks: [
    Plot.dot(icu5b, {x: "sx", y: "sy", r: 1.6, fillOpacity: 0.25, fill: "currentColor"}),
    Plot.dot(icu5obs, {x: "sofa", y: "p", r: 4, symbol: "square", fill: "#b35c00"}),
    Plot.line(d3.range(-0.5, 18.51, 0.1).map(s => [s, sig(b0 + b1 * s)]), {stroke: "#1f6f8b", strokeWidth: 3})
  ]
})










The best curve you can find with SOFA alone has a log-loss of about 0.57, and its slope is positive: each extra SOFA point raises the log-odds of AKI. With more features the computer does the same search in many dimensions at once.
Logistic regression can also be drawn as a small network (Figure 5.3): each feature is multiplied by a weight, the products are added to a constant, and the sum passes through the sigmoid. This is exactly a single artificial neuron. In Chapter 7 we stack many of them to build neural networks, and when there are more than two classes (normal, pneumonia, tuberculosis) the sigmoid is replaced by its many-class generalisation, the softmax, which returns one probability per class (Goodfellow, Bengio, and Courville 2016, ch. 6). The same softmax chooses the next word in the language models of Part V.






flowchart LR
    x1["x₁ (SOFA)"] --> w1["× β₁"]
    x2["x₂ (lactate)"] --> w2["× β₂"]
    xp["xₚ (…)"] --> wp["× βₚ"]

Before fitting the Ward 7 model, a small worked example shows how to read logistic coefficients. Suppose that among 200 patients with a suspected infection, 100 were immunosuppressed and 100 were not (Table 5.2).

Definition 5.3 (Odds ratio) The odds ratio (OR) compares the odds of an event in two groups: \(\text{OR} =
\text{odds}_1 / \text{odds}_0\). An OR above 1 means higher odds in group 1, below 1 lower odds, and exactly 1 no difference. In logistic regression, \(e^{\beta_j}\) is the odds ratio for a one-unit increase in feature \(x_j\), holding the other features fixed.

In Table 5.2 the odds ratio is \(0.43 / 0.14 \approx 3.1\): the odds of sepsis are about three times higher in immunosuppressed patients. A logistic regression of sepsis on immune status would return a coefficient of \(\log 3.1 \approx 1.13\), and \(e^{1.13} \approx 3.1\) brings us back. Note that the risk ratio (the ratio of probabilities) is only \(0.30/0.12 = 2.5\). The odds ratio and the risk ratio are close only when the outcome is rare; for common outcomes the odds ratio is further from 1 and should not be read as “three times the risk” (Zhang and Yu 1998). AKI on Ward 7 is anything but rare.
Now the real thing. Table 5.3 shows a logistic regression for AKI fitted to the 1000 Ward 7 training patients with five admission features. Each odds ratio is reported for a unit of change that makes clinical sense: the size of an odds ratio depends on the unit, just as “per gram” and “per kilogram” give different numbers for the same drug.

Read the table row by row. Each extra SOFA point multiplies the odds of AKI by 1.50, holding the other four features fixed. A lowest blood pressure 10 mmHg higher multiplies them by 0.70: better perfusion, lower odds. A baseline creatinine 0.5 mg/dL higher multiplies them by 3.22, and 10 more percentage points of protocol adherence by 0.77. Two warnings from earlier chapters apply. These are associations: Chapter 1 showed that the adherence coefficient is confounded by severity if severity is not in the model (Section 1.10). And an odds ratio multiplies odds, not probabilities: the same OR moves a 10 % risk much less, in absolute terms, than a 50 % one.

5.5 A second example: who responds in ONCO-1?
In the ONCO-1 trial, patients were randomised to chemotherapy or no chemotherapy and tumour size was measured before and after. A patient is a high responder if the tumour shrank by at least 30 %, a rule modelled on the RECIST criteria for partial response (Eisenhauer et al. 2009). The binary column high_response records it. Table 5.5 shows the outcome by treatment arm in the browser version of the trial.




Table 5.5: High response by treatment arm in ONCO-1 (1 000 patients).






Arm
Not high responders
High responders
Total




Chemotherapy
104

Only 2 of the 504 untreated patients were high responders. The odds ratio for chemotherapy is therefore enormous, about 950, and a logistic regression returns a coefficient near 6.9 with a very wide confidence interval. Do not read this as “chemotherapy multiplies the odds of response by nearly a thousand”. When one group has almost no events, the data come close to separation: a feature (here, treatment) predicts the outcome almost perfectly, and the maximum-likelihood estimate drifts towards infinity; with perfect separation it does not exist at all (Albert and Anderson 1984). The honest summary is “almost nobody responds without chemotherapy”, not a precise odds ratio. Penalised estimation (Section 5.12) or Firth’s bias-reduced likelihood (Firth 1993) give finite, more sensible estimates.
The clinically interesting question is a different one: among patients who receive chemotherapy, who responds? That is a decision about whom to treat, or whom to treat with something else. Fitted to the 412 chemotherapy patients in the book’s shared training set, with dose intensity, tumour grade, performance status, age and three genes, the model gives the odds ratios in Table 5.6. Genes are measured in standard deviations, so their odds ratios compare patients one standard deviation apart.

Higher dose and a higher grade go with higher odds of response, a worse performance score with lower odds; gene_01 and gene_12 raise the odds and gene_05 lowers them sharply. In this simulated trial older patients respond slightly more often. That is how the data were generated, not a clinical claim, and a reminder to check every sign against what you expect. Notice also what is not in the model: genes 08, 14 and 19. In the simulation they are noisy copies of the tumour shrinkage itself, the leakage trap described in Chapter 3. A model that used them would look superb and be useless, because they are only “known” once the response is.
Patients #0042 and #0917, whom we met in Chapter 4, are two of the chemotherapy patients in the test set, so the model was fitted without them. On paper they look alike: the same dose intensity (1.07), grade G1 tumours, the same performance score (2), aged 37 and 46. Their responses differed: #0042’s tumour shrank by 36.6 % (a high responder), #0917’s by 20.4 % (not a high responder). The model of Table 5.6 gives them probabilities of high response of 0.78 and 0.02: the right direction, but a near-certain “no” for a patient whose clinical profile is almost identical to that of a responder, driven by small differences in three genes. The lasso model of Section 5.12, the chapter’s headline model for ONCO-1, is more cautious: 0.75 and 0.18. As for Aoife, the model provides information. Had it been available before their treatment, what the oncologist and each patient would have done with an 18 % chance of high response, given the toxicity of treatment and the alternatives, is a decision that needs their values, and two patients who look the same on paper can still respond differently.

A colleague fits a logistic regression to the whole ONCO-1 dataset and reports: “Chemotherapy has an odds ratio of about 950 (95 % CI from about 230 to 3 900).” What is the main problem?

Nothing; a huge effect is good news for the trial The trial does show that chemotherapy works, but the number itself is not trustworthy.
Almost no untreated patient responded, so the estimate is driven by near-separation and is unstable Correct. With 2 events in one arm, the odds ratio is close to dividing by zero. Report the counts, or use penalised or bias-reduced estimation, rather than a precise-looking odds ratio.
Odds ratios cannot be computed for randomised trials They can; randomisation actually makes them easier to interpret causally. The problem is the near-absence of events in one arm.
The confidence interval should be symmetric around 950 Confidence intervals for odds ratios are symmetric on the log scale, not on the original scale; asymmetry is expected.

section: 5.6 From probability to decision: the confusion matrix
text:
5.6 From probability to decision: the confusion matrix
The model gives Aoife a probability. The flag on Emma’s screen needs a yes or a no. The bridge between the two is a threshold.

Definition 5.4 (Classification threshold) A classification threshold \(t\) turns a predicted probability into a decision: classify as positive (and act) when \(\hat p \ge t\), as negative otherwise. The threshold is not a property of the model: the same model can be used with different thresholds for different purposes.

Once the threshold is fixed, each test patient falls into one of four cells (Figure 5.4), and the table of counts is the confusion matrix.





What actually happens

Figure 5.4: The confusion matrix for the Ward 7 flag. The shaded cells are correct decisions; the other two are the two kinds of error.




Definition 5.5 (Confusion matrix, accuracy, precision, recall and F1) The confusion matrix cross-tabulates predicted and actual classes into true positives (TP), false positives (FP), false negatives (FN) and true negatives (TN). From it: accuracy \(= (\text{TP}+\text{TN})/n\) is the proportion classified correctly; precision \(= \text{TP}/(\text{TP}+\text{FP})\) is the positive predictive value; recall \(= \text{TP}/(\text{TP}+\text{FN})\) is the sensitivity; and the F1 score \(= 2 \cdot \text{precision} \cdot \text{recall} / (\text{precision} + \text{recall})\) is their harmonic mean (Fawcett 2006; Rijsbergen 1979).

Sensitivity, specificity and the predictive values were introduced for diagnostic tests in Chapter 2; machine learning often calls sensitivity recall and PPV precision. The names change, the counts do not. Table 5.7 applies the five-feature model to the 250 Ward 7 test patients with the hospital’s threshold of 0.5 and with Seán’s 0.25.

Lowering the threshold from 0.5 to 0.25 catches more of the patients who go on to develop AKI (sensitivity rises from 0.83 to 0.95, so false negatives fall from 25 to 7) at the price of more unnecessary bundles (false positives rise from 25 to 63). Accuracy falls from 0.80 to 0.72, yet for a team that fears missed AKI more than an extra bundle, 0.25 may be the better choice. Accuracy counts every error as equally bad, and that is rarely true in medicine. It is also misleading when one class is rare: if only 2 % of patients had an event, a “model” that never flags anyone would be 98 % accurate and useless.

title: 5  Classification, thresholds and calibration
text:
5.7 ROC curves and AUC
Each threshold gives one confusion matrix, one sensitivity and one specificity. Sliding \(t\) from 1 down to 0 traces a curve.

Definition 5.6 (ROC curve and AUC) The receiver operating characteristic (ROC) curve plots sensitivity (true-positive rate) against \(1-\)specificity (false-positive rate) for every possible threshold. The area under the ROC curve (AUC) summarises it in one number: the probability that a randomly chosen patient with the event receives a higher predicted risk than a randomly chosen patient without it. An AUC of 0.5 is no better than a coin; 1 is perfect ranking.

The probability reading of the AUC, due to Hanley and McNeil (1982), is worth remembering: it says that the AUC measures discrimination, how well the model ranks patients, and nothing else. It does not depend on the threshold, and it does not care whether the predicted probabilities are right in absolute terms. Multiplying every risk by one half would leave the AUC unchanged.
Figure 5.5 shows what ROC curves look like in six simulated situations, unrelated to our running examples (Fawcett 2006). An excellent model hugs the top-left corner; a reasonable one bows above the diagonal; a model that guesses follows the diagonal; an inverted model, whose scores run the wrong way, falls below it (a sign that something in the data or labels is reversed: flipping its scores would make it excellent). The fifth panel has heavily imbalanced classes, one positive for every 19 negatives: its ROC curve looks respectable, a point we return to in Section 5.8. The last panel marks the thresholds along the reasonable model’s curve: lowering \(t\) moves you up and to the right.








Figure 5.5: ROC curves for six simulated situations. The dashed diagonal is a model that guesses. Panel F marks thresholds along the curve of panel B.





Rules of thumb are often quoted (AUC 0.7–0.8 “acceptable”, 0.8–0.9 “excellent”) (Hosmer, Lemeshow, and Sturdivant 2013), but a number on its own means little. On the Ward 7 test set the five-feature model has an AUC of 0.85. Is that good? It depends on the alternatives. The SOFA-only model reaches 0.77, and “no model” (the same risk for everyone) has an AUC of exactly 0.5. This is the benchmark rule: every new model must be compared with a simple baseline and with current practice, on the same patients. An AUC of 0.81 reported without a baseline has told you nothing; a deep network that reaches 0.83 where logistic regression reaches 0.82 may not be worth its opacity. Across many clinical prediction studies, flexible machine-learning methods have on average not outperformed well-built logistic regression (Christodoulou et al. 2019).

A vendor’s AKI model has an AUC of 0.85 on your hospital’s data. Which statement follows?

85 % of the model’s predictions are correct That would be accuracy at some threshold. The AUC does not depend on any threshold.
If you pick one patient who developed AKI and one who did not, the model gives the higher risk to the first about 85 % of the time Correct. This is the ranking interpretation of the AUC.
A patient with a predicted risk of 0.85 will develop AKI The AUC says nothing about the meaning of an individual probability; that is calibration (Section 5.10).
The model is good enough to deploy Discrimination is one ingredient. You still need to know how it compares with current practice, whether its probabilities are calibrated, and whether acting on it does more good than harm (Section 5.11).

title: 5  Classification, thresholds and calibration
section: 5.8 Precision–recall curves when positives are rare
text:
5.8 Precision–recall curves when positives are rare
The ROC curve has a blind spot. Its two axes are each computed within one class (sensitivity among patients with the event, false-positive rate among those without), so the ROC curve and the AUC ignore how common the event is. When the event is rare, even a small false-positive rate can mean many false positives in absolute numbers, swamping the true ones.

Definition 5.7 (Precision–recall curve) The precision–recall (PR) curve plots precision (PPV) against recall (sensitivity) for every threshold. A model that guesses has a flat PR curve at the prevalence of the event; the area under the PR curve is often reported alongside the AUC when positives are rare.

Figure 5.6 compares the reasonable balanced model (panel B above) with the imbalanced one (panel E). On the ROC plot the imbalanced model looks merely mediocre; on the PR plot its weakness is obvious: to catch half of the positives it flags many more negatives than positives, and its precision hovers not far above the 5 % prevalence. For rare outcomes such as a rare adverse drug reaction or a rare disease in screening, report PR curves as well as ROC curves (Saito and Rehmsmeier 2015). Ward 7 is the opposite case: with AKI in more than half of patients, the two curves tell similar stories.








Figure 5.6: The same two simulated models on a ROC plot (left) and a precision–recall plot (right). Dotted lines on the right show each model’s prevalence, the precision of a model that guesses.

section: 5.9 The threshold is a value judgement

title: 5  Classification, thresholds and calibration
section: 5.10 Calibration: can you trust the number?
text:
5.10 Calibration: can you trust the number?
Seán’s second question was whether “50 %” means 50 %. The AUC cannot answer it, because the AUC only looks at the order of the predictions. A model can rank patients perfectly and still announce risks that are systematically too high or too low.

Definition 5.8 (Calibration) A model is calibrated when its predicted probabilities match observed frequencies: among patients given a risk of about 30 %, about 30 % have the event. A calibration plot groups patients by predicted risk and plots the observed proportion with the event against the average prediction in each group; a calibrated model lies on the diagonal. The calibration intercept (or calibration-in-the-large) checks whether predictions are too high or too low on average (ideal 0); the calibration slope checks whether they are too extreme or too timid (ideal 1) (Van Calster et al. 2019).

Calibration has been called the Achilles heel of predictive analytics (Van Calster et al. 2019): it is reported far less often than the AUC, yet a miscalibrated model can lead to harmful decisions, because Equation 5.4 compares the predicted risk with a threshold as if it were the true risk (Steyerberg 2019). A simple overall measure that rewards both discrimination and calibration is the Brier score, the mean squared difference between predicted probabilities and outcomes (0 is perfect) (Brier 1950). On the Ward 7 test set the model’s Brier score is 0.149, against 0.242 for giving everyone the average risk.
Figure 5.7 shows two calibration plots. On the left, the model is checked on the random test set from the same four hospitals: the points follow the diagonal closely (calibration intercept 0.04, slope 1.01). On the right, the same five features were used to fit a model on hospitals A–C only, and that model was then applied to hospital D, where AKI is more common (68 % instead of 55 %). Its AUC in hospital D is still 0.82, as good as at home, but its predictions are systematically too low: on average 54 % predicted against 68 % observed (calibration intercept 0.90). In hospital D, a patient flagged as 20 % is really at higher risk, and a threshold chosen with Equation 5.4 would under-treat.








Figure 5.7: Calibration plots. Each point is one tenth of the patients, grouped by predicted risk; vertical bars are 95 % confidence intervals for the observed proportion. Left: Ward 7 test set (same hospitals as the training data). Right: a model developed in hospitals A–C applied to hospital D.





The lesson generalises: discrimination often travels better than calibration. Case mix, local practice and the way outcomes are recorded all shift the baseline risk between hospitals and over time. The usual remedy is recalibration: keep the model’s coefficients but re-estimate the intercept (and perhaps the slope) on local data (Steyerberg 2019). Calibration matters well beyond logistic regression. Flexible models such as boosted trees and neural networks are often overconfident (Niculescu-Mizil and Caruana 2005; Guo et al. 2017), and in Chapter 18 we ask the same question of a language model that says it is “90 % sure”.

After the model is moved to hospital D, its AUC is unchanged but its calibration intercept is clearly positive. What does this mean for Emma, if she works in hospital D?

Nothing: the AUC is the same, so the model is as useful as before The ranking is as good, but the numbers are not. Decisions that compare a risk with a threshold depend on the numbers.
The model ranks patients well but underestimates their risk, so a fixed threshold will flag too few patients Correct. A positive intercept means observed risk is higher than predicted. Recalibrating the intercept on local data would fix most of the problem.
The model overestimates risk, so it will flag too many patients The opposite. Predictions are too low on average in hospital D, where AKI is more common.
The model must be rebuilt from scratch Often it need not be: re-estimating the intercept (and perhaps the slope) on local data restores calibration while keeping what the model learned.

title: 5  Classification, thresholds and calibration
section: 5.11 Decision curves: is the model worth using?
text:
5.11 Decision curves: is the model worth using?
We now have a model that discriminates, a threshold that reflects values, and a check that the probabilities can be trusted. One question remains, the one a hospital should ask before switching the flag on: does acting on this model do more good than harm, compared with the simple alternatives of treating everyone or treating no one? Decision curve analysis answers it (Vickers and Elkin 2006; Vickers, Van Calster, and Steyerberg 2016).

Definition 5.9 (Net benefit and decision curve) At threshold \(t\), the net benefit of acting on a model is \[\text{NB}(t) = \frac{\text{TP}}{n} - \frac{\text{FP}}{n}\cdot\frac{t}{1-t},\] the proportion of true positives minus the proportion of false positives weighted by the threshold odds, which (by Equation 5.4) equal the harm ratio \(C_{\text{FP}}/C_{\text{FN}}\). A decision curve plots NB\((t)\) against \(t\) over a range of reasonable thresholds, for the model and for the strategies “treat all” and “treat none” (whose net benefit is 0) (Vickers and Elkin 2006).

Net benefit is measured in units of true positives: a net benefit of 0.30 is as good as finding 30 true AKI cases per 100 patients with no unnecessary bundles. The weight \(t/(1-t)\) converts false positives into the same currency: at \(t = 0.25\) the team accepts three unnecessary bundles to prevent one AKI, so each false positive costs one third of a true positive. “Treat all” has \(\text{TP}/n\) equal to the prevalence and \(\text{FP}/n\) equal to one minus the prevalence.

A decision curve for Ward 7. Net benefit on the 250 test patients for the five-feature model, the SOFA-only model, treating everyone and treating no one. Choose the threshold range your team considers reasonable and read off which strategy is best.

viewof tDca5 = Inputs.range([0.02, 0.85], {value: 0.25, step: 0.01, label: "Your threshold t"})
nb5 = (key, t) => { const n = w7p.length; let tp = 0, fp = 0;
  for (const d of w7p) if (d[key] >= t) { d.aki === 1 ? tp++ : fp++; }
  return tp / n - fp / n * t / (1 - t); }
prev5 = d3.mean(w7p, d => d.aki)
dca5 = d3.range(0.02, 0.8501, 0.01).flatMap(t => [
  {t, s: "Five-feature model", nb: nb5("p_model", t)},
  {t, s: "SOFA only", nb: nb5("p_sofa", t)},
  {t, s: "Treat all", nb: prev5 - (1 - prev5) * t / (1 - t)},
  {t, s: "Treat none", nb: 0}])
{
  const m = nb5("p_model", tDca5), so = nb5("p_sofa", tDca5), all = prev5 - (1 - prev5) * tDca5 / (1 - tDca5);
  const best = [["the five-feature model", m], ["the SOFA-only model", so], ["treat all", all], ["treat none", 0]].sort((a, b) => b[1] - a[1])[0][0];
  return html`<p>At t = ${tDca5.toFixed(2)} (you accept ${((1 - tDca5) / tDca5).toFixed(1)} unnecessary bundles per AKI prevented):
  net benefit — model <strong>${m.toFixed(3)}</strong> · SOFA only <strong>${so.toFixed(3)}</strong> ·
  treat all <strong>${all.toFixed(3)}</strong> · treat none <strong>0</strong>.<br>
  Best strategy here: <strong>${best}</strong>. Compared with treating everyone, the model is worth
  <strong>${(100 * (m - all)).toFixed(1)}</strong> net true positives per 100 patients.</p>`;
}



































Plot.plot({
  height: 300, grid: true,
  x: {label: "Threshold probability t", domain: [0, 0.85]},
  y: {label: "Net benefit", domain: [-0.1, 0.6]},
  color: {legend: true, domain: ["Five-feature model", "SOFA only", "Treat all", "Treat none"],
          range: ["#1f6f8b", "#b35c00", "#7a7a7a", "currentColor"]},
  marks: [
    Plot.line(dca5.filter(d => d.nb > -0.1), {x: "t", y: "nb", stroke: "s", strokeWidth: 2.5}),
    Plot.ruleX([tDca5], {strokeDasharray: "3,3"})
  ]
})









Three readings stand out. At very low thresholds, when the team would give the bundle to almost anyone, treating everyone is as good as the model (at \(t = 0.10\): 0.548 for the model, 0.542 for treat all), so the model adds little: if everyone is treated anyway, a prediction changes nothing. Around the team’s threshold of 0.25 the model is better than treating everyone (0.476 against 0.451), and better than the SOFA-only model (0.459). And at high thresholds, treating everyone becomes harmful (negative net benefit) while the model stays above zero. This is the value of information of Chapter 1 made measurable: a model is worth using only where it can change decisions for the better.

At a threshold of 0.25, a model has a net benefit of 0.40 and “treat all” has 0.38. What is the best summary?

The model is 2 % more accurate than treating all Net benefit is not accuracy; it weighs false positives by the threshold odds.
Using the model is equivalent to finding 2 more true cases per 100 patients, with no extra unnecessary treatments, compared with treating everyone Correct. Differences in net benefit are in units of true positives per patient. Whether that small gain justifies the cost of running the model is a further judgement.
The model should not be used, because 0.40 is less than 0.5 Net benefit has no 0.5 benchmark. The comparison is with the default strategies at the same threshold.
The model halves the number of false positives Net benefit alone does not tell you that; you would need the confusion matrices.

5.12 Penalised logistic regression
When there are many features and relatively few events, an ordinary logistic regression overfits just as linear regression does, and near-separation makes it worse: some coefficients run off towards infinity. The remedies of Chapter 4 carry over unchanged. Ridge (an L2 penalty) shrinks all coefficients towards zero; lasso (L1) can set some exactly to zero, selecting features; the elastic net mixes the two (Hoerl and Kennard 1970; Tibshirani 1996; Zou and Hastie 2005). The only change is that the penalty is added to the log-loss of Equation 5.3 instead of the sum of squared errors, and the strength \(\lambda\) is chosen by cross-validation, for example with glmnet and family = "binomial" (Friedman, Hastie, and Tibshirani 2010).
We return to the ONCO-1 chemotherapy patients and give the models everything: dose, grade, performance score, age and all 47 genes of the browser dataset except the three leaky ones, 51 predictors for a training set of 412 patients of whom only about a fifth are not high responders. Where this chapter sits in the decision loop: from a probability to an action, with calibration and values in between.

In the decision loop of Chapter 1, this chapter is the hinge between information and decision. Logistic regression (Section 5.3) turns data into a probability; odds ratios (Section 5.4) tell us how each feature moves it; ROC and PR curves (Section 5.7, Section 5.8) measure how well it ranks patients; calibration (Section 5.10) checks that the number itself can be believed; the threshold (Section 5.9) is where the values of patients and clinicians enter; and the decision curve (Section 5.11) asks whether the whole chain does more good than harm. What can go wrong? An impressive AUC with no baseline; a default threshold of 0.5 that silently treats all errors as equal; a model that ranks well in a new hospital but whose probabilities are off; odds ratios read as risk ratios, or taken literally under separation. Who stays in control? Whoever sets the threshold, which is why it should be set openly, by the people who live with the consequences.

text:
5.15 Exercises

Odds by hand. Convert the probabilities 0.05, 0.20 and 0.95 to odds and log-odds. Which pairs are symmetric on the log-odds scale?
Risk ratio or odds ratio? In Table 5.2, change the counts so that only 3 of 100 immunosuppressed and 1 of 100 other patients develop sepsis. Compute the risk ratio and the odds ratio. Why are they now close?
Units. In Table 5.3, what is the odds ratio for an increase of 20 mmHg in the lowest mean arterial pressure? For an increase of 0.1 mg/dL in baseline creatinine?
Accuracy paradox. A rare-disease screening test is applied to 10 000 people, 50 of whom have the disease. A model flags 100 people, 40 of them correctly. Compute accuracy, sensitivity, precision and F1, and compare with a “model” that flags nobody.
Your threshold. In the threshold widget, set the harm of a missed AKI to 1, 3 and 9. Report \(t^{*}\) for each and how many of the 250 test patients would receive the bundle.
Calibration. Explain to Emma, in three sentences and without formulas, why a model with an AUC of 0.82 in hospital D can still lead her to under-treat.
Decision curve. In the decision-curve widget, find the range of thresholds where the five-feature model beats both “treat all” and “treat none”. What does it mean for a team whose threshold lies outside that range?
Code. Modify the Lab to fit the model on hospitals A–C and test it on hospital D. Compute the AUC, the Brier score and the calibration table. Then recalibrate by refitting only the intercept on half of hospital D’s patients (hint: glm(aki ~ offset(qlogis(p)), family =    binomial)) and check calibration on the other half.







Selected answers





1. Odds 0.053, 0.25 and 19; log-odds −2.94, −1.39 and +2.94. The probabilities 0.05 and 0.95 are symmetric: their log-odds differ only in sign.
2. Risk ratio \(0.03/0.01 = 3\); odds ratio \((3/97)/(1/99) \approx 3.06\). When the outcome is rare, \(1-p \approx 1\), so odds and probabilities are almost the same and so are their ratios.
3. For 20 mmHg the odds ratio is \(e^{20\beta}\): the square of the 10 mmHg odds ratio, about 0.49. For 0.1 mg/dL of baseline creatinine it is \(e^{0.1\beta} \approx\) 1.26.
4. TP = 40, FP = 60, FN = 10, TN = 9 890. Accuracy 0.993, sensitivity 0.80, precision 0.40, F1 ≈ 0.53. Flagging nobody gives accuracy 0.995 (higher!), sensitivity 0 and an undefined precision: accuracy rewards ignoring the disease.
6. The model still puts patients in the right order, so the sickest are still at the top of its list. But in hospital D more patients develop AKI than the model expects, so all its numbers are too low. If Emma treats only patients above a fixed cut-off, some patients who need the bundle will fall below it.
7. The model is useful only where its net benefit exceeds both default strategies. A team whose threshold is very low would treat nearly everyone anyway; for them the model changes few decisions and is not worth the effort.

title: 5  Classification, thresholds and calibration
text:
5.16 Summary

A binary outcome needs a model whose predictions stay between 0 and 1. Logistic regression is linear on the log-odds scale and S-shaped on the probability scale, \(p = \sigma(\beta_0 + \beta_1 x_1 + \dots)\); it is fitted by maximum likelihood (minimum log-loss).
\(e^{\beta_j}\) is an odds ratio per unit of \(x_j\). Its size depends on the unit; it approximates a risk ratio only for rare outcomes; under (near-)separation it is unstable and should not be read literally.
A threshold turns a probability into an action and produces a confusion matrix. Accuracy treats all errors as equal; sensitivity, specificity, precision and F1 separate them.
The ROC curve and its AUC measure discrimination (ranking) across all thresholds; precision–recall curves are more informative when positives are rare. Always compare with a baseline.
The best threshold follows from values: \(t^{*} = C_{\text{FP}}/(C_{\text{FP}}+C_{\text{FN}})\). A default of 0.5 is itself a value judgement.
Calibration asks whether predicted risks match observed frequencies. It often degrades when a model moves to a new setting, even when the AUC does not; recalibration can fix it.
Decision curves compare the net benefit of acting on a model with treating all or none, across reasonable thresholds.
Penalised logistic regression (ridge, lasso, elastic net) tames overfitting when there are many features and few events.
