text:
How to use this chapter






Starting here?





This chapter borrows a few ideas from earlier chapters. In one line each:

Training and test sets. A model is fitted on training data and judged on a test set it has never seen (Section 1.8). This chapter uses the book’s shared splits from Chapter 3, stored in data/splits/: 1 000 training and 250 test patients for Ward 7, 800 and 200 for ONCO-1, with the training patients divided into five fixed cross-validation folds. Every model in Part II is judged on the same patients.
Overfitting and cross-validation. A flexible model can memorise noise; \(V\)-fold cross-validation estimates performance on new data while choices are being made (Definition 1.8, Definition 1.9). A hyperparameter is a setting that controls how a model is learned rather than being learned itself (Chapter 3).
Error metrics. The mean absolute error (MAE) and root mean squared error (RMSE) measure how far numerical predictions are from the truth (Chapter 3).
Linear and logistic regression predict with a weighted sum of the features (Chapter 4, Chapter 5); the area under the ROC curve (AUC) is the probability that a randomly chosen patient with the event receives a higher score than one without it (Chapter 5).
Leakage is information in the features that would not be available, honestly, at the time of prediction (Chapter 3). Entropy measures surprise (Chapter 2).

This chapter is about models made of questions. It has fourteen sections and a Lab, seven quick checks, three “Try it” widgets (grow a tree, draw bootstrap samples, step through boosting), a challenge and three coding missions in R and Python. Allow about two hours. Forests with hundreds of trees and XGBoost models are trained once, outside the browser, and their results are loaded here; everything else runs live.

title: 6  Trees and ensembles
text:
6.1 A tree you can read
Before we let a tree loose on clinical data, it helps to see one recover rules we already know. We simulate 200 instances with two features, \(X_1\) (think of something like age, between 0 and 10) and \(X_2\) (think of a biomarker, centred on zero), and an outcome \(Y\) produced by if–else rules plus a little noise:
\[
Y = \begin{cases}
5 + \varepsilon, & \text{if } X_1 \le 4,\\
10 + \varepsilon, & \text{if } X_1 > 4 \text{ and } X_2 \le 0,\\
14 + \varepsilon, & \text{if } X_1 > 4 \text{ and } X_2 > 0,
\end{cases}
\qquad \varepsilon \sim \mathcal{N}(0,\ 0.8^2).
\qquad(6.1)\]

set.seed(2026)                                   # fixed seed: same data every time
n  <- 200
X1 <- runif(n, 0, 10)                            # "age-like"
X2 <- rnorm(n, 0, 1)                             # "biomarker-like"
y  <- ifelse(X1 <= 4, 5, ifelse(X2 <= 0, 10, 14)) + rnorm(n, 0, 0.8)
toy <- data.frame(X1, X2, y)

toy_tree <- rpart(y ~ X1 + X2, data = toy,
                  control = rpart.control(cp = 0, maxdepth = 3, minsplit = 15))
# prune with the 1-SE rule (explained in the pruning section)
cpt  <- toy_tree$cptable
best <- which.min(cpt[, "xerror"])
toy_pruned <- prune(toy_tree, cp = cpt[cpt[, "xerror"] <= cpt[best, "xerror"] + cpt[best, "xstd"], "CP"][1])
toy_pruned

Read the output from the top. Node 1 is the root: all 200 instances, with mean 8.89. The first question is “is \(X_1 < 4.04\)?”. Those who answer yes (92 instances) end in a final box, a leaf, that predicts 5.13. The others are asked a second question, “is \(X_2 < 0.01\)?”, which sends them to leaves predicting 9.93 or 13.94. The tree has rediscovered the three rules of Equation 6.1 almost exactly, with thresholds of about 4 and 0, from nothing but the data. Each path from the root to a leaf is one rule (Breiman et al. 1984; Hastie, Tibshirani, and Friedman 2009, ch. 9):

if \(X_1 < 4.04\) then predict 5.13;
if \(X_1 \ge 4.04\) and \(X_2 < 0.01\) then predict 9.93;
if \(X_1 \ge 4.04\) and \(X_2 \ge 0.01\) then predict 13.94.









Figure 6.1: The toy tree seen from above. Each dot is an instance, shaded by its outcome; the tree cuts the plane into three rectangles and predicts one constant (printed) in each.





This is what a regression tree does to any dataset: it chops the space of features into rectangles and predicts a constant in each. The rest of the chapter explains how it chooses where to cut, how deep to go, and why, in practice, we rarely trust a single tree.

title: 6  Trees and ensembles
text:
6.2 The anatomy of a tree
The vocabulary comes from botany, turned upside down: the root is at the top and the leaves at the bottom. Figure 6.2 shows the same toy example annotated by hand.






Figure 6.2: The anatomy of a decision tree, annotated on an earlier run of the toy simulation (so the numbers differ slightly from those above). Each box shows the predicted value, the number of instances and their percentage of the sample.




Definition 6.1 (Decision tree) A decision tree predicts an outcome by asking a sequence of yes/no questions about the features, each of the form “is \(x_j \le s\)?” for a feature \(j\) and a threshold \(s\) (or “is \(x_j\) in this group of categories?”). Its parts are:

the root node, which contains all training instances;
internal nodes, each holding a split (the question) that sends instances to its two child nodes;
leaves (terminal nodes), which make the prediction: the mean outcome of the training instances that reach them in a regression tree, or the class proportions in a classification tree.

The depth of a tree is the number of questions on its longest root-to-leaf path.

Each node also carries within-node information — its prediction, the number of instances and their share of the sample — that summarises the subgroup created by the questions above it, while the splits carry the between-node logic that routes each instance. A child either becomes an internal node, if splitting it further is worthwhile, or a leaf.
Trees have properties that make them attractive in health care (Breiman et al. 1984; James et al. 2021, ch. 8):

They read like clinical reasoning. Each prediction can be traced along one path of questions, which can be checked against clinical knowledge and written on Seán’s card.
They are local. Unlike a linear model, which assumes one relationship for everybody, each branch can behave differently. Thresholds, plateaus and abrupt changes are natural.
They find interactions on their own (see below).
They do not care about scale. A split depends only on the order of the values, so lactate in mmol/L or mg/dL gives the same tree, and there is no need to standardise features. Categorical features are handled directly, and some implementations route instances with missing values through surrogate splits.

Their weaknesses are just as real. Predictions jump from one constant to the next at each threshold; and, as we will see in Section 6.6, a small change in the data can produce a very different tree.

6.2.1 A very short introduction to interactions
Two features interact when the effect of one on the outcome depends on the value of the other. In a linear model an interaction must be written in by hand, as a product term such as \(\beta_3 x_1 x_2\) (Chapter 4). In a tree it appears by itself: a split on \(X_2\) that sits below a split on \(X_1\) applies only to the instances on that side of \(X_1\). In the toy example, \(X_2\) matters only when \(X_1 > 4\). Clinical examples are everywhere: a drug that works well in younger patients and less well in older ones, because of how they metabolise it; a gene whose expression predicts response only in high-grade tumours; a dose–response curve that is steep in patients with good performance status and flat in frail ones; and, in genetics, the interaction between genotype and environment that shapes a phenotype.
An interaction plot shows the mean outcome for each combination of two features. Parallel lines mean no interaction; lines that diverge or cross mean an interaction (Figure 6.3).








Figure 6.3: Left: simulated tumour response with no interaction — the effect of dose is the same in both tumour grades, so the lines are parallel. Right: the toy data — the effect of the biomarker X2 is zero when X1 ≤ 4 and large when X1 > 4, so the lines diverge.





In ONCO-1 there is a built-in interaction of the same kind: dose intensity can only matter for patients randomised to chemotherapy, because everyone in the control arm has a dose of zero. A tree discovers this by splitting on treatment first and on dose only within the chemotherapy branch.

Aoife (71, sepsis; on Ward 7) reaches a leaf of a regression tree for the change in creatinine that contains 464 training patients. What does the tree predict for her?

Her own measured change in creatinine The tree cannot know it: Aoife’s outcome is in the future. It predicts from patients seen in training.
The mean change in creatinine of the 464 training patients in that leaf Correct. A regression tree predicts the average outcome of the training instances that followed the same path of questions. Everyone in the leaf gets the same prediction.
A weighted sum of her features, as in linear regression That is a linear model. A tree’s prediction is constant within a leaf; her exact SOFA or lactate no longer matters once the path is fixed.
The prediction of the closest training patient That is a nearest-neighbour method (Chapter 3), not a tree.

text:
6.4 CART in practice: growing, stopping and pruning
Left alone, greedy splitting continues until every leaf is tiny. Two kinds of control prevent this.
Stopping rules halt growth early. In rpart they are hyperparameters: minsplit (the smallest node that may be split, default 20), minbucket (the smallest allowed leaf, by default a third of minsplit), maxdepth (the maximum depth) and cp, the complexity parameter: a split is kept only if it improves the overall fit by at least the fraction cp. For classification, parms = list(split = "gini") (the default) or "information" (entropy) chooses the impurity.
Pruning works in the opposite direction: grow a large tree first, then cut back the branches that do not earn their keep. Stopping early can miss a weak split that would have made a very good split possible further down; pruning does not have that blind spot.

Definition 6.3 (Cost-complexity pruning) For a tree \(T\) with \(\lvert T\rvert\) leaves and residual sum of squares \(\text{RSS}(T)\) on the training data, cost-complexity pruning minimises \[
\text{RSS}(T) + c_p\, \lvert T\rvert ,
\] where the complexity parameter \(c_p \ge 0\) charges a price for every leaf (Breiman et al. 1984). As \(c_p\) increases from zero, the best subtree loses branches one by one, giving a sequence of nested trees from the full tree down to the root alone. The value of \(c_p\) is chosen by cross-validation. The 1-SE rule picks the simplest tree whose cross-validated error is within one standard error of the minimum.

(rpart scales \(c_p\) relative to the error of the root node; the idea is the same. In other books the complexity parameter is called \(\alpha\); we keep \(\alpha\) for the elastic-net mixing parameter of Chapter 4.) Cost-complexity pruning is the tree version of the penalties of ridge and lasso: a measure of fit plus a price for complexity.
Here is the whole routine on Ward 7: grow a large regression tree on the training patients, look at the cross-validated error of each subtree, and prune.

# xval = folds: rpart's cross-validation uses the five shared folds, so no seed is needed
big <- rpart(delta_creatinine_48h ~ site + age + sofa + lactate + map_min + baseline_creat +
               protocol_adherence + bun + crp + albumin,
             data = train, control = rpart.control(cp = 0.001, minsplit = 20, xval = folds))
cpt  <- big$cptable                                # one row per subtree
best <- which.min(cpt[, "xerror"])                 # minimum cross-validated error
cp_min <- cpt[best, "CP"]
cp_1se <- cpt[cpt[, "xerror"] <= cpt[best, "xerror"] + cpt[best, "xstd"], "CP"][1]
tree_min <- prune(big, cp = cp_min)
tree_1se <- prune(big, cp = cp_1se)
tree_1se

Figure 6.4: Cross-validated error (relative to the root node) of the subtrees of the large Ward 7 tree, by number of leaves. The bars are ± one standard error; the dashed line is the minimum plus one standard error. The 1-SE rule picks the smallest tree below the line.





The large tree has 81 leaves. The subtree with the smallest cross-validated error has 6 and the 1-SE tree 6 — with the shared folds the two rules agree — and the pruned tree splits only on SOFA and baseline creatinine. These two trees are the ones compared with every other model of the book: the large tree (rpart, \(c_p = 0.001\), no pruning) and the 1-SE tree (the large tree pruned by the 1-SE rule). On the 250 test patients the mean absolute error is 0.195 mg/dL for the large tree and 0.186 for the 1-SE tree, against 0.236 for predicting the training average for everyone. Pruning removed most of the tree and made it more accurate: the extra leaves of the large tree were fitting noise. The small tree also fits on Seán’s card. When simplicity and accuracy pull in different directions, which to favour is not a statistical question: it depends on how the tree will be used, a theme we return to at the end of the chapter.

After growing a large tree, why choose the subtree given by the 1-SE rule rather than the one with the smallest cross-validated error?

Because the 1-SE tree always has a lower test error Not always — it can be a little less accurate than the minimum-error tree (on Ward 7, with the shared folds, the two happen to coincide). Its appeal is simplicity at nearly the same estimated error.
Because it is the simplest tree whose estimated error is statistically indistinguishable from the best Correct. Differences in cross-validated error smaller than one standard error are mostly noise, so among trees that good we prefer the simplest: easier to read, more stable.
Because it removes the need for a test set Cross-validation guides the choice of tree; an untouched test set is still needed for an honest final estimate.
Because it has the smallest training error The deepest tree has the smallest training error; that is exactly what pruning protects us from.

6.5 Trees for classification
Everything so far carries over to a categorical outcome. A classification tree chooses splits by Gini or entropy instead of variance, and each leaf stores the proportion of each class among its training instances (Breiman et al. 1984; James et al. 2021, ch. 8). That proportion is the predicted probability; a class prediction follows from a threshold, which, as Chapter 5 showed, is a decision about costs rather than a property of the model.
The tree in the gate was grown exactly like this, on Ward 7 with AKI (yes/no) as the outcome and a maximum depth of 2:

aki_tree <- rpart(aki ~ site + age + sofa + lactate + map_min + baseline_creat +
                    protocol_adherence + bun + crp + albumin,
                  data = train, method = "class",
                  control = rpart.control(maxdepth = 2, cp = 0, xval = 0))
aki_tree

The yprob column gives, for each node, the proportion without and with AKI. SOFA below 8.5 means SOFA of 8 or less, which is why the gate asked “SOFA ≥ 9?”. Read the leaf for Aoife: a risk of about one in three, above the threshold of 0.25 that her team set in Chapter 1 (Section 1.5), so the tree supports starting the kidney-protective bundle. Notice that Aoife and Tomás receive exactly the same risk, although Tomás is younger, less sick and has better blood pressure: a two-question tree cannot tell them apart. Coarseness is the price of a rule that fits on a card.
The gate tree is a teaching tree: its depth was fixed at 2. The tree that enters the book’s AKI comparison is grown the honest way, on the five predictors of the headline logistic model of Chapter 5 (SOFA, lactate, lowest blood pressure, baseline creatinine and protocol adherence) and pruned by the 1-SE rule with the shared folds. It keeps 4 leaves and gives tonight’s three patients the same risks (0.34, 0.34 and 0.84). On the 250 test patients its AUC is 0.733, against 0.855 for that logistic regression, which gives Aoife 0.49 and Tomás 0.07. A handful of leaves cannot rank patients as finely as a weighted sum of five features.

6.6 Why one tree is not enough
Trees are unstable: small changes in the training data can change the first split, and then everything below it. To see this, draw five new training sets by resampling the 1 000 Ward 7 patients with replacement (we will name this procedure in a moment) and grow a depth-2 tree on each.

SOFA dominates every time, as it should — it is the strongest predictor of kidney injury in these data — but the threshold moves, and the second question on the left changes from one sample to the next. Imagine five hospitals each printing “their” card. With more depth and weaker signals, as with thousands of genes, the disagreement becomes much larger. A single deep tree has low bias and high variance. The rest of the chapter is about fixing that by combining many trees.

title: 6  Trees and ensembles
6  Trees and ensembles
text:
6.8 Random forests
Bagged trees grown on the same data tend to look alike: if SOFA is the strongest feature, nearly every tree splits on SOFA first, and their errors are strongly correlated (a large \(\rho\) in the formula above). A random forest breaks this pattern with one more source of randomness (Breiman 2001).

Definition 6.7 (Random forest) A random forest is a bagged ensemble of deep trees in which, at every split, only a random subset of \(m_{\text{try}}\) of the \(p\) features is considered as candidates. Common defaults are \(m_{\text{try}} \approx \sqrt{p}\) for classification and \(p/3\) for regression (Liaw and Wiener 2002; Hastie, Tibshirani, and Friedman 2009, ch. 15). With \(m_{\text{try}} = p\) a random forest is ordinary bagging.

Forcing some trees to do without SOFA at some splits lets other features — baseline creatinine, lactate, blood pressure — have their say, so the trees disagree more and their average is more stable. Random forests have few hyperparameters that matter (the number of trees, which only needs to be “large enough”, \(m_{\text{try}}\) and the minimum leaf size), they rarely do badly with the defaults, and they come with an out-of-bag error estimate (James et al. 2021, ch. 8). In R the classic implementation is randomForest (Liaw and Wiener 2002); ranger (Wright and Ziegler 2017) is a faster alternative.
Figure 6.6 shows a forest of 500 trees grown on Ward 7, trained outside the browser.








Figure 6.6: Out-of-bag error (on the 1 000 training patients) and test error (on the 250 test patients) of a random forest and of plain bagging on Ward 7, as trees are added. Precomputed with scikit-learn.





Three lessons. First, more trees never hurt: the error falls and then flattens, so \(B\) is not a dial that causes overfitting — it only costs computing time. Second, the out-of-bag error tracks the test error closely, and if anything errs on the pessimistic side (0.165 against 0.153 for the forest at 500 trees), so in practice the forest can be tuned without touching the test set. Third, with only ten features, one of which dominates, the random forest and plain bagging end up about equally good here (test MAE of 0.153 and 0.156): decorrelating the trees helps most when many features carry overlapping signal.
You can grow a smaller forest yourself (200 trees take a second or two in the browser). Its errors will differ a little from those of the 500-tree scikit-learn forest above, which is the one used in every comparison of the book:

RPython























Variable importance. A forest is no longer a rule anyone can read, but it can still say which features it relies on. Impurity importance adds up, over all trees, the impurity reduction of the splits on each feature; permutation importance shuffles one feature at a time and measures how much worse the predictions become (Breiman 2001). On Ward 7 the impurity importances of the precomputed forest rank sofa, bun, baseline_creat at the top. Both measures are useful screening tools and both can mislead: impurity importance favours features with many possible split points, and correlated features share or steal each other’s credit (Strobl et al. 2007). Importance says what the model uses, not what causes the outcome. Chapter 12 returns to importance, explains it properly and criticises it.

title: 6  Trees and ensembles
section: 6.9 Boosting: learning from the ensemble’s mistakes

title: 6  Trees and ensembles
text:
6.10 XGBoost
XGBoost (extreme gradient boosting) is a fast, carefully engineered implementation of gradient boosting that has become a default choice for tabular prediction (Chen and Guestrin 2016). On top of the basic algorithm it adds:

a penalty on the complexity of each tree — on the number of leaves and on the size of the leaf values (L1 and L2 penalties, the same ideas as lasso and ridge in Chapter 4);
shrinkage by the learning rate \(\eta\) (called eta or learning_rate);
row and column subsampling: each tree sees a random fraction of the patients (subsample) and of the features (colsample_bytree), an idea borrowed from bagging and random forests (Friedman 2002);
efficient handling of sparse and missing values, and early stopping: training halts when the error on a validation set has not improved for a set number of rounds.

The main hyperparameters are the number of rounds, \(\eta\), the depth of each tree (typically 2 to 6) and the subsampling fractions. They interact: a smaller \(\eta\) needs more rounds. The number of rounds should never be chosen by looking at the test set; early stopping on a validation set carved out of the training data, or cross-validation, does the job honestly.
Figure 6.9 shows XGBoost on Ward 7 with all ten features and trees of depth 3, trained for 600 rounds with two learning rates. We plot the test error here only to show what happens; in a real analysis this curve is the one you are not allowed to look at.








Figure 6.9: XGBoost on Ward 7 (depth-3 trees): training and test MAE after each boosting round, for a small (η = 0.05) and a large (η = 0.3) learning rate. Precomputed in Python.





With \(\eta = 0.3\) the test error is lowest after about 33 rounds (0.148 mg/dL); after 600 rounds the training error has fallen to 0.011 while the test error has crept back up to 0.168. That is boosting overfitting: the later trees fit the noise of the training patients. With \(\eta = 0.05\) the best test error comes later, after about 314 rounds, and the curve is flatter, so stopping a little too late costs less. The model in the comparison of Section 6.13 used \(\eta = 0.05\), and the number of rounds was chosen by cross-validation on the five shared folds of the training patients: for each number of rounds, average the validation error over the five folds, take the minimum, then refit on all 1 000 training patients. That chose 152 rounds.
The code that produced it is short (Python, from ledger.py, the script that fits every model compared in the book):
import numpy as np, xgboost as xgb
par = dict(learning_rate=0.05, max_depth=3, subsample=0.8, colsample_bytree=0.8,
           reg_lambda=1.0, eval_metric="mae", random_state=2026)
curves = []
for v in range(1, 6):                         # the five shared folds of the TRAINING patients
    fit, val = fold != v, fold == v
    m = xgb.XGBRegressor(n_estimators=1000, **par).fit(
        X[fit], y[fit], eval_set=[(X[val], y[val])], verbose=False)
    curves.append(m.evals_result()["validation_0"]["mae"])
best = int(np.argmin(np.mean(curves, axis=0))) + 1   # rounds with the lowest mean CV error
model = xgb.XGBRegressor(n_estimators=best, **par).fit(X, y)
The R package xgboost implements the same algorithm. Its interface has changed between major versions (older tutorials, including the first edition of this chapter, use argument names that recent versions have renamed or removed), so follow the documentation of the version you install. XGBoost is not available in the in-browser R used by this book, which is why its results here are precomputed.

You halve the learning rate \(\eta\) of a boosted model and keep everything else the same. What should you expect?

Fewer rounds are needed to reach the best validation error The opposite: each tree now makes a smaller correction, so more rounds are needed.
More rounds are needed, and the best validation error is usually similar or slightly better Correct. Smaller steps make learning slower but steadier; the validation curve is flatter around its minimum, so early stopping is less critical.
The model can no longer overfit A small learning rate delays overfitting; with enough rounds it still happens.
Each tree becomes deeper Depth is a separate hyperparameter (max_depth); η does not change it.

title: 6  Trees and ensembles
text:
6.11 Stacking
Bagging and boosting combine many copies of the same kind of model. Stacking combines different kinds (Wolpert 1992).

Definition 6.9 (Stacking) In stacking, several base models (for example a penalised linear model, a random forest and a boosted model) are fitted to the training data, and a meta-model learns how to combine their predictions into a final one. To avoid rewarding base models that merely memorise the training data, the meta-model is trained on out-of-fold predictions obtained by cross-validation (Breiman 1996b).

Stacking can squeeze out a little extra accuracy, especially when the base models make different kinds of mistakes. It also makes the final model harder to explain, to validate and to maintain — costs that matter in a hospital far more than in a prediction competition.

Which ensemble method does each statement describe best?

Trees are grown one after another, each fitted to the residuals of the ensemble so far. Boosting
Deep trees are grown on bootstrap samples and averaged, and every split may use any feature. Bagging
At each split only a random subset of the features is considered, so that the trees disagree more. Random forest
A logistic regression, a forest and a boosted model each predict, and a meta-model learns how to weigh them. Stacking
A learning rate shrinks each new tree’s contribution. Boosting
Its default \(m_{\text{try}}\) for regression is about one third of the features. Random forest

6.12 Too good to be true? A checklist for near-perfect models
Back to the ONCO-1 report from the opening. The consultant used the trial’s clinical variables and the gene-expression profiles, removed the obvious culprits (the patient identifier and the tumour sizes before and after treatment, from which the response is calculated), and trained four classifiers for high_response (tumour shrinkage of at least 30 %). We repeated the analysis on the browser version of ONCO-1 with the book’s shared split (800 training and 200 test patients); the models were trained outside the browser.




Table 6.3: ONCO-1, predicting high response (shrinkage ≥ 30 %) from all clinical and gene-expression features: AUC on the training and test patients.

Test AUCs of 1.000 for the forest and 0.999 for XGBoost: on the face of it, an almost perfect test of who will respond. (The first edition of this chapter reported 0.998 for XGBoost on the full 10 000-patient trial and celebrated it.) In medicine a discrimination that good is so rare that it should trigger an investigation before anything else. Here is a checklist; each item is a question you can ask of any model, including ones built by others (Kaufman et al. 2012; Kapoor and Narayanan 2023).
1. Is the error estimated on data the model has not seen? Yes: the AUCs above are on the 200 test patients. (The training AUCs of 1.000 for the forest say nothing either way: a forest almost always fits its own training data perfectly; its out-of-bag error is the honest in-sample number.) So this is not simple overfitting.
2. What does the simplest possible model achieve? Patients were randomised to chemotherapy or nothing, and chemotherapy shrinks tumours. Predicting “high response” for everyone treated and “low response” for everyone else — no model at all — gives a test AUC of 0.923. Most of the impressive number comes from knowing who received the drug. The interesting clinical question, which treated patients will respond?, is a different and harder one.
3. Which features does the model rely on, and is that plausible? The ten most important features of the forest:

Three genes — 08, 14 and 19 — sit at the top, ahead of treatment and dose, and each correlates at about 0.98 with the measured shrinkage. No gene measured before treatment predicts a tumour’s response to chemotherapy that precisely. A correlation like this is the signature of a variable that is, in effect, a copy of the outcome. In ONCO-1 that is literally what happened: in the simulation these three columns were overwritten with noisy copies of the shrinkage (see sim_onco1.R). In real data the same pattern arises when a “baseline” measurement was in fact taken after treatment, when a derived variable encodes the outcome, or when a laboratory value is ordered because the outcome was suspected: leakage (Chapter 3).
4. Would the feature be available, honestly, when the prediction is made? For a model meant to guide the decision to treat, a feature that reflects the response cannot exist at that moment. If the answer is “no” or “not sure”, remove the feature and refit.
5. What happens without the suspicious features, and on the harder question?

Removing the three genes changes the overall AUC only a little (treatment and dose still do most of the work), but it reveals what the genes were doing elsewhere: the random forest’s error in predicting the amount of shrinkage rises from 1.55 to 3.40 percentage points, and among treated patients its AUC drops from 0.999 to 0.957. The honest models are still good — these are simulated data, with far less noise than real tumours — but now their performance comes from things that could truly be known before treatment: the drug, its dose and the genuinely predictive genes (01, 05 and 12 in the simulation).
Notice also which model wins the honest question among treated patients. The first row is not plain logistic regression: it is a ridge logistic regression (C = 1), scikit-learn’s default, which shrinks the coefficients. With the 51 predictors it reaches a test AUC of 0.977, ahead of XGBoost (0.971), the forest (0.957) and the tree (0.890). Plain, unpenalised logistic regression on the same 51 predictors does much worse (0.896, Chapter 5): with 412 patients it nearly separates the two classes and its coefficients explode. The best of all is still the 7-predictor logistic regression of Chapter 5 (0.987). For the amount of shrinkage, on the other hand, XGBoost has the edge: 2.72 against 3.47 percentage points for linear regression (OLS). Which model wins depends on the question, not on the fame of the algorithm.
6. Does it hold up elsewhere? Even a model that passes every check above has been tested only on patients from the same trial. External validation in other hospitals, and prospective evaluation, come before clinical use (Chapter 5; Collins et al. (2015)).






The checklist in one breath



When a model looks too good: (1) confirm the test data were truly unseen; (2) compare with the simplest baseline; (3) look at what the model relies on; (4) ask whether each of those features exists at the moment of decision; (5) refit without the suspects and on the question that matters; (6) validate somewhere else.



A colleague’s model predicts 30-day mortality after surgery with a test AUC of 0.99. Its most important feature is “number of days in hospital”. What is the most likely explanation?

The model has found a strong new risk factor Possibly, but a near-perfect AUC driven by one variable deserves suspicion first.
Leakage: length of stay is only known after the outcome has (or has not) happened, and patients who die early have short stays Correct. The feature is not available when the prediction would be made — before or just after surgery — and it partly encodes the outcome. Remove it and refit.
Overfitting, because the AUC was measured on the test set Measuring on a test set is what protects against overfitting. The problem here is what the features contain, not where the error was measured.
Random chance: with enough patients AUCs are always high Large samples make estimates more precise, not higher.



Spot the leak. Before modelling anything, a quick screen can catch the most blatant leaks: compute the correlation of every gene with the outcome in the training patients and look at the top. Fill in the blank with the name of the outcome column (tumour shrinkage, in %).

RPython

















Look at the column names with names(train): the shrinkage column ends in _percent.


r <- sapply(train[genes], function(g) cor(g, train$response_percent))


















Look at the column names with train.columns: the shrinkage column ends in _percent.


r = train[genes].corrwith(train["response_percent"])




A correlation screen catches only the crudest leaks. A leak can hide in a combination of variables, or in how patients were selected; the checklist above, and knowledge of how each variable was recorded, catch more.

title: 6  Trees and ensembles
section: 6.14 Where this fits in the decision loop
text:
6.14 Where this fits in the decision loop


  The decision loop, with this chapter's contribution highlighted
  A cycle of five boxes: data feed a model; the model produces information; people combine the information with values to make a decision; the decision leads to actions and outcomes, recorded as new data. The model box is labelled tree, forest or boosting, and the information box reads a rule, or a risk with a check for leakage.
  
  Data
  
  Model
  tree · forest · boosting
  
  Information
  a rule, or a checked risk
  
  Decision
  + values, human in the loop
  
  Action and outcome
  recorded as new data

The decision loop. Trees and ensembles sit in the Model step; what they hand to the Decision is either a readable rule or a risk that has survived the "too good to be true?" checks.

Trees and ensembles offer the decision-maker two different kinds of information. A single, pruned tree offers a rule: Seán’s card, which can be followed at 3 am, checked against clinical knowledge and argued with — at the price of coarse risks that cannot tell Aoife from Tomás. Forests and boosted models offer a sharper risk for each patient — at the price of transparency, so that what they rely on has to be examined with the tools of Chapter 12. Which one serves the decision depends on who will use it, when, and how much the extra accuracy changes what they do: if the forest and the card put the same patients above the threshold of Chapter 1, the card is the better information. What can go wrong? Deep trees overfit; importance is mistaken for cause; and, above all, a near-perfect score built on leaked information looks like the best model in the room. Who stays in control? The clinicians who decide whether a feature would really be known at the bedside, and whether a rule makes clinical sense.

title: 6  Trees and ensembles
text:
6.16 Exercises

Gini by hand. A node holds 80 CellWorks batches, 20 of which failed their potency release test. Compute its Gini index and its entropy. A split sends 30 batches left (18 failures) and 50 right (2 failures). Compute the impurity reduction with the Gini index.
Reading a tree. In the depth-2 Ward 7 classification tree, which patients end in the 61 % leaf? Write the rule in words a nurse could use. What clinical information does the tree ignore completely?
Depth and overfitting. In the grow-a-tree widget, record the depth with the lowest test error for (a) SOFA and baseline creatinine, (b) age and CRP. Explain the difference.
Bootstrap. Show that \((1 - 1/n)^n\) is 0.25 for \(n = 2\), about 0.349 for \(n = 10\) and about 0.366 for \(n = 100\). What does this say about out-of-bag estimates for very small datasets?
Forest by hand. In the Lab, change mtry in the random forest from 3 to 1 and to 10 (the total number of features). What happens to the OOB error? Which value corresponds to bagging?
Boosting. In the boosting stepper, set \(\eta = 1\) and then \(\eta = 0.05\). How many rounds does each need to reach a test MAE below 0.205? Why?
CellWorks. Fit a regression tree for potency_score in cell.csv (first 320 batches for training, last 100 for testing). Which process variable appears at the root? Is the tree better than predicting the average potency for every batch?
Leakage hunt. For each candidate feature, say whether it could leak information in a model that predicts AKI at ICU admission: (a) creatinine measured 24 hours after admission; (b) SOFA on admission; (c) whether the patient later received dialysis; (d) hospital site.







Selected answers





1. Failure proportion 0.25: Gini \(= 1 - (0.25^2 + 0.75^2) = 0.375\); entropy \(= -(0.25 \log_2 0.25 + 0.75 \log_2 0.75) \approx 0.811\) bits. Left child: 18/30 = 0.6, Gini 0.48; right child: 2/50 = 0.04, Gini \(= 1 - (0.04^2 + 0.96^2) = 0.0768\). Impurity reduction \(= 0.375 - (30/80)(0.48) - (50/80)(0.0768) = 0.375 - 0.18 - 0.048 = 0.147\).
2. Patients with SOFA of 8 or less and baseline creatinine of at least 1.13 mg/dL. The tree ignores age, lactate, blood pressure, inflammation markers, albumin, protocol adherence and site: every patient on the same path receives the same risk.
4. For \(n = 2\), \((1/2)^2 = 0.25\); for \(n = 10\), \(0.9^{10} \approx 0.349\); for \(n = 100\), \(0.99^{100} \approx 0.366\). The proportion left out is a little smaller than 1/e in tiny datasets, and with so few patients each out-of-bag prediction rests on few trees and little data, so OOB estimates are noisier.
5. mtry = 10 is bagging. With set.seed(2026) and 300 trees the OOB mean squared error is about 0.044 for mtry = 1, 0.042 for mtry = 3 and 0.042 for mtry = 10: forcing most splits onto weak features (mtry = 1) hurts a little, and with one dominant feature (SOFA) decorrelation helps only modestly.
8. (a) Leaks: measured after the moment of prediction, and part of the outcome definition. (b) Fine: known at admission. (c) Leaks: it happens after, and because of, kidney injury. (d) Fine, although a model that relies heavily on site may not transfer to other hospitals.

title: 6  Trees and ensembles
text:
6.17 Summary

A decision tree predicts by a sequence of yes/no questions; it splits the feature space into rectangles and predicts a constant (the mean, or the class proportions) in each leaf.
Trees are grown greedily by CART: at each node, choose the feature and threshold with the largest impurity reduction (variance for numbers; Gini or entropy for classes).
Deep trees overfit. Stopping rules (minsplit, maxdepth, cp) and cost-complexity pruning with cross-validation and the 1-SE rule keep them in check.
Trees are readable, handle interactions and mixed feature types without preparation, and do not need scaling — but they are coarse and unstable.
Bagging averages trees grown on bootstrap samples; each leaves out about 37 % of the data, which gives a free out-of-bag error. Random forests also sample \(m_{\text{try}}\) features at each split to decorrelate the trees.
Boosting adds shallow trees in sequence, each fitted to the remaining errors and shrunk by a learning rate \(\eta\); XGBoost adds penalties, subsampling and early stopping. Boosting can overfit: choose the number of rounds on validation data, never on the test set.
Stacking learns how to combine different models.
A near-perfect score is a reason to check for leakage and to compare with the simplest baseline. On data with linear structure, simple models are hard to beat.

text: References

title: 7  Neural networks and deep learning
text:
How to use this chapter






Starting here?





This chapter borrows a few ideas from earlier ones:

A model is a simplified representation of reality, \(y = f(\mathbf{x}) + \varepsilon\), and learning means estimating \(f\) from data (Definition 1.3). Each row of a dataset is an instance with features \(\mathbf{x}_i\) and an outcome \(y_i\) (Definition 1.7).
Models are fitted on a training set and judged on a test set they never saw (Section 1.8); a model that is too flexible overfits (Definition 1.8). Choices made during training use a separate validation set (Chapter 3).
A loss function \(\mathcal{L}\) measures how wrong a model’s predictions are (Chapter 3).
Logistic regression turns a weighted sum into a probability with the logistic (sigmoid) function \(\sigma(z) = 1/(1+e^{-z})\). A classifier’s errors are summarised in a confusion matrix, from which come sensitivity (the share of sick people it flags) and specificity (the share of healthy people it clears); a threshold \(t\) turns a probability into a decision (Chapter 5).
The learning rate \(\eta\) controls how big a step a learning algorithm takes (Chapter 6, boosting).










Example
Who or what

title: 7  Neural networks and deep learning
text:
7.1 From brains to artificial neurons
Artificial neural networks began as an attempt to capture, in a very simplified mathematical form, how nerve cells compute. This idea is sometimes called neuromorphism: representing computation with units loosely inspired by the brain, where “neurons” receive signals, combine them and pass on a response, and “synapses” decide how strongly each signal counts. The goal was never to copy biology faithfully — biological systems are far too complex for that — but to borrow its ability to detect patterns, integrate evidence and generalise (Mead 1990).
Neurons were first described in detail by the Spanish histologist Santiago Ramón y Cajal, whose drawings showed that the nervous system is made of separate cells connected at contact points, and who is regarded as a founder of modern neuroscience (Ramón y Cajal 1909). Although there are many types of neuron, a “canonical” one has the parts sketched in Figure 7.1.






Figure 7.1: A sketch of a nerve cell: dendrites around the cell body (soma) with its nucleus, an axon wrapped in myelin produced by Schwann cells with gaps called nodes of Ranvier, and the axon terminals.




Dendrites, the input tree. Branched projections that receive signals. A neuron typically receives thousands of synaptic inputs across its dendrites and cell body. They arrive as excitatory postsynaptic potentials, which push the membrane voltage up, and inhibitory ones, which push it down.
Synapses, the weighted connections. Each contact point between two neurons is a synapse. Synapses differ in strength, and their strength changes with use. This plasticity is the biological basis of learning and memory.
The soma, the integrator. The cell body sums the incoming excitatory and inhibitory potentials — in effect a biophysical weighted sum, shaped by the electrical properties of the membrane and the shape of the dendrites.
The axon initial segment, the decision point. At the base of the axon, densely packed voltage-gated sodium channels decide whether to fire. If the summed membrane potential crosses a threshold (typically around −55 mV), a rapid depolarisation — the action potential, or spike — begins.
The axon and its terminals, the output cable. The spike travels along the axon, often insulated by myelin that speeds conduction. At the terminals it releases neurotransmitters that influence the next cells.

In short, a nerve cell receives many signals, weights and sums them, fires if the sum crosses a threshold, and passes the result on (Kandel et al. 2021). Keep these four verbs in mind: the artificial neuron keeps exactly these and drops almost everything else.

section: 7.4 From one neuron to a network
text:
7.4 From one neuron to a network
Why should a single straight boundary not be enough? Think of a vascular surgeon estimating the risk that an abdominal aortic aneurysm ruptures. Age, smoking, hypertension, coronary disease and the size of the aneurysm all matter (Wanhainen et al. 2024), but not simply by adding up: a large aneurysm in a frail smoker with coronary disease is far more dangerous than the sum of its parts suggests. A clinician reasons through intermediate concepts — “how much physiological reserve does this patient have?”, “how heavy is the atherosclerotic burden?” — and then combines them. One neuron cannot do this. A layer of neurons can: each hidden neuron computes its own weighted combination of the inputs, which can play the role of such an intermediate feature, and the next layer combines those. The difference from the clinician is that the network is not told which intermediate features to build; it learns whatever combinations reduce the loss, and they need not correspond to any named clinical concept.

Definition 7.5 (Multilayer perceptron (feed-forward network)) A multilayer perceptron (MLP) arranges neurons in layers. The input layer holds the features (it does no computation). Each hidden layer \(l\) takes the outputs of the previous layer, computes weighted sums and applies an activation: \[
\mathbf{h}^{(1)} = g\big(\mathbf{W}^{(1)} \mathbf{x} + \mathbf{b}^{(1)}\big), \qquad
\mathbf{h}^{(2)} = g\big(\mathbf{W}^{(2)} \mathbf{h}^{(1)} + \mathbf{b}^{(2)}\big), \quad \dots
\qquad(7.4)\] where row \(k\) of the weight matrix \(\mathbf{W}^{(l)}\) holds the weights of neuron \(k\) in layer \(l\) and \(\mathbf{b}^{(l)}\) its biases. The output layer turns the last hidden representation into the prediction — for example one sigmoid neuron for a probability. When every neuron of a layer is connected to every neuron of the next, the layers are fully connected (dense). A network with many hidden layers is called deep.

































x₁

Figure 7.4: A multilayer perceptron with two hidden layers. Each line is one weight; each hidden neuron also has a bias.




7.4.1 Why the activation must be nonlinear
Suppose we left out the activation, so that each layer only computed a weighted sum. Two layers would give \[
\mathbf{W}^{(2)}\big(\mathbf{W}^{(1)}\mathbf{x} + \mathbf{b}^{(1)}\big) + \mathbf{b}^{(2)}
= \underbrace{\mathbf{W}^{(2)}\mathbf{W}^{(1)}}_{\text{one matrix}}\,\mathbf{x}
+ \underbrace{\mathbf{W}^{(2)}\mathbf{b}^{(1)} + \mathbf{b}^{(2)}}_{\text{one vector}} ,
\] which is again a single weighted sum. However many layers we stack, a network without nonlinear activations collapses into one linear layer: it can draw only straight boundaries, exactly like one neuron. The bends introduced by ReLU or the sigmoid at every hidden neuron are what allow the network to represent curved boundaries and interactions such as the one in the playground.

A team builds a ten-layer network but, by mistake, uses no activation function in any hidden layer (the output layer has a sigmoid). What can this network represent?

Much more than logistic regression, because it has ten layers Without nonlinear activations the ten weighted sums multiply out into a single weighted sum. Depth adds nothing.
Exactly what logistic regression can represent: a single straight boundary Correct. The hidden layers collapse into one linear map, which the output sigmoid turns into a logistic regression — with many more parameters to fit and nothing gained.
Nothing: the network will not train at all It trains, and gradient descent works; it simply cannot learn anything beyond a linear boundary.


How flexible can a network with nonlinear activations be? The universal approximation theorem answers this: a network with a single hidden layer, using a nonlinear activation such as the sigmoid, can approximate any continuous function on a bounded region as closely as we like, provided it has enough hidden neurons (Cybenko 1989; Hornik, Stinchcombe, and White 1989). The theorem is often quoted too generously. It guarantees that a good approximation exists; it does not say how many neurons are needed (possibly an enormous number), that gradient descent will find it, or that a network fitted to a finite sample will generalise to new patients. In practice deeper networks with fewer neurons per layer tend to be easier to train for images and signals, because each layer can build on the features of the one before (LeCun, Bengio, and Hinton 2015; Goodfellow, Bengio, and Courville 2016).


7.4.2 Backpropagation
With thousands of weights spread over several layers, how do we get the gradient of the loss with respect to each one? The answer is backpropagation (Rumelhart, Hinton, and Williams 1986).

Definition 7.6 (Backpropagation) Backpropagation computes the gradient of the loss with respect to every weight of a network by applying the chain rule of calculus layer by layer, from the output back towards the input. A forward pass computes the predictions and the loss; a backward pass sends the error back, each layer passing on to the previous one how much its outputs contributed to the loss. The gradients are then used in Equation 7.3.

The intuition: a weight in the first layer affects the loss only through the hidden neurons it feeds, which affect it through the output. The chain rule multiplies these effects along every path. Deep-learning libraries such as PyTorch (Paszke et al. 2019) and TensorFlow do this automatically — you write the forward pass and they compute the gradients.


7.4.3 More than two classes: softmax
For a yes/no outcome one sigmoid output neuron suffices. For \(C\) mutually exclusive classes — say normal, bacterial pneumonia and viral pneumonia — the output layer has \(C\) neurons with weighted sums \(z_1, \dots, z_C\), and the softmax function (Goodfellow, Bengio, and Courville 2016) turns them into probabilities that add up to 1: \[
P(\text{class } c \mid \mathbf{x}) = \frac{e^{z_c}}{\sum_{c'=1}^{C} e^{z_{c'}}} .
\qquad(7.5)\] With \(C = 2\) the softmax reduces to the logistic function. Softmax returns in Part V, where a language model uses it to give a probability to every possible next word.

title: 7  Neural networks and deep learning
text:
7.5 Images are numbers: tensors
Neural networks are at their best on data with structure that a table hides: images, signals and text. Before we feed them an X-ray we need one piece of vocabulary.

Definition 7.7 (Tensor) A tensor is an array of numbers with any number of dimensions (axes). A single number is a rank-0 tensor, a vector rank 1, a matrix rank 2; adding axes gives rank 3, rank 4 and so on. The shape of a tensor lists the length of each axis.

A tensor is not an exotic object: it is the familiar vector and matrix extended to more axes. In R:

v <- c(1, 2, 3)                           # rank 1: a vector
M <- matrix(1:6, nrow = 2)                # rank 2: a matrix
A <- array(1:24, dim = c(2, 3, 4))        # rank 3: a stack of four 2 x 3 matrices
c(length(v)); dim(M); dim(A)

[1] 3


[1] 2 3


[1] 2 3 4


A grey-scale image is a matrix: height × width, one number per pixel, small for dark and large for bright. A chest radiograph of 512 × 512 pixels is a rank-2 tensor of shape (512, 512). Colour images (dermoscopy, retinal photographs, stained histology) add a channel axis — red, green, blue — giving shape (height, width, 3). Networks are trained on batches of images, which adds one more axis: a batch of 64 grey-scale X-rays is a rank-4 tensor of shape (64, 1, 28, 28) in PyTorch’s convention (batch, channels, height, width). A CT or MRI scan is a stack of slices, (depth, height, width), and multi-sequence MRI (T1, T2, FLAIR…) adds channels; ultrasound cine loops add time. Whatever the modality, a network sees a tensor of numbers with a label attached. It does not see lungs or tumours.
This chapter uses PneumoniaMNIST (Yang et al. 2023), a standardised version of a public collection of paediatric chest X-rays from Guangzhou, labelled by expert physicians (Kermany et al. 2018) and also distributed on Kaggle (Mooney 2018). MedMNIST shrinks each image to 28 × 28 pixels so that a network can be trained on a laptop in a minute. Is that too small? Figure 7.5 compares X-rays from the same collection at their original resolution and resized: shrinking softens fine textures but keeps the large-scale patterns of density.






Figure 7.5: Chest X-rays of two children without pneumonia and two with pneumonia, at their original resolution (top) and resized to 512 × 512 pixels (bottom). Note the letter “R” printed on each image.



In the normal images the lung fields are dark and fairly uniform, because air-filled alveoli absorb little radiation; vessels appear as fine branching lines, and the heart and diaphragm borders are sharp. In the pneumonia images there are whiter, denser areas — alveoli filled with inflammatory material — that blur the vascular markings and the heart borders and break the symmetry between the two lungs. These large-scale patterns survive resizing; a 28 × 28 version keeps less, but still enough for a network to do far better than chance. Keep an eye on the letter “R”: we return to it in Section 7.9.








Figure 7.6: One PneumoniaMNIST image as the network receives it: a 28 × 28 matrix of numbers between 0 (black) and 255 (white). Left, drawn as an image; right, the top-left corner of the same matrix.

text:
7.7 A small CNN for paediatric pneumonia
We now train three models on the 4 708 training images of PneumoniaMNIST (Yang et al. 2023; Kermany et al. 2018), use the 524 validation images to monitor training, and judge them once on the 624 test images, of which 62 % show pneumonia:

One neuron — logistic regression on the 784 raw pixels (785 parameters).
A multilayer perceptron — 784 pixels → 64 ReLU neurons → one sigmoid neuron, no convolutions (50 305 parameters).
The small CNN of Figure 7.7 (26 401 parameters).

The networks were trained with the Adam optimiser (Kingma and Ba 2015) (learning rate 0.001), batches of 64 and the log-loss of Equation 7.2, for at most 10 epochs, on an ordinary laptop processor in about a minute each. The script is ch07_pneumonia_cnn.py; it fixes the random seed so that the numbers below can be reproduced.

7.7.1 Watching training: overfitting, early stopping, dropout








Figure 7.8: Training and validation loss of the small CNN, epoch by epoch.





Figure 7.8 shows the learning loop at work. Both losses fall quickly over the first three epochs and then more slowly; the small bump at epoch 7 is the noise of stochastic gradient descent. The two curves stay together, so after 10 epochs this small network shows no sign of overfitting. Had we trained for much longer, the training loss would have kept falling while the validation loss levelled off and began to rise: the network would be starting to memorise the training images (Definition 1.8). Two standard defences:

Definition 7.11 (Early stopping and dropout) Early stopping monitors the loss on a validation set during training and keeps the weights from the epoch with the lowest validation loss, stopping when it has not improved for a while (Prechelt 1998). Dropout randomly switches off a fraction of the hidden neurons (for example 20 %) at every training step, so that the network cannot rely on any single neuron; all neurons are used when predicting (Srivastava et al. 2014). Both are forms of regularisation: they trade a little training fit for better generalisation.

Our script keeps the weights of the epoch with the lowest validation loss — here the last one, epoch 10, because the validation loss was still falling.

Three things stand out in Table 7.1. First, the baseline is strong: one neuron looking at raw pixels already reaches an AUC of 0.918, and every fancier model must be judged against it — “an AUC of 0.92” with no baseline tells you nothing. Second, the MLP, with 64 times as many parameters, is no better than one neuron: more parameters are not the same as a better design. Third, the CNN is the best of the three, mainly because it is more specific — it wrongly flags fewer normal X-rays — with an accuracy of 0.862 and an AUC of 0.922, using fewer parameters than the MLP. (In a classroom run of a similar exercise, with a different small network and a much smaller test sample, the accuracy came out at about 0.91; with a few hundred test images, differences of a few percentage points are within the play of chance.)
There is a fourth, more uncomfortable observation. On the validation images the CNN’s accuracy at epoch 10 was 0.954; on the test images it is 0.862. The validation images were carved out of the same pool as the training images, whereas the test images come from a separate part of the original collection (Yang et al. 2023), and the network finds them harder. A model is validated on whose patients? This small drop, inside a single public dataset, is a mild version of what happens when a model meets a new hospital.

text:
7.8 Deeper is not automatically better: find the bug
The vendor’s tool has fifty layers; ours has two convolutional layers. Surely deeper is better? Here is a comparison from the first edition of this book, of the kind that circulates in tutorials and slide decks, obtained by training four networks on PneumoniaMNIST and evaluating them on the same 624 test images:



Table 7.3: A comparison that tells a tempting — and wrong — story.









Model
Test accuracy reported




TinyCNN (two convolutional layers)
0.625


ResNet-18, pretrained on ImageNet (He et al. 2016)
0.870


ResNet-50, pretrained on ImageNet (He et al. 2016)
0.389


EfficientNet-B0, pretrained on ImageNet (Tan and Le 2019)
0.556






The tempting story writes itself: the tiny network is too weak, ResNet-18 hits the sweet spot, and the bigger networks are “too sensitive” to work on medical images. None of the numbers in Table 7.3 can be trusted: each comes from a broken pipeline. Before reading on, look for the clues.

0.625 is exactly the prevalence of pneumonia in the test set. A model that answers “pneumonia” for every child scores 0.625. An accuracy equal to the prevalence is the signature of a model that predicts a single class.
ResNet-50 at 0.389 is barely above 0.375, the accuracy of calling every child normal: the same signature in the other direction. EfficientNet at 0.556 is below the 0.625 that requires no model at all. Something systematic is wrong.

Two of the bugs are visible in code like this (simplified from the original training scripts):
# Bug A: a generator as the training data
def convert_to_rgb(loader):
    for imgs, lbls in loader:
        yield imgs.repeat(1, 3, 1, 1), lbls     # grey-scale -> 3 channels
train_rgb = convert_to_rgb(train_loader)       # a generator: it can be read only ONCE
for epoch in range(3):
    for images, labels in train_rgb:           # epochs 2 and 3 see no data at all
        ...
# Bug B: different preprocessing in training and testing
resize_to_224 = transforms.Resize((224, 224))
# training: images enlarged to 224 x 224 before entering ResNet-50 / EfficientNet
# testing:  test_loader_rgb feeds the original 28 x 28 images -- no resize
Bug A silently turns “3 epochs” into one: a Python generator is exhausted after a single pass, and the later loops simply do nothing — no error, no warning. Bug B trains the network on large images and tests it on small ones. Why does this not crash? Because ResNet and EfficientNet end with global average pooling (Lin, Chen, and Yan 2014), which averages each feature map whatever its size; the network accepts a 28 × 28 image as happily as a 224 × 224 one, and produces confident nonsense. Bug A affected the ResNet-18 run, whose “three epochs” were one; Bug B affected the ResNet-50 and EfficientNet runs.
We cannot retrain the large pretrained networks in a browser, but the bugs do not depend on the size of the network. We reproduced each one with a small CNN that, like ResNet, ends in global average pooling, trained for 10 epochs, and then fixed it:

With Bug A the training log shows 74 batches in the first epoch and 0 in every later one. After a single epoch our network had not yet learned to separate the classes, called every child “pneumonia” and scored exactly the prevalence, 0.625 — the TinyCNN’s number in Table 7.3. Fixed, the same network reaches 0.825. With Bug B the network, shown images half the size it was trained on, calls almost every child “normal” and misses 293 of the 390 pneumonias; fixed, it reaches 0.835. When the pipelines are correct, published benchmarks put ResNet-18 and ResNet-50 on PneumoniaMNIST in the same region as our two-layer CNN, with accuracies of roughly 0.85 to 0.89 (Yang et al. 2023).
So, is deeper better? Not automatically. Depth helps when there are many images, rich detail (full-resolution scans rather than 28 × 28 thumbnails) and a correct pipeline. On small, low- resolution data a small network can match a large one, and a large network is more fragile: more settings to get right, more ways to fail quietly. Vendors sell depth; clinicians should buy fit — evidence that the system works on patients like theirs, through a pipeline someone has checked.

A colleague’s pneumonia classifier has a test accuracy of 0.742. In their test set, 74.2 % of the images show pneumonia. What should you check first?

Nothing: 0.742 is a respectable accuracy for a first model On this test set, a “model” that answers pneumonia for everyone also scores 0.742. The number says nothing until compared with that baseline.
Whether the model predicts the same class for every image Correct. An accuracy equal to the prevalence is the signature of a constant prediction. Look at the confusion matrix: if one column is empty, the model (or its pipeline) is broken.
Whether a deeper architecture would do better Changing architecture before ruling out a pipeline bug only adds a second unknown to the first.



7.8.1 Transfer learning
Why were ResNet and EfficientNet “pretrained on ImageNet” in the first place?

Definition 7.12 (Transfer learning) Transfer learning reuses a network trained on a large dataset for one task as the starting point for another. A CNN trained on millions of everyday photographs — the ImageNet collection (Deng et al. 2009; Krizhevsky, Sutskever, and Hinton 2012) — has learned general visual features (edges, textures, shapes) in its early layers (Yosinski et al. 2014). Its final layer is replaced by one suited to the new task (for example a single sigmoid neuron for pneumonia), and the network is fine-tuned on the new images, often with a small learning rate.

Transfer learning can greatly reduce the number of labelled medical images needed, which matters because expert labels are expensive. Its benefits for medical images are, however, smaller and less consistent than often assumed: X-rays differ from holiday photographs, and small networks trained from scratch can do as well on some medical tasks (Raghu et al. 2019). Pretrained networks also expect inputs that look like their training data — three colour channels, a certain size, a certain normalisation — and, as Bug B shows, nothing stops you from feeding them something else. Finally, the original data bring their own biases with them.

Diagnose each pipeline. Which problem explains the symptom?

The training log shows 74 batches in epoch 1 and 0 batches in every later epoch. Exhausted generator
A network trained on 56-pixel images scores 0.53 on 28-pixel test images and calls almost every child “normal”. Preprocessing mismatch
A tumour-response model on ONCO-1 reaches a test AUC of almost 1 because three “genes” in the data are noisy copies of the outcome. Data leakage
A pneumonia detector learns which hospital an X-ray came from, using text and markers burned into the image, because pneumonia was more common at one hospital. Shortcut learning
The training images were rescaled with the ImageNet mean and standard deviation; the test images were left as raw pixel values. Preprocessing mismatch
Flipped and rotated copies of each image were made before splitting, so copies of the same X-ray sit in both the training and the test set. Data leakage

title: 7  Neural networks and deep learning
text:
7.9 Shortcut learning
Look again at the letter “R” in Figure 7.5. It is a laterality marker placed by the radiographer, and its style, size and position differ between machines and hospitals. A network does not know which parts of an image are anatomy and which are labels. If something other than the disease predicts the diagnosis in the training data, the network may learn that instead (DeGrave, Janizek, and Lee 2021).
This is not hypothetical. A CNN trained to detect pneumonia on chest X-rays from several hospital systems learned to recognise which hospital an image came from — and since pneumonia was more common at one of them, that information helped its predictions. In most comparisons its performance was significantly worse on X-rays from hospital systems it had not seen in training (Zech et al. 2018).

Definition 7.13 (Shortcut learning) Shortcut learning occurs when a model achieves good performance by exploiting features that are associated with the outcome in the training data but are not the reason for it — a marker, a scanner type, a hospital, a ruler placed beside suspicious skin lesions — so that it fails when that association changes (Geirhos et al. 2020).

Shortcuts are hard to spot from accuracy alone, because on data from the same source they do predict the outcome. They are found by testing on data from other sites, by checking performance in subgroups (Oakden-Rayner et al. 2020), and by examining what the model attends to (Chapter 12 covers explanation methods and their limits).

A CNN detects pneumothorax very accurately on a hospital’s archive. Many of the pneumothorax images were taken after treatment and show a chest drain. What is the main concern?

None: high accuracy on many images shows the network has learned pneumothorax High accuracy on images from the same archive cannot distinguish “learned pneumothorax” from “learned to spot chest drains”.
The network may have learned to detect the chest drain, which is visible only after the diagnosis has been made and treated Correct. A drain is a shortcut: it is associated with the label in the archive but is absent in exactly the patients who need the tool — untreated ones. Test on images without drains before trusting it.
The network should be made deeper so that it can learn the anatomy instead Depth does not prevent shortcuts; a more powerful network can find shortcuts even more easily. The fix is in the data and the evaluation.

7.10 Neural networks for tables: Ward 7 and the ONCO-1 trial
Neural networks are not only for images. Since Chapter 1 the book has compared every new method with the earlier ones on the same patients, split, features and metrics; the network takes its turn. On Ward 7 we trained a small multilayer perceptron (two hidden layers of 32 and 16 ReLU neurons, scikit-learn (Pedregosa et al. 2011)) on the same 1 000 training patients as every other model, after standardising the features with the training-set means and standard deviations. The number of epochs was chosen by cross-validation on the five shared folds, as XGBoost’s rounds were in Chapter 6. For the change in creatinine it used the ten admission features (P10); for AKI, the five features of Chapter 5’s headline model (P5), with a sigmoid output neuron.

Why does the network win here and lose on Ward 7? Look at how ONCO-1 was simulated (sim_onco1.R). Shrinkage is not a weighted sum of the features. The effect of chemotherapy follows a saturating dose–response curve, with a small toxicity penalty at high doses; dose matters only for patients who received chemotherapy (an interaction between treatment and dose); and the percentage is cut off at 0, so a tumour that grows is recorded as no shrinkage. A linear model has to fit one flat surface through all of this. The ReLU units of the hidden layers, like the splits of XGBoost’s trees, can bend that surface and switch parts of it on and off. The gain comes from the shape of the data, not from the network being a network. On Ward 7, where the truth is linear, the same flexibility buys nothing. And on tabular data of this size, carefully tuned tree ensembles often match or beat neural networks (Grinsztajn, Oyallon, and Varoquaux 2022), as XGBoost does here.

title: 7  Neural networks and deep learning
text:
7.11 Costs, regulation and trust
Hospitals do not adopt a model because it scores well on a benchmark; they adopt it when the whole system is clinically useful, affordable, auditable and legal (Kelly et al. 2019). Several costs and obligations come with deep learning in particular.

Labels. Deep networks need many labelled examples, and in medical imaging each label is usually the time of a specialist. Delineating tumours or adjudicating disagreements between readers multiplies it. Acquiring images is easy; turning them into trustworthy training data is slow and expensive, and often dominates the budget.
Computing and maintenance. Training deep networks needs accelerators, and the cost recurs: models must be re-validated, and often retrained, when scanners, imaging protocols or patient populations change.
Drift. A model that performs well at launch can degrade as practice evolves (Finlayson et al. 2021). Regulators expect manufacturers and hospitals to monitor performance after deployment, which requires ongoing data collection and evaluation.
Regulation. In the European Union, software intended for diagnosis is a medical device (European Parliament and Council of the European Union 2017), and AI used as, or in, such a device is classed as high-risk under the AI Act, with obligations on data governance, documentation, transparency, human oversight and post-market monitoring (European Parliament and Council of the European Union 2024). Manufacturers must document how training data were collected, labelled and quality-checked, so annotation protocols become part of the regulatory file.
Opacity and responsibility. A network with thousands or millions of weights cannot be read like a logistic regression. Saliency maps and similar tools offer partial glimpses with their own uncertainties (Chapter 12). Most frameworks therefore keep AI assistive, with a clinician responsible for the decision — which in turn demands good interface design, workflow integration and training.

High accuracy is not adoption. Back at Emma’s committee, the useful questions for the vendor are now clear: Against which simple baseline was the 95 % measured? On whose patients — which hospitals, which scanners, which ages? What are the sensitivity and specificity at the threshold you propose, and who chose it? How was the pipeline checked? What happens when our scanner changes?

  A cycle: a chest X-ray is the data; the CNN is the model; it produces a probability of pneumonia, the information; a clinician applies a threshold chosen with clinical values and decides between sending the child home and further tests; the outcome, including drift and errors, is monitored and becomes new data.

A pneumonia classifier in the decision loop. The network supplies a probability; the threshold, and the decision, belong to people.

Neural networks are a way of building the model step when the data are images, signals or other inputs whose useful features nobody can write down in advance: the network learns its own features, layer by layer (Section 7.4, Section 7.6). The information it produces is still a probability — a single sigmoid neuron at the end is logistic regression — and it enters the decision exactly as in Chapter 5: through a threshold that reflects what a missed pneumonia and an unnecessary test are worth (Section 7.7). What can go wrong? Pipeline bugs that fail silently (Section 7.8), shortcuts that vanish at a new hospital (Section 7.9), leakage that makes any model look brilliant (Section 7.10), and drift after deployment (Section 7.11). Who stays in control? The clinicians who choose the threshold, the teams who check the pipeline and the external evidence, and the patients whose values the threshold should reflect.

7.13 Lab: one neuron, a hidden layer and a CNN on chest X-rays
The Lab works with a browser-sized sample of PneumoniaMNIST: 200 training and 200 test images (file data/pneumonia_subset.csv, one row per image, 784 pixel columns). It shows images as tensors, shrinks them by pooling, trains one neuron and a small hidden-layer network (with nnet (Venables and Ripley 2002) in R, and scikit-learn, NumPy and pandas (Pedregosa et al. 2011; Harris et al. 2020; McKinney 2010) in Python), and compares them with the CNN trained on all 4 708 images. Run it here, or download it: ch07_lab.R · ch07_lab.py.

RPython























Two observations to take forward. First, on these 200 test images the one-neuron model and the small hidden-layer network, trained on only 200 pooled images, come out about level with the CNN trained on 4 708 full images. With 200 test images a difference of 0.01 is two images: the test sample is too small to rank the models, and on the full 624-image test set the CNN is ahead (Table 7.1). Second, step 3 matters: without standardising the pooled features, the Python hidden-layer network can get stuck predicting one class — another pipeline detail that fails silently. Delete that line and see.

title: 7  Neural networks and deep learning
text:
7.14 Exercises

Neuron by hand. A sigmoid neuron has weights 0.8 (for age, in decades) and −1.2 (for vaccinated, 1 = yes) and bias −4. Compute its output for an unvaccinated 70-year-old and a vaccinated one. What are the odds ratios for ten years of age and for vaccination?
The playground. In the perceptron playground, find weights that give a log-loss below 0.57 on Ward 7. Compare them with the coefficients of a two-feature logistic regression on the standardised features, fitted to all 1 250 patients (intercept 0.416, SOFA 1.111, lactate 0.308). Which feature matters more?
Learning rates. In the gradient-descent stepper, find the smallest learning rate that reaches the bottom within 10 steps, and the learning rate at which the path starts to overshoot. Explain what you see in terms of the curvature of the loss.
Collapse. Show with two 2 × 2 weight matrices of your choice that two linear layers without activation equal one linear layer. Then apply ReLU between them to the input \((1, -1)\) and show that the result differs.
Counting parameters. Verify that the small CNN of Figure 7.7 has 26 401 parameters: count the weights and biases of the two convolutional layers (3 × 3 filters), the dense layer and the output neuron. How many parameters would a dense layer of 32 neurons need on a 224 × 224 image?
Threshold. Using the test-set predictions file, compute sensitivity and specificity of the CNN at thresholds 0.1, 0.3, 0.5 and 0.7. Which would you choose for a paediatric emergency department, and why? Who should be involved in that choice?
Find the bug. A colleague’s evaluation loop reports an accuracy of 0.375 for a binary classifier on the PneumoniaMNIST test set. What has almost certainly happened? (Hint: 0.375 = 1 − 0.625.)
Vendor questions. Write five questions Emma’s committee should send to the vendor before agreeing to a pilot, and say which section of this chapter motivates each one.







Selected answers





1. For the unvaccinated 70-year-old, \(z = 0.8 \times 7 - 4 = 1.6\) and \(\sigma(1.6) \approx
0.83\); for the vaccinated one, \(z = 0.4\) and \(\sigma(0.4) \approx 0.60\). The odds ratios are \(e^{0.8} \approx 2.2\) per decade and \(e^{-1.2} \approx 0.30\) for vaccination.
4. For any \(\mathbf{W}^{(1)}, \mathbf{W}^{(2)}\), the composition is the single matrix \(\mathbf{W}^{(2)}\mathbf{W}^{(1)}\). With ReLU in between, negative entries of the first layer’s output are set to zero before the second layer, which a single matrix cannot reproduce for all inputs.
5. First convolution: \(8 \times (3 \times 3 \times 1) + 8 = 80\). Second: \(16 \times (3 \times 3
\times 8) + 16 = 1\,168\). Dense: \(784 \times 32 + 32 = 25\,120\). Output: \(32 + 1 = 33\). Total \(26\,401\). On a 224 × 224 image a dense layer of 32 neurons would need \(224 \times 224 \times 32 + 32 = 1\,605\,664\) parameters.
7. The predictions are inverted: the model (or the evaluation) is predicting “normal” for every image, or the labels and predictions are swapped, so the accuracy equals the proportion of normal images. Check the confusion matrix and the label coding.

title: 7  Neural networks and deep learning
text:
7.15 Summary

An artificial neuron computes a weighted sum of its inputs plus a bias and passes it through an activation function (step, sigmoid, ReLU). The analogy with nerve cells is loose.
A single sigmoid neuron is logistic regression: its weights are log-odds ratios, and it draws a straight boundary.
Networks learn by minimising a loss with gradient descent; the learning rate sets the step size, backpropagation computes the gradients, and training proceeds in batches and epochs.
Hidden layers with nonlinear activations let networks represent interactions and curved boundaries; without nonlinearity, layers collapse into one. Softmax extends the sigmoid to many classes.
Images are tensors. Convolutional networks reuse small learned filters across the image and pool the results, which suits images far better than fully connected layers.
Honest evaluation still rules: compare with a simple baseline, read the confusion matrix and choose the threshold from clinical values. Early stopping and dropout limit overfitting.
On the book’s running examples a small network is no magic: on Ward 7, which is linear, it does not beat linear or logistic regression; on ONCO-1, where the dose–response is curved and treatment and dose interact, it beats the linear models but not XGBoost.
Deeper is not automatically better: silent pipeline bugs, shortcut learning and leakage can produce impressive or disastrous numbers that mean nothing. Transfer learning helps when labels are scarce but brings its own assumptions.

text:
How to use this chapter






Starting here?





This chapter borrows a few ideas from earlier chapters. In one line each:

Models and decisions. A model (Definition 1.3) turns data into information; a decision

combines that information with values. With the scores used in Chapter 1, the kidney-protective bundle is the better choice whenever the probability of AKI is above the threshold \(t = 0.25\) (Section 1.5).

Probability, likelihood and Bayes’ theorem (Chapter 2). The likelihood \(L(\theta)\) measures how well each value of a parameter \(\theta\) explains the data; Bayes’ theorem turns a prior into a posterior: posterior ∝ likelihood × prior. The threshold for acting is \(t = C_{\text{FP}}/(C_{\text{FP}} + C_{\text{FN}})\), set by the losses of the two kinds of error.
Training and test sets (Chapter 3). Models are judged on patients they have not seen; Ward 7 uses the book’s shared split (1 000 training and 250 test patients). The root mean squared error (RMSE) and mean absolute error (MAE) measure numerical errors.
Linear and logistic regression (Chapter 4, Chapter 5). A linear model predicts \(\beta_0 + \beta_1 x_1 + \dots\); a logistic model passes the same sum through the S-shaped logistic function to give a probability. Chapter 4 also met confidence intervals and prediction intervals.
Trees and forests (Chapter 6). Random forests and boosting add up many trees; they predict well but give a single number with no statement of uncertainty.
