title: 8  Bayesian learning and predictive uncertainty
section: 8.1 From Bayes’ theorem to Bayesian learning
text:
8.1 From Bayes’ theorem to Bayesian learning
In Chapter 2, Bayes’ theorem updated the probability of a condition — frailty, AKI — once a piece of evidence arrived: a fast heart rate, a positive urine test. The rule was always the same, posterior ∝ likelihood × prior. Bayesian learning applies exactly the same rule to the parameters of a model: the AKI rate of a hospital, the average heart rate of a population, the slope of a regression line (Gelman et al. 2013; McElreath 2020).
Chapter 2 also introduced the two schools of inference. In the frequentist view a parameter is a fixed, unknown constant; we compute one best estimate (often by maximum likelihood) and describe how that estimate would vary over repeated samples. In the Bayesian view the data, once observed, are fixed, and what we are uncertain about is the parameter; that uncertainty is described with a probability distribution, before the data (the prior) and after them (the posterior). Both views use the same likelihood. The difference is in what they let you say: only the Bayesian view lets you say “the probability that this AKI rate is above 60 % is 0.9” — a sentence that clinicians and managers usually want to hear (Spiegelhalter, Abrams, and Myles 2004).

Definition 8.1 (Prior and posterior distribution of a parameter) For a parameter \(\theta\) and data \(\mathbf{y}\), the prior distribution \(p(\theta)\) describes what is known or assumed about \(\theta\) before seeing the data, and the posterior distribution describes what is known after:
\[
p(\theta \mid \mathbf{y}) = \frac{p(\mathbf{y} \mid \theta)\, p(\theta)}{p(\mathbf{y})}
\;\propto\; \underbrace{p(\mathbf{y} \mid \theta)}_{\text{likelihood}} \times \underbrace{p(\theta)}_{\text{prior}} .
\]
The denominator \(p(\mathbf{y})\) does not depend on \(\theta\); it only makes the posterior integrate to 1. Every summary we need — a best guess, an interval, the probability that \(\theta\) exceeds a value — is read from the posterior (Gelman et al. 2013).








Prior
what we believed

Likelihood
what the data say

Posterior
what we believe now
×


today's posterior is tomorrow's prior




Figure 8.1: Bayesian learning as a loop. The posterior after one batch of data becomes the prior for the next.



The loop in Figure 8.1 is how clinicians already reason. Emma has an expectation about a new patient before the first blood test; each result shifts it; the shifted expectation is where she starts when the next result comes in. A Bayesian model does the same, explicitly and with numbers. Three consequences follow, and the rest of the chapter illustrates each. With little data, the prior matters and the posterior is wide. With a lot of data, the likelihood dominates and Bayesian and frequentist answers nearly coincide. And because the output is a whole distribution, it can be carried forward into predictions and decisions with its uncertainty intact.

text:
8.3 Bayesian linear regression
A proportion has one parameter. A regression has several, and Bayesian learning treats all of them as uncertain together. We return to the HomeBeat trial and ask how resting heart rate is related to frailty — a frailty index between 0 (fit) and about 0.8 (very frail), recorded at enrolment. The simplest model is the straight line of Chapter 4:
\[
\text{HR}_i \sim \mathcal{N}\!\left(\beta_0 + \beta_1\, \text{frailty}_i,\; \sigma^2\right),
\qquad i = 1, \dots, 500 .
\qquad(8.2)\]
Read it as: participant \(i\)’s resting heart rate is drawn from a normal distribution whose mean lies on the line \(\beta_0 + \beta_1\,\text{frailty}_i\) and whose standard deviation, \(\sigma\), describes the scatter around the line. Least squares (Chapter 4) gives a single slope, \(\hat\beta_1 =\) 47.6 bpm per unit of frailty, with a 95 % confidence interval from 40.4 to 54.8. A Bayesian model adds a prior for each unknown:
\[
\beta_0 \sim \mathcal{N}(60, 20^2), \qquad \beta_1 \sim \mathcal{N}(0, 20^2), \qquad
\sigma \sim \text{half-normal}(10) .
\qquad(8.3)\]
These are weak priors. The intercept prior says that the heart rate of a participant of average frailty is probably somewhere between 20 and 100 bpm.1 The slope prior is centred on zero — no association — and allows associations of either sign up to about 40 bpm per unit of frailty. The half-normal prior for \(\sigma\), a normal distribution folded at zero, says that the scatter around the line is positive and probably below 20 bpm (Gelman 2006). Bayes’ theorem then gives the joint posterior of all three unknowns,
1 The R package used below, rstanarm, applies the intercept prior to the value of the line at the average of the predictors, not at frailty = 0, because that intercept is far less uncertain and easier to think about. It reports the intercept back on the usual scale.\[
p(\beta_0, \beta_1, \sigma \mid \mathbf{y}) \;\propto\;
\prod_{i=1}^{500} \mathcal{N}\!\left(\text{HR}_i \mid \beta_0 + \beta_1\,\text{frailty}_i, \sigma^2\right)
\; p(\beta_0)\, p(\beta_1)\, p(\sigma) .
\]

Definition 8.3 (Bayesian regression) A Bayesian regression is a regression model — linear, logistic or other — in which the coefficients and any other unknowns (such as \(\sigma\)) receive prior distributions, and the result of fitting is their joint posterior distribution rather than a single set of estimates. Point summaries (posterior mean or median), intervals and probabilities such as \(P(\beta_1 > 0 \mid \text{data})\) are all read from that posterior (Gelman et al. 2013, ch. 14).

With three unknowns there is no simple formula for the posterior. In practice it is computed by sampling, with software such as Stan (Carpenter et al. 2017) and its R interface rstanarm (Goodrich et al. 2024). This is the code that produced the draws used in this chapter; it runs in a few seconds on a laptop, but not in the browser, so its results are loaded from a file.
library(rstanarm)
fit_simple <- stan_glm(
  resting_hr ~ frailty, data = hb, family = gaussian(),
  prior_intercept = normal(60, 20, autoscale = FALSE),
  prior           = normal(0, 20, autoscale = FALSE),
  prior_aux       = normal(0, 10, autoscale = FALSE),   # sigma: a half-normal(10)
  chains = 2, iter = 2000, seed = 2026)
autoscale = FALSE makes rstanarm use exactly the priors written above, instead of rescaling them to the spread of the data, as it does by default. The result is a table of 2 000 posterior draws: 2 000 plausible combinations of \((\beta_0, \beta_1, \sigma)\), each consistent with the data and the priors. Summaries are simply summaries of the draws (Table 8.1).

The posterior mean of the slope, 46.2, sits slightly closer to zero than the least-squares slope 47.6: the prior, centred on zero, pulls a little. This is the same shrinkage you met with ridge regression in Chapter 4: with a normal prior centred on zero, the most probable value of the coefficients is exactly a ridge estimate (Hastie, Tibshirani, and Friedman 2009, sec. 3.4). Notice also that the posterior is centred beyond the range of slopes the prior considered most plausible (±40): 500 participants are enough to overrule a weak prior, at the price of a small pull towards zero. With 30 participants the pull would be much larger.

section: 8.4 How the posterior is computed: MCMC
text:
8.4 How the posterior is computed: MCMC
The idea behind modern Bayesian computation is to replace a formula with a sample. If we could draw thousands of values \(\theta^{(1)}, \dots, \theta^{(S)}\) from the posterior, every question would become a count: the posterior mean is the average of the draws, a 95 % interval runs from the 2.5th to the 97.5th percentile of the draws, and \(P(\beta_1 > 0 \mid \text{data})\) is the proportion of draws above zero. This is the Monte Carlo idea, named after the casino (Metropolis and Ulam 1949).
The difficulty is to obtain the draws when the posterior is known only up to the constant \(p(\mathbf{y})\). Markov chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) solves it with a random walk. Picture a walker on the landscape of the posterior. At each step the walker proposes a move to a nearby point; moves uphill (to more plausible values) are always accepted, moves downhill only sometimes, with a probability equal to the ratio of the two heights. Only that ratio is ever needed, so the unknown constant cancels. After a while, the walker visits each region of the landscape in proportion to its posterior probability. This is the Metropolis algorithm (Metropolis et al. 1953; Hastings 1970). Stan uses a more efficient relative, Hamiltonian Monte Carlo with the No-U-Turn sampler, which uses the slope of the landscape to make long, well-aimed moves instead of short random ones (Neal 2011; Hoffman and Gelman 2014; Carpenter et al. 2017).

Definition 8.4 (Markov chain Monte Carlo (MCMC); trace plot, R-hat, effective sample size) MCMC produces a sequence of draws (a chain) whose distribution approaches the posterior. The first part of each chain, the warm-up, is discarded. Several chains are run from different starting points and checked for agreement with three standard diagnostics (Gelman and Rubin 1992; Vehtari et al. 2021; Gabry et al. 2019):

a trace plot shows each chain’s value against iteration; healthy chains overlap and look like a “fuzzy caterpillar”, with no trend and no flat stretches;
R-hat (\(\widehat{R}\)) compares the variation between chains with the variation within them; values close to 1 (in current practice, below 1.01) suggest the chains agree;
the effective sample size (ESS) is the number of independent draws that would carry the same information as the correlated draws of the chains; a few hundred is usually enough for means and 95 % intervals.


Diagnostics are a skill of the eye. The four panels in Figure 8.2 show three chains each for the same parameter — the frailty slope of Equation 8.2 — produced by four differently tuned samplers. Only one of them can be trusted.

Only panel C passes: R-hat close to 1 and an effective sample size close to the 1 500 draws themselves (Vehtari et al. 2021). Panel A’s chains have not yet reached the posterior: discard more warm-up or run longer. Panel B is in the right region, but each chain explores it so slowly that 1 500 draws carry the information of only a handful of independent ones. Panel D proposes moves so large that almost all are rejected, and the chains stand still. Running B or D longer would eventually help, but the real fix is a better-tuned sampler — which is what Stan’s warm-up does automatically (Hoffman and Gelman 2014; Carpenter et al. 2017).



The real fit is healthy. For both HomeBeat models, every parameter has \(\widehat{R} \le\) 1.006 and a bulk ESS of at least 1586; Figure 8.3 shows the trace and the posterior density of the slope.

A colleague’s Bayesian model for HomeBeat stress scores reports \(\widehat{R} = 1.08\) for one coefficient and a bulk ESS of 40. What should they do before reading its credible interval?

Nothing: R-hat is close to 1, and 40 draws are enough Values of 1.08 indicate that the chains disagree, and 40 effective draws give an unreliable interval. Current guidance asks for R-hat below 1.01 and an ESS of a few hundred.
Look at the trace plots, run longer or improve the sampler, and refit until the diagnostics are acceptable Correct. The diagnostics say the chains have not yet explored the posterior well enough. Common remedies are more warm-up and iterations, rescaling predictors, or a simpler parameterisation.
Report the interval, because Bayesian intervals are always valid A credible interval is valid only if the draws really come from the posterior. Unconverged chains can give intervals that are too narrow, too wide or in the wrong place.
Switch to a flat prior, which always fixes convergence problems Flat priors often make sampling harder, because they leave implausible regions open. Weakly informative priors usually help.

8.5 Reading the posterior: credible intervals and the probability of an effect

Definition 8.5 (Credible interval; posterior probability of an effect) A 95 % credible interval is an interval that contains 95 % of the posterior probability; the usual choice runs from the 2.5th to the 97.5th percentile of the posterior draws. Given the model, the priors and the data, there is a 95 % probability that the parameter lies inside it. The posterior probability of an effect, such as \(P(\beta_1 > 0 \mid \text{data})\), is the proportion of the posterior above zero, estimated by the proportion of draws above zero (Gelman et al. 2013).

A confidence interval (Chapter 4) answers a different question (Neyman 1937). Its “95 %” describes the procedure: if the study were repeated many times, 95 % of the intervals computed in this way would contain the true value. It does not say that this particular interval contains the value with probability 0.95, although that is how it is very often read (Morey et al. 2016). With weak priors and plenty of data the two intervals are usually close numerically — for the HomeBeat slope, 40.4–54.8 versus 39.0–53.5 — so the practical difference lies in what you are allowed to say.

For the simple HomeBeat model, every one of the 2 000 draws of the frailty slope is positive: \(P(\beta_1 > 0 \mid \text{data}) \approx\) 1.00. Given this model and these priors, it is practically certain that resting heart rate rises with frailty in this population — by about 4.6 bpm for every 0.1 of frailty.

8.5.1 A probability is only as good as its model
Now the important caveat. HomeBeat is simulated, so we know the truth: in the code that generated it (sim_homebeat.R), frailty raises resting heart rate by 4 bpm per unit — 0.4 bpm per 0.1 of frailty, ten times less than the model above suggests. Where does the rest come from? Older participants are both frailer and have faster resting heart rates, and so do participants with more inflammation. Age and inflammation are confounders (Hernán and Robins 2020) (Section 1.10): they push frailty and heart rate up together, and the simple model credits frailty with their effect. Adding them to the model,
\[
\text{HR}_i \sim \mathcal{N}\!\left(\beta_0 + \beta_1\,\text{frailty}_i + \beta_2\,\text{age}_i + \beta_3\,\text{inflammation}_i,\; \sigma^2\right),
\]
changes the answer completely (Figure 8.4): the frailty slope becomes 4.2 bpm per unit (95 % credible interval 0.4 to 8.0), close to the true 4, and \(P(\beta_1 > 0 \mid \text{data})\) falls from 1.00 to 0.98.








Figure 8.4: Posterior of the frailty slope in two models of HomeBeat resting heart rate. Not adjusting for age and inflammation (orange) gives a confident but wrong answer; adjusting (blue) recovers the value used to simulate the data (dashed line).





The lesson is not about Bayes, and it is the one the first HomeBeat model nearly hid. Every posterior probability is conditional on the model. The simple model was completely sure of something that is wrong as a statement about cause, because the model left out the confounders. More data would only have made it surer. Bayesian methods quantify uncertainty within a model; they do not protect against a model that answers the wrong question (Gelman et al. 2013, ch. 6). For questions of the form “what would happen if frailty changed?”, Chapter 13 provides the tools.

The simple model reports \(P(\beta_1 > 0 \mid \text{data}) \approx 1\) for frailty. Which reading is correct?

Frailty certainly causes a faster resting heart rate, by about 46 bpm per unit Two errors. A regression coefficient describes an association, and the adjusted model shows that most of this one is due to age and inflammation; the causal effect in the simulation is 4 bpm per unit.
There is a 1 % chance that frailty raises heart rate When all draws are above zero, the probability of a positive slope is close to 100 %, not 1 %. Reading the proportion of draws the wrong way round is an easy slip.
Given this model and its priors, the association between frailty and heart rate is almost certainly positive Correct. The probability is real, but it is a statement about the model’s parameter. Whether that parameter measures what we care about depends on what the model leaves out.
The prior must have been too strong The prior was centred on zero and weak; it pulled the slope slightly towards zero. The problem is confounding, not the prior.

8.8 Bayesian trees: BART
The regressions so far assume straight-line relationships. Physiological data are often less tidy: thresholds, curves and interactions that are hard to specify in advance. Chapter 6 handled them with trees, forests and boosting, which predict well but give a single number. Bayesian additive regression trees (BART) keep the idea of adding up many small trees, and put the whole ensemble inside a Bayesian model (Chipman, George, and McCulloch 2010):
\[
y_i = \sum_{j=1}^{m} g(\mathbf{x}_i;\, T_j, M_j) + \varepsilon_i, \qquad \varepsilon_i \sim \mathcal{N}(0, \sigma^2),
\qquad(8.4)\]
where \(T_j\) is the structure of the \(j\)-th tree (its questions), \(M_j\) the values in its leaves, and \(g(\mathbf{x}_i; T_j, M_j)\) the leaf value that tree \(j\) gives to instance \(i\). Typically \(m = 50\) to \(200\) trees.

prediction = sum of the leaf values reached in all m trees
priors keep each tree shallow and each leaf value small; MCMC samples thousands of whole ensembles




Figure 8.5: BART adds up many small trees, each contributing a little. Every posterior draw is a complete ensemble, so every prediction comes with a distribution.



What makes BART Bayesian is a set of priors that keep every tree a weak learner (Chipman, George, and McCulloch 2010):

Tree structure. A node at depth \(d\) (the top node has \(d = 0\)) is allowed to split with probability \(0.95\,(1 + d)^{-2}\) in the usual default, so most trees have only one to three questions.
Leaf values. Each leaf value has a normal prior centred on zero with a variance that shrinks as the number of trees \(m\) grows, so that no single tree dominates the sum.
Noise. The residual variance \(\sigma^2\) has an inverse-gamma prior (a conventional choice for variances).

These priors play the role that the learning rate and the tree depth play in boosting (Chapter 6), but instead of a single fitted ensemble, MCMC samples thousands of different ensembles from the posterior, each one a plausible explanation of the data. Averaging their predictions gives a point prediction; their spread gives a credible interval, and adding \(\sigma\) gives a prediction interval, exactly as for Lena.

Definition 8.7 (Bayesian additive regression trees (BART)) BART models the outcome as a sum of \(m\) small regression trees plus normal noise (Equation 8.4), with priors that favour shallow trees and small leaf values. Its posterior, sampled by MCMC, is a distribution over whole ensembles; predictions are averages over the posterior draws, and their spread quantifies uncertainty (Chipman, George, and McCulloch 2010). BART has been extended, for example, to separate main effects from interactions between genotypes and environments in plant breeding trials (Sarti et al. 2023).


8.8.1 An honest comparison
How does BART compare with the forests (Breiman 2001) and boosting (Chen and Guestrin 2016) of Chapter 6? On HomeBeat we predicted resting heart rate from age, frailty and inflammation, training on 400 participants and testing on the other 100 (the book’s HomeBeat split, data/splits/homebeat_split.csv), with BART fitted by the pymc-bart library (Quiroga et al. 2022) (the R package dbarts (Dorie, Chipman, and McCulloch 2025) fits the same model). Every model in Table 8.5 was fitted on the same 400 participants and scored on the same 100 test participants; the numbers come from the book’s model ledger, which later chapters also use.

Three lessons, each worth more than the ranking.

Training error flatters flexible models. The random forest’s training RMSE, 2.11 bpm, is less than half its test RMSE, 5.54. Compared on the data they were trained on, the forest would look by far the best model; compared honestly, it is not. This is the lesson of Chapter 3, and it is easy to forget when a table looks impressive.
The true shape wins. HomeBeat’s heart rate was simulated as a straight-line function of these three features, so linear regression, the model with the right shape, has the lowest test error (MAE 3.75, RMSE 4.83 bpm), and the Bayesian linear regression is practically identical (3.75 and 4.83). BART comes next (4.07 and 5.06) without being told the shape, ahead of XGBoost and the forest. On real data nobody knows the shape in advance, which is BART’s appeal.
Only models with a probability model say how wrong they might be. BART’s 95 % prediction intervals contained 98 % of the test participants’ heart rates (98 of 100), more than the promised 95 %: on this test set the intervals were somewhat too wide, that is, conservative (on average 20.8 bpm from end to end). The classical prediction intervals of linear regression did the same (98 %). With only 100 test participants, a coverage a few points away from 95 % can arise by chance, but an interval that errs on the wide side overstates the uncertainty rather than hiding it. The forest and XGBoost give no such statement at all.

For Lena, the model we name for her prediction is the Bayesian linear regression fitted on the 400 training participants: a mean resting heart rate of 85.0 bpm for people like her, against 85.2 bpm from the same model fitted on all 500 participants in Section 8.6. The other models in Table 8.5 agree within about two beats per minute (BART 85.3, XGBoost 85.8, the forest 86.7); only the training mean, which ignores her age, frailty and inflammation, is far off (69.5). Tonight’s 88 bpm is a little above what every model expects for her.






A classic slip: average over draws, not over patients



BART software returns predictions as a matrix with one row per posterior draw and one column per patient. The point prediction for each patient is the mean of its column — colMeans() in R, .mean(axis=0) in numpy (Dorie, Chipman, and McCulloch 2025; Chipman, George, and McCulloch 2010). Taking row means instead averages over patients within each draw and throws the individual predictions away. On the HomeBeat test set this slip turns BART’s RMSE of 5.06 bpm into 13.54, roughly the error of predicting the average for everyone (13.71). If a flexible model performs like no model at all, check the bookkeeping before the method.


On Ward 7, with the shared split and the ten predictors (P10) of Chapters 4 and 6, BART predicts the 48-hour change in creatinine with a test MAE of 0.146 and an RMSE of 0.182 mg/dL: better than the random forest (0.153 and 0.191) and XGBoost (0.148 and 0.184) of Chapter 6, slightly worse than the linear regression of Chapter 4 (0.141 and 0.174). Its 95 % prediction intervals cover 96.8 % of the 250 test patients, again a little above the nominal 95 % (linear regression: 97.2 %). Because the prediction is a distribution of creatinine changes, it also gives a probability of AKI directly: the share of Aoife’s predictive draws at or above 0.3 mg/dL is 0.48, close to the 0.49 of the Bayesian logistic model, even though BART never saw the AKI label. Two very different models, built in different ways, agreeing on Aoife’s risk is itself a reassuring piece of evidence.

Since Chapter 1 every Ward 7 model has been fitted on the same 1 000 training patients and tested on the same 250, so this chapter’s two regressions can join the table (Table 8.6; this chapter’s rows in bold). The Bayesian linear regression, with weak priors and 1 000 patients, is the OLS model of Chapter 4 in all but name: test MAE 0.141 against 0.141. The linear models of Chapter 4 (OLS, and ridge and lasso at λ min) and the Bayesian linear regression still have the lowest MAE, 0.141. A report compares BART, a random forest and XGBoost on the data used to train them and concludes that the forest is best because its RMSE is lowest. What is the main problem?

BART should always win, because it is Bayesian Being Bayesian adds uncertainty statements, not guaranteed accuracy. On HomeBeat, linear regression beat BART on the test set.
Training-set errors reward memorisation; the comparison must be made on held-out data Correct. A forest can fit its training data very closely. On HomeBeat its training RMSE was less than half its test RMSE. Only errors on unseen patients compare models fairly (Chapter 3).
RMSE cannot be computed for BART, because its predictions are distributions The posterior mean of each patient’s predictive distribution is a perfectly good point prediction, and its RMSE can be compared with any other model’s.
Forests cannot be compared with Bayesian models Any two models that predict the same outcome for the same patients can be compared on the same metric. What forests lack is a built-in statement of uncertainty.

title: 8  Bayesian learning and predictive uncertainty
section: 8.9 Where this fits in the decision loop
text:
8.9 Where this fits in the decision loop


  The decision loop, with this chapter's contribution
  A cycle of five boxes: data feed a model; the model produces information, here a posterior distribution rather than a single number; people combine it with values to make a decision, and the spread of the posterior says whether more information is worth seeking; the decision leads to actions and outcomes, which are recorded as new data. The model and information boxes are highlighted.
  
  Data
  
  Model
  prior × likelihood
  
  Information
  a posterior, not a point
  
  Decision
  act, or learn more first
  
  Action and outcome
  recorded as new data
  
  
  
  
  

The decision loop. Bayesian learning changes the Information step: the model hands over a distribution, and its spread tells the decision-maker whether to act now or to learn more first.

Which decision does this chapter support? Any decision in which it matters how sure the model is: whether to start Aoife’s bundle tonight or order a test first; whether a heart-rate alert from Lena’s watch deserves a phone call; whether a new hospital’s AKI rate is really higher than its neighbours’. A Bayesian model hands the decision-maker a distribution; its mean feeds the expected loss, and its spread says whether more information is worth its cost.
What can go wrong? A strong prior that nobody justified; chains that never converged; a credible interval for the average reported as if it were a prediction interval for one patient; a confident posterior from a model that omits a confounder; a flexible model compared with others on its own training data.
Who stays in control? The prior is an explicit, inspectable statement of what was assumed, and should be agreed with the clinicians who own that knowledge. The threshold still comes from the values of patients and clinicians. And when the posterior straddles the threshold, the model’s most useful output is an honest “I am not sure” that hands the case back to a person.

RPython























Two observations to take forward. First, with 1 000 patients the Bayesian logistic model and the maximum-likelihood model of Chapter 5 agree on every patient; the Bayesian model’s added value is the honest spread, which becomes decisive when data are few or when a patient sits near the threshold. Second, the confounding lesson of section 3 does not depend on the method: change the model, not the inference engine, to answer a different question.

Prior sensitivity. In the prior–posterior widget, compare a flat prior (mean 0.5, strength 2) with the sceptical prior (mean 0.55, strength 100) at \(n = 5\), \(50\) and \(313\). Report the two posterior means at each \(n\) and explain the pattern in two sentences.

2. Prior \(\text{Beta}(6, 14)\) (mean 0.30, strength 20). Posterior \(\text{Beta}(6 + 6, 14 + 6) = \text{Beta}(12, 20)\), mean \(12/32 = 0.375\): between the prior 0.30 and the observed 0.50, closer to the prior because 20 imaginary patients outweigh 12 real ones.

Credible: “Given our model and the data, there is a 95 % chance that each 0.1 of frailty is associated with between 3.9 and 5.4 bpm more.” Confidence: “If we repeated the study many times, 95 % of intervals calculated this way would contain the true association.” Only the first is a probability statement about the slope.

title: 8  Bayesian learning and predictive uncertainty
text:
8.12 Summary

Bayesian learning applies Bayes’ theorem to model parameters: posterior ∝ likelihood × prior. The posterior distribution describes what is known about a parameter after the data.
Priors should be stated, justified and checked by sensitivity analysis. They matter when data are few and fade when data are many. Conjugate priors, such as the beta prior for a proportion, make updating a matter of adding counts.
In a Bayesian regression all coefficients receive priors; a normal prior centred on zero shrinks coefficients like ridge regression.
MCMC draws samples from the posterior. Before trusting them, check trace plots, R-hat (below 1.01) and the effective sample size.
A credible interval contains the parameter with stated probability, given the model; a confidence interval describes a procedure. \(P(\text{effect} > 0)\) is read directly from the draws — and is only as trustworthy as the model, which must include the confounders.
The posterior predictive distribution adds person-to-person scatter to parameter uncertainty; a prediction interval for one patient is much wider than a credible interval for the average.
A Bayesian risk is a distribution. Its mean decides today’s best action under expected loss; its spread says whether more information could change the decision, and lets a model say “I don’t know”.
BART is a Bayesian sum of small trees: flexible like boosting, with predictive distributions and prediction intervals. Check the intervals’ coverage on held-out data (here 98 % on HomeBeat and 97 % on Ward 7 for a nominal 95 %: slightly conservative), and compare it, like any model, on held-out data.

title: 9  When data are missing
text:
How to use this chapter






Starting here?





This chapter borrows a few ideas from earlier chapters. In one line each:

Instances, features and outcome (Definition 1.7). A dataset has one row per instance (patient, participant) and one column per feature; the outcome is the column we want to explain.
Train, test and leakage (Section 1.8; Chapter 3). A model is judged on patients it has never seen; any step that learns from data, imputation included, must learn from the training rows only, or information leaks into the evaluation.
Probability and the logistic function (Chapter 2, Chapter 5). A probability lies between 0 and 1; the logistic function \(\sigma(z) = 1/(1+e^{-z})\) turns any number into one, and logistic regression models a yes/no outcome with it.
Linear regression, coefficients and standard errors (Chapter 4). A linear model predicts \(\hat y = \beta_0 + \beta_1 x_1 + \dots + \beta_p x_p\); each coefficient comes with a standard error that measures how much it would vary from sample to sample.
Trees and surrogate splits (Chapter 6). Some tree implementations can route a patient with a missing feature down the tree using other, correlated features.

title: 9  When data are missing
section: 9.1 Even a mean needs an assumption
text:
9.1 Even a mean needs an assumption
Missing data are often treated as a technical nuisance, something that “just happens” and is cleaned away before the real analysis begins. Their consequences go much deeper, and the simplest statistic of all is enough to show why: the average.

Definition 9.1 (Missing value and missingness indicator) A missing value is a value that was meant to be recorded but was not: a laboratory test that was never ordered, a questionnaire item left blank, a night on which a watch recorded nothing. In R and pandas it appears as NA or NaN. For each cell of a data table we write the missingness indicator \(R_{ij} = 1\) if the value of feature \(j\) for instance \(i\) is observed and \(R_{ij} = 0\) if it is missing. The table of all the \(R_{ij}\) is the missingness pattern (Little and Rubin 2020, ch. 1).

The sample mean of \(n\) values is
\[
\bar{x} = \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n} x_i = \frac{x_1 + x_2 + \dots + x_n}{n} .
\qquad(9.1)\]
The formula quietly assumes that every \(x_i\) exists. Take four HRV readings, 10, 12, 14 and 16 ms: their mean is \((10+12+14+16)/4 = 13\). Now suppose the third reading was never recorded. The formula asks for \((10 + 12 + {?} + 16)/4\), and it has no instruction for the question mark.

x <- c(10, 12, NA, 16)
mean(x)                  # R refuses: the answer is unknown

[1] NA

mean(x, na.rm = TRUE)    # the mean of the values that were recorded

[1] 12.66667


R’s refusal is honest. Adding na.rm = TRUE (“remove the NAs”) gives \((10 + 12 + 16)/3 = 12.67\), but notice what changed: one value was dropped, the number of values went from four to three, and the result answers a different question — what is the average of the readings we happen to have? With the indicator \(R_i\) it reads
\[
\bar{x}_{\text{obs}} = \frac{\sum_{i=1}^{n} R_i\, x_i}{\sum_{i=1}^{n} R_i} ,
\qquad(9.2)\]
which estimates the mean of everybody only if the recorded readings are a fair sample of all the readings. When they are not — when, as with Lena’s watch, the low readings are the ones that go missing — \(\bar{x}_{\text{obs}}\) is biased, and no amount of extra data fixes it.
Other quick fixes fare no better. Filling the gap with zero gives \((10+12+0+16)/4 = 9.5\), a mean driven by an arbitrary choice. Filling it with the average of the other three gives back 12.67, but now looks as if it rests on four measurements when only three were made. Even for a mean, then, missing data make the answer undefined without an assumption, sensitive to the assumption chosen, and biased if the assumption is wrong. Regression models, which combine many variables, are more exposed still.

Lena’s dashboard shows the average of the HRV values her watch recorded over 30 nights. Under which condition is this a fair estimate of her average HRV over all 30 nights?

Always, as long as at least 20 nights were recorded More nights make the average more precise, not less biased. If the missing nights are systematically the bad ones, the average of the recorded nights stays too high however many there are.
If the nights without a recording are like the recorded ones, so that the gaps have nothing to do with her HRV Correct. Then the recorded nights are a fair sample and Equation 9.2 is unbiased. The two flat-battery nights meet this condition; the seven restless nights almost certainly do not.
If the missing nights are replaced by zeros first Zero is not a plausible HRV, so this drags the average down by an amount that depends only on how many nights are missing.

title: 9  When data are missing
section: 9.2 Naive fixes and what they do to the data
text:
9.2 Naive fixes and what they do to the data
Before principled methods, it helps to see the three shortcuts that analysts most often reach for. They are popular because they are easy and look assumption-free. They are not assumption-free, and the HomeBeat data show what they do. In the version of the data the trial team actually has (homebeat_missing.csv), four wearable signals have gaps: resting heart rate (30 missing), HRV (48), skin temperature (31) and the activity index (45). Because the data are simulated, we also have the complete version (homebeat.csv) and can compare every shortcut with the truth — a luxury no real study has.

Definition 9.2 (Complete-case analysis and pairwise deletion) Complete-case analysis (also listwise deletion) keeps only the rows in which every variable used is observed. Pairwise deletion (also available-case analysis) uses, for each calculation, every row in which the variables of that calculation are observed, so different quantities rest on different subsets of rows.

Complete-case analysis is the default of most software, so it often happens silently. 134 of the 500 HomeBeat participants (27 %) have at least one gap, so a complete-case analysis of the whole table works with 366 people. The participants who are dropped are not a random slice: the mean HRV of everyone is 42.2 ms, the mean of all recorded HRV values is 43.7 ms, and the mean HRV of the complete cases is 46.4 ms. Each step away from “everyone” removes more of the low readings.
Pairwise deletion keeps more data for each calculation: the correlation of HRV with frailty uses 452 participants, that of HRV with resting heart rate 427, and that of frailty with resting heart rate 470. Each correlation describes a slightly different group of people, so together they can form a matrix that no single dataset could produce, which makes methods built on that matrix (principal components, factor analysis, some learning algorithms) fail or behave erratically (Little and Rubin 2020).

Definition 9.3 (Imputation and single imputation) Imputation replaces each missing value with a value predicted or drawn from the data. Single imputation fills every gap once — with zero, the mean, the median, a regression prediction — and then analyses the completed table as if it had been fully observed.

Single imputation with the mean makes a table look complete at a price. Figure 9.1 shows HRV after every missing value was replaced by the observed mean. The 48 filled-in participants pile up at a single value, the standard deviation falls from 21.0 to 19.9 ms, and the correlation between HRV and frailty is pulled towards zero, from -0.50 to -0.48. Zero is worse: an HRV of 0 ms is physiologically impossible, so it creates a cluster of fake extreme patients. The median behaves like the mean: more robust to outliers, but with the same spike and the same loss of spread.








Figure 9.1: What mean imputation does to HomeBeat’s HRV. Left: the distribution of HRV after every missing value was replaced by the observed mean; the filled-in values form a spike. Right: frailty against HRV; the imputed participants (orange) sit on a flat line at the mean and weaken the relationship.





All three shortcuts handle the gaps by convention rather than by reasoning about why the values are missing. Single imputation has a second, subtler flaw: it treats a guess as a measurement, so every standard error computed afterwards is too small (Little and Rubin 2020; Buuren 2018).

A colleague fills the missing HRV values with the mean and then reports a correlation between HRV and frailty. What is the most likely consequence?

The correlation is unchanged, because the mean does not move The mean of the column does not move, but the filled-in participants all share one HRV value whatever their frailty, which breaks the link between the two variables.
The correlation is pulled towards zero and its uncertainty is understated Correct. Imputed values carry no information about frailty, so they dilute the relationship; and because the software counts them as real measurements, the confidence interval is too narrow.
The correlation becomes stronger, because the data are now complete Completeness is only apparent. Adding values that sit at the centre regardless of frailty can only weaken the association.



Count the gaps. The HomeBeat data with missing values are loaded as hb. Fill in the blank with the function that marks each cell as missing (TRUE) or present (FALSE), so that the line counts the missing values in every column.

RPython

















The function is is.na(). Applied to a data frame, it returns a table of TRUE/FALSE, and colSums() counts the TRUEs in each column.


colSums(is.na(hb))


















The method is .isna(); .sum() then counts the True values in each column.


hb.isna().sum()

section: 9.3 How gaps change a model: bias or bad luck?
text:
9.3 How gaps change a model: bias or bad luck?
Means and correlations are only the start. Suppose the HomeBeat team wants to know how the stress score depends on frailty, HRV and resting heart rate, and fits the linear model of Chapter 4,
\[
\text{stress score} = \beta_0 + \beta_1\,\text{frailty} + \beta_2\,\text{HRV} + \beta_3\,\text{resting HR} + \varepsilon .
\]
R’s lm() silently drops every participant with a gap in any of these variables, so the model uses 427 of the 500 participants. Table 9.1 compares that complete-case fit with the fit on the complete data, which in this simulation plays the role of the truth, and with mean imputation and multiple imputation, which we build later in the chapter.

The complete-case frailty coefficient is 9.41 against 11.07 in the complete data. It is tempting to read that drop as a bias: frailer participants lose their resting heart rate more often, so, the argument goes, the frailest people are under-represented and the frailty effect is underestimated. It is a natural story. Is it true?
Look at the standard errors first. A difference of 1.65 is well inside one standard error (about 3.2), so a single dataset cannot tell bias from bad luck. A simulation can. We took the complete data, deleted values again and again with exactly the same rules (HRV more often missing above age 60, resting heart rate more often missing among the frailest), refitted the complete-case model each time, and averaged (Table 9.2, scenario A). Over 200 repetitions the complete-case frailty coefficient averages 11.02 — the truth, give or take simulation noise. The drop in our one dataset was bad luck. What complete-case analysis really cost here was precision: fewer participants, larger standard errors, estimates that wander more from one deletion to the next.

The lesson is general, and it corrects a claim that appears in many textbooks. In a regression, complete-case analysis is unbiased whenever the chance of a row being incomplete depends only on the model’s predictors, and not on the outcome — whatever the pattern of missingness looks like (Little and Rubin 2020; White and Carlin 2010; Hughes et al. 2019). In scenario A, missingness depends on frailty, a predictor, and on age, which is not in the model; because age also affects the stress score, a small bias remains (compare resting heart rate with its truth), but it is tiny next to the spread from one deletion to the next. Scenario B is different: HRV goes missing more often when the stress score is high, so the rows that survive are selected on the outcome. Now the complete-case coefficient of resting heart rate is 0.622 against a truth of 0.679, a shift of about 2.1 spreads: a genuine bias. Multiple imputation, which uses the stress score to fill in the missing HRV values, brings it much closer, to 0.695.
Mean imputation is the clear loser in Table 9.1: it moves the frailty coefficient to 16.81, because the participants whose HRV was replaced by the average now look as if their stress were explained by frailty instead. Ignoring missing data is never a neutral choice. Whether it does harm depends on how the data went missing, which is where we turn next.

In a regression of the stress score on frailty, HRV and resting heart rate, resting heart rate is missing more often for frailer participants, and for no other reason. What does complete-case analysis do to the coefficients?

They stay unbiased, but are less precise Correct. Missingness depends only on a predictor in the model, so the complete cases have the same relationship between outcome and predictors as everybody else. The price is fewer rows and wider intervals.
They are biased towards zero, because frail participants are under-represented Under-representation of a range of a predictor does not bias a correctly specified regression; it only makes that range less well estimated. This is the error the repeated-deletion experiment exposed.
They are biased, because complete-case analysis is valid only when data are missing completely at random That rule is too strict for regression. For means and other summaries it is close to right; for regression coefficients what matters is whether missingness depends on the outcome.

title: 9  When data are missing
section: 9.4 Why values go missing: MCAR, MAR and MNAR

title: 9  When data are missing
text:
9.5 Diagnosing missingness
The mechanism is an assumption about the world, but the data can still tell us a good deal. A standard diagnostic routine has three steps.
1. How much is missing, and where? Count the gaps per variable (you did this in the mission) and per row, and look at which variables tend to be missing together. In HomeBeat, 9.6 % of HRV values and 9.0 % of activity values are missing, and 27 % of participants have at least one gap.
2. Do participants with and without a gap differ on what we can see? Compare, for each variable with gaps, the distribution of the fully observed variables between the two groups (Figure 9.3). Participants with and without an activity value have almost the same frailty (mean 0.397 against 0.396), as MCAR predicts. Participants missing HRV are older (mean age 68.4 against 47.3); those missing resting heart rate are frailer; those missing skin temperature have higher stress scores. Each of these rules out MCAR for that variable.








Figure 9.3: Who has gaps? For each HomeBeat signal with missing values, a fully observed variable is compared between participants whose value is recorded and those whose value is missing. Similar boxes (activity index) are compatible with MCAR; shifted boxes show that missingness depends on an observed variable.





3. Model the indicator. A logistic regression with the missingness indicator as outcome (Chapter 5) shows which observed variables predict a gap, adjusting for the others:

glm(is.na(resting_hr) ~ frailty, data = hm, family = binomial)


Call:  glm(formula = is.na(resting_hr) ~ frailty, family = binomial, 
    data = hm)

Coefficients:
(Intercept)      frailty  
     -9.915       14.560  

Degrees of Freedom: 499 Total (i.e. Null);  498 Residual
Null Deviance:      227 
Residual Deviance: 157.1    AIC: 161.1


The log-odds of a missing resting heart rate rise by 1.5 for every 0.1 increase in frailty: a strong, systematic link. More formal checks exist, such as Little’s test of MCAR (Little 1988a), but none of them is a verdict, for a reason worth stating plainly: the data cannot distinguish MAR from MNAR. Every diagnostic compares things we observe; MNAR is about the values we do not observe. The shifted boxes in Figure 9.3 show that missingness depends on something observed. They cannot show that it depends on nothing else. That judgement comes from knowing how the data were collected — the device, the clinic, the patients — which is why the people who collected the data must be part of the analysis.

In HomeBeat, the logistic regression of the HRV missingness indicator on age, frailty, stress and the other observed variables fits well. Which conclusion is justified?

The data are MAR, so multiple imputation will remove all bias The regression shows that missingness depends on observed variables. It cannot show that it does not also depend on the missing HRV values.
The data are not MCAR; whether they are MAR or MNAR must be argued from how the data were collected Correct. Observed data can refute MCAR, but MAR versus MNAR depends on unobserved values. Knowledge of the device and of the participants has to fill that gap.
The data are MNAR, because missingness is predictable Predictable from observed variables is the definition of MAR, not MNAR. Predictability alone does not tell the two apart.



9.5.1 The same questions on Ward 7
The Ward 7 records have gaps too. In icu_aki_missing.csv, a version of the Ward 7 data made for this chapter, albumin is missing for 7 % of patients, lactate for 21 % and baseline creatinine for 22 %; 529 of the 1 250 patients have at least one gap. The deletion script, sim_ward7_missing.R, documents the mechanisms, and you are invited to diagnose them before reading it.

Who goes without a lactate? The Ward 7 data with gaps are loaded as icu. Fill in the blank so that the line compares the mean SOFA score of patients whose lactate is recorded (FALSE) and missing (TRUE).

RPython

















The SOFA score is in the column sofa.


tapply(icu$sofa, is.na(icu$lactate), mean)


















The SOFA score is in the column "sofa".


icu.groupby(icu["lactate"].isna())["sofa"].mean()




Patients without a lactate have a mean SOFA of 4.5, against 7.8 for the others: lactate is ordered less often for patients who look well. In these simulated data lactate itself is unrelated to SOFA, so the observed mean lactate is barely affected — a reminder that MAR leads to bias only when the cause of the gaps is also related to the value. Baseline creatinine is a different story, to which we return in Section 9.10.

title: 9  When data are missing
section: 9.6 How much missingness is too much?
text:
9.6 How much missingness is too much?
Once the mechanism has been thought through, the next practical question is the amount. Analysts often look for a threshold — impute below 5 %, worry above 20 %, discard above 50 % — and such conventions are widespread. They are rough guides, not rules (Madley-Dowd et al. 2019), and three points matter more than any cut-off.

A small amount can still bias. What matters is the mechanism and how strongly the gaps are related to the quantity of interest. Under MNAR, 5 % missing values that are all extreme can move a mean more than 30 % that are missing completely at random.
What is lost is information, not rows. The relevant quantity is the fraction of missing information about the parameter of interest (Section 9.7), which depends on how well the observed variables predict the missing ones. A variable with 40 % gaps that is strongly predicted by other recorded variables loses less than one with 15 % gaps and no good predictors.
Heavy missingness is a finding. A key biomarker missing in half the participants usually signals a problem in data collection — a device that failed halfway through the trial, a test that only some sites order — and that problem should be reported and understood, not only imputed. A scientifically indispensable variable may be kept and imputed even with many gaps, provided the imputation model is strong and the uncertainty is reported honestly; a weakly relevant one with many gaps is often better left out (Buuren 2018; Sterne et al. 2009).

Every principled method treats missing values for what they are: unknown quantities with a probability distribution, given what was observed. The more is missing, the wider that distribution, and the more uncertainty must be carried into the final result. That is exactly what multiple imputation is designed to do.

title: 9  When data are missing
text:
9.7 Multiple imputation: the idea
Single imputation fails because it pretends to know what it does not. Multiple imputation (MI) replaces each missing value not with one best guess but with several plausible values, each drawn from a model of how the missing value relates to what was observed (Rubin 1987). The missing values become what they really are: uncertain quantities with a distribution — the same view of unknowns that runs through the Bayesian chapter of this book (Chapter 8).

Definition 9.5 (Multiple imputation) Multiple imputation creates \(M\) completed copies of a dataset, in each of which every missing value is replaced by a random draw from its predictive distribution given the observed data. The analysis of interest is run separately on each copy, and the \(M\) results are combined with Rubin’s rules into one estimate whose uncertainty includes the uncertainty about the missing values.

Multiple imputation has three steps (Figure 9.4).

Impute. Create \(M\) completed datasets \(\mathbf{D}^{(1)}, \dots, \mathbf{D}^{(M)}\). If HRV is related to age, frailty, resting heart rate and the stress score, those variables are used to draw plausible HRV values. Because the draws are random, the completed datasets differ exactly where the data were missing.
Analyse. Fit the intended model — here the stress-score regression — to each completed dataset, giving estimates \(\hat\theta_1, \dots, \hat\theta_M\) and their standard errors.
Pool. Combine the \(M\) results with Rubin’s rules.






  
  
  Incomplete
  data
  with gaps (?)
  1. Impute M times
  dataset 1
  dataset 2
  dataset M
  ⋮
  
  2. Analyse each
  estimate θ̂₁
  estimate θ̂₂
  estimate θ̂ₘ
  ⋮
  
  3. Pool
  
  Rubin's rules
  one estimate,
  honest standard error
  




Figure 9.4: The three steps of multiple imputation. The completed datasets differ only where values were missing; how much their estimates differ measures how much the missing values matter.




9.7.1 Rubin’s rules
Suppose analysis \(m\) gives an estimate \(\hat\theta_m\) (say, the frailty coefficient) with squared standard error \(\widehat{\mathrm{SE}}_m^2\). Rubin’s rules (Rubin 1987; Little and Rubin 2020) combine them in four lines:1
1 Rubin writes \(\bar Q\), \(\bar U\), \(B\) and \(T\). We use \(\bar\theta\) and \(V_W, V_B, V_T\) because \(B\) and \(T\) already mean the number of bootstrap samples and a tree in Chapter 6.\[
\begin{aligned}
\bar\theta &= \frac{1}{M}\sum_{m=1}^{M}\hat\theta_m && \text{pooled estimate}\\
V_W &= \frac{1}{M}\sum_{m=1}^{M}\widehat{\mathrm{SE}}_m^2 && \text{within-imputation variance}\\
V_B &= \frac{1}{M-1}\sum_{m=1}^{M}\left(\hat\theta_m - \bar\theta\right)^2 && \text{between-imputation variance}\\
V_T &= V_W + \left(1 + \frac{1}{M}\right) V_B && \text{total variance}
\end{aligned}
\qquad(9.3)\]
The pooled standard error is \(\sqrt{V_T}\). Each term has a plain meaning. \(V_W\) is the uncertainty we would have even with no missing data: the ordinary sampling variability, averaged over the completed datasets. \(V_B\) is the extra uncertainty because values are missing: if the imputations disagree a lot, the missing values matter a lot. The factor \(1 + 1/M\) corrects for using a finite number of imputations. The share of the total variance due to missingness, \((1 + 1/M)V_B / V_T\), approximates the fraction of missing information about \(\theta\).
Confidence intervals use a \(t\) distribution with degrees of freedom \(\nu = (M-1)\left[1 + V_W/\big((1 + 1/M)V_B\big)\right]^2\), so few imputations and much missing information give wider intervals; software such as mice applies a small-sample refinement of this formula (Barnard and Rubin 1999).

Definition 9.6 (Rubin’s rules) Rubin’s rules pool the results of \(M\) analyses of multiply imputed data: the pooled estimate is the average of the \(M\) estimates, and its variance is the average within-imputation variance plus \((1 + 1/M)\) times the variance between the estimates (Equation 9.3).

For the frailty coefficient in the first five HomeBeat imputations, the estimates average \(\bar\theta =\) 11.19, the within-imputation variance is \(V_W =\) 8.26 and the between-imputation variance \(V_B =\) 0.60, so \(V_T =\) 8.26 \(+ (1 + 1/5) \times\) 0.60 \(=\) 8.98 and the pooled standard error is 3.00. About 8 % of the variance is due to the missing values. With all 50 imputations, the fraction of missing information is about 6 % for frailty and 8 % for resting heart rate, which itself has gaps.
How many imputations? Early advice said three to five were enough for a good point estimate (Rubin 1987); for stable standard errors and \(p\)-values, White, Royston, and Wood (2011) suggest at least as many imputations as the percentage of incomplete cases. In HomeBeat that is 27 %, so \(M \ge\) 27.

Pool it yourself. The dots are the estimates of one coefficient from \(M\) completed HomeBeat datasets (made with mice, M up to 50), each with its own 95 % interval. The bar at the top is the pooled result from Rubin’s rules; the vertical line is the estimate from the complete data, which only a simulation knows. Switch the between-imputation variance off to see what single imputation would claim. Target: set \(M\) to at least the percentage of incomplete cases (27), with \(V_B\) included.

miw = FileAttachment("data/precomputed/ch09/mi_estimates.csv").csv({typed: true})
mods9 = FileAttachment("data/precomputed/ch09/hb_models.csv").csv({typed: true})
hbmw = FileAttachment("data/homebeat_missing.csv").csv()
mRule = Math.ceil(100 * hbmw.filter(d => Object.values(d).some(v => v === "NA" || v === "")).length / hbmw.length)
viewof term9 = Inputs.select(new Map([["Frailty", "frailty"], ["HRV (per ms)", "hrv"], ["Resting heart rate (per bpm)", "resting_hr"]]), {label: "Coefficient"})
viewof M9 = Inputs.range([2, 50], {value: 5, step: 1, label: "Number of imputations, M"})
viewof withB = Inputs.toggle({label: "Include the between-imputation variance", value: true})



















































pool9 = {
  const rows = miw.filter(d => d.term === term9 && d.m <= M9);
  const M = rows.length, th = d3.mean(rows, d => d.estimate);
  const VW = d3.mean(rows, d => d.se * d.se), VB = d3.variance(rows, d => d.estimate);
  const VT = VW + (withB ? (1 + 1 / M) * VB : 0);
  const nu = withB ? (M - 1) * Math.pow(1 + VW / ((1 + 1 / M) * VB), 2) : 1e6;
  const z = 1.959964;   // t quantile by a Cornish-Fisher expansion
  const tq = z + (z ** 3 + z) / (4 * nu) + (5 * z ** 5 + 16 * z ** 3 + 3 * z) / (96 * nu * nu);
  const truth = mods9.find(d => d.term === term9 && d.analysis.startsWith("Complete data")).estimate;
  return {rows, M, th, VW, VB, VT, se: Math.sqrt(VT), lo: th - tq * Math.sqrt(VT), hi: th + tq * Math.sqrt(VT),
          fmi: withB ? (1 + 1 / M) * VB / VT : 0, truth};
}
{
  const dg = term9 === "frailty" ? 2 : 3;
  const hit = M9 >= mRule && withB;
  if (hit && window.aihs) window.aihs.complete("ch09-tryit-pool");
  return html`<p>M = ${pool9.M}: pooled estimate <strong>${pool9.th.toFixed(dg)}</strong>, 95 % interval
  ${pool9.lo.toFixed(dg)} to ${pool9.hi.toFixed(dg)} · V<sub>W</sub> = ${pool9.VW.toPrecision(3)},
  V<sub>B</sub> = ${pool9.VB.toPrecision(3)}${withB ? "" : " (ignored)"}, V<sub>T</sub> = ${pool9.VT.toPrecision(3)}
  · fraction of missing information ≈ ${(100 * pool9.fmi).toFixed(0)} %
  ${hit ? "<br>✓ Enough imputations for stable standard errors by White's rule of thumb." : ""}</p>`;
}














Plot.plot({
  height: 90 + 7 * M9, marginLeft: 50, grid: true,
  x: {label: "Estimated coefficient"}, y: {type: "point", label: "Imputation", domain: [-1, ...d3.range(1, M9 + 1)], tickFormat: d => d === -1 ? "pooled" : (M9 > 20 && d % 5 ? "" : d)},
  marks: [
    Plot.ruleY(pool9.rows, {y: "m", x1: d => d.estimate - 1.96 * d.se, x2: d => d.estimate + 1.96 * d.se, stroke: "#1f6f8b", strokeOpacity: 0.4}),
    Plot.dot(pool9.rows, {y: "m", x: "estimate", fill: "#1f6f8b", r: 3}),
    Plot.ruleY([-1], {x1: pool9.lo, x2: pool9.hi, stroke: "#b35c00", strokeWidth: 6}),
    Plot.dot([{y: -1, x: pool9.th}], {x: "x", y: "y", fill: "currentColor", r: 5}),
    Plot.ruleX([pool9.truth], {strokeDasharray: "4,3"})
  ]
})










Two things to notice. With \(V_B\) switched off the pooled interval shrinks — that is the false confidence of single imputation. And as \(M\) grows, the pooled estimate and its interval stop jumping around: more imputations do not add information about the missing values, but they make the Monte Carlo part of the answer stable.

In Rubin’s rules, why is the total variance \(V_T\) larger than the average within-imputation variance \(V_W\)?

Because imputed datasets have more rows than the original Each completed dataset has exactly as many rows as the original; imputation fills cells, it does not add people.
Because the imputations disagree, and that disagreement measures the uncertainty about the missing values Correct. \(V_B\) is the variance of the estimates across imputations: if the missing values could plausibly be quite different, the estimates differ, and the total uncertainty grows.
Because the \((1 + 1/M)\) factor always doubles it The factor is close to 1 for large \(M\) (1.02 for \(M = 50\)); it is a small correction for using finitely many imputations.



Rubin’s rules by hand. The frailty estimates and standard errors from the first five HomeBeat imputations are loaded as est and se. Complete the line that computes the total variance; the last line returns the pooled standard error.

RPython

















Look at the last line of Equation 9.3: \(V_T = V_W + (1 + 1/M)\,V_B\).


VT    <- VW + (1 + 1/M) * VB       # total variance


















Look at the last line of Equation 9.3: \(V_T = V_W + (1 + 1/M)\,V_B\).


VT = VW + (1 + 1/M) * VB            # total variance





Why does it work? Each completed dataset is one plausible version of the full data. No single imputed value is trusted, but across the copies the spread of the imputed values — and therefore of the estimates — reflects how uncertain we are about them. Compared with complete-case analysis, MI uses every participant’s observed values, which gains precision, and it removes the bias that arises when missingness depends on the outcome or on variables outside the analysis model, as long as those variables are in the imputation model. Compared with single imputation, MI restores the spread of the data, keeps correlations intact and gives standard errors that admit what is not known. Both properties rest on the MAR assumption (or MCAR) and on a sensible imputation model (Sterne et al. 2009; Buuren 2018).

title: 9  When data are missing
text:
9.8 Multiple imputation in practice: MICE
How do we draw plausible values for several variables with gaps at once? The most widely used answer is multiple imputation by chained equations (MICE), also called fully conditional specification, implemented in the R package mice (Buuren and Groothuis-Oudshoorn 2011; Buuren 2018).

Definition 9.7 (MICE (chained equations)) MICE imputes several incomplete variables by cycling through them: each variable with gaps is imputed from a regression model on all the other variables, using the current imputed values of the others, and the cycle is repeated a number of times (iterations) until the imputations stabilise. Running \(M\) independent chains gives \(M\) completed datasets.

In HomeBeat, one cycle imputes resting heart rate from the other variables, then HRV from the others (including the freshly imputed resting heart rate), then skin temperature, then the activity index; ten cycles are usually ample for data like these. The model for each variable is chosen by its type. For continuous variables the default is predictive mean matching.

Definition 9.8 (Predictive mean matching (PMM)) Predictive mean matching imputes a missing value by (1) predicting it with a regression whose coefficients are drawn to reflect their uncertainty, (2) finding a few observed participants whose predictions are closest, and (3) copying the actual observed value of one of them, chosen at random. Imputed values are therefore always values that really occur in the data (Little 1988b).

PMM is robust: it cannot produce an impossible HRV of −5 ms, and it keeps the shape of skewed distributions (Buuren 2018). The whole analysis takes a few lines. (The mice package does not run in the browser, so this chunk is shown rather than run; its results were computed when the book was built, by ch09_mice.R.)
library(mice)
hm   <- read.csv("data/homebeat_missing.csv")
vars <- c("age", "baseline_inflammation", "frailty", "resting_hr", "hrv",
          "skin_temp", "activity_index", "stress_score", "event_occurred")
imp  <- mice(hm[, vars], m = 50, method = "pmm", maxit = 10, seed = 2025)

plot(imp)                      # trace plots: have the chains mixed?
densityplot(imp, ~ hrv)        # imputed (red) against observed (blue) values

fit <- with(imp, lm(stress_score ~ frailty + hrv + resting_hr))   # analyse each copy
summary(pool(fit), conf.int = TRUE)                                # Rubin's rules
Two decisions in this code deserve attention. The identifier is left out, because it carries no information. And the outcome, stress_score, is in the imputation model. This surprises many people — is it not circular? It is not: leaving the outcome out would impute HRV as if it were unrelated to stress, and would bias the HRV coefficient towards zero. The imputation model should contain every variable in the analysis model, the outcome included, plus auxiliary variables that predict the gaps or the missing values (White, Royston, and Wood 2011; Sterne et al. 2009).
Before trusting the result, look at two diagnostics (Figure 9.5). The trace plot follows the mean of the imputed values in each chain across iterations: the chains should intermingle without a trend. The density plot compares imputed with observed values; under MAR they need not be identical — here imputed HRV values are lower, because the participants who lost them are older — but they should be plausible.








Figure 9.5: Checking a mice run on HomeBeat (M = 5, 10 iterations). Left: mean of the imputed HRV values in each of the five chains, by iteration; the chains mix with no trend. Right: distribution of observed HRV (blue) and of the imputed values in the five completed datasets (orange); the imputed values are plausible, and lower on average because older participants lost more readings.





The pooled results are in the last row of Table 9.1. The coefficients are close to the complete-data truth, with standard errors between those of the complete data and those of the complete-case analysis: MI recovered some, not all, of the information lost to the gaps. Do not read too much into how close one dataset comes to the truth; as Table 9.2 showed, the fair comparison is over many repetitions.

9.8.1 Other imputation methods in mice
PMM is a robust default for continuous variables, but the method argument of mice() can be set separately for each variable (Buuren and Groothuis-Oudshoorn 2011; Buuren 2018):



Table 9.3: Some imputation methods available in mice (version 3.16).





Method
Variable type
What it does




"pmm"
continuous (any numeric)
predictive mean matching: copies an observed value from a donor with a similar prediction


"norm"
continuous, roughly normal
Bayesian linear regression: draws the coefficients and residual variance from their posterior, then adds random noise


"norm.nob"
continuous
linear regression with random noise but without drawing the coefficients; understates uncertainty


"norm.boot"
continuous
linear regression refitted on a bootstrap sample, then noise added


"norm.predict"
continuous
the regression prediction itself, no noise: a single deterministic imputation that shrinks variance; for teaching or as a baseline only


"logreg"
binary (two-level factor)
logistic regression


"polyreg"

multinomial logistic regression


"polr"

proportional-odds model, which respects the order


"cart", "rf"
any
classification and regression trees, random forests (Chapter 6); capture interactions and non-linearity


"2l.norm", "2l.pan", "2l.lmer"

multilevel models, for repeated measures within participants or patients within hospitals


"~ I(...)"

passive imputation: recomputes a variable from others at each iteration






Passive imputation keeps derived variables consistent. If body-mass index is computed from weight and height, impute weight and height and let mice recompute BMI each time, with method["bmi"] <- "~ I(weight / (height / 100)^2)", instead of imputing BMI separately and risking impossible combinations. For HomeBeat’s nightly readings — many nights per participant — a multilevel method would be the natural next step, because readings from the same person are more alike than readings from different people.

title: 9  When data are missing
section: 9.9 When gaps depend on what we cannot see: MNAR and sensitivity analysis
text:
9.9 When gaps depend on what we cannot see: MNAR and sensitivity analysis
Everything so far assumed MAR. Lena’s watch does not oblige: its gaps fall on her worst nights. To see what happens then, we add to HomeBeat a fictitious marker, hydration_level (mean 50, standard deviation 10), and delete its values with a probability that rises as hydration falls — a textbook MNAR mechanism, unrelated to any other variable. About 20 % of values go missing (Figure 9.6).








Figure 9.6: A textbook MNAR mechanism. Left: true hydration levels of participants whose value was recorded or deleted — the deleted values are much lower. This comparison is possible only in a simulation. Right: the probability of deletion built into the simulation, which rises as hydration falls.





The mean of the recorded values is 52.6, against a true mean of 49.9. Now run multiple imputation exactly as before, under MAR. The pooled mean is 52.5: no better than the naive average. MI could not help, because nothing observed is related to hydration; under MAR it fills the gaps with values like the observed ones, which are the wrong values. Imputing such a variable together with the others, as if it were MAR, is a common and silent error: with real data we would not know the true mean, so we would not even see the failure.
What can be done? Since the data cannot reveal the MNAR mechanism, the honest approach is a sensitivity analysis: ask how much the conclusion changes under a range of plausible departures from MAR (Carpenter and Kenward 2013; Buuren 2018).

Definition 9.9 (Sensitivity analysis (δ-adjustment)) A sensitivity analysis repeats an analysis under different assumptions to see whether the conclusion holds. In the δ-adjustment approach to MNAR, values are imputed under MAR and then shifted by an amount \(\delta\) (“missing values are on average \(\delta\) units lower than observed values that are otherwise similar”); the analysis is repeated over a range of \(\delta\) chosen with people who know the data, and the results are reported side by side.


How far from MAR? Each value of \(\delta\) shifts every imputed hydration value by that amount before pooling (20 imputations, precomputed with mice’s post argument). Move \(\delta\) and watch the pooled mean and its 95 % interval. Then reveal the truth, which in real life you would never see.

hdw = FileAttachment("data/precomputed/ch09/hydration_delta.csv").csv({typed: true})
viewof dl = Inputs.range([-15, 0], {value: 0, step: 1, label: "Shift δ applied to imputed values"})
viewof reveal = Inputs.toggle({label: "Reveal the true mean (only a simulation can)", value: false})























{
  const r = hdw.find(d => d.delta === dl);
  if (reveal && window.aihs) window.aihs.complete("ch09-tryit-delta");
  return html`<p>δ = ${dl}: pooled mean <strong>${r.estimate.toFixed(1)}</strong> (95 % interval ${r.lower.toFixed(1)} to ${r.upper.toFixed(1)})
  · mean of recorded values ${r.observed_mean.toFixed(1)}${reveal ? html` · <strong>true mean ${r.true_mean.toFixed(1)}</strong>` : ""}</p>`;
}







Plot.plot({
  height: 260, grid: true,
  x: {label: "Shift δ applied to imputed values", domain: [-15, 0]},
  y: {label: "Pooled mean hydration"},
  marks: [
    Plot.areaY(hdw, {x: "delta", y1: "lower", y2: "upper", fill: "#1f6f8b", fillOpacity: 0.2}),
    Plot.line(hdw, {x: "delta", y: "estimate", stroke: "#1f6f8b", strokeWidth: 2.5}),
    Plot.dot(hdw.filter(d => d.delta === dl), {x: "delta", y: "estimate", r: 6, fill: "#b35c00"}),
    Plot.ruleY([hdw[0].observed_mean], {strokeDasharray: "6,4"}),
    reveal ? Plot.ruleY([hdw[0].true_mean], {stroke: "#b35c00", strokeWidth: 2}) : null
  ]
})








Dashed line: mean of the recorded values. Blue band: 95 % interval of the pooled mean.


Here the truth is reached at about \(\delta =\) -13: the deleted values were much lower than the recorded ones. In a real study the analyst would present the whole curve and ask the clinical team which shifts are plausible. If the conclusion survives every plausible \(\delta\), it is robust to the MNAR worry; if it flips within the plausible range, the data cannot settle the question, and that too is worth knowing. More formal MNAR models exist — selection models, which model the probability of a gap as a function of the missing value, and pattern-mixture models, which model the data separately for each missingness pattern — and mice offers some of them, but all rest on assumptions that the data cannot check (Little and Rubin 2020; Carpenter and Kenward 2013).
For Lena, the lesson is practical. Her dashboard average treats the gaps as if they were MCAR, in a situation that is probably MNAR. If her HRV on restless nights is even somewhat lower than on the nights recorded, her true average is lower than the dashboard shows — and seven bad nights in a month are a signal in their own right. The nurse should call.

title: 9  When data are missing
text:
9.10 Missing data in prediction models
Most of this chapter concerned inference: estimating a mean or a coefficient without bias, with honest uncertainty. Prediction models — the risk scores of Part II — change the priorities, and three points follow (Sperrin et al. 2020).

Missingness must be handled at deployment too. A model fitted on complete cases cannot produce a prediction for a new patient with a gap. Whatever handling is chosen must be available at the bedside, for one patient at a time, using only what is known then.
Imputation is part of the model, so it must learn from the training data only. An imputation model fitted on all patients lets the test patients’ values shape the training data: this is the train–test contamination of Chapter 3. Fit the imputation on the training set (or inside each cross-validation fold) and apply it, frozen, to the test set.
The fact of missingness can carry information. A lactate that was never ordered says something about how ill the clinicians thought the patient was. In prediction it can be useful to add a missing-indicator feature, \(1 - R_{ij}\), next to the imputed value, and some methods — trees with surrogate splits (Breiman et al. 1984), XGBoost’s default directions (Chen and Guestrin 2016) (Chapter 6) — handle gaps natively. The indicator approach that is acceptable for prediction is generally not acceptable for estimating effects, where it can bias the coefficients (Sperrin et al. 2020; Groenwold et al. 2012; Buuren 2018). And informative missingness is fragile: if a new hospital orders lactate for everyone, the indicator’s meaning changes.

The Ward 7 baseline creatinine shows all three. In the deletion script, a baseline creatinine exists only if the patient had a blood test before admission, which healthier people rarely have: the gap depends on the unseen value itself (MNAR). The recorded values average 1.15 mg/dL against a true 1.07 mg/dL. The Lab below fits a prediction model with training-set mean imputation and missing indicators, on the shared Ward 7 split and with the ten predictors (P10, site included) used for Ward 7 since Chapter 4, and you will see that the indicator for a missing baseline creatinine picks up some of the information that the gap itself carries.

9.10.1 Ward 7: the comparison so far
The gaps were deleted from the same 1 250 Ward 7 patients, so models fitted to the gappy data can join the comparison of the earlier chapters (Table 9.4; this chapter’s rows in bold): fitted on the same 1 000 training patients, now with gaps, and tested on the same 250 test patients, gaps included. With complete data, the linear regression (OLS) of Chapter 4 has a test MAE of 0.141 mg/dL. With the gaps, training-mean imputation with missing indicators gives 0.144, and multiple imputation (mice, 20 imputations, imputation model fitted on the training rows only) gives 0.147. The gaps cost little: mean imputation with indicators still does better than the random forest (0.153) and XGBoost (0.148) of Chapter 6 and BART (0.146, Chapter 8), all fitted to complete data, and multiple imputation falls between BART and XGBoost. That multiple imputation, the better method for inference, predicts slightly worse here is no paradox: imputing under MAR, it has no way to use the information that a missing baseline creatinine carries, which the indicator captures.
A complete-case model is not in the table, because it cannot be scored on the same patients. Fitted on the 553 training patients without a gap, it can predict for only 168 of the 250 test patients and is silent for the other 82. On those 168 patients its MAE is 0.140, but on the same 168 patients the imputation model scores 0.140 and the complete-data OLS model 0.141: the complete-case model is about as accurate, only less available.

You are building a Ward 7 AKI risk model and want to impute missing albumin with mice before splitting the data into training and test sets, “to use all the information”. What is the problem?

None: imputation does not use the outcome, so it cannot leak The imputation model learns from every patient’s predictors (and should include the outcome when used for inference). Either way, test patients shape the training data, so the test error is no longer an honest estimate.
The test patients help to impute the training data, so the test error is optimistic; the imputation should be fitted on the training set and applied to the test set Correct. Imputation is a learned step of the pipeline, like scaling or feature selection, and belongs inside the training data (or inside each fold).
mice cannot be used for prediction models at all It can, as long as it is fitted on training data and the same procedure can be applied to new patients; simpler imputations are often preferred in prediction because they are easy to apply at the bedside.
