section: 9.11 Where this fits in the decision loop
text:
9.11 Where this fits in the decision loop


  The decision loop, with missing data at the data step
  A cycle of five boxes: data feed a model; the model produces information; people combine the information with values to make a decision; the decision leads to actions and outcomes, recorded as new data. In this chapter the data box is highlighted: what was recorded, and why some values were not, decides what the model can say.
  
  
  Data
  what was recorded
  and why not
  
  Model
  
  Information
  
  Decision
  + values, human in the loop
  
  Action and outcome
  recorded as new data
  
  
  
  
  

The decision loop. This chapter is about the Data step: the gaps in a dataset, and the reasons for them, shape every piece of information that follows.

This chapter sits at the very start of the loop, where data become the raw material of a model. Data with gaps (Section 9.1) are not a smaller version of the complete data; they are a selected version, and the selection rule — MCAR, MAR or MNAR (Section 9.4) — decides whether the information a model returns is trustworthy. What can go wrong? A dashboard average that silently drops the worst nights (Lena); a complete-case regression selected on the outcome (Section 9.3); single imputation that understates uncertainty (Section 9.2); an imputation fitted on the test set (Section 9.10); and above all an MNAR mechanism treated as MAR (Section 9.9). Who stays in control? The people who know how the data were collected: they judge which mechanism is plausible and which range of \(\delta\) is credible, and the decision-makers then see a range of answers instead of a single, falsely precise number. For the decision itself, the gaps are evidence too: a watch that stops recording on bad nights is telling the nurse something.

title: 9  When data are missing
text:
9.12 Lab: missing values on Ward 7
The Lab gathers the chapter’s code in one place and ends on the running example: diagnose the gaps in the Ward 7 data, then build a prediction model that handles them without leakage (in Python with scikit-learn’s SimpleImputer (Pedregosa et al. 2011)), on the shared training/test split. Run it here, or download it and run it on your computer: ch09_lab.R · ch09_lab.py.

RPython























Three observations to take forward. The complete-case model can produce a prediction for only 168 of the 250 test patients — at the bedside it would be silent for anyone with a gap — and on those 168 it is about as accurate as the others (MAE 0.140, against 0.140 for the imputation model on the same patients). Training-set mean imputation with indicators predicts for everyone, and its test MAE on all 250 patients, 0.144, is close to the 0.141 of the model fitted to the complete data (Table 9.4), because in a prediction model the goal is accuracy, not unbiased coefficients. And the indicator for a missing baseline creatinine has a clearly negative coefficient (-0.085 mg/dL): the gap itself tells the model that the patient was probably healthy before admission — useful here, and a reason to watch for changes in testing practice when the model moves to a new hospital.

title: 9  When data are missing
text:
9.13 Exercises

The mean, again. Five HbA1c values are 48, 52, (missing), 61 and (missing) mmol/mol. Compute the mean of the recorded values. Give one reason the missing values might be higher, and one reason they might be lower, than the recorded ones. Which mechanism is each?
Mechanisms in your practice. Describe one MCAR, one MAR and one MNAR example from a clinical setting you know. For the MAR example, name the recorded variable that explains the gaps.
Complete-case regression. In the mechanism widget, choose MAR with strength 3. Is the average of the recorded HRV values biased? Now think of a regression of HRV on age fitted to the complete cases. Would its slope be biased? Explain using Section 9.3.
Rubin’s rules. Three imputations give frailty coefficients 10.2, 11.5 and 12.1 with standard errors 2.9, 3.0 and 2.8. Compute \(\bar\theta\), \(V_W\), \(V_B\), \(V_T\) and the fraction of missing information.
How many imputations? In the pooling widget, compare the pooled standard error of resting heart rate at \(M = 5\) and \(M = 50\). Why might the answer at \(M = 5\) change if mice were run again with a different seed, while the answer at \(M = 50\) would barely move?
The outcome in the imputation model. Explain to a colleague, in three sentences, why stress_score belongs in the imputation model for HRV even though it is the outcome of the analysis.
Sensitivity analysis. In the δ widget, suppose the clinical team believes that missing hydration values are between 0 and 5 units lower than similar recorded ones. Report the range of pooled means. Would a conclusion such as “mean hydration is above 51” survive?
Code. Modify the Lab so that missing values are imputed with the training median instead of the mean. Then remove the three indicator columns. Which change matters more for the test error? Look at sim_ward7_missing.R and explain why.







Selected answers





1. The mean of 48, 52 and 61 is 53.7 mmol/mol. The missing values might be higher if people with poorly controlled diabetes miss clinic appointments (MNAR if it depends on the HbA1c itself; MAR if it is fully explained by recorded variables such as previous HbA1c); lower if well-controlled people are tested less often (same reasoning).
3. Yes: older participants lose more readings and have lower HRV, so the recorded average is too high. But a regression of HRV on age fitted to complete cases has an unbiased slope, because missingness depends only on the predictor (age); it is merely less precise.
4. \(\bar\theta = 11.27\); \(V_W = (2.9^2 + 3.0^2 + 2.8^2)/3 = 8.42\); \(V_B = [(10.2 - 11.27)^2 + (11.5 - 11.27)^2 + (12.1 - 11.27)^2]/2 = 0.94\); \(V_T = 8.42 + (4/3)(0.94) = 9.67\), so the pooled standard error is 3.11; the fraction of missing information is \((4/3)(0.94)/9.67 \approx 0.13\).
6. Imputation should preserve the relationships the analysis will look at. If the outcome is left out, imputed HRV values are drawn as if HRV had nothing to do with stress, so in the completed data the HRV–stress association is diluted and the HRV coefficient is biased towards zero. Including the outcome is not circular: it only makes the imputed values consistent with the observed relationship.
7. From the widget, the pooled mean falls from about 52.5 at \(\delta = 0\) to about 51.5 at \(\delta = -5\). The lower end of the interval at \(\delta = -5\) is 50.7: the point estimate stays above 51 across the whole range, but at its edge the interval no longer excludes values below 51, so the claim is not secure. If the team thinks larger shifts are possible, it fails.

title: 9  When data are missing
text:
9.14 Summary

A missing value is a value that should exist but was not recorded; the indicator \(R_{ij}\) marks which values are observed. Even a mean needs an assumption once a value is missing.
Naive fixes have costs: complete-case analysis loses precision and can be biased; pairwise deletion produces inconsistent summaries; single imputation (mean, median, zero) distorts spreads and correlations and understates uncertainty.
MCAR: gaps unrelated to anything. MAR: gaps explained by observed variables. MNAR: gaps depend on the unobserved values. Observed data can refute MCAR but cannot distinguish MAR from MNAR.
In regression, complete-case analysis is unbiased when missingness depends only on the predictors, and biased when it depends on the outcome. One dataset cannot tell bias from bad luck; repeated simulation can.
Multiple imputation creates \(M\) completed datasets, analyses each and pools them with Rubin’s rules: \(V_T = V_W + (1 + 1/M)V_B\). MICE with predictive mean matching is the standard tool; the imputation model must include the analysis outcome.
Under MNAR, imputation under MAR does not remove bias; a sensitivity analysis such as δ-adjustment shows how far conclusions move.
In prediction, imputation is part of the model, must be fitted on training data only, and missing indicators can carry useful (but fragile) information.

Starting here?





This chapter borrows a few ideas from earlier chapters. In one line each:

Instances and features. Each row of a dataset is an instance (a patient), each column a feature; there are \(n\) instances and \(p\) features, and \(\mathbf{x}_i\) collects the features of instance \(i\) (Definition 1.7).
Unsupervised learning looks for structure in the features without using an outcome (Section 1.6.2). Everything in this chapter is unsupervised; outcomes appear only as colours laid over the results afterwards.
From Chapter 3. \(k\)-nearest neighbours predicts from the most similar past patients, “similar” meaning close in Euclidean distance on standardised features (each feature minus its mean, divided by its standard deviation). From Chapter 4. Collinearity (strongly related predictors) makes regression coefficients unstable; ridge and lasso tame models with more predictors than patients. In ONCO-1, genes 08, 14 and 19 are leaky copies of the outcome and are left out unless we are studying leakage.

title: 10  High-dimensional data and dimension reduction
text:
10.1 What is a dimension?
Start with the dermatology cohort, which we call Dermato-ATT. Psoriasis is a chronic inflammatory skin disease in which skin cells multiply too fast and the immune system, in particular the interleukin-17 and interleukin-23 pathway, is over-active; drugs that block IL-17 are among the most effective treatments (Griffiths et al. 2021). Severity is scored with the Psoriasis Area and Severity Index (PASI), from 0 (clear) to 72 (Fredriksson and Pettersson 1978). Before the first injection, the unit recorded for each of 200 patients the blocks in Table 10.1; the outcome is the change in PASI after 12 weeks of treatment. Like every dataset in this book, the cohort is simulated: the gene and microbe names are labels, not real genes, and we will look inside the simulator in Section 10.5.4.

Each column is an axis. A patient described by two measurements is a point on a sheet of paper; by three, a point in a room. A Dermato-ATT patient is a point in a space with 1 850 axes.

Definition 10.1 (Dimension) The dimension of a dataset is its number of features \(p\): each feature is one axis, and each instance is a point \(\mathbf{x}_i = (x_{i1}, \dots, x_{ip})\) in a \(p\)-dimensional space. A dataset is high-dimensional when \(p\) is large relative to the number of instances \(n\); when \(p\) is much larger than \(n\) we write \(p \gg n\). Dermato-ATT has \(n = 200\) and \(p = 1\,850\); the full ONCO-1 trial has 2 000 genes.

We can look at a few axes at a time. Figure 10.1 (left) places every patient by baseline PASI and nitrogen dioxide (NO2) exposure and colours them by their 12-week change in PASI. No pattern jumps out: patients who improved a lot and patients who barely changed are scattered everywhere. Adding a third axis (a gene) gives a cloud you could rotate on screen, and it is still a diffuse cloud. The data contain strong relationships by construction, but they are not visible through two or three coordinates.








Figure 10.1: Two ways of looking at more than one dimension. Left: 200 patients placed by two of their 1 850 measurements and coloured by their 12-week change in PASI. Right: a parallel-coordinate plot, in which each patient is a line crossing six vertical axes (all standardised); the 40 patients with the largest change are highlighted.





Graphics can stretch a little further. In a parallel-coordinate plot (Figure 10.1, right) each variable becomes a vertical axis and each patient a line that crosses them all; bundles of lines that travel together reveal shared profiles (Inselberg 1985). Here the highlighted patients, those who improved most, tend to cross the NO2 axis low: a first hint, which we will need later. Conditioning plots (trellis or lattice displays) draw the same scatter plot in several panels, one for each band of a third variable, so that you can see how a relationship changes across groups (Cleveland 1993; Sarkar 2008). Both stop working long before 1 850 variables. To see the whole cloud we need either a way of measuring how far apart patients are in all dimensions at once, or a way of reducing the dimensions to a few that matter. This chapter does both, in that order.

section: 10.2 How far apart are two patients? Distances
text:
10.2 How far apart are two patients? Distances
Every method in this chapter, and the \(k\)-nearest neighbours of Chapter 3, begins with the same question: how far apart are two patients?

10.2.1 Euclidean distance, from two dimensions to \(p\)
On a sheet of paper, the distance between patients A and B is the length of the straight line that joins them. If A is at \((x_{A1}, x_{A2})\) and B at \((x_{B1}, x_{B2})\), Pythagoras gives
\[
d(A, B) = \sqrt{(x_{B1} - x_{A1})^2 + (x_{B2} - x_{A2})^2} :
\]
the horizontal difference squared, plus the vertical difference squared, square-rooted (Figure 10.2, left). In three dimensions a third squared difference joins the sum. Nothing stops us from continuing: with \(p\) features, the Euclidean distance between instances \(i\) and \(i'\) is
\[
d(\mathbf{x}_i, \mathbf{x}_{i'}) = \sqrt{\sum_{j=1}^{p} (x_{ij} - x_{i'j})^2} ,
\qquad(10.1)\]
the same recipe over \(p\) coordinates: one squared difference per feature, added up, then the square root.




  Three ways of measuring how far apart two patients are
  Three panels. Left, Euclidean: two points A and B joined by a straight diagonal line, with dashed horizontal and vertical legs forming a right triangle. Middle, Manhattan: the same two points joined by a path that goes along the horizontal leg and then up the vertical leg, like walking city blocks. Right, cosine: two arrows from the origin, one to A and one to a point twice as far along the same direction labelled 2A, and a third arrow to B at an angle; the angle between the arrows is what cosine distance measures, so A and 2A are at cosine distance zero.

Figure 10.2: Three notions of distance. Euclidean: the straight line. Manhattan: the sum of the differences along each axis. Cosine: the angle between two profiles, whatever their length.





10.2.2 Other distances
Euclidean distance is one choice among several, and each choice encodes a different idea of what “similar” means (Hastie, Tibshirani, and Friedman 2009, ch. 14).

Manhattan distance adds the absolute differences instead of squaring them, \(d_{\text{Man}}(\mathbf{x}_i, \mathbf{x}_{i'}) = \sum_j |x_{ij} - x_{i'j}|\): the distance a taxi drives along a grid of streets (Figure 10.2, middle). Because differences are not squared, one large difference weighs less, and for random data the contrast between near and far points fades more slowly than with Euclidean distance as dimensions are added (Aggarwal, Hinneburg, and Keim 2001).
Cosine distance looks only at the direction of the two profiles, not at their length: \(d_{\cos}(\mathbf{x}_i, \mathbf{x}_{i'}) = 1 - \dfrac{\sum_j x_{ij}x_{i'j}}{\sqrt{\sum_j x_{ij}^2}\,\sqrt{\sum_j x_{i'j}^2}}\). The fraction is the cosine of the angle between the two arrows of Figure 10.2 (right): 1 when they point the same way, so the distance is 0. It suits profiles in which the proportions matter and the total does not: two skin swabs with the same mix of bacteria, one sequenced twice as deeply as the other, have cosine distance 0. Chapter 15 uses exactly this idea to compare documents of different lengths.
Mahalanobis distance takes the correlations between features into account (Mahalanobis 1936): \(d_{\text{Mah}}(\mathbf{x}_i, \mathbf{x}_{i'}) = \sqrt{(\mathbf{x}_i - \mathbf{x}_{i'})^\top \mathbf{S}^{-1} (\mathbf{x}_i - \mathbf{x}_{i'})}\), where \(\mathbf{S}\) is the covariance matrix of the features. Two cytokines that rise and fall together (in Dermato-ATT, cytokine_1 and cytokine_2 have a correlation of 0.81) carry largely the same information. A patient one standard deviation above average on both is unremarkable: Mahalanobis distance 1.05 from the average patient. A patient one standard deviation above on one and one below on the other has an unusual combination: distance 3.22, although both patients are exactly the same standardised Euclidean distance (\(\sqrt 2\)) from the average. The catch is that \(\mathbf{S}\) must be estimated and inverted, which is impossible when \(p \ge n\): with 1 850 features and 200 patients the matrix has no inverse.


Definition 10.2 (Distance) A distance \(d(\mathbf{x}_i, \mathbf{x}_{i'})\) is a rule that turns two feature vectors into a non-negative number, zero for identical instances and larger for less similar ones. The Euclidean distance (Equation 10.1) sums squared differences; the Manhattan distance sums absolute differences; the cosine distance measures the angle between profiles and ignores their length; the Mahalanobis distance rescales the space by the inverse covariance matrix so that correlated features are not counted twice (Mahalanobis 1936). Choosing a distance is choosing what “similar” means (Hastie, Tibshirani, and Friedman 2009, ch. 14; Kaufman and Rousseeuw 1990).


Two microbiome profiles have exactly the same proportions of every bacterium, but sample B was sequenced to twice the depth of sample A, so every count in B is double the count in A. Which statement is true?

Their Euclidean distance is zero Euclidean distance compares the raw counts, which differ by a factor of two in every coordinate, so it is far from zero.
Their cosine distance is zero Correct. B is A multiplied by 2: the two arrows point in exactly the same direction, so the angle between them, and hence the cosine distance, is zero. That is why cosine distance is popular for profiles in which only proportions matter.
Their Manhattan distance is zero Manhattan distance adds the absolute differences in counts, and every count differs.
All distances agree that they are identical Only distances that ignore the overall magnitude (cosine) see them as identical; Euclidean and Manhattan see a large difference.

On the raw scale NO2 is measured in tens of units and gene_1 in fractions of a unit, so NO2 decides almost everything: of the squared distance between A and C, 91% comes from NO2 and only 9% from PASI, although A and C differ by eight PASI points, a clinically large gap. After each variable is divided by its standard deviation in the cohort (PASI 3.1, NO2 8.1, gene_1 1.16), PASI’s share rises to 40%. Nothing about the patients changed; only the units did. This is the scaling lesson of Chapter 3, now with many variables of wildly different units, and it applies to every distance, to PCA and to every map in this chapter.

Definition 10.3 (Standardisation (scaling)) To standardise a feature, subtract its mean and divide by its standard deviation: \(x^{*}_{ij} = (x_{ij} - \bar x_j)/s_j\). Every standardised feature has mean 0 and standard deviation 1, so distances and principal components no longer depend on the units of measurement. In a prediction pipeline the means and standard deviations are computed on the training data only (Chapter 3); for a purely descriptive map of a cohort they come from the whole cohort.

Standardising is a choice, not a law. It gives every feature the same weight, which is right when units are arbitrary (NO2 against PASI) and can be wrong when all features share a unit and their spread is informative, or when many noisy features would be inflated to the same importance as a few strong ones (Jolliffe 2002, ch. 2). Make the choice deliberately, and report it.

You compute Euclidean distances between Dermato-ATT patients on the five named exposome variables (NO2, PM10, UV index, temperature, humidity) without standardising. Their standard deviations are about 8, 6, 1, 5 and 12. Which variable dominates the distances?

UV index, because ultraviolet light matters most for psoriasis Clinical importance plays no part in the arithmetic. UV index has the smallest spread, so it contributes least.
Humidity, because it has the largest spread Correct. Squared differences in humidity are typically (12/1)² = 144 times larger than those in UV index. Unstandardised distances are mostly distances in humidity.
They contribute equally, because they are all exposome variables Belonging to the same block does not put them on the same scale. Only standardising does.



How far apart are two ONCO-1 patients? The 47 genes of ONCO-1 that are not leaky copies of the outcome are loaded as genes (one row per patient). Standardise every gene, then compute the Euclidean distance between the first two patients. Fill in the blank with the function that standardises.

RPython

















The function has the same name as the idea: it scales the columns.


z <- scale(genes)                     # standardise every gene (column)


















The method is short for standard deviation: three letters.


z = (genes - genes.mean()) / genes.std()        # standardise every gene (column)




On the raw expression values the same two patients are a different distance apart, because genes with a large spread dominate. pandas and R both divide by the standard deviation computed with \(n-1\), so the two languages agree to the last digit.

title: 10  High-dimensional data and dimension reduction
text:
10.4 Correlation and redundancy
Biological measurements come in teams. Genes switched on by the same transcription programme rise and fall together; bacteria that share a niche flourish together; pollutants from the same traffic move together. Figure 10.3 shows the correlations among a sample of Dermato-ATT variables.








Figure 10.3: Correlations among 58 Dermato-ATT variables: 25 genes, 15 microbiome features, 8 cytokines and 10 exposome variables. Orange = positive, blue = negative, white = none.






Definition 10.5 (Correlation and collinearity) The correlation between two features measures, from −1 to 1, how closely they follow a straight line together. A set of features is collinear when one of them can be written, exactly or nearly, as a weighted sum of others. Collinear features carry overlapping information: the data cloud occupies a space of fewer dimensions than the number of columns suggests. Its intrinsic dimension is the number of independent directions it really uses.

Collinearity is a nuisance and a gift. It is a nuisance because, as Chapter 4 showed, regression coefficients of collinear predictors become unstable, and because distances count redundant information many times over: 1 500 genes moving together weigh 1 500 times in a Euclidean distance. It is a gift because it tells us that the 1 850 columns are not 1 850 separate pieces of information. If a handful of directions carry most of the variation, we can describe each patient by their position along those directions instead. Finding them is the job of principal component analysis.

title: 10  High-dimensional data and dimension reduction
text:
10.5 Principal component analysis

10.5.1 PCA as a rotation
Look at the cloud of patients in the widget below: each point is a patient, placed by two standardised genes. The cloud is a tilted ellipse. Along the original axes it spreads moderately in both directions; along its long diagonal it spreads a lot; across the diagonal, very little. If you had to describe each patient with one number instead of two, the best single number would be the patient’s position along the long diagonal. That is the idea of principal component analysis (Pearson 1901; Hotelling 1933).

Find the first principal component by hand. The line through the centre is a candidate new axis. Each patient is projected onto it (the small marks on the line), and the variance captured is the variance of those projected positions. Turn the axis and watch the variance change. The total variance of two standardised genes is 2. Target: capture at least 99% of the largest variance that any single axis can capture.

dermRaw = FileAttachment("data/dermato.csv").csv({typed: true})
rotPts = {
  const zs = v => { const m = d3.mean(v), s = d3.deviation(v); return v.map(x => (x - m) / s); };
  const x = zs(dermRaw.map(d => d.gene_1)), y = zs(dermRaw.map(d => d.gene_2));
  return x.map((xi, i) => ({x: xi, y: y[i]}));
}
rotInfo = {
  const varAt = deg => { const t = deg * Math.PI / 180, c = Math.cos(t), s = Math.sin(t); return d3.variance(rotPts, p => p.x * c + p.y * s); };
  const curve = d3.range(0, 180.01, 0.5).map(a => ({a, v: varAt(a)}));
  const best = d3.greatest(curve, d => d.v);
  const total = d3.variance(rotPts, p => p.x) + d3.variance(rotPts, p => p.y);
  return {varAt, curve, best, total};
}
viewof rotTheta = Inputs.range([0, 180], {value: 0, step: 0.5, label: "Angle of the new axis (degrees)"})
viewof rotCurve = Inputs.toggle({label: "Show the variance for every angle", value: false})





































{
  const v = rotInfo.varAt(rotTheta), share = v / rotInfo.total, ofMax = v / rotInfo.best.v;
  const hit = ofMax >= 0.99;
  if (hit && window.aihs) window.aihs.complete("ch10-tryit-rotation");
  return html`<p>Variance captured: <strong>${v.toFixed(2)}</strong> of ${rotInfo.total.toFixed(2)}
  (<strong>${(100 * share).toFixed(1)}%</strong> of the total; ${(100 * ofMax).toFixed(1)}% of the best possible)
  ${hit ? html` — ✓ you found the first principal component, at about ${rotInfo.best.a.toFixed(0)}°. The axis at right angles to it is the second component, carrying the remaining ${(100 * (1 - rotInfo.best.v / rotInfo.total)).toFixed(1)}%.` : ""}</p>`;
}







{
  const t = rotTheta * Math.PI / 180, c = Math.cos(t), s = Math.sin(t), L = 4;
  const proj = rotPts.map(p => { const z = p.x * c + p.y * s; return {x: p.x, y: p.y, px: z * c, py: z * s}; });
  return Plot.plot({
    width: 420, height: 420, grid: true,
    x: {domain: [-L, L], label: "gene_1 (standardised)"}, y: {domain: [-L, L], label: "gene_2 (standardised)"},
    marks: [
      Plot.link(proj, {x1: "x", y1: "y", x2: "px", y2: "py", stroke: "currentColor", strokeOpacity: 0.12}),
      Plot.dot(proj, {x: "x", y: "y", r: 2.5, fill: "currentColor", fillOpacity: 0.45}),
      Plot.line([[-L * c, -L * s], [L * c, L * s]], {stroke: "#1f6f8b", strokeWidth: 3}),
      Plot.dot(proj, {x: "px", y: "py", r: 1.8, fill: "#1f6f8b"})
    ]
  });
}







(rotCurve || rotInfo.varAt(rotTheta) / rotInfo.best.v >= 0.99) ? Plot.plot({
  height: 190, grid: true,
  x: {label: "Angle (degrees)", domain: [0, 180]}, y: {label: "Variance captured", domain: [0, 2]},
  marks: [Plot.line(rotInfo.curve, {x: "a", y: "v", stroke: "#1f6f8b", strokeWidth: 2}),
          Plot.ruleX([rotTheta], {strokeDasharray: "3,3"}), Plot.ruleY([rotInfo.total], {stroke: "#b35c00", strokeDasharray: "5,3"}),
          Plot.text([[178, rotInfo.total - 0.08]], {text: ["total variance"], textAnchor: "end", fontSize: 11})]
}) : html`<p class="muted">Turn on the toggle to see the variance for every angle.</p>`








You have just done PCA in two dimensions: you rotated the coordinate system so that the first axis points along the direction of greatest spread. The second axis is forced to be at right angles to the first, and here it carries what is left. Nothing about the patients changed; we only looked at them from a better angle, much as the cylinder of Chapter 1 looked like an ellipse, a triangle or an arch depending on the point of view (Figure 1.1).


10.5.2 The algorithm
With \(p\) standardised features, the same idea runs in \(p\) dimensions. A direction is a list of \(p\) coefficients \(\mathbf{u} = (u_1, \dots, u_p)\) with \(\sum_j u_j^2 = 1\), and the position of patient \(i\) along it is a weighted sum of the patient’s features:
\[
z_{i} = u_1 x_{i1} + u_2 x_{i2} + \dots + u_p x_{ip} .
\qquad(10.2)\]
PCA chooses the first direction \(\mathbf{u}_1\) to make the variance of these positions as large as possible; the second, \(\mathbf{u}_2\), to make the remaining variance as large as possible while being at right angles to \(\mathbf{u}_1\); and so on, up to \(p\) directions (or \(n - 1\), whichever is smaller). Linear algebra solves this in one step: the directions are the eigenvectors of the correlation matrix \(\mathbf{S}\) of the standardised features, and the variance along each one, \(s_m^2\), is the corresponding eigenvalue (Jolliffe 2002; Jolliffe and Cadima 2016). You do not need to compute eigenvectors by hand; you do need to know what comes out.

Definition 10.6 (Principal component analysis (PCA)) Principal component analysis replaces \(p\) correlated features by new variables, the principal components, that are weighted sums of the originals (Equation 10.2), uncorrelated with one another and ordered by the variance they carry: the first has the largest possible variance, each next one the largest variance at right angles to all the previous ones. Keeping the first \(q\) components gives the best \(q\)-dimensional linear summary of the data, in the sense of losing the least variance. PCA is unsupervised: it never sees the outcome.


Definition 10.7 (Scores and loadings) The score \(z_{im}\) is the position of instance \(i\) along component \(m\); the scores of the first \(q\) components, \(\mathbf{z}_i = (z_{i1}, \dots, z_{iq})\), are the instance’s coordinates on the PCA map. The coefficients \(u_{jm}\) say how much feature \(j\) weighs in component \(m\) (R’s prcomp calls them rotation). For standardised data the loading of feature \(j\) on component \(m\) is usually reported as the correlation between the feature and the component, \(u_{jm} s_m\); this is what FactoMineR calls the variable’s coordinate. A large loading, positive or negative, means the feature moves strongly with the component.


Definition 10.8 (Explained variance) The proportion of variance explained by component \(m\) is \(s_m^2 / \sum_k s_k^2\). With \(p\) standardised features the total variance is \(p\), so it equals \(s_m^2 / p\). A scree plot shows these proportions in order; the point where the curve flattens (the “elbow”) suggests how many components carry structure rather than noise (Cattell 1966).


After a PCA of Dermato-ATT, patient P17 has a score of +40 on the first component. What does that number describe?

How much the outcome of P17 changed PCA never sees the outcome. The score is about the features only.
Where P17 lies along the first new axis: far on the positive side of the direction of greatest variation Correct. A score is a coordinate on the PCA map, a weighted sum of P17’s standardised features.
The correlation between P17 and the first component Correlations with components belong to features (loadings), not to patients.
The percentage of P17’s variance explained Explained variance describes components, not individual patients.




10.5.3 PCA of the Dermato-ATT cohort
The full cohort (200 patients, 1 850 standardised variables) was analysed with the PCA() function of the R package FactoMineR (Lê, Josse, and Husson 2008); the code is in scripts/precompute/ch10_pca.R and, on the browser copy of the data, in the Lab. Two lines do the work:
library(FactoMineR)
res <- PCA(X, scale.unit = TRUE, ncp = 10, graph = FALSE)   # X: the 1 850 columns, no outcome
scale.unit = TRUE standardises every variable first; the outcome and the patient identifier are left out because PCA is unsupervised. The result holds the eigenvalues (res$eig), and for the variables their coordinates (loadings), squared cosines and contributions (res$var$coord, res$var$cos2, res$var$contrib), with the same three for the patients in res$ind.








Figure 10.4: Scree plot of the Dermato-ATT PCA: the percentage of the total variance carried by each of the first 15 components.





The scree plot (Figure 10.4) has a sharp elbow. The first component carries 64.0% of the total variance, the second 11.0%, the third 2.6%; together the first three carry 77.6%, and every later component carries less than 0.4%. In other words, 1 850 columns behave as if they were about three, plus noise.

10.5.3.1 Which variables build each component? Contributions done right
FactoMineR reports, for each variable and component, a contribution: the percentage of the component’s variance that comes from that variable. For standardised data it equals \(100 \times u_{jm}^2\), so it is always positive and, for every component, the contributions of all variables add up to 100%. With 1 850 variables, the average contribution is \(100 / 1850 = 0.054\%\). Keep that baseline in mind when you read the numbers in Table 10.4.

The top gene on the first component contributes 0.078%: barely above the average of 0.054%. That is not a weakness; it is the signature of a component built from a whole block. Each of the 1 500 genes contributes a little, most of them with loadings between 0.80 and 0.94, and together the genes make up 99.2% of the first component. The second component is the microbiome block (99.0% of it, top contribution 0.394%: fewer variables share the load, so each takes a larger slice). The third is more mixed: the 18 cytokines together make up 13.3% of it, with individual contributions near 0.83%, and the genes most of the rest, some with positive and some with negative loadings.
Three quantities are easily confused, and the confusion leads to wrong biology:

the loading says how strongly a variable moves with the component (and in which direction);
the cos², the loading squared, says how much of that variable the component captures: about 92% of the top gene’s variance is on the first component;
the contribution says how much of the component that variable makes up. A single variable can only contribute a large percentage if few variables share the component.

A contribution of several percent from one gene in a component built from 1 500 similar genes is arithmetically impossible: ten genes at that level would make up most of the axis on their own. Always check that contributions add up to 100, and compare them with \(100/p\).








Figure 10.5: Correlation circles for the first two components. Left: all 1 850 variables, each drawn as the tip of its arrow; the plot is a ‘hairball’ in which individual variables cannot be read. Right: a reduced circle with a few representatives of each block and two exposome variables. The closer an arrow reaches the circle, the better the two components represent that variable.





A correlation circle (Figure 10.5) draws each variable as an arrow whose coordinates are its loadings on two components. Arrows that point the same way belong to correlated variables; arrows at right angles to uncorrelated ones; an arrow that reaches the circle is almost entirely captured by the two components, and a short arrow lives mostly in other dimensions. With 1 850 variables the full circle is unreadable, so draw a reduced one with the variables you want to discuss. Notice the two short arrows near the centre: NO2 and humidity are almost invisible on this map. Remember NO2.


10.5.3.2 Where do the patients sit?








Figure 10.6: Left: the 200 patients on the first two principal components, coloured by their 12-week change in PASI (an outcome PCA never saw). Right: the same outcome against a single exposome variable, NO2.





The scores place every patient on the map (Figure 10.6, left). Patients close together have similar values on the dominant directions of variation; with three components carrying 77.6% of the variance, distances on the map approximate distances in the full space reasonably well, though not perfectly. Colouring by the outcome reveals almost nothing: the first three components together explain only 13% of the variance of the 12-week change in PASI, the first ten 26%. Yet a single variable, NO2, explains 52% of it on its own (Figure 10.6, right). The variable that matters most for the outcome is one of the two short arrows near the centre of the circle; its largest loading among the first ten components is 0.40, on component 9.



10.5.4 What the simulation really contains
Because the data are simulated, we can open the box. The simulator (scripts/simulate/sim_dermato_att.R) draws four hidden factors for each patient, \(G_1\), \(G_2\), \(M_1\) and \(M_2\), all independent standard normal variables, and builds every block from them:
\[
\begin{aligned}
\text{gene}_j &= a_j G_1 + b_j G_2 + \text{noise}, &\quad a_j, b_j &\sim \mathcal{N}(0.7,\ 0.2^2) \text{ (the same distribution)} \\
\text{ASV}_j &= c_j M_1 + d_j M_2 + \text{noise}, &\quad c_j, d_j &\sim \mathcal{N}(0.5,\ 0.1^2) \\
\text{cytokine}_j &= 2\,G_1 + \text{noise} \\
\text{exposome} &= \text{independent noise, on very different scales} \\
\text{Outcome} &= 20 - 2\,G_1 + 1.5\,M_1 - 0.5\,\text{NO}_2 + \text{noise} .
\end{aligned}
\]
The comments in the code call \(G_1\) an “IL-17/IL-23 inflammatory axis” and \(G_2\) a “barrier” signature, but nothing in the numbers makes them so: every gene mixes both factors with weights drawn from the same distribution, and no pathway, IL-17 or otherwise, is simulated. Table 10.5 shows how the components line up with the hidden factors.

Read the table row by row and the components tell an honest story:

PC1 is the sum of the two gene factors (\(G_1 + G_2\)), because every gene loads positively on both. It is not an inflammatory axis; it is “how much of the shared gene programme this patient expresses”.
PC2 is the sum of the two microbiome factors.
PC3 is the contrast \(G_1 - G_2\): the direction along which genes that lean towards \(G_1\) separate from genes that lean towards \(G_2\). The cytokines follow \(G_1\) alone, so this is the component on which they stand out. PC4 is the microbiome contrast.
The outcome depends on \(G_1\), \(M_1\) and above all on NO2, an independent variable with a large spread that PCA treats as one standardised column among 1 850.

Three lessons follow, and they hold far beyond this dataset.

Directions of large variance are not necessarily directions that matter. PCA summarises what varies most among the features. Whether that relates to the outcome is a separate question that PCA cannot answer. Using the first few components as predictors (principal components regression) can throw away exactly the signal you need (James et al. 2021, sec. 6.3); supervised methods such as the lasso of Chapter 4 look at the outcome when they choose.
Components are mathematical objects; names are hypotheses. Calling a component “inflammation” is a claim to be tested against external knowledge, not a result of the PCA.
Read the numbers before the story. Contributions add up to 100; loadings are correlations; a block of many similar variables produces a component with many small contributions.


In the Dermato-ATT PCA, a gene has a contribution of 0.078% to the first component. A colleague concludes: “Each gene is irrelevant to PC1.” Is that right?

Yes, 0.078% is negligible It is small for one variable, but the average contribution with 1 850 variables is 100/1 850 ≈ 0.054%. This gene contributes more than average, and so do most of the 1 500 genes.
No: the component is built from the whole gene block, each gene contributing a little; together they make up about 99% of it Correct. Many small contributions from strongly correlated variables are the signature of a block-wide component. Most genes have loadings between 0.8 and 0.95: they move almost in lockstep with PC1.
No: contributions are not percentages, so 0.078 means 7.8% FactoMineR reports contributions in percent and they sum to 100 for each component. 0.078 means 0.078%.



The first three principal components of Dermato-ATT explain about 78% of the variance of the features but less than 15% of the variance of the outcome. What should you conclude?

The PCA was done wrongly Nothing is wrong: PCA maximises variance among the features and never looks at the outcome. There is no guarantee that the two align.
The outcome cannot be predicted from these data NO₂ alone explains about half of the outcome’s variance. The signal is there, in a direction PCA does not favour.
The directions of greatest variation among the features are not the ones that drive the outcome here; to predict, let the outcome guide the choice of features Correct. Unsupervised summaries are for describing the data. For prediction, use supervised methods (Chapters 4–6), or at least check what the components discard.



Match each description to the PCA quantity it describes.

Where patient P17 sits along the first component. Score
The correlation between NO2 and the ninth component. Loading
The amount of variance carried by the second component. Eigenvalue
The share of gene_538’s own variance that the first component captures. cos²
The percentage of the first component built from gene_538; summed over all variables it gives 100. Contribution




10.5.5 Scaling, once more
What if we skip scale.unit = TRUE? Take the 30 exposome variables alone. Unstandardised, the first component explains 49% of their variance, and the variable with the largest coefficient is humidity: the component is simply “humidity”, because humidity has the largest standard deviation (12 percentage points) and the 25 expo_ variables have standard deviation 1. Standardised, the first component explains 6%. That is about what 30 unrelated variables give: with no structure each would carry \(1/30 \approx 3.3\%\), and with 200 patients chance alone lets the first component catch a little more. It is the truth: the exposome variables were simulated independently. An unscaled PCA would have announced a “humidity axis” discovered by the data; it was discovered by the units.

How many genes’ worth of information? Run a PCA on the 47 non-leaky ONCO-1 genes and report the proportion of variance explained by the first component. Remember to standardise.

RPython

















scale. = TRUE standardises every gene before the components are computed.


pca <- prcomp(genes, scale. = TRUE)


















The standardised matrix is already stored in z.


pca = PCA().fit(z)




The first two components together carry 70% of the variance of the 47 genes: the ONCO-1 simulator builds its gene expression from two hidden factors, and PCA finds them. Unscaled, the first component alone would claim 51%.

text:
10.6 When straight lines are not enough
PCA looks at the data through flat sheets: its map is a projection onto the plane of greatest spread. If the patients lie on a curved surface, a projection squashes parts of it on top of each other, as a rolled-up carpet seen from above hides most of its pattern. For such data, nonlinear methods try to keep each patient next to its true neighbours instead of keeping straight-line distances.
To meet them we switch to the third request of the Monday morning. The Digital Trial dataset describes 500 participants of a decentralised trial with eleven features: four circulating cytokines (cytokine_1–cytokine_4), four summaries of wearable-sensor signals such as rest–activity rhythm and movement variability (wearable_1–wearable_4), three clinical assessments (clinical_1–clinical_3), and a treatment response, delta_score, with a binary responder label (above or below the median response). The dataset is simulated, and its simulator hides a secret that we keep for Section 10.9. All maps below use the eleven features, standardised; delta_score and responder are left out and used only as colours.
A PCA of the eleven features spreads the variance over several components: the first two carry 28% and 20%, the third still 12%. A two-dimensional PCA map shows only about half of the picture. You can see it in the widget at the end of the next section.
crumbs: 10  High-dimensional data and dimension reduction

title: 10  High-dimensional data and dimension reduction
text:
10.7 t-SNE: keeping neighbours together
t-distributed stochastic neighbour embedding (t-SNE) gives up on preserving distances in general and concentrates on one thing: who is close to whom (Maaten and Hinton 2008). It works in three steps.

Neighbourhoods in the original space. For each participant \(i\), t-SNE turns distances into probabilities of being neighbours: participant \(i'\) is picked as a neighbour of \(i\) with probability \[
p_{i' \mid i} = \frac{\exp\!\big(-d(\mathbf{x}_i, \mathbf{x}_{i'})^2 / 2\sigma_i^2\big)}
                      {\sum_{k \ne i} \exp\!\big(-d(\mathbf{x}_i, \mathbf{x}_k)^2 / 2\sigma_i^2\big)} :
\] close participants get high probabilities, distant ones almost zero. The width \(\sigma_i\) is chosen separately for each participant so that the neighbourhood has a fixed perplexity, \(\text{Perp} = 2^{H_i}\), where \(H_i\) is the entropy (in bits) of the probabilities \(p_{\cdot \mid i}\) (Chapter 2). Perplexity reads as the effective number of neighbours: in a dense region \(\sigma_i\) shrinks, in a sparse one it grows, until each participant has roughly Perp neighbours. The probabilities are then made symmetric, \(p_{ii'} = (p_{i' \mid i} +
p_{i \mid i'})/2n\).
Neighbourhoods on the map. Each participant gets a position \(\mathbf{z}_i\) in two dimensions, at first at random, and the same kind of probability \(q_{ii'}\) is computed on the map, but with the heavy-tailed Student t curve, \(q_{ii'} \propto (1 + \lVert \mathbf{z}_i - \mathbf{z}_{i'}
\rVert^2)^{-1}\). The heavy tails let moderately dissimilar participants sit far apart on the map, which relieves the crowding problem: there is far less room in two dimensions than in eleven.
Make the two agree. The positions are moved, step by step by gradient descent (Chapter 7), to reduce the mismatch between the two sets of probabilities, measured by the Kullback–Leibler divergence \(\sum_{i \ne i'} p_{ii'} \log (p_{ii'} / q_{ii'})\) (Kullback and Leibler 1951). Mismatches are penalised heavily when close neighbours are put far apart, and only lightly when distant participants are put close together.


Definition 10.9 (t-SNE) t-SNE places each instance on a two- (or three-) dimensional map so that instances that are neighbours in the original space remain neighbours on the map. It converts distances into neighbour probabilities (with a neighbourhood size set by the perplexity), uses a heavy-tailed Student t curve on the map, and minimises the Kullback–Leibler divergence between the two by gradient descent, starting from random positions (Maaten and Hinton 2008).

The R package Rtsne implements a fast approximation (Maaten 2014; Krijthe 2015):
library(Rtsne)
X <- scale(dt[, features])                         # the 11 features, standardised
set.seed(1)
fit <- Rtsne(X, perplexity = 30, max_iter = 1000, pca = FALSE)
plot(fit$Y, col = hcl.colors(100)[cut(dt$delta_score, 100)])








Figure 10.7: The 500 Digital Trial participants on a t-SNE map (perplexity 30) and a UMAP map (15 neighbours), coloured by treatment response. The axes have no units and no meaning; only who is next to whom does.





Figure 10.7 (left) is the kind of picture that arrived on Monday morning. The participants fall into a handful of islands, some round, some long; colours change smoothly along each island, so participants with similar profiles have similar responses. Tempting conclusions crowd in: “eight subtypes”, “the islands at the top respond best”, “the left island is closer to the centre island than to the right one”. Most of them are not supported by a t-SNE map (Wattenberg, Viégas, and Johnson 2016; Kobak and Berens 2019):

Sizes mean little. t-SNE adapts the neighbourhood width to the local density, so dense and sparse groups come out with similar sizes on the map.
Distances between islands mean little. The optimisation cares about keeping neighbours together; where whole islands end up relative to one another depends on the random start and the perplexity. The axes have no units.
The map is random. Each run starts from random positions; a fixed seed makes it reproducible, not right. Another seed gives another, equally valid, arrangement.
Perplexity changes the picture. Small values fragment the data into many small islands; large values merge them. There is no single correct setting, which is why you should always look at several.
Islands are not clusters, until proven. A map can split a continuous structure into pieces, and noise can form convincing-looking groups.

What a t-SNE map does show reliably is local: participants placed next to each other were, in almost all cases, close in the original space.

section: 10.9 Revealing the truth: a helix and a Swiss roll
text:
10.9 Revealing the truth: a helix and a Swiss roll
Now open the simulator (scripts/simulate/sim_digital_trial.R). It does not simulate patients at all in the biological sense. It draws points on two geometric shapes in three dimensions:

350 participants on a curve. The code calls it an “S-curve”, but with coordinates \(X_1 = \sin t\), \(X_2 = t\), \(X_3 = \cos t\) for \(t\) between \(-3\pi/2\) and \(3\pi/2\) it is a helix, a spring of one and a half turns: a one-dimensional object.
150 participants on a Swiss roll, a sheet rolled up like a pastry: a two-dimensional object, a classic test case for nonlinear maps (Tenenbaum, Silva, and Langford 2000).

Every “biological” feature is then computed from the three coordinates: cytokines are smooth functions of them, wearables are fast oscillations (wearable_4 \(= \sin(10(X_1 + X_2))\) plus noise, which wiggles so fast that it behaves almost like noise), and the three clinical variables contain jumps. clinical_1 is 3 on the helix and 5 on the roll; clinical_2 jumps where \(X_2\) changes sign; clinical_3 jumps where \(X_1\) changes sign. Those three ifelse() lines cut the two shapes into 8 pieces: shape × sign of \(X_1\) × sign of \(X_2\).








Figure 10.8: The hidden truth of the Digital Trial. Left: the two shapes the simulator draws, seen at an angle (circles: helix; triangles: Swiss roll). Middle and right: the t-SNE and UMAP maps of the figure above, now coloured by the eight pieces created by the step-shaped clinical variables. Almost every island is a single piece.





Figure 10.8 settles the Monday-morning question. The “eight subtypes” are the eight pieces, and the pieces were made by three lines of code that switch a clinical variable on and off. The maps did their job honestly: in the space of the eleven features those pieces really are separated by jumps, and t-SNE and UMAP kept each piece together (two pieces that are close in the eleven features can end up sharing an island). What the maps cannot tell you is why the islands exist. Here the reason is an artefact of how the features were built, and the biggest split of all is a single column: clinical_1 alone identifies the shape of 99.6% of the participants. Notice also what the maps lost. The helix is one continuous curve, yet it appears as four separate islands, and nothing on the map says that the islands join end to end.

What created the eight islands of the Digital Trial maps?

Eight biological subtypes with distinct immune and behavioural profiles Nothing biological was simulated. The participants are points on two geometric shapes.
Random noise that t-SNE and UMAP turned into clusters The islands are stable across seeds and methods, and each one matches a piece of the simulation. They are real structure in the features, not noise.
Three step-shaped clinical variables that cut two shapes into pieces, which the maps faithfully kept apart Correct. The maps reported a real feature of the data. The structure is real, but it says nothing about biology: it comes from three if-else rules in the simulator.
The choice of perplexity Perplexity changes how finely the data are fragmented, but these eight islands appear for most settings, because the jumps are in the features themselves.



One column, two “groups”. Check how well a single variable, clinical_1, identifies which shape each participant was drawn from. Choose a threshold: participants above it are labelled “Swiss roll”. The last line computes the share of participants labelled correctly.

RPython

















clinical_1 is about 3 on the helix and about 5 on the roll. A threshold half-way between works.


rule <- dt$clinical_1 > 4         # TRUE means "Swiss roll" according to one column


















clinical_1 is about 3 on the helix and about 5 on the roll. A threshold half-way between works.


rule = dt["clinical_1"] > 4         # True means "Swiss roll" according to one column





The lesson travels well beyond simulated helices. Real data have their own “three lines of code”: batch effects (Leek et al. 2010), a change of laboratory kit, a sensor firmware update, a coding rule that sets a variable to 0 for one group. Each can carve a cohort into islands that look like biology. Before naming an island, ask which features separate it, colour the map by every technical variable you have (site, batch, date, device), and check that the islands survive other seeds and settings.






Two more methods you may meet: self-organising maps and locally linear embedding





A self-organising map (SOM) places a grid of “prototype” profiles in the data space and lets each prototype move towards the instances closest to it, dragging its grid neighbours along, so that neighbouring cells of the grid end up with similar profiles (Kohonen 1982). The result is a map on a fixed grid, popular for summarising sensor and omics data. Locally linear embedding (LLE) describes each instance as a weighted average of its nearest neighbours and then looks for low-dimensional positions that keep the same weights, unrolling curved surfaces such as the Swiss roll when the neighbourhoods are well chosen (Roweis and Saul 2000). Both share the strengths and the cautions of t-SNE and UMAP: they rely on distances, need standardised features, depend on tuning choices and produce maps whose structure must be checked, not believed.

section: 10.10 Where this fits in the decision loop
text:
10.10 Where this fits in the decision loop


  Dimension reduction in the decision loop
  A cycle: thousands of measurements per patient are the data; PCA, t-SNE or UMAP is the model; a map and a few component scores are the information; people decide which hypotheses to test, which features to keep and which patients to compare; the follow-up study or validation produces new data. A note at the decision step says that maps generate hypotheses and do not confirm them.
  
  
  Data
  1 850 measurements
  
  Model
  PCA, t-SNE, UMAP
  
  Information
  a map, a few scores
  
  Decision
  what to test, keep, compare
  
  Action and outcome
  a follow-up study, a validation
  
  
  
  
  
  maps suggest; they do not confirm

Dimension reduction in the decision loop. The information it produces feeds research and modelling decisions more often than bedside ones.

Dimension reduction rarely decides anything at the bedside. Its information is a map or a few summary scores, and the decisions it serves are upstream: which hypotheses to test, which variables to measure in the next study, which features to give a predictive model, which patients to compare. For the three Monday-morning requests:

ONCO-1. “Patients most similar to #0042 in 2 000 genes” is a question the curse of dimensionality makes treacherous (Section 10.3). Standardise, then compare on a few principal components or on genes chosen with the outcome (Chapter 4), and check that the neighbours found are stable.
Dermatology. PCA gives an honest, checkable map (Section 10.5): three components summarise 1 850 columns, and their contributions and loadings can be read. But the map is organised by what varies most, and the outcome is driven mostly by something it barely shows. Name components cautiously, and do not use them as predictors without checking what they discard.
The digital trial. The eight islands are real structure in the features, created by three step-shaped variables, not eight biological subtypes (Section 10.9). A paper would need the islands to survive other settings and seeds, a check against technical variables, and confirmation in new data.

What can go wrong? Unscaled data that let units decide (Section 10.2); distances drowned in noise dimensions (Section 10.3); components named before they are read; maps over-read. Who stays in control? The analysts and clinicians who decide which structure is worth a new study, and who treat every island as a hypothesis.

10.11 Lab: from 1 850 columns to a map
The Lab gathers the chapter’s code in one place. It uses the browser copy of Dermato-ATT (200 of the 1 850 variables), so its numbers differ from those of the full-data analysis above. t-SNE and UMAP are too heavy for the browser, so the Lab reads the precomputed maps; the R version recomputes them if the packages Rtsne and uwot are installed on your computer; the Python version uses scikit-learn (Pedregosa et al. 2011). Run it here, or download it: ch10_lab.R · ch10_lab.py.

RPython























Three observations to take forward. First, the browser copy, with only 100 of the 1 500 genes, gives the same structure as the full data: one component for the genes, one for the microbiome, one for the gene contrast, and contributions that add up to 100. Second, five components explain far less of the outcome than NO2 alone. Third, a table of clinical_1 against the hidden shape is almost perfectly diagonal: one column explains the biggest split on every map.

title: 10  High-dimensional data and dimension reduction
text:
10.12 Exercises

Units. Recompute the distances of Table 10.2 with NO2 in mg/m³ instead of µg/m³ (divide by 1 000). Which pair of patients is now closest? Why does standardising make the question disappear?
Cosine or Euclidean? For each comparison say which distance you would choose and why:

two skin swabs, compared by the proportions of 300 bacteria; (b) two ICU patients, compared by standardised SOFA, lactate and creatinine; (c) two discharge letters, compared by how often each word occurs.

Concentration. In the concentration widget, compare the two kinds of data at \(p = 1\,000\). Explain in two sentences why shared hidden factors protect distances from concentrating.
Contributions. A PCA of 40 standardised variables gives a variable a contribution of 15% to the first component. Is that a lot? What would it be if all 40 contributed equally?
Reading the components. Use Table 10.5 to explain why the cytokines, which depend only on \(G_1\), contribute most to PC3 and not to PC1.
PCA and leakage. Run a standardised PCA on all 50 ONCO-1 genes, including the leaky genes 08, 14 and 19, and correlate the first five components with response_percent. What do you find, and how could PCA help you spot a leak?
The grid of maps. In the widget, find the t-SNE setting that splits the data into the most islands, and the UMAP setting with the best distance agreement. Does any setting join the four pieces of the helix into one curve?
Code. Modify the Lab so that the PCA of Dermato-ATT leaves out the gene block. Which block now dominates the first component, and how much of the outcome do the first five components explain?







Selected answers





1. In mg/m³ the NO2 differences shrink to a few hundredths, so PASI dominates: A and B (PASI 10 and 12) become the closest pair, while on the original scale B and C were. After standardising, the units cancel out (dividing by the standard deviation removes any change of scale), so the answer is the same whichever unit was used.
4. The average contribution with 40 variables is 100/40 = 2.5%, so 15% is six times the average: a substantial share. With equal contributions every variable would have 2.5%.
5. PC1 is the sum \(G_1 + G_2\) shared by all 1 500 genes; the 18 cytokines follow only \(G_1\), so their correlation with PC1 is moderate and their share of a component built from 1 500 genes is tiny. PC3 is the contrast \(G_1 - G_2\), the one direction along which “\(G_1\) only” stands out, so the cytokines’ loadings and contributions are largest there.
6. With the leaky genes included, component 3 has a correlation of -0.79 with the response: the three leaky genes are copies of the outcome, so they move together and form a component of their own. A component built from just a few variables that is suspiciously strongly related to the outcome is a reason to inspect those variables, exactly as a near-perfect predictor is in Chapter 6.
7. Small perplexities (5) fragment the pieces further. In our runs none of the settings in the grid joins the helix into one curve, because clinical_2 and clinical_3 jump where the coordinates change sign and those jumps are real in the eleven features.

title: 10  High-dimensional data and dimension reduction
text:
10.13 Summary

The dimension of a dataset is its number of features; with thousands of features and hundreds of patients, \(p \gg n\).
A distance encodes what “similar” means: Euclidean, Manhattan, cosine (direction, not length) and Mahalanobis (correlations taken into account). Standardise first, or the units decide.
The curse of dimensionality: data become sparse and distances concentrate, so neighbourhood methods falter when many features are noise. Shared hidden factors protect structure; noise dimensions erode it.
Collinearity means the data use fewer directions than they have columns, which is what dimension reduction exploits.
PCA rotates standardised data onto uncorrelated components ordered by variance. Scores locate patients, loadings relate variables to components, eigenvalues give the variance explained, and contributions add up to 100 per component. Components summarise variation, not relevance to an outcome, and names given to them are hypotheses.
t-SNE and UMAP keep local neighbourhoods on a two-dimensional map. Sizes of islands, distances between them and the axes carry little meaning; maps change with seeds and settings; islands are hypotheses that need checking, as the helix and the Swiss roll showed.

How to use this chapter






Starting here?





This chapter borrows a few ideas from earlier ones:

Each row of a dataset is an instance with features \(\mathbf{x}_i\) (Definition 1.7). Unsupervised learning looks for structure in data that have no outcome (Section 1.6.2).
A model that is too flexible overfits: it fits noise that will not come back in new data (Definition 1.8). Settings chosen by the analyst rather than learned, such as the \(k\) of \(k\)-nearest neighbours, are hyperparameters (Chapter 3).
The normal distribution describes measurements that scatter symmetrically around a mean, and the likelihood measures how well a model with given parameters explains the data (Chapter 2).
The distance \(d(\mathbf{x}_i, \mathbf{x}_{i'})\) between two patients is usually Euclidean; features are standardised (centred and divided by their standard deviation) so that each counts equally; PCA summarises many correlated features by a few new axes, the principal components, that keep as much of the variation as possible (Chapter 10).
Real records have missing values, and how they went missing matters (Chapter 9).

title: 11  Clustering patients
text:
11.1 What is a cluster?

Definition 11.1 (Cluster and clustering) A cluster is a group of instances that are more similar to one another than to instances in other groups, according to a stated measure of similarity. Clustering is the task of finding such groups in data that carry no outcome labels. A partition assigns every instance to exactly one of \(K\) clusters \(C_1, \dots, C_K\), with \(n_k\) instances in \(C_k\).

Notice the phrase according to a stated measure. There is no single, method-free definition of a “true” cluster: a group that is obvious under one notion of similarity can vanish under another (Hennig 2015). Every clustering method in this chapter makes its own choice — round groups around a centre, dense regions separated by sparse ones, overlapping bell curves, a tree of nested merges — and finds groups of that kind.
Clustering methods come from two broad perspectives. Flat (partitioning) methods look for one partition into a chosen number of groups \(K\); \(k\)-means, \(k\)-medoids and Gaussian mixtures are of this kind. Hierarchical methods do not commit to one \(K\): they build a tree of nested groups, from every patient on their own up to everyone together, which can be cut at any level. We start flat and finish with trees.
Many flat methods summarise a cluster by a representative point.

Definition 11.2 (Centroid and medoid) The centroid of cluster \(C_k\) is the mean of its members, \(\mathbf{\mu}_k = \frac{1}{n_k}\sum_{i \in C_k} \mathbf{x}_i\): the coordinate-wise average, a synthetic point that need not coincide with any real patient. The medoid is the member of the cluster with the smallest average distance to all other members: always a real patient.

The centroid is to the medoid what the mean is to the median. A single faulty sensor reading of 40 000 steps drags a centroid towards it; a medoid, anchored to an actual person, barely moves. That robustness is why \(k\)-medoids (Kaufman and Rousseeuw 1990) is popular with messy clinical data, at a higher computational cost.

You run a clustering algorithm on the HomeBeat pilot and ask for four clusters. It returns four groups. What have you learned?

That the population contains four distinct kinds of participant Not yet. Most clustering algorithms return exactly as many groups as you ask for, whether or not the data contain groups. Four groups are a proposal, not a finding.
That, under this algorithm’s notion of similarity, this is its best division into four groups — which may or may not reflect real structure Correct. The output is a hypothesis. The rest of the chapter is about testing it: internal indices, stability, comparison with known labels when they exist, and, above all, external validation against outcomes.
Nothing, because unsupervised results cannot be evaluated They can — with care. Internal indices, stability, agreement with known structure and links with outcomes all provide evidence.

The data were simulated with five digital phenotypes of 160 people each: healthy active (low heart rate, many steps), high stress (fast heart rate, low heart-rate variability, few steps), sedentary calm (slow heart rate, few steps), fever or infection (warm skin, lower oxygen saturation) and post-operative (the fastest heart rate and almost no steps). In real remote monitoring nobody knows the phenotypes, and perhaps there are none. Here we know them, and that lets us do something rarely possible in practice: check what each method gets right and wrong. Sleep efficiency is a share of time in bed spent asleep; the simulation lets some values exceed 1 (124 of the 800), a reminder that simulated data are a teaching device, not a mirror of reality.

11.2.1 Preparing the data: one scale for all
Clustering is driven by distances between patients (Chapter 10). Steps run into the thousands, skin temperature varies by a couple of degrees, and sleep efficiency lives between 0 and 1. On the raw scales the Euclidean distance between two participants is almost entirely a difference in steps, and the other five signals are ignored. The usual remedy is to standardise each feature to mean 0 and standard deviation 1 before clustering (Kaufman and Rousseeuw 1990, ch. 1). Keep in mind that this is a modelling choice, not a neutral step: it decides how much each signal is allowed to matter (Hastie, Tibshirani, and Friedman 2009, ch. 14). We will see it come back to bite.








Figure 11.1: The pilot before any clustering: standardised resting heart rate against standardised steps for the 800 participants. Several dense clumps are visible; how many groups would you say there are?






You run \(k\)-means on the pilot data without standardising. Which signal will dominate the clusters?

Steps per day Correct. Its values differ between people by thousands, so squared differences in steps swamp everything else in the Euclidean distance. The clusters would be “step-count bands”, whatever the other signals say.
Sleep efficiency, because it is a proportion Its differences are at most about 1, so on the raw scale it contributes almost nothing to the distance.
All six equally, because \(k\)-means treats every column the same It treats every unit the same. One step and one degree Celsius count as one unit each, which is exactly the problem.








Figure 11.2: The clustering workflow used in this chapter: prepare (and usually standardise) the feature matrix, choose the number of clusters \(K\), fit the algorithm, and validate the clusters.



Figure 11.2 shows the workflow we follow. Unlike supervised learning there is no outcome to predict and no test error to report, so the last box, validate, carries most of the weight.

title: 11  Clustering patients
11  Clustering patients
section: 11.4 How many clusters? Internal indices and stability
text:
11.4 How many clusters? Internal indices and stability
\(K\) is a hyperparameter, and choosing it is the central modelling decision of \(k\)-means. Too few clusters underfit: distinct states are lumped together. Too many overfit: a genuine group is chopped into fragments that would not reappear in new data. Without labels, we lean on two kinds of evidence.

Definition 11.4 (Internal validation index) An internal index scores a partition using only the data and the cluster labels, by balancing how compact the clusters are against how separated they are. Comparing the index across values of \(K\) suggests which \(K\) fits the data best — by the index’s own notion of a good cluster.

Four indices are in common use.

Silhouette (Rousseeuw 1987). For patient \(i\), let \(\bar d_{\text{own}}(i)\) be the average distance to the other members of its cluster and \(\bar d_{\text{near}}(i)\) the average distance to the members of the nearest other cluster. Then \[
s(i) = \frac{\bar d_{\text{near}}(i) - \bar d_{\text{own}}(i)}{\max\{\bar d_{\text{own}}(i),\ \bar d_{\text{near}}(i)\}} ,
\qquad(11.3)\] which lies between −1 and 1: close to 1 when \(i\) sits snugly in its cluster, near 0 when it is on a border, negative when it would fit better next door. The average silhouette summarises a partition; higher is better.
Davies–Bouldin (Davies and Bouldin 1979). For each cluster, take the worst ratio of (its scatter + a neighbour’s scatter) to the distance between their centroids, then average over clusters. Lower is better.
Calinski–Harabasz (pseudo-F) (Caliński and Harabasz 1974): \(\text{CH} = \dfrac{\text{BSS}/(K-1)}{\text{WSS}/(n-K)}\), the ANOVA-style ratio of

Higher is better.

Dunn (Dunn 1973): the smallest distance between two patients in different clusters divided by the largest distance between two patients in the same cluster. It looks at the worst case, so a single outlier can sink it. Higher is better.

A second kind of evidence is stability (Hennig 2007): a cluster structure that is real should reappear when the data are perturbed. We draw bootstrap samples of the 800 participants, rerun \(k\)-means on each, assign everyone to the nearest bootstrap centroid, and measure the agreement with the original partition (with the adjusted Rand index introduced in the next section; 1 = identical). One can also borrow the logic of cross-validation: fit the clusters on some folds and compute the indices on the held-out participants, so that \(K\) is judged on people the clustering never saw (Rhys 2020, ch. 16).








Figure 11.3: Choosing \(K\) for \(k\)-means on the six standardised signals (20 starts for each \(K\)). Silhouette, Davies–Bouldin and Dunn all point to \(K = 4\) (dashed line); Calinski–Harabasz prefers \(K = 2\), with \(K = 4\) a close second; bootstrap stability is highest at \(K = 4\).





The verdict looks unanimous (Figure 11.3). Silhouette peaks at \(K = 4\), Davies–Bouldin is lowest at \(K = 4\), Dunn peaks at \(K = 4\), and the four-cluster solution is the most stable one (0.998). Only Calinski–Harabasz dissents, preferring \(K = 2\) with four a close second. A careful analyst would report four digital phenotypes, and would have good reason to feel confident.
And would be wrong: the data were generated with five.

title: 11  Clustering patients
section: 11.5 Four or five? The adjusted Rand index
text:
11.5 Four or five? The adjusted Rand index
When true labels exist — in a simulation, or when clusters are compared with an established classification — we can measure how well a partition recovers them. Cluster numbers are arbitrary (cluster 2 in one run may be cluster 4 in the next), so we cannot simply count matching labels. Instead we look at pairs of patients: a good partition puts together the pairs that belong together and separates the pairs that do not.

Definition 11.5 (Adjusted Rand index (ARI)) Consider all \(\binom{n}{2}\) pairs of instances. The Rand index is the proportion of pairs on which two partitions agree (both put the pair together, or both keep it apart). The adjusted Rand index corrects it for the agreement expected by chance (Hubert and Arabie 1985): \[
\text{ARI} = \frac{\text{Rand index} - \text{expected Rand index}}{\text{maximum Rand index} - \text{expected Rand index}} .
\] ARI = 1 for identical partitions (whatever the label names), about 0 for a partition no better than random, and it can be slightly negative.

The lesson



Internal indices and stability measure how well the data fit the method’s own idea of a cluster. They cannot tell you whether the clusters are real. Four agreeing indices and a stable solution added up to a confident, reproducible, wrong answer. Two remedies follow, and the rest of the chapter uses both: try methods with different notions of a cluster, and, above all, validate clusters against knowledge that the algorithm did not see.



A colleague clusters 100 patients into three groups labelled 1, 2, 3. The true subtypes are A, B, C, and every A patient is in cluster 3, every B in cluster 1 and every C in cluster 2. What is the ARI?

1 Correct. The two partitions put exactly the same pairs together, so the agreement is perfect; only the names differ.
About 0.33, one in three by chance The ARI is already adjusted for chance: random labels give about 0, not 0.33.

In real data there is no phenotype_true column. What would have warned us? Looking at each signal on its own scale (a histogram of steps among the fast-heart-rate participants shows two separate humps); asking clinicians whether “fast heart rate, no steps” lumps together people who should be managed differently; and fitting a method whose clusters may be elongated, which we do in Section 11.7.

11.5.1 Strengths and limits of \(k\)-means
\(k\)-means is fast, scales to millions of rows, is easy to explain, and its centroids are readable summaries: a centroid at +1.8 standard deviations of steps and −0.9 of heart rate is the healthy-active profile. Its limits follow from its objective. It needs \(K\) in advance; it works only with numerical features (categories such as device type or diagnosis need other methods, such as \(k\)-medoids with a suitable dissimilarity); it depends on scaling; its result depends on the starts; a few outliers pull centroids away; and it favours round clusters of similar size. It also assigns every patient to some cluster, however unusual the patient.

title: 11  Clustering patients
text:
11.6 Density-based clustering: DBSCAN and OPTICS
Density-based methods take a different view: a cluster is a region where patients are crowded together, separated from other such regions by sparse space. Clusters can then have any shape, and a patient who lives in an empty region need not belong to any cluster at all. In remote monitoring that is often exactly what we want: an unusual episode or a faulty sensor should be flagged, not forced into the nearest group.

Definition 11.6 (DBSCAN) DBSCAN (density-based spatial clustering of applications with noise) (Ester et al. 1996) uses two hyperparameters, a radius \(r\) (called eps in software) and a count minPts. A core point has at least minPts points, itself included, within distance \(r\). A border point has fewer, but lies within \(r\) of a core point. Every other point is noise. A cluster is grown from a core point by adding everything within \(r\) of it, then everything within \(r\) of each new core point, and so on, until nothing more can be reached.

















r
✕
core points
≥ minPts within r
border point
reached from a core point
noise
no dense neighbourhood




Figure 11.4: The three kinds of point in DBSCAN, here with minPts = 4. Clusters grow outwards from core points; noise belongs to no cluster.



The classic demonstration uses shapes that defeat \(k\)-means. Below, 150 points form an inner ring, 260 an outer ring, and 40 are scattered at random.








Figure 11.5: Two rings with background noise (left), clustered by \(k\)-means with \(K = 2\) (middle) and by DBSCAN with \(r = 0.3\) and minPts = 5 (right; noise in grey).





\(k\)-means cuts the plane into two halves, each containing pieces of both rings (ARI on the ring points 0.008, no better than chance). DBSCAN follows the rings, because neighbouring points along a ring keep handing the cluster on, and it leaves 21 of the scattered points as noise. Now find good settings yourself.

Tune DBSCAN by hand. Move the radius \(r\) and minPts. Grey crosses are noise; open circles are border points. Watch what happens when \(r\) is too small (the rings shatter into fragments, and much becomes noise) and too large (the rings merge with each other and with the background). Target: exactly two clusters that recover the two rings (ARI on the ring points ≥ 0.95).

rings = FileAttachment("data/precomputed/ch11/rings.csv").csv({typed: true})
viewof epsR = Inputs.range([0.05, 1.2], {value: 0.12, step: 0.01, label: "Radius r (eps)"})
viewof minPtsR = Inputs.range([2, 20], {value: 5, step: 1, label: "minPts"})
dbRes = {
  const P = rings, n = P.length, r2 = epsR * epsR;
  const nb = P.map(p => { const out = []; for (let j = 0; j < n; j++) { const dx = p.x - P[j].x, dy = p.y - P[j].y; if (dx * dx + dy * dy <= r2) out.push(j); } return out; });
  const core = nb.map(a => a.length >= minPtsR), lab = new Array(n).fill(0);
  let c = 0;
  for (let i = 0; i < n; i++) {
    if (lab[i] !== 0 || !core[i]) continue;
    c++; lab[i] = c; const stack = [i];
    while (stack.length) { const j = stack.pop(); if (!core[j]) continue;
      for (const k of nb[j]) if (lab[k] === 0) { lab[k] = c; stack.push(k); } }
  }
  const ringIdx = d3.range(n).filter(i => P[i].truth !== "background");
  const ariRings = ariJS(ringIdx.map(i => lab[i]), ringIdx.map(i => P[i].truth));
  const type = lab.map((l, i) => l === 0 ? "noise" : core[i] ? "core" : "border");
  return {lab, type, nclus: c, noise: lab.filter(l => l === 0).length, ariRings};
}

  · ARI on the ring points: <strong>${dbRes.ariRings.toFixed(2)}</strong>
