title: 12  Interpretable and explainable AI
text:
12.11 How sure is the explanation?
Every number in this chapter is an estimate. Fit the forest on a slightly different sample of patients and its importance ranking, its curves and its interactions all change a little — sometimes a lot. An explanation that is large but unstable is a poor basis for a clinical story.
Bayesian models make this uncertainty explicit. Chapter 8 introduced Bayesian additive regression trees (BART), which write the prediction as a sum of many small trees, \[
\hat f(\mathbf{x}) = \sum_{t=1}^{m} g(\mathbf{x}; T_t, M_t),
\] where \(T_t\) is the structure of tree \(t\) and \(M_t\) the values in its leaves, with priors that keep every tree small and a posterior distribution over the whole ensemble (Chipman, George, and McCulloch 2010). The fitted model is not one function but a sample of plausible functions, one per posterior draw. Any summary computed from the trees — how often each feature is used in a split, how often two features appear one directly below the other on a branch — can be computed for every draw, giving a distribution for each entry of the VIVID matrix rather than a single number. The R package bartMan does exactly this (Inglis, Parnell, and Hurley 2024). In the first edition of this book BART was the most accurate model for the lung clinic, and its explanations were summarised in this way; we repeat that analysis here. (In Python, BART is available through PyMC-BART (Quiroga et al. 2022), but there is no equivalent of bartMan’s displays. For any model, the bootstrap (Efron 1979) offers a simpler route: refit the model on many bootstrap samples and recompute the explanation each time.)

library(dbarts)
library(bartMan)
test <- lung[split$set == "test", c(feats, "time")]
# 80 trees and 200 burn-in iterations as in the first edition; 200 posterior draws.
# Write the settings as numbers: extractTreeData() reads them back from the call.
set.seed(2026)
bart_fit <- bart(x.train = as.matrix(train[feats]), y.train = train$time,
                 x.test = as.matrix(test[feats]), ntree = 80L, nskip = 200L,
                 ndpost = 200L, keeptrees = TRUE, verbose = FALSE, seed = 2026)
post_mean <- colMeans(bart_fit$yhat.test)          # posterior mean for each test patient
cred_int  <- apply(bart_fit$yhat.test, 2, quantile, c(0.025, 0.975))   # 95% credible intervals

trees   <- extractTreeData(model = bart_fit, data = data.frame(train[feats], y = train$time))
vsupMat <- viviBartMatrix(trees = trees, type = "vsup", metric = "propMean", metricError = "CV")
viviBartPlot(vsupMat, max_desat = 1, pow_desat = 0.6, max_light = 0.6, pow_light = 1, label = "CV")
set.seed(2026)
permVimp(model = bart_fit, data = data.frame(train[feats], time = train$time),
         response = "time", numTreesPerm = 20)  # inclusion proportion minus that of a null model

The posterior mean predicts the 57 test patients with a test MAE of 33.2 days, in the range of the forests of Table 12.5. Each patient also gets a 95% credible interval, of median width 71 days — but only 35 of the 57 observed follow-up times fall inside theirs. That is not a failure of BART: the interval describes the uncertainty about the model’s average prediction for patients like this one, \(\hat f(\mathbf{x})\), not about one patient’s outcome, which also scatters around that average with a residual standard deviation of about 31 days. Adding that scatter gives prediction intervals that contain 51 of the 57 outcomes. Know which of the two uncertainties a display shows.
How should the value of an explanation and its uncertainty be shown together? Two separate heatmaps invite the eye to read only the first. A value-suppressing uncertainty palette (VSUP) merges them (Correll, Moritz, and Heer 2018).

Definition 12.7 (Value-suppressing uncertainty palette (VSUP)) A VSUP is a colour scale with two inputs, a value and its uncertainty. When uncertainty is low, many shades distinguish small differences in value; as uncertainty grows, neighbouring values are merged into fewer, paler shades, until at the highest uncertainty every value gets the same grey. Entries that are both large and reliable stand out; large but unreliable ones are deliberately suppressed.







Figure 12.8: Value-suppressing uncertainty palette for the BART model of the lung clinic, drawn by bartMan::viviBartPlot(). Diagonal (green to blue, Vimp): inclusion proportion, the share of all splits in the posterior trees that use the feature. Off-diagonal (yellow to red, Vint): the share of pairs of splits, one directly below the other, that use the two features. In each fan-shaped legend the value grows from left to right and the uncertainty — the coefficient of variation (CV) across 200 posterior draws — grows from the outer ring to the tip, where all values share one grey.



Read the legend first. The importance scale runs only from about 0.17 to 0.23: every feature is used in roughly a fifth of all splits — 0.22 for weight loss, 0.20 for ECOG, 0.20 for age — which is what you would see if the 80 trees chose their split variables almost at random (1/5 = 0.20). The strong blue of weight loss and age and the grey-blue of ECOG are differences of one or two percentage points, and ECOG is desaturated because its proportion varies a little more between draws (CV 0.16 against 0.14). Why does age, which every other method found irrelevant, look as important as ECOG? With many trees, BART has room to use every feature, useless ones included, so inclusion proportions separate features well only when the number of trees is small — about 20 has been suggested for variable selection (Chipman, George, and McCulloch 2010; Bleich et al. 2014). And, like impurity importance, split counts favour features with many possible split points: age takes dozens of values, ECOG only four. bartMan’s permVimp() corrects for both by subtracting the inclusion proportions of a null model fitted to a shuffled outcome. For the lung clinic only ECOG stays clearly above the null (0.033; weight loss 0.007, the others zero or almost).
The off-diagonal is more informative. The strongest interaction, ECOG × weight loss (0.062), is also the most stable one (CV 0.37), so it keeps its deep red: in the posterior trees a split on weight loss often sits directly below a split on ECOG, or above it. This is the interaction that the first edition built into the simulation. ECOG × Karnofsky, by contrast, is the rarest and least stable pair (0.029, CV 0.70), shown in grey: the two scores are substitutes, and a tree that has already split on one rarely needs the other on the same branch. The forest’s VIVID display ranked the same pair second, because the H statistic measures something else — a departure from additivity in the partial dependence — so the two displays need not agree. The remaining pairs are small and uncertain (CVs around 0.5), and the palette deliberately fades them. A VSUP makes it hard to tell a story about an explanation the data do not support; it cannot tell you whether the quantity displayed is the right one. That judgement remains yours.

title: 12  Interpretable and explainable AI
text:
12.12 Using explanations responsibly
Explanation methods are powerful, and in health care they are also easy to misuse. Ghassemi, Oakden-Rayner, and Beam (2021) warn that explanations of individual predictions can give clinicians false reassurance: a plausible list of contributions or a heatmap on an image looks like understanding, even when the model is wrong for reasons the explanation does not show. Explanations of image models are a striking case. Saliency maps (Simonyan, Vedaldi, and Zisserman 2014) colour the pixels that most influence a network’s output, and can reveal shortcuts — models that read the hospital’s marker on a chest X-ray instead of the lungs (Zech et al. 2018; Geirhos et al. 2020) — but some saliency methods produce almost the same map for a trained network and for one with random weights (Adebayo et al. 2018). A map that does not depend on the model cannot explain it.
A short checklist distils the chapter.

Start from the question and the audience. Global or local? For whom, and to decide what?
Prefer an interpretable model when it predicts about as well (Rudin 2019). Then the explanation is the model.
Check the outcome and the data first. A faithful explanation of a model of a censored or leaky outcome is still misleading.
Use held-out data, and repeat. Permutation importance on the test set; several shuffles; bootstrap or posterior uncertainty for the explanation itself.
Watch correlated features. Group them, shuffle them together, prefer ALE to PDP, and report that the credit between them is not identifiable.
Compare methods and models. If importance, Shapley values and coefficients disagree, find out why before telling a story.
Never read an explanation as a cause. Explanations describe what the model does with the data it was given; what would happen if we intervened is a causal question.

title: 12  Interpretable and explainable AI
section: 12.13 Where this fits in the decision loop
text:
12.13 Where this fits in the decision loop


  The decision loop, with this chapter's contribution highlighted
  A cycle of five boxes: data feed a model; the model produces information; people combine the information with values to make a decision; the decision leads to actions and outcomes, recorded as new data. The information box reads a prediction with an explanation, and an extra label between information and decision reads: check, contest, trust.
  
  Data
  
  Model
  any model, queried
  
  Information
  prediction + explanation
  
  Decision
  + values, human in the loop
  check · contest · trust
  
  Action and outcome
  recorded as new data

The decision loop. Explanations travel with the model's output to the people who decide, so that they can check it, contest it and decide how far to trust it.

This chapter adds nothing to a model’s accuracy. What it adds is the ability of the people in the loop to examine the information a model hands them. Seán can check what the forest relies on and notice when it leans on a proxy (BUN) or on a leak (the ONCO-1 genes). Emma can tell Aoife’s son why her risk is 49 % — mostly the base rate of AKI on Ward 7, slightly lowered by her moderate severity — and what the team will do about it. The governance committee can see how stable those explanations are. What can go wrong? An explanation can be faithful to a model of the wrong outcome, can split credit arbitrarily between correlated features, can look authoritative while being unstable, and can be mistaken for a statement about causes — the counterfactual that “full adherence would cut her risk” is the most tempting error of all. Who stays in control? The people who judge whether an explanation makes clinical sense, and who decide which changes are actionable and worth testing.

title: 12  Interpretable and explainable AI
text:
12.15 Exercises

Audiences. Write three explanations of Aoife’s 49 % risk: one for Emma, one for Aoife’s son and one for the hospital’s AI governance committee. What does each contain that the others do not?
The sign. A classifier is evaluated with the Brier score (lower is better) and with the AUC (higher is better). Write the permutation importance formula for each so that a positive value always means “the model relies on this feature”.
Shuffling together. In the Lab, shuffle ph.ecog and ph.karno together (the same row permutation for both columns) in the forest. Is the importance of the pair larger than the sum, smaller, or about equal to the two separate importances? Why?
Impurity versus permutation. Using the Ward 7 widget and Table 12.7, list the features whose rank changes most between impurity importance and permutation importance. Propose an explanation for each, using the correlations between features.
Extrapolation. In the ICE widget, choose the Karnofsky score and the forest. For which values are there few observed patients? Why should the PDP be read with care there? Would you expect ALE to differ most for ECOG or for age?
Censoring. Using lung_sim_complete.csv, compare the average time of patients with status == "alive" and "dead" within each ECOG level. Explain why a regression of time that ignores censoring underestimates the follow-up of patients in good condition more than that of patients in poor condition.
Shapley by brute force. Modify the Lab so that the linear model’s Shapley values for Aoife are computed with a background of 20, 100 and 300 training patients (in Python, repeat it for the forest of step 6, passing lambda d: rf7.predict(design(d)); it takes a few minutes). How much do they change? What does this say about reporting them to two decimal places?
Counterfactuals and causes. In the what-if widget, find two different counterfactuals that bring Aoife’s risk below 0.25. Which one would you present to the team, and what evidence would you need before acting on it?
Who needs which explanation? Suppose CellWorks uses a model to flag batches such as CW-118 before release. Add rows to Table 12.2 for the quality team and for the person who certifies the batch for release. Which methods of this chapter would each need, and what would you record in the batch documentation?







Selected answers





2. Brier score: \(\text{imp}_j = \frac{1}{N_s}\sum_m \text{Brier}(D^{(j,m)}) - \text{Brier}(D)\) (shuffled minus original). AUC: \(\text{imp}_j = \text{AUC}(D) - \frac{1}{N_s}\sum_m \text{AUC}(D^{(j,m)})\) (original minus shuffled).
3. Shuffling both removes the information that each could otherwise take from the other, so the importance of the pair is usually larger than either one alone, and can be larger than their sum when the model uses them as substitutes. This is why correlated features should be reported as a group.
4. BUN drops sharply: it is correlated with SOFA and baseline creatinine, which carry its information when it is shuffled, and impurity importance rewards it for being split on during training. Site rises a little in the linear model, which uses one coefficient per site, and is small in the forest.
6. Among patients in good condition (low ECOG) most are still alive at the end of follow-up, so their recorded time is a lower bound of their survival; among patients in poor condition most have died, so their time is close to their true survival. Ignoring censoring therefore shortens the apparent survival of the healthier patients most — and makes the effect of ECOG look smaller than it would be for survival.
8. For example: MAP 76 mmHg with adherence 1.00, or MAP 86 mmHg with adherence 0.85. Whichever is presented, the adherence part is confounded by severity in observational data; acting on it requires a causal estimate — from a randomised trial or a carefully adjusted analysis (Chapter 13) — and the MAP target requires clinical judgement about how it would be reached and what else would change.

title: 12  Interpretable and explainable AI
text:
12.16 Summary

Interpretability is the ability to understand a model from its structure; explainability methods build simpler descriptions of a model’s behaviour. Both are relative to an audience and a purpose. When an interpretable model predicts about as well, prefer it.
Explanations matter beyond the bedside. The AI Act requires high-risk systems — most AI in medical devices among them — to be interpretable by their deployers (Article 13) and designed for human oversight (Article 14); the GDPR, the MDR, the FDA, Health Canada and MHRA principles, the EMA and draft GMP rules ask for transparency in their own terms. Explanations also catch leaks and shortcuts, support fairness audits and generate scientific hypotheses.
Methods are model-specific (coefficients, tree rules, impurity importance) or model-agnostic (they only query the model); intrinsic (the model is interpretable by design) or post hoc; and global (the whole model) or local (one prediction).
Permutation importance is the increase in error on held-out data when a feature is shuffled (shuffled minus original for an error; original minus shuffled for a score). Correlated features share or steal credit; group them.
Partial dependence shows the average prediction as a feature varies; ICE curves show one curve per patient and reveal heterogeneity. Beware of extrapolation; use ALE for correlated features.
The H statistic measures departures from additivity; read the normalised and the unnormalised versions together. VIVID shows importance and interactions in one display; the R package vivid computes it (vivi()) and draws heatmaps, networks and generalised partial dependence pairs plots.
Shapley values share one prediction among the features so that the contributions add up to the prediction minus the average; for linear and logistic models they are \(\beta_j(x_j - \bar x_j)\). They depend on the background data.
Counterfactual explanations say what change would alter the model’s output; they describe the model, not the effect of an intervention.
Explanations are estimates with uncertainty (bootstrap, BART posteriors summarised with bartMan); a value-suppressing uncertainty palette shows value and uncertainty together. It shows which numbers are stable, not whether they measure the right thing: BART inclusion proportions with many trees say little about importance.
An explanation is only as good as the model and the outcome it explains — time with censoring ignored is not survival — and it is never a statement about causes.

title: 13  From prediction to causation
text:
How to use this chapter






Starting here?





This chapter borrows a few ideas from earlier chapters. In brief:

Observational and experimental data (Definition 1.2). Observational data record what happened in routine care; experimental data come from a design in which the investigator assigns the exposure, ideally at random, as in the ONCO-1 trial.
Confounding, first look (Section 1.10). On Ward 7, sicker patients (higher SOFA score) receive less of the care protocol and have larger creatinine rises. A regression of the creatinine rise on adherence alone gives −0.53 per unit of adherence; adding SOFA gives −0.30; the value used to simulate the data is −0.28.
Coefficients (Chapter 4, Chapter 5). In a linear model, \(\beta_j\) is the expected difference in the outcome between two patients who differ by one unit in \(x_j\) and are alike in the other predictors in the model; in a logistic model \(e^{\beta_j}\) is an odds ratio. Both are associations.
Expectation (Chapter 2). \(\mathbb{E}[Y]\) is the long-run average of \(Y\); \(\mathbb{E}[Y \mid A = 1]\) is the average among those with \(A = 1\).
Train and test sets, leakage (Section 1.8, Chapter 3). Predictive models are judged on patients they have not seen. In ONCO-1, genes 08, 14 and 19 are noisy copies of the outcome (leakage); the genes that truly influence shrinkage are 01, 05 and 12.

title: 13  From prediction to causation
text:
13.1 Three kinds of question
Every chapter so far has built a model that predicts: from what is known about a patient today, estimate what will happen to her. Prediction is enormously useful — it tells Emma that Aoife’s risk is close to the threshold and Tomás’s is low — but it is only one of three things we ask of data (Hernán, Hsu, and Healy 2019):

Predict. What will happen to this patient? A good prediction uses any feature that carries information, whatever the reason it carries it. It is judged on new patients, by its error, its discrimination and its calibration (Chapters 3–8).
Explain (or describe). What patterns are there in the data, and how do groups differ? How many patients developed AKI in each hospital; which genes are associated with response; which patients form natural groups (Chapters 4, 10–12). These are summaries of the world as it was.
Intervene. What would happen if we changed something? If we gave chemotherapy, stopped a drug, raised protocol adherence, funded a nurse. This is a causal question: it asks about a world we did not observe.

The third kind is the one decisions are made of: every alternative in Emma’s set \(\mathcal{A}\) is an action, and choosing among actions needs to know what each action would cause. In practice the “explain” kind often slides quietly into the third. “Patients with high adherence do better” is a description; “so raising adherence will make patients do better” is a causal claim that the description alone does not support.
A classic example comes from the lecture hall. Yellow-stained fingers predict lung cancer very well: people with them are many times more likely to develop it. A risk model could use them with profit. But nobody would prevent lung cancer by scrubbing fingers clean, because the stains do not cause the cancer. Both are consequences of a third factor, smoking, whose causal role was established by careful epidemiology (Doll and Hill 1950; Hill 1965). Yellow fingers are a good predictor and a useless intervention target.






flowchart TD

    Q1 -- "yes" --> I["INTERVENE<br/>What would happen if we did A?<br/>Needs a trial, or a causal diagram<br/>plus adjustment (this chapter)"]
    Q1 -- "no" --> Q2{"Do you need a number for a new person<br/>whose outcome is not yet known?"}
    Q2 -- "yes" --> P["PREDICT<br/>What will happen to this person?<br/>Supervised learning, judged on unseen data<br/>(Chapters 3 to 8)"]
    Q2 -- "no" --> E["EXPLAIN / DESCRIBE<br/>What patterns are in the data?<br/>Associations, groups, explanations<br/>(Chapters 4, 10 to 12)"]
    P --> Q3{"Will the prediction be used<br/>to choose a treatment?"}

Figure 13.1: Which question do I have? Start from what you will do with the answer. A prediction that will be used to choose a treatment is, underneath, a question about intervening.






Seán’s hospital wants a model to decide which ICU patients should have their vancomycin dose reduced to protect their kidneys. A vendor offers a model that predicts AKI with an AUC of 0.85. Which kind of question is the hospital really asking?

Predict: the model predicts AKI well, so it answers the question It answers “who is at risk under current care?”. The hospital wants to know for whom reducing the dose would lower that risk — a different quantity, which the AUC does not measure.
Intervene: they need to know what would happen to each patient’s kidneys if the dose were reduced Correct. The model will be used to choose an action, so the question underneath is causal. A high-risk patient may be high-risk for reasons a dose change cannot touch.
Explain: they want to understand why some patients develop AKI Understanding is welcome, but the hospital will act on the answer, patient by patient. That makes it an intervention question.

title: 13  From prediction to causation
text:
13.2 Interventions and counterfactuals
To ask causal questions precisely we need a language for “what would happen if”. The one used in medicine and epidemiology is that of potential outcomes, developed by Neyman for experiments (Splawa-Neyman, Dabrowska, and Speed 1990) and by Rubin for observational studies (Rubin 1974; Holland 1986; Hernán and Robins 2020).

Definition 13.1 (Intervention and counterfactual) An intervention sets a variable to a chosen value — give chemotherapy, set adherence to 90 % — instead of letting it take the value it would have taken on its own. A counterfactual is a statement about what would have happened under an intervention that did not, in fact, take place: “had Aoife received the bundle, her creatinine would have…”.

Write \(A\) for the treatment (or exposure) and \(Y\) for the outcome. In ONCO-1, \(A = 1\) means chemotherapy and \(A = 0\) none; \(Y\) is tumour shrinkage in percent.

Definition 13.2 (Potential outcomes) Each patient \(i\) has two potential outcomes: \(Y_i(1)\), the outcome she would have if treated, and \(Y_i(0)\), the outcome she would have if not treated. For an exposure with many levels, such as protocol adherence, there is one potential outcome \(Y_i(a)\) for every level \(a\). The individual causal effect is the difference \(Y_i(1) - Y_i(0)\).

Patient #0042 (trial record P5440), the 37-year-old with a grade G1 tumour whom you met in Chapters 4 and 5, received chemotherapy in ONCO-1, and her tumour shrank by 36.6 %: that is \(Y_{0042}(1)\). We will never observe \(Y_{0042}(0)\), the shrinkage her tumour would have shown without chemotherapy, because she cannot both receive and not receive it. Her near twin #0917 (P9541: same grade, dose and performance score, 46 years old) shrank by only 20.4 %, and the lasso logistic model of Chapter 5 gave them probabilities of a high response of 0.75 and 0.18. Those are predictions of what happens under chemotherapy; neither says what chemotherapy did for either of them. This is the fundamental problem of causal inference (Holland 1986): for every patient, at most one potential outcome is observed; the others are counterfactual. Individual causal effects are therefore never seen directly.
Only in a simulation can we fill in both columns, because there we wrote the rules that generate the outcome and can rerun them with the exposure changed while keeping everything else about each patient the same (Section 13.6 explains how). Table 13.1 shows six past Ward 7 patients with their recorded adherence and creatinine change, and two of their potential outcomes, at 50 % and at 90 % adherence.

Look at patient ICU_0048. Her recorded adherence was 0.907, very close to 90 %, and her observed change (0.053) is almost exactly her \(Y(0.9)\) (0.055). This is consistency: the observed outcome is the potential outcome under the exposure actually received. In the last column every patient has the same effect, −0.112 mg/dL, because the simulator’s rule is a straight line with no interactions (\(-0.28 \times 0.4\)). Real patients surely differ in how much they benefit.
Since individual effects cannot be observed, we aim at averages.

Definition 13.3 (Average and conditional average treatment effects) The average treatment effect (ATE) in a population is \[
\text{ATE} = \mathbb{E}[Y(1)] - \mathbb{E}[Y(0)] ,
\qquad(13.1)\] the difference between the average outcome if everyone were treated and the average outcome if no one were. The conditional average treatment effect (CATE) is the same contrast within a subgroup of patients with features \(\mathbf{x}\): \(\tau(\mathbf{x}) = \mathbb{E}[Y(1) - Y(0) \mid \mathbf{X} = \mathbf{x}]\).

Compare Equation 13.1 with what data show directly: \[
\mathbb{E}[Y \mid A = 1] - \mathbb{E}[Y \mid A = 0] ,
\qquad(13.2)\] the difference between the average outcome of those who happened to be treated and those who happened not to be. Equation 13.1 compares the same population under two interventions; Equation 13.2 compares two different groups of people. The two coincide only when the treated and untreated are alike in everything that affects the outcome — when they are exchangeable. On Ward 7 they are not: patients with high adherence are, on average, less sick.
Hernán and Robins (2020) list three conditions under which a causal effect can be computed from data:

Exchangeability: given the measured covariates, who received which treatment is unrelated to the potential outcomes (no unmeasured confounding).
Positivity: every kind of patient had a real chance of receiving each treatment.
Consistency: the treatment is defined clearly enough that “the outcome under \(A = a\)” means one thing, and the observed outcome equals the potential outcome under the treatment received.

Consistency sounds pedantic until you try a real question. In Chapter 4 Seán asked whether raising Aoife’s albumin would protect her kidneys. Albumin can be higher because a patient is less inflamed, better nourished or because she received an albumin infusion; these are different interventions, which may have different effects. A dataset of naturally varying albumin levels says little about infusions. Before asking “what is the effect of \(A\)?”, say exactly what you would do.

An analyst says: “To find the effect of chemotherapy for patient #0917, compare her tumour shrinkage under chemotherapy with her shrinkage without it.” What is the difficulty?

There is none; it is the standard way of measuring an individual effect It is the definition of an individual effect, but it cannot be carried out: patient #0917 can be observed under only one of the two conditions.
Only one of the two potential outcomes can ever be observed for her Correct. This is the fundamental problem of causal inference. We can estimate average effects, in the whole population or in subgroups like hers, but her individual effect remains unobserved.
Tumour shrinkage is measured with error Measurement error adds noise, but the deeper problem would remain even with perfect measurement: one of the two outcomes does not exist in the data.
The trial is too small No sample size can reveal both potential outcomes of the same patient.

text:
13.4 Randomisation: ONCO-1
If confounding is the problem, the cleanest solution is to remove the arrows into the treatment. That is what a coin does.

Definition 13.9 (Randomisation) In a randomised experiment the treatment is assigned by a chance mechanism that the investigators control and that is unrelated to any characteristic of the patients. Then no arrow enters \(A\) except from the coin, there is no backdoor path, and treated and untreated groups are exchangeable — for measured and unmeasured characteristics alike (Fisher 1935; Hernán and Robins 2020, ch. 2).






  
  
  Coin (1:1)
  Chemotherapy
  Tumour shrinkage
  Age, grade, performance status,genes 01, 05, 12, unmeasured factors
  
  
  
  
  
  
  
  ✕




Figure 13.4: In ONCO-1 a coin decided who received chemotherapy, so nothing about the patient points into the treatment.



In the ONCO-1 sample of 1000 patients, 496 were randomised to chemotherapy and 504 to no chemotherapy. Randomisation does not make the two arms identical, but it makes their differences small and due to chance alone. A standard way to check is the standardised mean difference (SMD): the difference between the arms’ means divided by the pooled standard deviation. Values below about 0.1 are usually taken as good balance (Austin 2011). The first column of Table 13.3 shows that every covariate is balanced in the trial.
Because the arms are exchangeable, the simplest comparison estimates the average treatment effect: average shrinkage was 37.8 % with chemotherapy and 4.9 % without, a difference of 32.9 percentage points (95 % confidence interval 31.8 to 34.0). No model, no adjustment, no assumption about which genes matter — that is the power of randomisation. It is why regulators ask for randomised trials before approving treatments, and why a new drug discovered with AI still has to pass one (Chapter 18 returns to this).
Randomisation has limits too. Trials are expensive and slow; they enrol selected patients, who may differ from those treated in practice; some exposures (smoking, severity, a hospital’s staffing) cannot be randomised; and patients do not always take the treatment they were assigned. For these reasons most of the data a health system holds are observational, and the next section is about analysing them as if they came from a trial.

The trial’s answer. In ONCO-1 treatment was randomised, so the difference between the average shrinkage of the two arms estimates the effect of chemotherapy. Complete the last line.

RPython

















The first term already uses mean(); the second must use the same function.


mean(treated) - mean(control)


















The first term already uses .mean(); the second must use the same method.


treated.mean() - control.mean()






Why does randomisation remove confounding even by factors nobody measured?

Because randomised trials measure every relevant variable No trial measures everything. The point is that it does not need to.
Because a coin cannot depend on the patient’s characteristics, so no backdoor path into the treatment exists Correct. Whatever influences the outcome — measured or not — has the same distribution in both arms, apart from chance, which the confidence interval accounts for.
Because the arms are made exactly equal on every characteristic Randomisation balances characteristics only on average; in any one trial small chance differences remain, as the SMDs show.
Because trials are analysed with regression models The simple difference in means is already unbiased in a randomised trial; regression may add precision but is not what removes confounding.

title: 13  From prediction to causation
text:
13.5 Adjustment without randomisation
When the treatment was not randomised, we try to make the comparison fair by adjustment: comparing treated and untreated patients who are alike in every confounder. The backdoor criterion tells us which variables to adjust for; this section shows how. All methods here rest on the same assumption — that the chosen set blocks every backdoor path (no unmeasured confounding) — and they differ in how they use the data.

13.5.1 Regression adjustment on Ward 7
The simplest way is the one Chapter 1 used: put the confounders in a regression model with the treatment. If the model’s form is right, the treatment coefficient estimates the effect. Table 13.2 shows the adherence coefficient under several adjustment sets, with the value used in the simulation for comparison.

Regression adjustment works well when the outcome model is right. With many confounders, non-linear relationships or a binary treatment given to very different kinds of patients, it is easy to get the model wrong without noticing. The next three methods move the effort from modelling the outcome to modelling the treatment.


13.5.2 ONCO-1 in routine practice
To have a benchmark, we turn the ONCO-1 trial into an observational study. Imagine that, instead of a coin, oncologists had chosen: they offered chemotherapy more often to younger and fitter patients, to higher-grade tumours and to patients with low expression of gene_05 (which a previous study had linked with poor response). We mimic this by keeping each trial patient with a probability that depends on the arm and on these characteristics (sim_ch13_onco1_routine.R). The result, onco1_routine.csv, has 509 patients, 252 of them treated. Since every patient comes from the trial, we know what the right answer should be: the trial’s 32.9 percentage points.
In this “routine practice” dataset, treated patients are fitter (mean performance score 0.40 against 0.67) and have lower gene_05, both of which predict better shrinkage. The naive comparison gives 38.7 percentage points, an overestimate of about 6 points: part of the apparent benefit is the better prognosis of the patients oncologists chose to treat.

Definition 13.10 (Propensity score) The propensity score of a patient with covariates \(\mathbf{x}\) is her probability of receiving the treatment, \(e(\mathbf{x}) = P(A = 1 \mid \mathbf{X} = \mathbf{x})\). Rosenbaum and Rubin (1983) showed that if adjusting for \(\mathbf{X}\) removes confounding, then so does adjusting for the single number \(e(\mathbf{X})\): treated and untreated patients with the same propensity score are, on average, alike in all the covariates that went into it.

In observational data the propensity score is unknown, so we estimate it, usually with a logistic regression of the treatment on the confounders (Chapter 5). It is a model of the doctors’ decision, not of the outcome. Two warnings: put in the confounders (causes of treatment that also affect the outcome), not variables caused by the treatment — dose_intensity is zero for every untreated patient and would predict treatment perfectly, but it is a consequence of the decision; and do not judge the propensity model by its AUC, because what matters is the balance it achieves (Austin 2011).
Look at the estimated scores before going further (Figure 13.5). For an adjustment to be possible, the two histograms must overlap: for every kind of treated patient there must be untreated patients with a similar score, and vice versa. This is positivity in practice. Where the groups do not overlap, any method must extrapolate.








Figure 13.5: Estimated propensity scores in ONCO-1 routine practice. Treated patients (top) tend to have high scores, untreated (bottom) low ones; the overlap in the middle is where fair comparisons can be made.





Three ways of using the propensity score follow.

Definition 13.11 (Inverse probability weighting (IPW)) Inverse probability weighting gives each treated patient the weight \(w_i = 1/e(\mathbf{x}_i)\) and each untreated patient \(w_i = 1/\{1 - e(\mathbf{x}_i)\}\), then compares weighted averages: \[
\widehat{\text{ATE}}_{\text{IPW}} =
\frac{\sum_{i:A_i=1} w_i\, y_i}{\sum_{i:A_i=1} w_i} -
\frac{\sum_{i:A_i=0} w_i\, y_i}{\sum_{i:A_i=0} w_i} .
\qquad(13.3)\] The weighting creates a pseudo-population in which treatment no longer depends on the covariates, as in a trial (Hernán and Robins 2020, ch. 12; Austin 2011).

The intuition: a treated patient with \(e(\mathbf{x}) = 0.2\) belongs to a kind of patient who usually goes untreated; she is rare in the treated group, so she must stand in for five patients like her. A treated patient with \(e(\mathbf{x}) = 0.9\) represents only about one.

Definition 13.12 (Matching) Matching pairs each treated patient with one (or more) untreated patients who are similar — here, whose propensity scores are close — and discards those without a good partner. The outcome is then compared within pairs. Because it keeps the treated patients and finds controls for them, matching usually estimates the effect in the treated (ATT) rather than the ATE (Stuart 2010).

Stratification on the propensity score (comparing treated and untreated within, say, its fifths) is a fourth option with the same logic (Rosenbaum and Rubin 1983). Whatever the method, check whether it actually balanced the covariates: Table 13.3 shows the SMDs before and after.

      Plot.link(rows, {x1: "lo", x2: "hi", y1: "label", y2: "label", stroke: "#1f6f8b", strokeWidth: 6, strokeOpacity: 0.45}),
      Plot.dot(rows, {x: "mean", y: "label", r: 5, fill: "#1f6f8b"}),

    ]
  });
}







Plot.plot({
  height: 220, grid: true,
  x: {domain: [0, 1], label: "Estimated propensity score (one simulated dataset)"},
  y: {label: "Patients"},
  fy: {label: null, axis: null},
  color: {domain: ["chemotherapy", "no chemotherapy"], range: ["#1f6f8b", "#b35c00"], legend: true},
  marks: [
    Plot.rectY(selData.ps.filter(d => d.k === selK).map(d => ({...d, arm: d.chemo === 1 ? "chemotherapy" : "no chemotherapy"})),
      Plot.binX({y: "count"}, {x: "ps", fy: "arm", fill: "arm", thresholds: d3.range(0, 1.0001, 0.05)})),
    Plot.ruleY([0])
  ]
})








As selection grows, the propensity scores of the two groups pull apart towards 0 and 1. A few treated patients with scores near 0 (or untreated near 1) receive enormous weights, and IPW becomes unstable: positivity is almost violated. Regression adjustment stays tight here because its model happens to match how these data were generated; in real data that would be an assumption, and with little overlap it would be extrapolating silently. Matching copes by discarding the patients it cannot match, which changes the population the answer describes. When overlap is poor, the honest conclusion is often that the data cannot answer the question for everyone.

Weight the patients. The propensity score ps of every patient in ONCO-1 routine practice has already been estimated with a logistic regression on age, grade, performance score and gene_05. Complete the weights for the untreated patients; the last lines compute the IPW estimate.

RPython

















The probability of not being treated is 1 - ps.


w <- ifelse(obs$chemo == 1, 1 / ps, 1 / (1 - ps))


















The probability of not being treated is 1 - ps.


w = np.where(obs["chemo"] == 1, 1 / ps, 1 / (1 - ps))






In an observational dataset, almost every patient with a performance score of 2 was left untreated (estimated propensity scores below 0.02). What is the main consequence for IPW?

None: IPW handles any propensity score automatically The formula runs, but the few treated patients with score 2 get weights above 50 and dominate the estimate.
Positivity is nearly violated: a handful of patients receive huge weights, and the estimate for that group rests on almost no data Correct. Remedies include restricting the question to patients with overlap, matching with a caliper, or trimming extreme weights — each of which changes the population the answer describes.
The propensity model has a low AUC and must be replaced The opposite: near-perfect prediction of treatment is exactly what signals a positivity problem. A propensity model is judged by balance and overlap, not by AUC.


All of these methods share an unverifiable assumption: that the measured covariates include every confounder. A careful analysis therefore starts by writing down the trial it would have liked to run — eligibility, treatment strategies, start of follow-up, outcome — and then emulates that target trial with the observational data (Hernán and Robins 2016), and ends with a sensitivity analysis of how strong an unmeasured confounder would have to be to change the conclusion (VanderWeele and Ding 2017). Methods that estimate how effects vary between patients, \(\tau(\mathbf{x})\), such as causal forests (Wager and Athey 2018) and their Bayesian versions for several treatments and correlated outcomes at once (Sarti 2026), rest on the same assumptions.

title: 13  From prediction to causation
text:
13.6 Using simulated truth
Real data never reveal the true effect, so we cannot check whether an adjustment worked. Simulated data can, and this book’s running examples were built so that you can. The Ward 7 simulator is a structural causal model: a list of equations, one per variable, each computing the variable from its causes plus random noise (Pearl 2009). The file ward7_scm.R rewrites it as a function that reproduces icu_aki.csv exactly and accepts an intervention: it sets a variable to a chosen value for every patient while keeping each patient’s random noise unchanged. Running it twice, with adherence set to 1 and to 0, gives both potential outcomes for all 1 250 patients, and their average difference is the true ATE: −0.28 per unit of adherence.
Now return to the committee’s question: bring every patient up to at least 90 % adherence. In the data, this raises adherence by 21 percentage points on average (patients already above 90 % are unchanged). Table 13.5 compares the truth, obtained by running the simulator under the policy, with what the naive and the SOFA-adjusted coefficients would predict.

The simulator also shows that a good predictor can give the wrong effect. Table 13.6 fits four linear models on the book’s shared training set and evaluates them on the test set (Chapter 3). The model with every variable except SOFA predicts far better than the SOFA-only model — blood pressure, BUN, CRP and albumin carry plenty of information — yet its adherence coefficient is badly confounded. The last row is the linear regression (OLS) of Chapter 4, with the same ten predictors and the same test MAE as in the model ledger (0.141 mg/dL); adherence + SOFA (0.187) predicts about as well as the SOFA-only line of Chapter 1 (0.191). Simulated truth is a laboratory, not a substitute for thinking: it shows whether a method recovers an effect when its assumptions hold, and how badly it fails when they do not. title: 13  From prediction to causation
text:
13.7 What this means for decisions
Prediction models used for intervention decisions. Many clinical models are built to predict an outcome and then used to decide who should be treated. Two things can go wrong. First, a model trained on routinely treated patients predicts risk under current care, treatment included. A famous example: a model of pneumonia mortality learned that patients with asthma had lower risk, because they were routinely sent straight to intensive care; used to decide who could go home, it would have sent the most vulnerable patients away (Caruana et al. 2015). Second, high risk is not the same as high benefit: the patients most likely to develop AKI may be those whose kidneys a bundle can help least. Choosing whom to treat needs the effect of treatment, \(\tau(\mathbf{x})\), or at least risk without treatment, estimated with causal methods (Geloven et al. 2020).
The Table 2 fallacy. A paper reports a multivariable model in “Table 2” and readers interpret every coefficient as an effect. Only the coefficient of the variable the model was built for has a chance of being causal; the others are adjusted for a set chosen with someone else in mind (Westreich and Greenland 2013). Ward 7 shows it numerically. In the regression of the creatinine change on all recorded variables, the SOFA coefficient is 0.041 — close to the simulator’s direct effect of SOFA, 0.04, because the model holds blood pressure, BUN, CRP, albumin and adherence fixed. But a patient one SOFA point sicker also has lower blood pressure, higher BUN and CRP, lower albumin and less adherence; running the simulator with SOFA raised by one gives a total effect of 0.060, about 45 % larger. Each question needs its own adjustment set, and a single model rarely answers more than one.
Explanations are not causes. Methods that explain a predictive model — feature importance, SHAP values, counterfactual explanations — describe how the model uses its inputs. They inherit every confounding of the data: a model could explain its prediction of lung cancer by yellow fingers. Chapter 12 treats these methods; read their output as hypotheses for a causal analysis, not as its result.

A published table reports a multivariable logistic model of AKI built to estimate the effect of a nephrotoxic antibiotic, adjusting for age, severity, baseline creatinine and blood pressure. The odds ratio for blood pressure is 0.80 per 10 mmHg. A reader concludes that raising blood pressure by 10 mmHg would cut the odds of AKI by 20 %. What is the problem?

None: every coefficient in an adjusted model is an adjusted effect This is the Table 2 fallacy. The adjustment set was chosen for the antibiotic, not for blood pressure.
The adjustment set was chosen for the antibiotic; for blood pressure it may adjust for mediators or miss its own confounders Correct. Severity may confound blood pressure in ways the model does not handle, and the antibiotic may lie on a path from blood pressure. Each exposure needs its own diagram and adjustment set — and “raising blood pressure” needs a defined intervention.
Odds ratios cannot be interpreted in logistic regression They can be interpreted as associations; the issue is whether this one is a causal effect.


So what should Emma and Seán tell the committee? Not “the consultancy’s coefficient says we will halve AKI”. Something like: the raw audit and the risk model exaggerate the benefit of adherence because sicker patients receive less of the protocol; after adjusting for severity, our best estimate is about −0.3 mg/dL per unit of adherence, so the proposed nurse would prevent roughly one AKI case for every 11 patients — if severity is the only important confounder. If the decision is expensive, the most reliable answer would come from randomising wards or months to the new nurse.

title: 13  From prediction to causation
section: 13.8 Where this fits in the decision loop
text:
13.8 Where this fits in the decision loop


  The decision loop
  A cycle of five boxes: data feed a model; the model produces information; people combine the information with values to make a decision; the decision leads to actions and outcomes, which are recorded as new data. In this chapter the model box holds a causal diagram plus an adjustment method or a randomised comparison, and the information box holds the effect of each alternative.
  
  
  Data
  trial or routine care
  
  Model
  causal diagram +
  randomisation or adjustment
  
  Information
  what each alternative
  would cause
  
  Decision
  + values, human in the loop
  
  Action and outcome
  recorded as new data
  
  
  
  
  

The decision loop. A decision compares alternatives, so the information it needs is causal: what each alternative would bring about.

Chapter 1 defined a decision as a choice among alternatives in \(\mathcal{A}\), made with knowledge \(\mathcal{K}\) about their consequences. Consequences of an alternative is another name for potential outcomes. A predictive model supplies one kind of knowledge — what is likely to happen under current practice — and that is often enough: to decide whom to watch closely tonight, to plan dialysis capacity, to warn a family. But when the alternatives are actions whose effects are uncertain, the information link of the decision-quality chain needs causal reasoning: a randomised comparison when it can be had, and otherwise a diagram that makes the assumptions explicit, an adjustment that respects it, and a check of overlap and balance. The values — how much one AKI avoided is worth a nurse’s salary — still belong to people.

RPython

title: 13  From prediction to causation
text:
13.10 Exercises

Name the question. For each running example (Ward 7, ONCO-1, HomeBeat, CellWorks), write one predict, one explain and one intervene question. For the intervene question, state the intervention precisely enough to satisfy consistency.
Draw it. Draw a DAG for the effect of an influenza vaccine on hospital admission in older adults, including frailty (frail people are vaccinated less often and admitted more often) and a variable of your choice that is a collider. Which variables would you adjust for?
Mediator or confounder? On Ward 7, Seán proposes to adjust the effect of adherence for “number of nephrotoxic drugs stopped in the first 24 hours”. Using Ward 7, extended, explain why this would underestimate the total effect, and when the adjusted number could still be useful.
Collider by selection. In the DAG widget’s data (ward7_dag.csv), estimate the effect of adherence adjusting for SOFA only among patients with seven or more creatinine tests. Compare with the estimate in all patients and explain the difference.
Proxies. Regress the Ward 7 creatinine change on adherence and CRP only. Then on adherence, CRP, BUN, blood pressure and albumin. Why does the estimate approach, but not reach, the SOFA-adjusted one?
Remove a confounder. In the Lab, drop gene_05 from the propensity model. Recompute the IPW estimate and the balance table. What happened, and why could no diagnostic computed from the data alone have warned you?
Policy arithmetic. Using Table 13.5, how many patients must reach 90 % adherence for one AKI case to be avoided, according to the truth and according to the naive coefficient? If a protocol nurse costs as much as treating 40 cases of AKI per year and Ward 7 admits 1 250 patients a year, is the nurse worth it under each answer?
Table 2. Choose a published clinical paper with a multivariable regression table. Which coefficient was the model built for? For one other coefficient, sketch a DAG showing why it might not be a causal effect.







Selected answers





3. The number of nephrotoxic drugs stopped is caused by adherence and affects the outcome: a mediator. Adjusting for it removes the part of the effect that works through stopping drugs, giving roughly the direct effect (about −0.19 in Ward 7, extended, against a total of −0.28). It is useful if the question is how much of the benefit comes from stopping drugs — a mediation question, which needs its own assumptions.
4. Restricting to patients with many tests selects on a collider. Among them, a patient with low adherence must have reached many tests through a rising creatinine, so low adherence and high creatinine appear together more often than they should, and the estimate is pushed away from the truth.
5. CRP, BUN, blood pressure and albumin all depend on SOFA, so adjusting for them removes part of the confounding. But each also has its own noise, so together they do not reproduce SOFA exactly: residual confounding remains (−0.40 with every variable except SOFA).
6. gene_05 is a strong confounder in routine practice; without it the weights do not remove its imbalance and the estimate moves back towards the naive one. The balance table would look good for the covariates still in the model — balance can only be checked for what was measured and included, which is why the list of confounders must come from subject-matter knowledge, drawn as a DAG.
7. True: the policy avoids about 85 cases per 1 000 patients, one for every 12 patients, or about 106 a year. Naive: 156 per 1 000, one for every 6, or about 195 a year. With the stated cost, the nurse pays for itself under both answers, but the margin under the truth is about half of what the naive analysis promises — and with a costlier intervention the two answers could lead to opposite decisions.

title: 13  From prediction to causation
text:
13.11 Summary

Data answer three kinds of question: predict (what will happen?), explain (what patterns are there?) and intervene (what would happen if we acted?). Decisions are made of the third kind.
Potential outcomes \(Y(1)\) and \(Y(0)\) define causal effects; only one is observed per patient, so we estimate averages such as the ATE, \(\mathbb{E}[Y(1)] - \mathbb{E}[Y(0)]\), and the CATE. Identification needs exchangeability, positivity and consistency.
A DAG makes causal assumptions explicit. Confounders open backdoor paths and must be adjusted for; mediators carry the effect and must not be, for a total effect; colliders are closed until adjusted for or selected on. The backdoor criterion says which sets suffice.
Randomisation removes every arrow into the treatment, measured or not; in ONCO-1 a simple difference in means estimates the effect.
Without randomisation, regression adjustment, propensity scores, inverse probability weighting and matching can recover the effect if no confounder is missing. Check overlap and balance; poor overlap makes weights unstable and answers narrower.
Simulated truth lets us test methods: on Ward 7 the naive estimate doubles the benefit of adherence, and a model can predict well while giving a confounded coefficient.
Do not read every coefficient in a model as an effect (Table 2 fallacy), and do not use a prediction of risk under current care as if it were a prediction of benefit.

title: 14  Sequential decisions: reinforcement learning
text:
How to use this chapter






Starting here?





This chapter borrows a few ideas from earlier chapters. In brief:

Decisions (Definition 1.4, Section 1.5). A decision chooses one alternative \(a\) from a set \(\mathcal{A}\) using what is known, \(\mathcal{K}\). With probabilities and values, the best alternative is the one with the highest expected value — the probability-weighted average of the scores of its consequences.
Expectation and the Bernoulli distribution (Chapter 2). \(\mathbb{E}[Y]\) is the long-run average of \(Y\); a yes/no outcome with probability \(p\) of “yes” has expectation \(p\). Information has value only if it can change a decision (value of information).
The beta posterior (Chapter 8). Starting from a \(\text{Beta}(1, 1)\) (flat) prior for a proportion and observing \(k\) successes in \(n\) trials gives a \(\text{Beta}(1 + k,\, 1 + n - k)\) posterior.
Observational data and confounding (Definition 1.2, Section 1.10, Chapter 13). In routine care, treatment follows the patient’s condition, so comparing treated and untreated patients mixes the effect of treatment with the reasons for it. Causal estimates need exchangeability (no unmeasured confounding) and positivity (every kind of patient had a chance of each treatment).
Learning loop (Section 1.6). Guess, mark how wrong the guess is, adjust, repeat. Gradient descent in Chapter 7 uses a learning rate \(\eta\) to set the size of each adjustment.

title: 14  Sequential decisions: reinforcement learning
text:
14.1 Decisions that come back
Every decision in this book so far has been taken once. Emma decided on Monday night whether to start the kidney-protective bundle for Aoife; a model supplied a probability, the values supplied a threshold, and the decision was made (Section 1.5). Real care rarely stops there. On Tuesday morning Aoife’s creatinine is measured again and the team decides about fluids; the fluids change her blood pressure and her kidneys; on Wednesday the next creatinine reflects both her illness and Tuesday’s choice. Giving too little fluid risks under-perfusing the kidneys, giving too much risks fluid overload, and the right amount today depends on what was given yesterday. The insulin infusion works the same way, every two hours instead of every day.
Three features make these problems different from the prediction problems of Chapters 3–9:

Actions change the data. The glucose reading at 10 am depends on the rate chosen at 8 am. A model of “glucose next” that ignores the action is a model of the past policy, not of the patient.
Consequences are delayed. A large insulin increase may look good for two hours and cause hypoglycaemia four hours later. Credit and blame must be spread over a sequence of actions.
Nobody labels the right action. There is no column “correct rate” in the records, only what was done and what followed. The learner must discover good actions from their consequences.

Reinforcement learning (RL) is the branch of machine learning built for exactly this setting: an agent learns, from interaction and reward, a rule for acting that does well over time (Sutton and Barto 2018). Chapter 1 met it in one paragraph (Section 1.6.2); this chapter opens it up.

Definition 14.1 (Agent, environment, state, action, reward) An agent is whatever chooses the actions: a clinician, a protocol, an algorithm. The environment is everything the agent acts on and cannot fully control — here, the patient. At each decision time \(t\) the agent observes the state \(s_t\), a summary of what is known that matters for what happens next; it takes an action \(a_t\) from a set \(\mathcal{A}\); the environment responds by moving to a new state \(s_{t+1}\) and returning a reward \(r_{t+1}\), a number that scores how good that step was. The cycle then repeats (Sutton and Barto 2018, ch. 3).

The action set is Chapter 1’s set of alternatives, \(\mathcal{A}\), and the action \(a_t\) is the chosen alternative \(a\) — now chosen once per time step instead of once in total. Figure 14.1 draws the cycle for Aoife’s infusion.

Figure 14.1: The agent–environment loop for Aoife’s insulin infusion. The agent sees the state, acts, and receives a new state and a reward; the policy is the rule that maps states to actions.




Definition 14.2 (Policy) A policy is a rule for choosing actions from states. A deterministic policy names one action for each state; a stochastic policy gives a probability \(\pi(a \mid s)\) to each action \(a\) in state \(s\). A bedside protocol (“above 10 mmol/L increase, below 6 decrease, otherwise keep”) is a deterministic policy written by people; reinforcement learning learns a policy from rewards (Sutton and Barto 2018, ch. 3).

The symbol \(\pi\) meant a prevalence in Chapter 2; in this chapter, as everywhere in the reinforcement-learning literature, it means a policy. The reward also needs a word of warning before we use it. It is a design choice, not a fact about the patient: someone decides that a glucose in range earns \(+1\) and hypoglycaemia \(-10\). The agent will pursue exactly what the reward says, which may not be what we meant. We return to this in Section 14.5; keep it in mind as you read.
The Ward 7 kidney decisions fit the same frame. The state on Tuesday morning would include creatinine, urine output, fluid balance and blood pressure; the actions are fluids, a diuretic or nothing; a reward might penalise each rise in creatinine of 0.3 mg/dL or more and each litre of excess fluid. That problem is much harder to stylise honestly, which is why the worked example of this chapter is the simpler glucose problem.

A team has two years of Ward 7 records of insulin rates and glucose readings. Why is learning a dosing policy from them not an ordinary supervised-learning problem?

Because there are too few records for supervised learning Two years of two-hourly readings is plenty of rows. The difficulty is not the amount of data but what the data contain.
Because the records show what was done and what followed, not which rate would have been best, and each rate changes the next glucose reading Correct. There is no label “correct action”. Good actions must be inferred from their delayed consequences, and the data were produced by the clinicians’ own policy — a point that matters a great deal in Section 14.5.
Because glucose is a continuous outcome Continuous outcomes are routine in supervised learning (regression, Chapter 4). The problem is that the target of learning is an action, not an outcome.
Because reinforcement learning needs no data Reinforcement learning needs experience — interaction with an environment or, offline, records of past interaction. It is not data-free.

title: 14  Sequential decisions: reinforcement learning
text:
14.3 Planning ahead: Markov decision processes
In a bandit, today’s choice does not change tomorrow’s situation. On Aoife’s infusion it does: raising the rate now lowers the glucose the next nurse will find. To plan, we need a model of how states follow one another.

Definition 14.5 (Markov decision process (MDP)) A Markov decision process consists of a set of states, a set of actions, transition probabilities \(P(s' \mid s, a)\) — the chance that the next state is \(s'\) when action \(a\) is taken in state \(s\) — and a reward for each transition. It is Markov because the next state depends only on the current state and action, not on how the patient got there: the state must summarise everything about the past that matters for the future (Bellman 1957; Sutton and Barto 2018, ch. 3).

The Markov property is a demand on the state, and it is where clinical realism usually breaks first. If Aoife’s response to insulin depends on whether she was fed in the last four hours, then a state that contains only her current glucose is not Markov; the state must include feeding too.

14.3.1 The toy insulin problem
Here is the problem we will solve, learn and break for the rest of the chapter.

States. Glucose in one of five bands — below 4 mmol/L (hypoglycaemia), 4–6, 6–10 (the target range), 10–14, above 14 — combined with the current infusion rate: off, low, medium or high. That makes \(5 \times 4 = 20\) states. (10 mmol/L is about 180 mg/dL.)
Actions. Every two hours: decrease the rate by one level, keep it, or increase it by one level (you cannot go below off or above high).
Transitions. Over the next two hours, glucose moves down one band, stays, or moves up one band, with probabilities that depend on the new rate (Table 14.2). Without insulin, the stress of sepsis pushes glucose up; at the high rate it tends to fall.
Rewards. Ending a two-hour period in range earns \(+1\); above 14 mmol/L, \(-1\); below 4 mmol/L, \(-10\), because hypoglycaemia is dangerous; the other bands earn 0.

The intensive-care trial NICE-SUGAR is a reminder that targets are themselves decisions: aiming for glucose of 4.5–6.0 mmol/L instead of 10 mmol/L or less caused more severe hypoglycaemia and higher mortality (NICE-SUGAR Study Investigators 2009). Our target band of 6–10 mmol/L reflects that lesson.


14.3.2 Returns and discounting
A policy produces a sequence of rewards, and we need one number that says how good the sequence is.

Definition 14.6 (Return and discount factor) The return from time \(t\) is the discounted sum of the rewards that follow,
\[
G_t = r_{t+1} + \gamma\, r_{t+2} + \gamma^2 r_{t+3} + \dots = \sum_{k=0}^{\infty} \gamma^k\, r_{t+k+1},
\qquad(14.2)\]
where the discount factor \(\gamma\), between 0 and 1, sets how much a reward \(k\) steps away counts compared with an immediate one (Sutton and Barto 2018, ch. 3).

With \(\gamma = 0\) only the next reward matters: a perfectly short-sighted agent. As \(\gamma\) approaches 1 the agent cares about the distant future almost as much as about the next two hours. Discounting also keeps the infinite sum finite. For example, if Aoife’s next five periods earn rewards \(0, 0, 1, 1, 1\) (two more periods above range, then three in range) and we stop there, the return with \(\gamma = 0.9\) is \(0 + 0.9 \times 0 + 0.81 \times 1 + 0.729 \times 1 + 0.6561 \times 1
=\) 2.20. In this chapter \(\gamma = 0.9\): a reward ten steps (20 hours) away counts about a third as much as an immediate one.


14.3.3 Value functions and the Bellman equation

Definition 14.7 (Value functions) The value of a state under policy \(\pi\), \(V^\pi(s)\), is the expected return when starting in \(s\) and following \(\pi\). The action value \(Q^\pi(s, a)\) is the expected return when starting in \(s\), taking action \(a\) once, and following \(\pi\) afterwards. The best achievable values are written \(V^*(s)\) and \(Q^*(s, a)\); a policy that picks, in every state, an action with the highest \(Q^*(s,a)\) is an optimal policy (Sutton and Barto 2018, ch. 3).

(The letter \(V\) also counts cross-validation folds in Chapter 3; with its argument \((s)\) and its superscript there is no risk of confusion here.)
Values obey a simple recursion, first written by Richard Bellman (Bellman 1957): the value of where you are equals the expected reward of the next step plus the discounted value of where you land. For a fixed policy,
\[
V^\pi(s) = \sum_{a} \pi(a \mid s) \sum_{s'} P(s' \mid s, a)\,\bigl[\, r(s') + \gamma\, V^\pi(s') \,\bigr],
\qquad(14.3)\]
and for the best policy, which takes the best action instead of averaging over \(\pi\),
\[
V^*(s) = \max_{a} \sum_{s'} P(s' \mid s, a)\,\bigl[\, r(s') + \gamma\, V^*(s') \,\bigr]
       = \max_a Q^*(s, a).
\qquad(14.4)\]
Here \(r(s')\) is the reward for landing in \(s'\). The Bellman equation turns one hard question (what is the value of a whole future?) into many easy ones (what is one step worth, given the values of the next states?). Value iteration exploits this: start with all values at zero and apply Equation 14.4 to every state, again and again, until the values stop changing (Sutton and Barto 2018, ch. 4). Each sweep looks one step further into the future, and with \(\gamma < 1\) the values converge to \(V^*\).
Run on the toy insulin problem, value iteration gives the optimal policy in Table 14.3. One Bellman backup shows where its numbers come from. Take the state “glucose 10–14, infusion low” and the action increase: the rate becomes medium, so glucose falls to 6–10 with probability 0.30 (reward \(+1\)), stays at 10–14 with probability 0.60 (reward 0) or rises above 14 with probability 0.10 (reward \(-1\)). With the optimal values of the three landing states, 4.49, 4.33 and 3.03,
\[
Q^*(\text{10–14 low}, \text{increase}) = 0.30\,(1 + 0.9 \times 4.49) + 0.60\,(0 + 0.9 \times 4.33) + 0.10\,(-1 + 0.9 \times 3.03) = 4.03.
\]
The same calculation for keep gives 3.02 and for decrease 1.28, so increasing is the best action in that state.




Table 14.3: The optimal policy of the toy insulin problem (value iteration, γ = 0.9, rewards −10 / 0 / +1 / 0 / −1 from the lowest to the highest band). Each cell gives the best action and, in brackets, the value V*(s) of the state.

The policy is sensible but not obvious. Below 6 mmol/L it always lowers the rate (or leaves the infusion off). Above 10 it raises it, except at the high rate, where it holds. Inside the target range it does something a simple protocol would not: with the infusion off it starts it (because glucose will otherwise drift up), and at the medium or high rate it lowers it before glucose leaves the range (because glucose will otherwise keep falling). It anticipates. Compared with a bedside “sliding scale” (increase above 10, decrease below 6, otherwise keep), starting from glucose 10–14 with the infusion off, the optimal policy keeps glucose in range for 46 % of the next 24 hours against 34 %, and in hypoglycaemia for 0.7 % against 5.5 % — in this toy, whose transition probabilities we invented and therefore know exactly.

An agent dosing insulin uses a discount factor \(\gamma = 0\). What will its policy care about?

Only the reward of the next two-hour period Correct. With γ = 0, every term of the return after the first is multiplied by zero. Such an agent will happily choose an action that looks good for two hours and causes hypoglycaemia four hours later.
Only the long-term outcome, such as survival That would need γ close to 1 (or no discounting over a finite horizon), so that distant rewards count almost fully.
All future rewards equally Equal weighting corresponds to γ = 1, which over an endless horizon can make the return infinite.
Nothing: with γ = 0 the agent cannot learn It can learn perfectly well; it just learns to optimise the immediate reward, which is a bandit-like, short-sighted goal.



The value of a fixed rate. Suppose the nurse simply keeps the infusion at the low rate whatever happens. Glucose then moves between the five bands with the transition matrix P (rows: band now; columns: band in two hours), and r holds the expected reward of the next step from each band. Policy evaluation applies the Bellman equation Equation 14.3 over and over. Complete the update so that each new V is the expected immediate reward plus the discounted expected value of the next band. The last line shows the value of each band.

RPython

















The expected value of the next state, for every current band at once, is P %*% V.


V <- r + gamma * P %*% V


















The expected value of the next state, for every current band at once, is P @ V.


for k in range(200): V = r + gamma * P @ V
