text:
14.5 Reinforcement learning in health care: regimes, records and rewards
The toy problem made three assumptions that clinical reality breaks: the agent could experiment freely, the state captured everything that mattered, and the reward was what we wanted. This section takes each in turn.

14.5.1 Dynamic treatment regimes
Long before the term reinforcement learning reached medicine, statisticians had formalised sequential treatment decisions as dynamic treatment regimes (Murphy 2003; Chakraborty and Murphy 2014).

Definition 14.9 (Dynamic treatment regime) A dynamic treatment regime is a sequence of decision rules, one for each decision point, each mapping the information available about a patient at that time — the history of measurements and past treatments — to a recommended treatment. A regime is dynamic because the treatment adapts to how the patient evolves; an optimal regime maximises the expected value of a chosen final outcome (Murphy 2003).

A dynamic treatment regime is a policy in the language of this chapter, written for a few decision points (often two or three) with a patient’s whole history as the state. Figure 14.2 shows a two-stage regime for Ward 7 built on the kidney decisions of Chapters 1, 5 and 13.






flowchart LR
    A["Admission<br/>SOFA, lactate, blood pressure,<br/>baseline creatinine"] --> D1{"Stage 1 rule<br/>risk of AKI above threshold?"}
    D1 -- "yes" --> B["Start kidney-protective bundle"]
    D1 -- "no" --> C["Standard care"]
    B --> M["48 h later:<br/>creatinine change, urine output,<br/>fluid balance"]
    C --> M
    M --> D2{"Stage 2 rule<br/>creatinine rise ≥ 0.3 mg/dL?"}
    D2 -- "yes" --> E["Nephrology review,<br/>restrictive fluid plan"]
    D2 -- "no" --> F["De-escalate:<br/>restart paused drugs"]




Figure 14.2: A two-stage dynamic treatment regime for the Ward 7 kidney decisions (illustrative). Each stage maps what is known at that time to an action; the second rule uses the response to the first.





Optimal regimes can be estimated by a statistical cousin of Q-learning that works backwards: first model the outcome as a function of the stage-2 history and treatment, and choose the best stage-2 action for each history; then model the outcome that each patient would reach if treated optimally at stage 2 as a function of the stage-1 history and treatment (Murphy 2003; Chakraborty and Murphy 2014). The best data for this are not records but sequential multiple assignment randomised trials (SMARTs), which randomise patients again at each decision point, so that every stage’s treatment comparison is protected by randomisation (Murphy 2005). A SMART is to a dynamic regime what ONCO-1 is to a single treatment decision.


14.5.2 Offline reinforcement learning: learning from records
Nobody may experiment on Aoife to train an agent. The obvious alternative is to learn from records: millions of past decisions and their consequences. This is offline (or batch) reinforcement learning: learning a policy from a fixed set of logged transitions, collected under someone else’s policy, with no further interaction (Levine et al. 2020). It is attractive, and it inherits every problem of Chapter 13, plus one of its own.

Confounding. In the records, actions were chosen by clinicians who saw the patient. If sicker patients received more insulin, more fluid or more vasopressor, the data will associate those treatments with worse outcomes, and a naive learner will conclude that they are harmful — the Ward 7 adherence problem of Chapters 1 and 13, now repeated at every time step. Any variable that influenced the clinicians and is missing from the state (how the patient looked, a family’s wishes) is an unmeasured confounder that no algorithm can adjust for (Gottesman et al. 2019).
Positivity. An agent can only learn the consequences of actions that were actually taken in similar states. Where clinicians never did something, the data say nothing about it, and the learner’s estimates there are pure extrapolation.

The toy problem shows the second danger starkly. Suppose the records come from nurses who always follow the sliding scale. Replaying those logged transitions through the Q-learning update (the Lab does it), the agent never sees 68 % of the state–action pairs: their estimates stay at zero, the value they started with. In the states where every action that was tried led to bad outcomes (near hypoglycaemia, for example), an untried action with an estimate of zero looks better than all of them. The learned policy chooses it — and, simulated on the true toy patient, it spends 28 % of the next 24 hours in hypoglycaemia, against 5.5 % for the nurses it learned from. The records were perfectly accurate; the problem is that they never contained the information the agent needed. Offline methods counter this by penalising actions far from those in the data, at the cost of staying close to current practice (Levine et al. 2020).
The most cited example in critical care is the AI Clinician (Komorowski et al. 2018). Using records of tens of thousands of ICU patients with sepsis from two large US databases, it summarised each patient’s condition every four hours, from 24 hours before to 48 hours after the estimated onset of sepsis, in one of 750 states (found by clustering, as in Chapter 11), plus two terminal states for death and discharge. It chose among 25 actions — five dose levels of intravenous fluids combined with five of vasopressors — and received a reward only at the end of each patient’s record: \(+100\) if the patient survived to 90 days, \(-100\) if not. In retrospective analyses, the value estimated for its policy exceeded that of the clinicians’, and patients whose actual doses happened to be close to its recommendations had the lowest mortality. It was a research study; it was never used to treat patients.
The study triggered a useful debate. Critics argued that the retrospective evaluation gave little weight to the patients whose treatment differed from the policy, so that the estimates of its value rested on far fewer effective patients than the size of the databases suggested, and that a reward based only on 90-day survival ignored short-term goals such as blood pressure (Jeter et al. 2019); the authors replied, defending their methods and sensitivity analyses (Komorowski et al. 2019). Shortly afterwards, several of the same researchers and others published guidelines that boil down to three questions for any reinforcement learning study from health records (Gottesman et al. 2019):

Did the agent see all the variables that influenced the clinicians’ decisions? If not, confounding can make any policy look good or bad.
How much data supported the evaluation, really? Estimating a new policy’s value from records (off-policy evaluation) reweights the patients whose treatment happened to agree with it (Precup, Sutton, and Singh 2000); when few agree, the estimate rests on a handful of patients however large the database.
Will the policy behave as intended prospectively? Does it recommend actions clinicians never take, does it make clinical sense, and what happens when it is wrong?



14.5.3 Rewards that say what we mean
An agent optimises its reward with total literal-mindedness. If the reward is an imperfect proxy for what we want, a good optimiser will find and exploit the gap: this is reward hacking, or specification gaming, one of the central problems of AI safety (Amodei et al. 2016).
Take an automated insulin pump. “Time in range” — the share of the day with glucose between 3.9 and 10 mmol/L — is the headline target of modern continuous glucose monitoring, and an attractive reward. But the international consensus that defines it pairs it with explicit limits on time below range, because a policy can push time in range up while also pushing up hypoglycaemia (Battelino et al. 2019). A reward that rewards only one of these numbers invites the agent to trade the other away. The widget below lets you be the reward designer.

Design the reward. Choose how the agent is rewarded for ending a two-hour period in each glucose band. For each choice the optimal policy is recomputed by value iteration (arrows), and the patient of the toy problem — starting at 10–14 mmol/L with the infusion off — is followed exactly for 24 hours under that policy. Try “Below 10 mmol/L”, a natural-sounding reward for “control hyperglycaemia”, and look at the bars.

viewof rwPreset = Inputs.radio(new Map([
  ["Clinically weighted: hypo −10, > 14 −1, in range +1", "clinical"],
  ["Time in range only: +1 in 6–10, else 0", "tir_only"],
  ["Below 10 mmol/L: +1 whenever glucose < 10", "below_10"],
  ["Custom (sliders below)", "custom"]]), {value: "clinical", label: "Reward"})








Custom reward for each band


viewof rwC = Inputs.form([
  Inputs.range([-20, 2], {value: -10, step: 0.5, label: "< 4 mmol/L"}),
  Inputs.range([-5, 2], {value: 0, step: 0.5, label: "4–6"}),
  Inputs.range([-5, 2], {value: 1, step: 0.5, label: "6–10"}),
  Inputs.range([-5, 2], {value: 0, step: 0.5, label: "10–14"}),
  Inputs.range([-10, 2], {value: -1, step: 0.5, label: "> 14"})])








rwResult = {
  const rew = rwPreset === "custom" ? rwC : mdpSpec.presets[rwPreset];
  const sol = mdp.solve(rew), ev = mdp.evaluate(sol.policy);
  if (rwPreset === "below_10" && window.aihs) window.aihs.complete("ch14-tryit-reward");
  return {rew, sol, ev};
}







mdp.grid(x => ({fill: mdp.colour(rwResult.sol.V[x] / 2), label: mdp.arrows[mdp.eff(x, rwResult.sol.policy[x])]}),
  "Grid of 20 states showing the optimal action under the chosen reward.")







{
  const ev = rwResult.ev;
  const rows = [{k: "In range (6–10)", v: ev.inRange}, {k: "Hypoglycaemia (< 4)", v: ev.hypo}, {k: "Above range (> 10)", v: ev.hyper}];
  return Plot.plot({
    height: 140, marginLeft: 150, x: {domain: [0, 1], label: "Share of the next 24 hours", percent: true},
    y: {label: null},
    marks: [Plot.barX(rows, {y: "k", x: "v", fill: d => d.k.startsWith("Hypo") ? "#b03a2e" : d.k.startsWith("In") ? "#1f6f8b" : "#999"}),
            Plot.text(rows, {y: "k", x: "v", text: d => (100 * d.v).toFixed(1) + " %", dx: 22})]
  });
}








With the clinically weighted reward the agent keeps hypoglycaemia to 0.7 % of the day. Rewarding only time in range gives the same policy here, because in this toy leaving the range downwards is already costly enough. But “+1 whenever glucose is below 10 mmol/L” — a reward that sounds like “control hyperglycaemia” — produces a policy that turns the infusion up and keeps it up: hypoglycaemia for 48 % of the day, and time in range down to 15 %. The agent did exactly what it was asked. Nothing in its reward said that 3 mmol/L is worse than 9.
The same lesson runs through real cases. The AI Clinician’s reward ignored everything that happened between admission and day 90, including harms from the treatment itself. Language models are tuned with reinforcement learning from human ratings, and learn to produce answers that raters prefer, which is not always the same as answers that are true (Ouyang et al. 2022); Chapter 18 returns to this.


14.5.4 Evaluating and deploying a learned policy safely
Putting the pieces together, a clinical team facing a reinforcement-learning product — Emma and Seán with their brochure — can ask:

Which reward, and who chose it? Is it the outcome patients care about, or a convenient proxy? Are harms (hypoglycaemia, fluid overload, side effects) in it explicitly?
What was the state, and what was missing from it? Were the variables that drove clinicians’ decisions recorded? If not, how was confounding handled?
How was the policy evaluated? By off-policy estimates from records (how many effective patients?), in a simulator (how was it validated?), or prospectively? Does it recommend actions outside the range of current practice?
What constrains it? Hard limits on doses and rates of change; recommendations shown to a clinician rather than executed automatically; a way to override and to log overrides.
How will it be monitored? As practice changes, the data the policy sees drift away from the data it learned from (Chapter 3); performance and safety events need watching.

In the European Union, software that recommends doses for individual patients is a medical device (European Parliament and Council of the European Union 2017; Medical Device Coordination Group 2025), and AI systems used as safety components of medical devices are classed as high-risk, with obligations for risk management, data governance, human oversight and post-market monitoring (European Parliament and Council of the European Union 2024). A learned policy reaches the bedside, if at all, the way any new treatment strategy does: through prospective evaluation, ideally randomised.

An offline RL agent trained on Ward 7 records recommends less insulin for patients with very high glucose, because in the records those who received less insulin had better outcomes. What is the most likely explanation?

Less insulin really is better for very high glucose This contradicts physiology and trial evidence; before believing it, rule out the explanations below.
Confounding: the patients who received less insulin were probably less sick in ways the state did not capture Correct. Clinicians gave more insulin to patients who looked worse. If severity is incompletely recorded in the state, the agent credits insulin with outcomes caused by severity — Chapter 13’s confounding, at every time step.
The discount factor was too high The discount factor sets how far ahead the agent looks; it does not create a spurious association between insulin and outcomes.
The agent explored too little Offline agents cannot explore at all; but the specific pattern here — a treatment associated with worse outcomes because it is given to sicker patients — is confounding.



A hospital rewards an automated fluid-management agent with +1 for every six-hour period in which the patient’s urine output is at least 0.5 mL/kg/h. What is the most worrying way the agent could “succeed”?

It could learn slowly Slow learning wastes data, but it is not a way of gaming the reward.
It could keep urine output exactly at 0.5 mL/kg/h That satisfies the reward and is not, by itself, harmful.
It could give large volumes of fluid or diuretics to push urine output up, causing fluid overload or electrolyte problems that the reward does not see Correct. The reward measures a proxy (urine output), not the goal (kidney and patient wellbeing). An optimiser will find whatever raises the proxy most cheaply — reward hacking. Harms must be in the reward, or excluded by hard constraints.
It could stop all fluids to save costs Stopping fluids would lower urine output and lose reward, so the agent would avoid it.



Which formulation fits each problem best?

Estimate Priya’s probability of acute kidney injury from her admission data. Supervised learning
Each evening, choose one of three reminder messages for each HomeBeat participant, learning from whether they act on it. Bandit
Adjust Aoife’s insulin infusion every two hours, knowing that each rate affects the next glucose reading. Sequential decision (MDP)
Shift the allocation of newly enrolled patients towards whichever of two antibiotics is curing more patients so far. Bandit
Decide each morning whether to give fluids, a diuretic or neither, as creatinine and fluid balance evolve over the ICU stay. Sequential decision (MDP)
Classify paediatric chest X-rays as pneumonia or normal. Supervised learning
Choose the feeding schedule of a CellWorks culture day by day, where each feed changes the cell density on the next day. Sequential decision (MDP)

section: 14.6 Where this fits in the decision loop
text:
14.6 Where this fits in the decision loop


  The decision loop
  A cycle of five boxes: data feed a model; the model produces information; people combine the information with values to make a decision; the decision leads to actions and outcomes, which are recorded as new data. In this chapter the loop turns many times for the same patient, the model box holds a policy learned from rewards, and the values enter through the reward.
  
  
  Data
  states, actions, rewards
  
  Model
  value function and policy
  learned from rewards
  
  Information
  recommended action
  for this state, now
  
  Decision
  + values, human in the loop
  
  Action and outcome
  next state, every 2 hours
  
  
  
  
  

The decision loop, turning again and again. Reinforcement learning closes the loop: the outcome of each action becomes the next state, and the values enter through the reward.

Every earlier chapter drew the decision loop once per decision. Reinforcement learning is the decision loop run repeatedly, with the action–outcome arrow feeding straight back into the next decision and into the learning itself. That changes where things can go wrong. The values of Chapter 1 no longer enter only at the threshold: they are written into the reward, once, by someone, and then optimised relentlessly; a reward that misses a harm builds that blind spot into every future decision. The information link depends on causal knowledge: what each action would do in each state, which records alone supply only under strong assumptions (Chapter 13). And the human in the loop has a clear role: to own the reward, to check that recommendations make clinical sense, and to keep the authority to override. So what should Emma and Seán reply to the brochure? Show us the reward, the variables the agent saw, how its policy was evaluated and on how many effective patients, and the constraints it works within; then let us test it prospectively, with clinicians deciding.

text:
14.7 Lab: bandits, value iteration and Q-learning
The Lab gathers the chapter’s code in one place: the HomeBeat bandit, the toy insulin MDP, value iteration, Q-learning, a comparison of policies, a misspecified reward and offline learning from records. Run it here, or download it and run it on your computer: ch14_lab.R · ch14_lab.py. It takes a few seconds on a laptop and somewhat longer in the browser. The code uses R (R Core Team 2024) and, in Python, pandas and NumPy (McKinney 2010; Harris et al. 2020).

RPython























Three observations to take forward. First, Q-learning reaches essentially the same policy as value iteration, without knowing the transition probabilities — given a free simulator and thousands of episodes. Second, the policy is only as good as the reward: change the reward and the “optimal” policy changes with it. Third, learning from records of a single, fixed clinical policy leaves most actions untried, and an agent that is not told how little it knows will extrapolate into them.

title: 14  Sequential decisions: reinforcement learning
text:
14.8 Exercises

Name the parts. For the HomeBeat nudge problem, name the agent, the environment, the actions and the reward. Is there a state that carries over from one round to the next? What would have to change for the problem to become a full MDP?
Exploration budget. In the bandit widget, set ε to 0, 0.05, 0.2 and 0.5 with Average over 100 runs switched on. Which value gives the lowest regret after 500 nudges? After 100? Explain the difference.
When equal allocation wins. Set all three true engagement rates to 0.30. What happens to the regret of every strategy, and why? What would a trial statistician still want from the data?
Discounting by hand. Compute the return of the reward sequence \(1, 1, 0, 0, -10\) for \(\gamma = 0.5\) and \(\gamma = 0.9\). Which agent is more troubled by the hypoglycaemia at the end?
The sliding scale. Explain in words why the optimal policy of Table 14.3 lowers the rate in the target range when the infusion is at medium, whereas the sliding scale keeps it.
Code. In the Lab, change the hypoglycaemia reward from −10 to −2 and rerun value iteration. Which states change their action? What happens to the share of time in hypoglycaemia?
Offline data. In step 7 of the Lab, let the nurses deviate from the sliding scale at random in 10 % of their decisions (choose a random action instead). How does the share of state–action pairs never tried change, and how does the offline agent perform?
Reading a paper. A study reports that an RL policy learned from ICU records “would have reduced mortality by 3 percentage points”. Write the three questions of Gottesman et al. (2019) you would ask the authors, adapted to that study.







Selected answers





1. The agent is the app’s selection algorithm; the environment is the participant (and their evening); the actions are the three nudges; the reward is 1 if the participant does the activity within an hour. No state carries over: each round is treated as independent. It would become an MDP if, for example, today’s nudge changed tomorrow’s responsiveness (fatigue with repeated nudges), so that the history of nudges had to be part of the state.
3. With equal rates every strategy has zero regret, because no nudge is better than another. The bandit strategies still concentrate on whichever nudge had a lucky start, so a statistician would get unbalanced groups and a less precise comparison; equal allocation gives the most information that the nudges really are equivalent.
4. For \(\gamma = 0.5\): \(1 + 0.5 + 0 + 0 - 10 \times 0.0625 = 0.875\). For \(\gamma = 0.9\): \(1 + 0.9 + 0 + 0 - 10 \times 0.6561 = -4.661\). The far-sighted agent (\(\gamma = 0.9\)) is much more troubled by the hypoglycaemia four steps ahead.
5. At the medium rate glucose moves down with probability 0.30 and up with only 0.10 per step: left alone it tends to fall, eventually towards hypoglycaemia, which costs −10. Lowering the rate while still in range trades a small risk of drifting above 10 for a lower risk of a heavily penalised fall. The sliding scale reacts only after glucose has left the range.
7. Random deviations cover many more state–action pairs (positivity improves): in our run every pair was tried at least once, and the offline agent’s policy came close to the optimal one, with less hypoglycaemia than the nurses it learned from. This is why exploration, or randomisation in a SMART, makes data far more useful for learning policies — and why, without it, offline methods must stay close to the actions in the data.

title: 14  Sequential decisions: reinforcement learning
text:
14.9 Summary

Reinforcement learning learns a policy — a rule from states to actions — from the rewards that follow the actions. It suits decisions that recur, whose consequences are delayed, and where the actions change the data.
A multi-armed bandit is the simplest case: repeated choices with no state that carries over. The agent must balance exploration and exploitation; ε-greedy explores at random, Thompson sampling explores in proportion to the posterior probability that an arm is best. Bandits underlie response-adaptive trials, which trade some statistical information for better outcomes during the trial.
A Markov decision process adds states and transition probabilities. The return is the discounted sum of future rewards; value functions \(V^\pi\) and \(Q^\pi\) give its expectation; the Bellman equation writes each value as one step’s reward plus the discounted value of the next state. Value iteration solves known MDPs.
Q-learning estimates \(Q^*\) from experience alone with the update old + η × (target − old); it learns the greedy policy’s value while exploring. It needs every action to be tried.
In health care, sequential policies are dynamic treatment regimes, ideally learned from SMARTs. Offline RL from records inherits confounding and positivity problems, and off-policy evaluation can rest on few effective patients.
The reward encodes values. A proxy reward invites reward hacking; harms must be in the reward or excluded by constraints, and a learned policy needs prospective evaluation and human oversight.

How to use this chapter






Starting here?





This chapter borrows a few ideas from earlier chapters. In brief:

Instances, features and the train/test split (Definition 1.7, Section 1.8). A dataset has one row per instance and one column per feature; a model is built on a training set and judged on a test set it has never seen. Here each document is an instance, and every Ward 7 and ONCO-1 note follows the book-wide split of its patient (Chapter 3).
Sensitivity, specificity and predictive values (Chapter 2). Sensitivity is the share of true cases a test catches; specificity the share of non-cases it correctly leaves alone; the positive predictive value (PPV) the share of flagged cases that are real.
Logistic regression, ROC/AUC and thresholds (Chapter 5). A logistic model turns features into a probability \(\hat p\); the area under the ROC curve (AUC) measures how well it ranks cases above non-cases; a threshold \(t\) turns \(\hat p\) into an action, and the best threshold follows from the harms of the two errors, \(t^{*} = C_{\text{FP}}/(C_{\text{FP}}+C_{\text{FN}})\). Ridge penalties (Chapter 4) keep a model with many features from overfitting.
Cosine similarity (Chapter 10). Two profiles are compared by the angle between them, not by their length: a profile and the same profile doubled have cosine similarity 1.

title: 15  Text as data
section: 15.1 Language is symbols; computers need numbers
text:
15.1 Language is symbols; computers need numbers
We use language long before we can describe it. Natural languages such as English, Portuguese or Chinese, the mathematical language of equations and the programming languages of this book, R and Python, look very different, but they share one property: they encode information in symbols governed by rules, and they work in layers — symbols build structures, structures carry meaning, meaning serves an intention, and all of it depends on context (Figure 15.1).






Figure 15.1: Language as layers. Natural, mathematical and programming languages differ in purpose, but all encode information through structured symbols governed by rules: symbols, structure, meaning, intention and context.



Computers, however, do not handle symbols. They handle numbers, and ultimately binary numbers, sequences of 0s and 1s. Before a computer can do anything with a discharge summary, the text has to become numbers. The first step is to store it as a string.

Definition 15.1 (String and character encoding) A string is an ordered sequence of characters: letters, digits, spaces, punctuation and other symbols. A character encoding maps each character to a number and each number to bytes in memory. Today’s standard is Unicode, which gives every character of every writing system a number called a code point (The Unicode Consortium 2023), stored most often in the UTF-8 encoding, which uses one byte for the basic Latin letters and two to four bytes for everything else (Yergeau 2003).

Take the name of one of tonight’s patients. Table 15.1 shows what the computer actually holds.




Table 15.1: The five characters of ‘Tomás’ as Unicode code points and UTF-8 bytes (in hexadecimal). The accented á needs two bytes.






Character
Code point
UTF-8 bytes

Five characters, 6 bytes. The same holds for other scripts: the Chinese sentence 病人报告胸痛 (“the patient reports chest pain”) has 6 characters but takes 18 bytes. Encoding mistakes are mundane but real: a hospital system that assumes one byte per character turns Tomás into TomÃ¡s, and a search for his name then fails.
Meaning does not live inside the machine. It has to be reconstructed, by computation, from a chain of representations:
\[
\text{meaning} \;\rightarrow\; \text{symbols} \;\rightarrow\; \text{code points} \;\rightarrow\; \text{bits}.
\]
Once text is stored as an ordered, indexed sequence, a computer can measure its length, search it, cut it and compare it, all without understanding a word. In R, nchar(), grepl(), gsub() and substr() do exactly that; in Python, len(), in, str.replace() and slicing. The rest of the chapter follows the path
\[
\text{language} \;\rightarrow\; \text{numbers} \;\rightarrow\; \text{vectors} \;\rightarrow\; \text{models} \;\rightarrow\; \text{decisions},
\]
and Chapter 16 adds the next link, probability distributions over words.

How many bytes does UTF-8 use to store the name “Tomás”?

6 Correct. T, o, m and s take one byte each; á (code point U+00E1) takes two, C3 A1. Character counts and byte counts differ as soon as text leaves basic English.
10 That would be two bytes for every character, as in some older encodings. UTF-8 uses one byte for basic Latin letters.

15.2 What is natural language processing?
Natural language processing (NLP) is the discipline that builds computational systems able to work with human language, written or spoken: to classify it, extract facts from it, search it, translate it and generate it (Jurafsky and Martin 2026). It draws on linguistics, computer science, statistics and machine learning, and its practical promise in health care is to turn unstructured text into structured information (Figure 15.2). That promise matters because so much of what clinicians know about a patient is written, not coded: symptoms, reasons for stopping a drug, suspected reactions and plans are typically found in the free text of the record (Meystre et al. 2008; Wang et al. 2018).






NLP
natural language processing
Linguistics
Statistics
Computer science
Machine learning



Unstructured text
"Hives on the arms after meropenem;
treated with an antihistamine. No fever."


Structured information
drug: meropenem · reaction: hives
fever: negated · P(drug reaction) = 0.9




Figure 15.2: Natural language processing draws on four disciplines and turns unstructured text into structured information.



A collection of texts assembled for analysis is a corpus (plural corpora). Language models are trained on corpora of billions of words — encyclopaedias, web pages, books, and in medicine the abstracts and articles of PubMed — and what they learn depends on what those corpora contain. Our corpus is much smaller and entirely synthetic, but it has the shape of the real thing (Table 15.2). Each Ward 7 note is attached to one of the 1 250 simulated Ward 7 patients and each ONCO-1 note to a simulated trial participant, so every note inherits its patient’s train/test assignment. Two pharmacists labelled, in our story, whether each note reports a suspected adverse drug reaction; the leaflet sentences carry no label and are used only for searching.

Aoife’s, Tomás’s and Priya’s admission notes, written tonight, are kept apart: they are the notes the finished system will have to read, and they say nothing yet about how their stay will end. Here is Priya’s:

Ms Priya Nair, 38, admitted to ICU tonight with pneumonia with septic shock. Vancomycin 1500 mg and gentamicin 5 mg/kg given, with a noradrenaline infusion. Flushing and itching of the face within an hour of starting vancomycin, probably related to vancomycin. Infusion slowed and treated with an antihistamine. Reported to the pharmacy team.

A sentence can be represented in more than one way. As a sequence, it is a row of characters or words in order. As a tree, it is nested phrases: [the patient] [reports [chest pain]]. As a graph, it is a set of relations: reports has subject patient and object pain, and pain is modified by chest. The same surface can hide several structures — “the doctor saw the patient with the stethoscope” (who had the stethoscope?) — and much of the difficulty of NLP is ambiguity (Jurafsky and Martin 2026). In this chapter we stay with the simplest representation, the sequence, and see how far it takes us.

title: 15  Text as data
text:
15.3 Finding patterns: regular expressions
The simplest way to make text useful is to search it. Seán’s first idea is to find every note that mentions a rash.

Definition 15.2 (Regular expression) A regular expression (regex) is a compact language for describing patterns in text, used to find, extract or replace the fragments of a string that match the pattern (Friedl 2006).

A handful of symbols covers most clinical uses (Table 15.3).



Table 15.3: The regular-expression symbols used in this chapter.










Pattern
Matches
Example




rash
the letters r-a-s-h anywhere, also inside rashes or crash
grepl("rash", x)


\\b
a word boundary (in R strings the backslash is doubled)
\\brash\\b matches rash but not rashes


[0-9] or \\d
one digit
[0-9]+ mg matches 1000 mg


+, *, ?, {2}
one or more, zero or more, optional, exactly two of the previous item
[0-9]{4} matches 2026


[^a-z]
any character except the letters a–z
gsub("[^a-z]", " ", x)


(…)
a group, to combine or to extract
([0-9]+) mg captures the number






One more symbol completes the kit: a vertical bar means or, so (rash|hives|urticaria) matches any of the three words.
In our labelled notes, the pattern \\brash\\b (ignoring capitals) matches 181 notes. Only 70 of them were labelled as reporting a suspected drug reaction. The rest say “no rash”, “skin intact, no rash”, or describe a rash present before any antibiotic. A keyword finds the word, not what is said about it. The v1 edition of this book showed the same with pain: “the patient reports pain”, “the patient denies pain” and “pain was discussed as a possible risk” all match the same pattern.
Regular expressions are also brittle. The same fact can be written in many ways, and each way needs its own pattern. The Ward 7 notes record dates in four styles — 12/03/2026, 2026-03-12, 12 March 2026 and 12th of March — and a pattern written for one style finds only those dates:




Table 15.4: Ward 7 notes containing at least one date in each style, found with four different regular expressions.






Style
Pattern
Notes

\b[0-9]{2}/[0-9]{2}/[0-9]{4}\b
143

Together the four patterns find a date in 450 of the 450 notes; any one of them alone misses most. Every new style (“March 12th”, “12.03.26”) needs another rule, and rules start to overlap and conflict. This is the central weakness of hand-written rules, and the reason the rest of the chapter moves towards representations from which a model can learn patterns instead. Regular expressions remain indispensable for well-defined formats — doses, dates, laboratory values, identifiers — and for cleaning text before anything else is done with it.

The pattern \\brash\\b is run on four sentences. Which one does it not match?

“Itchy rash on the trunk.” It matches: rash is a whole word, with spaces on both sides.
“Rash-free since Tuesday.” It matches, perhaps surprisingly. A hyphen is not a letter, so there is a word boundary between rash and free. The pattern finds the word and happily reports a rash in a sentence that says there is none.
“Rashes on both arms.” Correct. After rash comes the letter e, so there is no word boundary and \\b fails. To catch plurals you need something like \\brash(es)?\\b.
“No rash.” It matches. The pattern has no idea that the sentence denies the rash: that is the problem of the next section.



Seán’s dose audit. The Ward 7 discharge summaries are loaded as w7. Extract every dose written as a number followed by a space and mg (such as 1000 mg) and count how often each one appears. Fill in the regular expression.

RPython

















“One or more digits” is [0-9]+. Follow it with a space and mg.


doses <- unlist(regmatches(w7$text, gregexpr("[0-9]+ mg", w7$text)))


















“One or more digits” is [0-9]+ or \d+. Follow it with a space and mg.


doses = [d for text in w7["text"] for d in re.findall(r"[0-9]+ mg", text)]

text:
15.5 Tokens and vocabularies
Regular expressions and negation rules work on the raw string. To learn from text, a model needs discrete units it can count and index. These units are called tokens.

Definition 15.4 (Token, tokenisation and vocabulary) A token is the basic unit into which a text is cut before it is processed: a word, a piece of a word, a character or a byte. Tokenisation is the cutting. The set of distinct tokens a system knows is its vocabulary \(\mathcal{V}\), of size \(\lvert\mathcal{V}\rvert\); each token in it is given an integer token ID, and a text becomes a sequence of tokens \(w_1, w_2, \dots, w_T\) — that is, a sequence of IDs.

Figure 15.4 follows one sentence through the steps. The token IDs are only labels — token 4 is not “twice” token 2 — so a model cannot use them as numbers directly. The classical solution is the one-hot vector: a vector as long as the vocabulary, with a 1 in the token’s own position and 0 everywhere else. Modern models instead learn a short dense vector for each token, an embedding; how such vectors are learned, and why similar words end up close together, is the subject of Chapter 16.

Figure 15.4: From text to numbers: tokens, token IDs from a vocabulary, and two numeric representations, one-hot (sparse) and dense (learned).




15.5.1 Words, characters and bytes
The most intuitive choice is word-level tokenisation: split at spaces and punctuation. It is transparent and works well when the vocabulary is stable, but it has two weaknesses. First, the vocabulary keeps growing: our 687 training notes contain 36 930 word tokens but already 376 distinct words (counting numbers such as 1000 as words), and every new drug, misspelling or abbreviation adds more. Second, a word that was never seen in training is out of vocabulary (OOV): a word-level model has no representation for it and usually replaces it with a generic <UNK> token. If we take the vocabulary of the training notes and read the leaflet sentences with it, 130 distinct leaflet words are unknown — dizziness, kidneys, bleeding, drowsy, toothbrush, fits among them — and 52 % of the leaflet’s word tokens become <UNK>. Word tokens also treat treat, treats, treated and treatment as unrelated, so nothing learned about one helps with the others.
Character-level tokenisation goes to the other extreme. The vocabulary is tiny — the training notes use only 44 distinct characters, counting letters, digits, spaces and punctuation — and there is no OOV problem: any new word, misspelling (“paim” for “pain”) or mixed-language note can be spelled out. The price is length. A typical training note has about 54 words but 299 characters, so a model must read many more steps and learn for itself that r-a-s-h is a unit. Byte-level tokenisation takes the idea one step further: 256 possible bytes cover every UTF-8 text in every script, with a fixed vocabulary (Radford et al. 2019). Chinese and accented characters then cost two to four tokens each, so the same message is longer, and more expensive to process, in some languages than in others (Petrov et al. 2023).

How big is the vocabulary? The training notes are loaded as train. Turn the text to lower case, replace every character that is not a letter a–z by a space, split at spaces and count the distinct words. Fill in the regular expression.

RPython

















Inside square brackets, ^ means not: [^a-z] is any character that is not a lower-case letter.


clean <- gsub("[^a-z]", " ", tolower(train$text))


















Inside square brackets, ^ means not: [^a-z] is any character that is not a lower-case letter.


clean = [re.sub(r"[^a-z]", " ", t.lower()) for t in train["text"]]

title: 15  Text as data
text:
15.7 Bag of words
We can now turn a whole document into a vector. The oldest and still useful way is to count.

Definition 15.6 (Bag of words and document-term matrix) A bag-of-words representation describes a document by how many times each vocabulary word occurs in it, ignoring the order of the words. Stacking the vectors of \(n\) documents gives the document-term matrix: \(n\) rows (documents, our instances), \(\lvert\mathcal{V}\rvert\) columns (words, our features), and in each cell the count of word \(w\) in document \(i\). Most cells are zero: the matrix is sparse.

In the language of Definition 1.7, each note becomes a row \(\mathbf{x}_i\) and each vocabulary word a feature. The training notes give a matrix with 687 rows and 376 columns, almost all of them zeros in any given row. Bag-of-words vectors made the first scalable text classifiers possible — spam filters, document routing, search engines (Manning, Raghavan, and Schütze 2008) — but the price of ignoring order is easy to see. Here are two sentences with opposite clinical meanings:




Table 15.5: Two sentences with opposite meanings and identical bag-of-words vectors.

Their vectors are identical, so their cosine similarity is 1.00: to a bag of words they are the same document. One remedy is to count pairs of adjacent words (bigrams) as extra features: “no fever” and “no rash” are different pairs. Another is to mark negated words before counting, turning “no rash” into a token NEG_rash (Pang, Lee, and Vaithyanathan 2002). Both appear in our classifier below. The deeper remedy, representations that read words in context, is the story of Chapters 16 and 17.

“Rash after vancomycin, no fever” and “Fever after vancomycin, no rash” are turned into bag-of-words vectors. What is the cosine similarity between them?

0, because they mean opposite things Meaning is exactly what a bag of words cannot see.
About 0.5, because half the words are in a different place Position is discarded before the vectors are made.
1, because they contain exactly the same words the same number of times Correct. Same counts, same vector, angle zero. Adding word pairs (bigrams) such as “no fever” and “no rash” would separate them.

title: 15  Text as data
section: 15.8 TF-IDF: weighting words by what they tell you
text:
15.8 TF-IDF: weighting words by what they tell you
Raw counts treat every word as equally informative. But a word that appears in almost every note — the, with, creatinine in an ICU archive — says little about any particular note, whereas a word that appears in a few — hives, tinnitus — says a lot. TF-IDF formalises this intuition (Spärck Jones 1972; Salton and Buckley 1988).

Definition 15.7 (TF-IDF) For a collection of \(n\) documents, the term frequency \(\text{tf}(w, i)\) is the number of times word \(w\) occurs in document \(i\); the document frequency \(\text{df}(w)\) is the number of documents that contain \(w\) at least once; the inverse document frequency is \[
\text{idf}(w) = \log \frac{n}{\text{df}(w)},
\] and the TF-IDF weight of \(w\) in document \(i\) is \[
\text{tfidf}(w, i) = \text{tf}(w, i) \times \text{idf}(w).
\qquad(15.1)\] A word that occurs in every document has \(\text{idf} = \log 1 = 0\) and weight 0; a word frequent in one document and rare elsewhere gets a large weight.

The idea of weighting a term by how specific it is, rather than how frequent, is due to Karen Spärck Jones (Spärck Jones 1972); it became, with term frequency, the standard weighting of search engines for decades (Salton and Buckley 1988; Manning, Raghavan, and Schütze 2008). Table 15.6 works it out on four miniature notes.




Table 15.6: TF-IDF on four miniature notes (A: ‘No rash. Vancomycin stopped.’ B: ‘Rash after vancomycin. Vancomycin stopped.’ C: ‘No nausea. Creatinine stable.’ D: ‘Rash after piperacillin. No fever.’), for six of their words. Natural logarithms.

Vancomycin occurs twice in note B and in only two of the four notes, so it gets the largest weight in B. No occurs in three notes and carries little weight anywhere; nausea and piperacillin occur in only one note each and are the most specific words of the collection. Software packages use small variants of Equation 15.1. scikit-learn, for example, adds one to the numerator and the denominator of the idf fraction and one to the logarithm (“smoothing”, so that no weight is exactly zero), and by default rescales every document vector to length 1 (Pedregosa et al. 2011). The ranking of words changes little; the exact numbers do, so always say which variant you used.

In the Ward 7 archive, every discharge summary contains the word creatinine. What is its inverse document frequency, using \(\text{idf}(w) = \log(n/\text{df}(w))\)?

It cannot be computed, because the fraction has no zero in it The fraction is \(n/n = 1\); its logarithm is 0.

section: 15.10 A first text classifier: flagging adverse drug reactions
text:
15.10 A first text classifier: flagging adverse drug reactions
Search answers Seán’s questions one at a time. What he really wants is a list, every morning, of the notes most likely to report a suspected adverse drug reaction (ADR): a harmful, unintended response to a medicine that warrants changing treatment, monitoring or future prescribing (Edwards and Aronson 2000). Reactions found in clinical notes are a recognised and under-used source of safety signals, and finding them automatically is a long-standing goal of clinical NLP (Harpaz et al. 2014; Wang et al. 2018).

Definition 15.9 (Text classifier) A text classifier is a supervised model whose input is a document, represented as a vector (for example TF-IDF weights), and whose output is a class or, better, a probability for each class. It is trained on documents whose class was assigned by people — the labels — and evaluated on documents it has not seen.

Nothing here is new except the input. The 687 training notes become a TF-IDF matrix; the label is 1 if the pharmacists judged that the note reports a suspected ADR (34 % of labelled notes) and 0 otherwise; and a logistic regression with a ridge penalty (Cessie and Houwelingen 1992) (Chapter 5, Chapter 4) estimates the probability \(\hat p\) that a note reports one. With hundreds of word features and a few hundred notes, the penalty is not optional: without it, the model would memorise the training notes. The fitted model is evaluated on the 163 test notes. Table 15.7 compares it with two rule-based screens, a keyword list of reaction words (rash, hives, nausea, neutropenia, …) and the same list with NegEx-lite ignoring negated mentions.

The keyword list catches 61 % of the reactions but flags so many notes without one that its PPV is only 0.41: reaction words appear just as often in notes saying “rash after gardening, unrelated to the study drug”. NegEx-lite removes the “no rash” mentions and raises the PPV to 0.57, at the cost of some sensitivity. The learned models do far better, with an AUC of 0.974 for single words and 0.976 when word pairs are added. Marking negations changes nothing here: in these notes, what decides the label is not whether a symptom is present but what it is attributed to, and that is carried by words such as related, attributed and unrelated. A different task — “does the patient have a rash?” — would reward negation handling much more.

unrelated (-2.56)


probably (3.67)
unrelated to (-2.56)


probably related (3.67)



likely (3.66)









Most of these make sense — related to, probably related, effect of up; not, unrelated to, the infection down. Others are artefacts of how notes are written: on day rises because the reaction sentences usually say when the reaction started. A model that leans on such phrasing will stumble when a new hospital writes differently. Reading the largest weights is the simplest way to look inside a text classifier, with all the caveats of Chapter 12: a weight is an association with the label in these notes, not a reason.
Finally, the model reads tonight’s notes. Tomás’s (“No adverse drug reactions so far”) gets \(\hat p\) = 0.06; Priya’s, with flushing and itching “probably related to vancomycin”, 0.99; Aoife’s, with a mild itch since the first antibiotic dose, “cause unclear”, 0.49. Aoife’s note is precisely the kind on which two pharmacists might disagree. These are probabilities that each note reports a suspected adverse drug reaction, not the risks of acute kidney injury that the logistic model of Chapter 5 gives the same three patients (0.49 / 0.07 / 0.99): the numbers happen to be close, but they answer a different question, and whether the kidneys will be injured belongs to the models of Part II.

title: 15  Text as data
section: 15.11 Who reads what? Thresholds and a review queue
text:
15.11 Who reads what? Thresholds and a review queue
A probability is not yet a decision. In Chapter 5 one threshold split patients into “give the bundle” and “do not”. Here a single threshold would split notes into “report” and “ignore”, and either error is costly: a missed reaction is a safety signal lost; a false report wastes a pharmacovigilance officer’s time and pollutes the database. But Seán has a third option, which a bundle decision on Ward 7 did not: read the note himself.

Definition 15.10 (Review queue) A review queue uses two thresholds on a classifier’s probability. Below \(t_{\text{low}}\) a document is cleared automatically; at or above \(t_{\text{high}}\) it is acted on automatically; in between it is sent to a person. Widening the band between the thresholds trades human workload for fewer automatic errors. Letting a classifier abstain when it is unsure is known as classification with a reject option (Chow 1970).







Cleared
automatically

Human review
Seán reads the note

Flagged
drafted for reporting

0
1
t_low
t_high
predicted probability of a suspected adverse drug reaction, p̂




Figure 15.5: A review queue: two thresholds split the notes into three streams, and only the uncertain middle reaches a person.



The two thresholds come from the same reasoning as \(t^{*}\) in Chapter 5, with a third action added. Suppose a missed reaction costs \(C_{\text{FN}}\), a false automatic report \(C_{\text{FP}}\), and a human review \(C_{\text{R}}\), smaller than both (Seán’s few minutes, assuming he then gets the note right). For a note with probability \(\hat p\), clearing it has expected cost \(\hat p\,C_{\text{FN}}\), flagging it \((1-\hat p)\,C_{\text{FP}}\), and reviewing it \(C_{\text{R}}\). Review is the cheapest option when \(\hat p\,C_{\text{FN}} > C_{\text{R}}\) and \((1-\hat p)\,C_{\text{FP}} > C_{\text{R}}\), that is, when \[
t_{\text{low}} = \frac{C_{\text{R}}}{C_{\text{FN}}} \;<\; \hat p \;<\; 1 - \frac{C_{\text{R}}}{C_{\text{FP}}} = t_{\text{high}} .
\qquad(15.3)\] The cheaper a review compared with an error, the wider the band. If reading a note costs one twentieth of a missed reaction and one third of a false report, review every note with \(\hat p\) between 0.05 and 0.67. As in Chapter 5, these numbers assume calibrated probabilities, and the costs are value judgements that the pharmacy team, not the software vendor, should make.

Seán’s review queue. Each dot is one of the 163 test notes, placed at its predicted probability; the upper row holds the 56 notes that really report a suspected ADR. Move the two thresholds. With both at 0.5 there is no review band: one threshold decides everything. Target: miss at most one reaction and send at most two false automatic reports, while Seán reads no more than a third of the notes.

rq = FileAttachment("data/precomputed/ch15/test_predictions.csv").csv({typed: true})
viewof tLo = Inputs.range([0, 1], {value: 0.5, step: 0.01, label: "t_low (clear below)"})
viewof tHi = Inputs.range([0, 1], {value: 0.5, step: 0.01, label: "t_high (flag at or above)"})
rqLo = Math.min(tLo, tHi)
rqHi = Math.max(tLo, tHi)
rqS = {
  const c = rq.filter(d => d.p < rqLo), r = rq.filter(d => d.p >= rqLo && d.p < rqHi), f = rq.filter(d => d.p >= rqHi);
  return {cleared: c.length, missed: c.filter(d => d.adr === 1).length, review: r.length,
    reviewAdr: r.filter(d => d.adr === 1).length, flagged: f.length, falseFlag: f.filter(d => d.adr === 0).length};
}
{
  const s = rqS, share = s.review / rq.length;
  const hit = s.missed <= 1 && s.falseFlag <= 2 && share <= 1 / 3;
  if (hit && window.aihs) window.aihs.complete("ch15-tryit-queue");
  return html`<table style="max-width:560px;text-align:center;margin:0.4rem 0">
  <thead><tr><th></th><th>Cleared</th><th>Human review</th><th>Flagged</th></tr></thead>
  <tbody><tr><th style="text-align:left">Notes</th><td>${s.cleared}</td><td><strong>${s.review}</strong> (${(100 * share).toFixed(0)} %)</td><td>${s.flagged}</td></tr>
  <tr><th style="text-align:left">Errors</th><td>${s.missed} reactions missed</td><td>${s.reviewAdr} reactions found by Seán</td><td>${s.falseFlag} false reports</td></tr></tbody></table>
  ${rqLo !== tLo ? html`<p class="muted">(t_low is above t_high; the two have been swapped.)</p>` : ""}
  ${hit ? html`<p>✓ target reached. Seán's reading is focused where the model is unsure.</p>` : ""}`;
}

















































Plot.plot({
  height: 220, grid: false, marginLeft: 60,
  x: {label: "Predicted probability of a suspected ADR", domain: [0, 1]},
  y: {domain: [-0.6, 1.6], ticks: [0, 1], tickFormat: d => d === 1 ? "ADR" : "no ADR", label: null},
  marks: [
    Plot.rect([{x1: rqLo, x2: rqHi}], {x1: "x1", x2: "x2", y1: -0.6, y2: 1.6, fill: "#1f6f8b", fillOpacity: 0.12}),
    Plot.dot(rq, {x: "p", y: (d, i) => d.adr + (((i * 7919) % 97) / 97 - 0.5) * 0.7, r: 3,
      fill: d => d.adr === 1 ? "#b35c00" : "#1f6f8b", fillOpacity: 0.75}),
    Plot.ruleX([rqLo, rqHi], {strokeWidth: 2})
  ]
})










With a single threshold of 0.5, the model misses 9 of the 56 reactions and sends 3 false reports. With \(t_{\text{low}} = 0.10\) and \(t_{\text{high}} = 0.65\), Seán reads 43 of the 163 notes (26 %), finds 18 reactions among them, and the automatic streams miss 1 reaction and send 1 false report. The notes in the band are the ones written ambiguously — “cause unclear”, “a drug cause cannot be excluded” — exactly where human judgement is worth its cost. With these thresholds Aoife’s note (0.49) goes to Seán for review, Tomás’s (0.06) to the cleared stream and Priya’s (0.99) to the flagged stream.
A review queue is also how a classifier keeps learning. The notes Seán reads, with his decisions, are new labelled examples from the place the model is used, and the ones in the band are the most informative of all, because the model was unsure about them. Feeding them back is a simple form of active learning (Settles 2009). It has a catch: if only the uncertain notes are ever checked, errors in the automatic streams go unseen. A sensible queue also sends a small random sample of cleared and flagged notes for review, to keep measuring the error rates the thresholds were chosen for.

The pharmacy team widens the review band, lowering \(t_{\text{low}}\) and raising \(t_{\text{high}}\). What happens?

The model becomes more accurate The model and its probabilities are unchanged. Only what is done with them changes.
Fewer errors are made automatically, and Seán reads more notes Correct. A wider band moves notes from the automatic streams to the human one: fewer misses and false reports, more reading. Equation 15.3 says the band should be wide when a review is cheap compared with an error.
Seán reads fewer notes, because the model is more confident The opposite: more notes fall between the thresholds.
Nothing, as long as the AUC is high The AUC summarises ranking over all thresholds; it says nothing about where the thresholds are or how many notes a person must read.



Which tool from this chapter fits each job best?

Pull every vancomycin dose written in milligrams from 450 discharge summaries. Regular expression
Decide whether “no evidence of rash” means that the patient has a rash. Negation detection
Find the five leaflet sentences most relevant to a family’s question about hearing loss. TF-IDF search
Estimate, for every new ONCO-1 note, the probability that it reports a suspected drug reaction. Text classifier
Check that every note contains a date written as YYYY-MM-DD. Regular expression
List last year’s notes most similar to Priya’s admission note. TF-IDF search

Text in the decision loop: the classifier ranks, the thresholds route, and a person decides where the model is unsure.

This chapter turned the least structured data in the hospital into information for a decision. Text is stored as strings of encoded characters (Section 15.1); regular expressions find well-defined patterns but not meaning (Section 15.3); negation rules catch the commonest way in which a mention means its opposite (Section 15.4); tokens and subwords cut text into countable units (Section 15.5, Section 15.6); bags of words and TF-IDF turn documents into vectors (Section 15.7, Section 15.8), which can be searched by cosine similarity (Section 15.9) and fed to a classifier (Section 15.10).
What can go wrong? Keywords find words, not facts; a bag of words cannot tell “rash, no fever” from “fever, no rash”; a classifier can learn the writing habits of one hospital; search can retrieve the exact opposite of what was asked. Who stays in control? The thresholds of the review queue (Section 15.11) are a value judgement about the cost of a missed reaction, a false report and a pharmacist’s time, and the person reading the uncertain notes is part of the system, not a fallback for it.

title: 15  Text as data
section: 15.13 Lab: screening notes for adverse drug reactions
text:
15.13 Lab: screening notes for adverse drug reactions
The Lab gathers the chapter’s steps in one place: regular expressions, NegEx-lite, tokens, TF-IDF, a ridge logistic classifier and a review queue. To keep R and Python comparable, both fit the classifier on single words that occur in at least two training notes, with the same penalty; R writes the ridge logistic regression in a few lines of base R, Python uses scikit-learn. Run it here, or download it and run it on your computer: ch15_lab.R · ch15_lab.py. The code uses R (R Core Team 2024) and, in Python, pandas, NumPy and scikit-learn (McKinney 2010; Harris et al. 2020; Pedregosa et al. 2011).

RPython























Three observations to take forward. First, R and Python give practically the same test AUC: the same features and the same penalty give the same model, whatever the language. Second, NegEx-lite fails on exactly the sentences the widget showed; rules do not improve with more data. Third, the review queue is where the classifier meets the pharmacist, and its thresholds are not in the data: they are set by people.

title: 15  Text as data
text:
15.14 Exercises

Encodings. Use nchar(x, type = "bytes") in R, or len(x.encode("utf-8")) in Python, to count the bytes of “Aoife”, “Tomás”, “Priya” and the Chinese sentence of Section 15.1. Which character costs the most bytes?
A better dose pattern. Extend the regular expression of Mission 1 so that it also captures doses in grams (4.5 g, 1 g) and keeps 5 mg/kg whole. How many distinct doses do you find now? What would still go wrong in real notes?
Your own negation rules. In the NegEx-lite widget, find a sentence of your own that the rules get wrong. Which rule would you add to fix it, and which correct sentence might that new rule break?
Merges. In the tokeniser explorer, why does cardiotoxic stay in many pieces even after all the merges? Add the word cardiology with frequency 10 to the corpus in your head: which merges would change?
Search. Search “kidney” and then “creatinine” in the search widget. Why are the results so different, although both words are about the same organ? What does this tell you about vocabulary mismatch between patients’ leaflets and clinicians’ notes?
Word pairs. In the Lab, change TfidfVectorizer(min_df=2) to TfidfVectorizer(min_df=2, ngram_range=(1, 2)). Does the AUC change? Which word pairs now have the largest coefficients?
Thresholds from costs. With Equation 15.3, find \(t_{\text{low}}\) and \(t_{\text{high}}\) if a review costs 1, a missed reaction 30 and a false report 4. Set them in the review-queue widget: how many notes does Seán read?
Generalisation. The classifier was trained on notes written from a fixed set of templates. Write three sentences that report a drug reaction in words the templates never use. Would the model flag them? What would you need before using such a model in a real hospital?







Selected answers





1. “Aoife” and “Priya” take 5 bytes each (one per letter); “Tomás” takes 6, because á takes 2; each Chinese character takes 3, so the six-character sentence takes 18 bytes.
4. Cardio occurs only in cardiotoxicity, which has frequency 2, so pairs inside cardio are never among the most frequent. With cardiology at frequency 10, pairs such as c+a, ar and rd would become frequent, and cardio would probably be merged into one token early on.
5. Kidney appears mainly in the leaflet sentences (“can affect your kidneys”) and creatinine in the clinical notes. TF-IDF matches strings, not concepts: it cannot know that kidney and creatinine belong together. Learned embeddings (Chapter 16) and medical vocabularies are two remedies.
7. \(t_{\text{low}} = 1/30 \approx 0.03\) and \(t_{\text{high}} = 1 - 1/4 = 0.75\): the band is wide, because a review is cheap compared with a missed reaction; Seán reads many more notes than with the thresholds 0.10 and 0.65.

title: 15  Text as data
text:
15.15 Summary

Computers store text as strings of characters, each character a Unicode code point stored as one to four UTF-8 bytes. Meaning is not in the machine; it is reconstructed by computation.
Regular expressions find and extract well-defined patterns (doses, dates, identifiers) but are brittle: every new way of writing the same fact needs another rule. A keyword finds a word, not what is said about it.
Negation detection (NegEx) uses trigger phrases, a limited scope, pseudo-negations and termination words to decide whether a finding is affirmed or denied. It handles the common patterns and misses the long tail.
Tokenisation cuts text into tokens with integer IDs from a vocabulary. Word tokens suffer from out-of-vocabulary words; characters and bytes have none but make sequences long; subwords (BPE, WordPiece, unigram LM) are the modern compromise and follow frequency, not meaning.
A bag of words turns a document into a vector of counts, a row of the document-term matrix, and loses word order: “rash, no fever” equals “fever, no rash”. TF-IDF weights words by how specific they are, \(\text{tf} \times \log(n/\text{df})\).
Cosine similarity compares documents by direction, not length, and turns search into geometry. Retrieval inherits the blindness of the bag of words.
A text classifier is ordinary supervised learning on document vectors: a penalised logistic regression on TF-IDF features clearly beats keyword rules for flagging suspected adverse drug reactions, and its largest weights show what it relies on.
A review queue uses two thresholds, \(t_{\text{low}} = C_{\text{R}}/C_{\text{FN}}\) and \(t_{\text{high}} = 1 - C_{\text{R}}/C_{\text{FP}}\), to send only the uncertain notes to a person.

text:
How to use this chapter






Starting here?





This chapter borrows a few ideas from earlier chapters.

Tokens and vocabulary (Chapter 15). A text is cut into tokens (words, pieces of words or characters, depending on the tokeniser); the set of distinct tokens is the vocabulary \(\mathcal{V}\), of size \(|\mathcal{V}|\), and the token at position \(t\) is written \(w_t\). Here the notes are already lower-case words and punctuation marks separated by spaces, so a token is simply a word or a punctuation mark.
Probability, conditional probability and maximum likelihood (Chapter 2). \(P(A \mid B)\) is the probability of \(A\) when \(B\) is known; the maximum likelihood estimate of a proportion is the count of successes divided by the number of trials, \(k/n\).
Entropy (Chapter 2): the average surprise of an outcome, \(-\log_2 P\), measured in bits. Chapter 2 promised that it returns as the loss that trains language models; it does in Section 16.5.
Softmax and gradient descent (Chapter 7): softmax turns a list of scores into probabilities that add up to one; gradient descent adjusts a network’s weights to reduce a loss.
Cosine similarity (Chapter 10, Chapter 15): the cosine of the angle between two vectors, 1 when they point the same way and 0 when they are perpendicular.
Training and test data (Section 1.8): a model is judged on data it did not see while it was being built.

section: 16.1 The data: eight thousand short notes
text:
16.1 The data: eight thousand short notes
Language models learn from text, so we need a corpus. Real clinical notes are protected health information and cannot be shipped with a book, so this chapter uses 8 000 simulated Ward 7 notes, generated by a small grammar with a fixed random seed (sim_ch16_ward7_notes.py). They describe no real person. Each note has one or two short clauses — a symptom, a drug started, a laboratory trend, a negation, a plan, a remark by a member of staff — and 7 147 of them form the training set, the remaining 853 the test set.

The training notes contain 65 431 tokens drawn from a vocabulary of only 129 distinct words and punctuation marks. That is tiny next to the hundreds of billions of tokens used to train modern language models (Brown et al. 2020), and the notes are far more repetitive than real clinical writing. This is deliberate: because the grammar that generated the notes is known, we can check what each model has learned, as we did with the simulated datasets of earlier chapters. The grammar also hides three traps that we will spring later: drugs of the same class appear in similar sentences; some notes name a drug and ask, a clause or two later, to check the level of that same drug; and the pronoun that follows each staff role is deliberately unbalanced, as it is in much real text.

title: 16  Predicting the next word: language models and embeddings
section: 16.2 A language model assigns probabilities to the next token
text:
16.2 A language model assigns probabilities to the next token
The autocomplete on Seán’s screen does one thing: given the text so far, it gives every token in its vocabulary a probability of coming next, and shows the most probable one. After “patient reports” the Ward 7 notes continue with a symptom or a body site. Counting what follows those two words in the training notes gives the probabilities in Figure 16.1.








Figure 16.1: What follows “patient reports” in the training notes: a probability for every possible next token (only tokens that ever follow are shown).






Definition 16.1 (Language model) A language model is a probability distribution over sequences of tokens. In practice it is specified by its next-token probabilities \(P_\theta(w_t \mid w_{<t})\): for every position \(t\) and every possible context \(w_{<t} = (w_1, \dots, w_{t-1})\), a probability for each token of the vocabulary, adding up to one. The parameters \(\theta\) are estimated from a training corpus (Jurafsky and Martin 2026, ch. 3).

Two operations follow from this definition. Scoring: the model can say how probable a whole text is, which lets us compare models and spot unusual text. Generation: the model can write, by choosing a next token from its distribution, appending it to the text, and repeating. A chatbot answering a question does exactly this, token after token; the rest of Part V explains how much machinery can sit inside \(P_\theta\), but the outer loop never changes.
The idea is older than computers. In 1913 Andrei Markov counted, by hand, how often a vowel follows a vowel or a consonant in 20 000 letters of Pushkin’s Eugene Onegin, to show that the letters of a text are not independent draws (Markov 2006). In 1951 Claude Shannon asked people to guess the next letter of an English text and used their success rate to estimate how predictable English is (Shannon 1951). A language model plays Shannon’s guessing game.

The autocomplete suggests gentamicin. What, exactly, has the model computed?

Whether gentamicin is the right drug for Tomás The model has no access to Tomás’s chart or to pharmacology. It has seen which words tend to follow “check” in past notes.
A probability for every token in its vocabulary, of which gentamicin got the highest Correct. The suggestion is the top of a distribution over the whole vocabulary; vancomycin had a probability too, just a lower one. Nothing in the computation checks the claim against the patient.
The single sentence from its training data that best matches what Seán typed A language model does not retrieve stored sentences: it computes a probability for each possible next token from the context. Sentences it never saw can get high probability.
The meaning of Seán’s sentence Nothing in the model represents meaning in that sense. As Section 1.6 put it, plausible is not the same as true.

title: 16  Predicting the next word: language models and embeddings
section: 16.3 The chain rule: the probability of a whole note
text:
16.3 The chain rule: the probability of a whole note
A note is a sequence of tokens \(w_1, w_2, \dots, w_N\). Its probability can always be written as a product of next-token probabilities. With two tokens, the definition of conditional probability from Chapter 2 gives \(P(w_1, w_2) = P(w_1)\,P(w_2 \mid w_1)\); applying it again and again gives the general rule.

Definition 16.2 (Chain rule of probability) For any sequence of tokens, \[
P(w_1, w_2, \dots, w_N) = P(w_1)\, P(w_2 \mid w_1)\, P(w_3 \mid w_1, w_2) \cdots P(w_N \mid w_1, \dots, w_{N-1})
= \prod_{t=1}^{N} P(w_t \mid w_{<t}) .
\qquad(16.1)\] The rule is exact: it involves no assumption. It turns the impossible task of assigning a probability to every possible text into a sequence of next-token predictions (Jurafsky and Martin 2026, ch. 3).

To mark where a note starts and ends we add two special tokens, <s> (start) and </s> (end): the first prediction is \(P(w_1 \mid \texttt{<s>})\), and the model must also predict </s>, so that it learns when a note is finished. Table 16.2 applies Equation 16.1 to the note “patient reports chest pain .”, with each factor estimated by counting in the training notes how often the word follows the previous one (the method of the next section).

  P(reports | <s>, patient)
  P(chest | all before)
  P(pain | all before)
  step 1step 2step 3step 4
  

The chain rule: the probability of a text is built from one next-token prediction per position, each conditioned on everything to its left.


One of the six probabilities in Table 16.2 is replaced by 0, because a model has never seen that pair of words. What happens to the probability of the whole note and to its total surprise?

Nothing much: one factor out of six barely matters In a product, a single zero makes everything zero, however large the other factors are.
The probability becomes 0 and the surprise becomes infinite Correct. \(-\log_2 0\) is infinite, so the model declares the note impossible. This is why count-based models need smoothing, the topic of the next section.
The probability becomes 0 but the surprise stays finite, because we add logarithms Adding logarithms avoids rounding problems with very small numbers; it cannot rescue a true zero, whose logarithm is minus infinity.

section: 16.5 Cross-entropy and perplexity: how surprised is the model?
text:
16.5 Cross-entropy and perplexity: how surprised is the model?
We now have several language models — bigram or trigram, with more or less smoothing — and need a way to compare them. As always, the comparison is made on text the models have not seen: the 853 test notes. A good model is one that is not surprised by them, that is, one that gave high probability to the tokens that actually came next. Chapter 2 measured surprise in bits; here is the general version.

Definition 16.5 (Cross-entropy) If outcomes follow a distribution \(P\) but we predict them with a model \(Q\), the cross-entropy is the average surprise we experience: \[
H(P, Q) = -\sum_{w} P(w) \log_2 Q(w) .
\] It is never smaller than the entropy \(H(P) = -\sum_w P(w) \log_2 P(w)\), and the difference is the Kullback–Leibler divergence, \(D_{\text{KL}}(P \,\Vert\, Q) = H(P, Q) - H(P) \ge 0\), which is zero only when \(Q = P\) (Cover and Thomas 2006; Kullback and Leibler 1951). For a language model on a test text of \(N\) tokens we do not know \(P\), but the text is a sample from it, so the cross-entropy is estimated by the average surprise per token: \[
\hat H = -\frac{1}{N} \sum_{t=1}^{N} \log_2 P_\theta(w_t \mid w_{<t}) .
\qquad(16.4)\]

A small example makes the identity concrete. If the true next-token distribution over three words is \(P = (0.7, 0.2, 0.1)\) and a model predicts \(Q = (0.6, 0.3, 0.1)\), then \(H(P) =\) 1.157 bits, \(H(P, Q) =\) 1.195 bits and the KL divergence is the difference, 0.039 bits: the extra surprise caused by using a slightly wrong model. Because \(H(P)\) does not depend on the model, minimising cross-entropy is the same as minimising the KL divergence from the truth, and it is also the same as maximising the likelihood of the training text (the average surprise is minus the log-likelihood divided by \(N\)). This is the loss that trains every language model in this chapter and the next two, exactly as it trained the classifiers of Chapter 5, where the “vocabulary” had only two entries, AKI or not.

Definition 16.6 (Perplexity) The perplexity of a model on a test text is two raised to its cross-entropy in bits: \[
\text{PPL} = 2^{\hat H} = \left( \prod_{t=1}^{N} P_\theta(w_t \mid w_{<t}) \right)^{-1/N} .
\] It can be read as the effective number of equally likely choices the model is hesitating between at each step: a model that spread its probability evenly over 8 tokens would have a perplexity of 8. Lower is better (Jurafsky and Martin 2026, ch. 3).

(With natural logarithms, as in most software, the same quantity is \(e^{\hat H}\); the number does not change. The “perplexity” setting of t-SNE in Chapter 10 is the same idea applied to a distribution over neighbours (Maaten and Hinton 2008).) Table 16.4 compares the models on the 8 639 predictions needed for the test notes.

Read it from top to bottom. A model with no context at all (unigram) hesitates between about 59 tokens at every step. Using one previous token cuts that to 3.2, using two to 2.6. Smoothing matters too, and not in an obvious way: with add-one smoothing the trigram model is no better than the bigram one (3.89 against 3.88), because adding 1 to each of 130 possible counts swamps the few observations available for each two-token context. A small \(\delta\) works much better here. (We chose \(\delta\) from a short list while looking at the test notes, which, as Chapter 3 warned, makes these test numbers slightly optimistic; a validation set would be the honest way.) Notice also how low all the numbers are: real English has perplexities in the tens or hundreds under good models (Jurafsky and Martin 2026, ch. 3; Radford et al. 2019), but the Ward 7 notes come from a small grammar and are very predictable. Perplexity measures a model on a particular text: numbers from different corpora or different tokenisers cannot be compared.

Model A has a perplexity of 3.2 on the Ward 7 test notes; model B has a perplexity of 45 on a collection of real discharge letters. Which model is better?

Model A, because its perplexity is lower Perplexities are comparable only on the same test text with the same tokeniser. The Ward 7 notes are far more predictable than real letters, so any model would score lower on them.
Model B, because it was tested on real text Testing on real text is more relevant, but it does not make the model better; we simply cannot rank the two from these numbers.
We cannot tell: the two numbers were measured on different texts Correct. To compare A and B, evaluate both on the same held-out text, cut into tokens in the same way. Perplexity is a property of a model and a text.

title: 16  Predicting the next word: language models and embeddings
text:
16.7 From one-hot vectors to embeddings
Count-based models treat every token as an unrelated symbol. To a bigram model, vancomycin and gentamicin are as different as vancomycin and tomorrow; what it learns about one tells it nothing about the other. In vector form, each token is a one-hot vector: a vector of length \(|\mathcal{V}|\) with a 1 in the token’s own position and 0 everywhere else. Any two different one-hot vectors are perpendicular, so their cosine similarity is exactly 0: every word is equally unlike every other.

Definition 16.8 (Embedding) An embedding represents each token \(w\) by a dense vector \(\mathbf{e}_w\) of \(d\) real numbers, with \(d\) much smaller than \(|\mathcal{V}|\) (here \(d =\) 24; in large models a few thousand). The vectors are the rows of an embedding matrix \(\mathbf{E}\) of size \(|\mathcal{V}| \times d\), and looking up a token’s embedding is the same as multiplying its one-hot vector by \(\mathbf{E}\). The entries of \(\mathbf{E}\) are parameters learned from data, so that tokens used in similar ways end up with similar vectors (Jurafsky and Martin 2026, ch. 5).

Why should usage give similar vectors? Because of an old idea from linguistics.

Definition 16.9 (Distributional hypothesis) Words that occur in similar contexts tend to have similar meanings (Z. S. Harris 1954). In Firth’s phrase, “you shall know a word by the company it keeps” (Firth 1957).

In the Ward 7 notes, vancomycin and gentamicin both appear in “started … for sepsis”, “… dose adjusted for kidney function” and “check … level tomorrow”. A method that places words with similar neighbours close together will therefore place these two close together, without being told that both are antibiotics. The best-known such method is word2vec.

Definition 16.10 (Skip-gram (word2vec)) The skip-gram model learns embeddings by turning the corpus into a prediction task: for each word, predict the words within a small window around it (here, two words on each side). Each word has an input vector and an output vector; the model is trained, by gradient descent, to give a high score \(\sigma(\mathbf{u}_{o}^\top \mathbf{e}_{c})\) to pairs that really occur together and a low score to random negative pairs (Mikolov, Chen, et al. 2013; Mikolov, Sutskever, et al. 2013). Once trained, the prediction task is thrown away and the vectors are kept. GloVe obtains similar vectors from a table of co-occurrence counts (Pennington, Socher, and Manning 2014).

We trained a skip-gram model with \(d =\) 24 on the training notes, in a few seconds, with the script ch16_language_models.py; as GloVe does, each word’s embedding is the sum of its input and output vectors (Pennington, Socher, and Manning 2014). No pharmacology, anatomy or staffing information went in: only the notes.

Explore the embeddings. Each dot is a word of the Ward 7 notes, placed by a two-dimensional projection (principal components, Chapter 10; Jolliffe and Cadima (2016)) of its 24-dimensional embedding. The projection keeps only 33 % of the variation, so judge closeness by the cosine similarities in the table, which use all 24 dimensions. Colours show categories we assigned; the model never saw them. The analogy box computes \(\mathbf{e}_b - \mathbf{e}_a + \mathbf{e}_c\) and lists the nearest words (excluding \(a\), \(b\) and \(c\)). Task: make the analogy box answer cardiology.

embW = embj.words.map(d => {
  const n = Math.sqrt(d3.sum(d.v, x => x * x));
  return {...d, u: d.v.map(x => x / n)};
})

}

    height: 430, grid: true, x: {label: "First principal component"}, y: {label: "Second principal component"},

      Plot.text(shown.filter(d => d.word !== eWord && !nbSet.has(d.word)), {x: "x", y: "y", text: "word", dy: -8, fontSize: 9}),
      Plot.text(shown.filter(d => d.word === eWord || nbSet.has(d.word)), {x: "x", y: "y", text: "word", dy: -9, fontSize: 12, fontWeight: "bold"})
    ]

}























Inputs.table(eNb, {format: {cosine: d => d.toFixed(3)}, header: {word: `Nearest to "${eWord}"`}, height: 250})

viewof aB = Inputs.select(embWords, {value: "creatinine", label: "is to b"})
viewof aC = Inputs.select(embWords, {value: "liver", label: "as c"})























aRes = {
  const va = embIdx.get(aA).u, vb = embIdx.get(aB).u, vc = embIdx.get(aC).u;
  const t = vb.map((x, i) => x - va[i] + vc[i]);
