The nearest neighbour of vancomycin is gentamicin (cosine 0.98), and the symptoms crowd together in one region. Two other things are worth noticing. The neighbours mix two kinds of relation: words used instead of each other (gentamicin for vancomycin) and words used with each other (level, today), because summing input and output vectors mixes both. And meropenem, always the drug switched to in these notes, has as neighbours to, piperacillin, dose: embeddings reflect how a word is used in a particular corpus, not what it is.

16.7.1 Analogies, and their biases
Embeddings became famous for analogies: in vectors trained on news text, the vector \(\mathbf{e}_{\text{king}} - \mathbf{e}_{\text{man}} + \mathbf{e}_{\text{woman}}\) lies close to \(\mathbf{e}_{\text{queen}}\) (Mikolov, Sutskever, et al. 2013). The Ward 7 embeddings do something similar (Table 16.5), and fail just as instructively.

Most of them work: kidney is to creatinine as liver is to bilirubin; kidney is to nephrology as liver is to hepatology. The last one fails: pain occurs far more often as a symptom (“patient reports chest pain”) than as the reason for giving a drug, so its vector says little about what analgesics are for. Analogy results are also flattered by a convention, the exclusion of the three query words, without which the answer is often simply \(c\) itself (Nissim, Noord, and Goot 2020). Treat them as a window into the geometry, not as reasoning.
The same geometry records whatever associations the corpus contains, including unwelcome ones. Embeddings trained on news text place man close to computer programmer and woman close to homemaker (Bolukbasi et al. 2016), and reproduce the implicit associations measured in people (Caliskan, Bryson, and Narayanan 2017). Clinical text is no exception: language models trained on intensive care notes complete sentences differently depending on a patient’s gender, ethnicity or insurance (Zhang et al. 2020). In our simulated notes, the pronoun after each staff role was deliberately unbalanced (she follows nurse in 88 % of mentions and surgeon in only 13 %). In the embeddings, furosemide and bumetanide are close neighbours. Why?

The model has learned that both are loop diuretics The model knows nothing about drug classes; no such information was given to it.
They appear in similar contexts in the notes (“given for fluid overload”, “started … for oedema”) Correct. That is the distributional hypothesis at work: similar company, similar vectors. It usually coincides with similar meaning, which is why embeddings are useful, but the cause is usage.
Their names are spelled similarly Word-level embeddings see each word as an indivisible token; spelling plays no role. (Subword tokenisers, Chapter 15, would share pieces between similar spellings.)



The embeddings put surgeon closer to he than to she. A colleague proposes to fix this by deleting the words he and she from the vocabulary. What is the main problem with that fix?

None: without the pronouns the bias disappears The association lives in the whole pattern of contexts, not only in two words; other gendered words (names, titles, “Mr”, “Ms”) carry the same signal, and the model’s predictions will still reflect the skew of its training text.
The bias comes from the training text, so it resurfaces through other words, and removing pronouns also breaks legitimate uses Correct. The geometry reflects the corpus. Real remedies start with the data (what text, written by and about whom), continue with measuring bias in the model’s outputs, and keep a human reviewing what the model writes.
Bias in embeddings is harmless, because embeddings are only an internal representation Embeddings feed the predictions. On Ward 7 the same skew made the autocomplete write he for a woman surgeon.

text:
16.8 A tiny neural language model, built once
We can now put the pieces together. In 2003, Yoshua Bengio and colleagues replaced the count table of an n-gram model with a small neural network that reads the embeddings of the previous few tokens and outputs a softmax over the vocabulary (Bengio et al. 2003). The network and the embeddings are trained together, by gradient descent on the cross-entropy loss. Because similar tokens get similar embeddings, what the network learns about one context transfers to similar ones, which a count table cannot do.






started
vancomycin
for
w(t−3)
w(t−2)
w(t−1)

look up in E
look up in E
look up in E


join: x
length 3d


hidden layer
h = tanh(W₁x + b₁)


z = W₂h + b₂
softmax
infection
sepsis
pneumonia …




Figure 16.3: The tiny neural language model of this section, after Bengio et al. (2003): embeddings of the previous three tokens, one hidden layer, and a softmax over the whole vocabulary.



Written out, with the embeddings of the previous three tokens joined end to end into \(\mathbf{x} = (\mathbf{e}_{w_{t-3}}, \mathbf{e}_{w_{t-2}}, \mathbf{e}_{w_{t-1}})\), the model is \[
\mathbf{h} = \tanh\!\big(\mathbf{W}^{(1)} \mathbf{x} + \mathbf{b}^{(1)}\big), \qquad
\mathbf{z} = \mathbf{W}^{(2)} \mathbf{h} + \mathbf{b}^{(2)}, \qquad
P_\theta(w_t = j \mid w_{t-3}, w_{t-2}, w_{t-1}) = \frac{e^{z_j}}{\sum_k e^{z_k}} .
\qquad(16.6)\] Everything in it has appeared before: a lookup in \(\mathbf{E}\) (this section), a hidden layer with a nonlinear activation and a softmax output (Chapter 7), trained with the cross-entropy of Equation 16.4. Ours uses 16-dimensional embeddings, 128 hidden units and a window of 3 tokens: in total 25 267 parameters, trained with the Adam optimiser (Kingma and Ba 2015) for 8 passes over the 72 578 training predictions. The Lab writes the same model in about forty lines of base R or numpy (with 64 hidden units and plain gradient descent, to keep it short) and trains it in your browser; the version used in this chapter was trained once by the precompute script.








Figure 16.4: Learning curve of the tiny neural language model: cross-entropy on the training and test notes. Most of the learning happens in the first pass over the data.





Untrained, the network spreads its probability almost evenly and has a cross-entropy of 7.05 bits, close to \(\log_2\) 131 \(=\) 7.03, the cost of guessing uniformly. After training it reaches 1.292 bits on the test notes, a perplexity of 2.45, better than the best trigram model (2.63). Its predictions are also sensible: after “started vancomycin for” it gives infection, pneumonia and sepsis probabilities of 0.41, 0.31 and 0.26, not far from the one-third each built into the grammar. Do not overrate it, though. It gives “started meropenem” a probability of about 0.00002, even less than add-one smoothing did, because in the notes meropenem never follows started or anything used like it. Sharing by similarity works only when the data provide the similarity.

16.8.1 Characters instead of words
The same recipe works with any tokens. Figure 16.5 follows a model that reads and writes one character at a time, trained on Tiny Shakespeare, a public-domain collection of Shakespeare’s plays (about 1 115 000 characters) that has become a standard teaching corpus (Karpathy 2015). We chose it over the Ward 7 notes because its vocabulary of 65 characters and its rich language make the stages of learning easy to see. The model is a recurrent network, the subject of the next section, with 333 169 parameters, trained for a few minutes on one processor.

Watch a model learn to write. Choose a stage of training and a sampling temperature. Each sample starts from the prompt ROMEO: and continues for 300 characters. The curve shows the validation cross-entropy in bits per character; the dashed line is a uniform guess among the 65 characters.

section: 16.9 Remembering further back, and why that is not enough
text:
16.9 Remembering further back, and why that is not enough
Seán’s problem was a long-range one. In “started vancomycin today, patient reports nausea, check …”, the word that settles the next token, vancomycin, is eight tokens back. Every model so far looks at a fixed window: one token for the bigram, two for the trigram, three for our neural model. Whatever lies outside the window is invisible (Figure 16.6).






Figure 16.6: A model with a short window sees only the nearby words; the information that settles the next word may lie much further back.



A recurrent neural network removes the fixed window by reading the text one token at a time and carrying a summary forward.

Definition 16.11 (Recurrent neural network and hidden state) A recurrent neural network (RNN) keeps a hidden state vector \(\mathbf{h}_t\) that is updated after each token from the previous state and the new token’s embedding, \[
\mathbf{h}_t = \tanh\!\big(\mathbf{W}_{h} \mathbf{h}_{t-1} + \mathbf{W}_{e}\, \mathbf{e}_{w_t} + \mathbf{b}\big),
\] with the same weights at every position; the next-token distribution is a softmax of a linear function of \(\mathbf{h}_t\) (Elman 1990; Mikolov et al. 2010). In principle \(\mathbf{h}_t\) can carry information from any distance.

In practice, plain RNNs forget quickly.

Definition 16.12 (Vanishing gradient; LSTM) Training an RNN by backpropagation multiplies one factor per step back in time. Over many steps the product usually shrinks towards zero (or, less often, explodes), so the network receives almost no signal about how a word far back should have influenced the present: the vanishing gradient problem (Bengio, Simard, and Frasconi 1994). The long short-term memory (LSTM) network adds a separate memory cell and learned gates that decide, at each step, what to keep, what to forget and what to output; information can then travel many steps without fading (Hochreiter and Schmidhuber 1997).

We trained a small word-level LSTM on the Ward 7 notes, again in advance, with PyTorch (Paszke et al. 2019). Its test perplexity is 2.32, the best in Table 16.4, and Table 16.7 shows why.

The bigram and trigram models give the same answer whichever drug was started: after check they always prefer gentamicin, the drug that follows check slightly more often in the training notes (286 times against 250). That is the suggestion Seán saw. The neural model with a window of three is no better off, since the drug is outside its window: its probabilities hover around one half and change only with the words that happen to precede check. The LSTM, which has read the whole note, gives the right drug a probability of about 0.93, even when the drug is twelve tokens back.
Recurrence is not the end of the story. An RNN must squeeze everything it has read into one fixed-length vector, updated strictly in order, so a long discharge letter is compressed through a bottleneck, and the computation cannot be spread over many processors at once because each step waits for the previous one. The fix, introduced first to help recurrent translation models (Bahdanau, Cho, and Bengio 2015) and then on its own (Vaswani et al. 2017), is to let the model look back directly at any earlier token and decide how much attention to pay to each. That is attention, the subject of Chapter 17.

Why can a trigram model never learn, however many notes it sees, to suggest the right drug after “started vancomycin today, patient reports nausea, check”?

Because vancomycin is a rare word Vancomycin is common in the notes. The problem is not frequency but distance.
Because the drug lies outside its two-token window, so its prediction after “, check” is the same whatever drug was started Correct. A fixed window throws away everything earlier. More data sharpen the estimate of P(drug | “, check”) but cannot make it depend on a word the model never sees.
Because trigram models need smoothing Smoothing deals with unseen sequences. Here the sequence “, check vancomycin” is common; the trouble is that the model cannot tell when it is the right one.
It can, if the temperature is lowered Lowering the temperature only makes the model commit harder to its preferred drug, which here is the wrong one half of the time.



Each problem below was met in this chapter. Which idea was introduced to address it?

A count-based model gives probability zero to “started meropenem”, so a whole note becomes impossible. Smoothing
What the model learns about vancomycin tells it nothing about gentamicin, because each word is an unrelated symbol. Embeddings
The model cannot use a drug mentioned eight tokens before the word it must predict, because it only sees a fixed window. Recurrence
A recurrent model must compress a whole discharge letter into one vector, processed strictly word by word. Attention
“furosemide” and “bumetanide” should share what is learned about them, since they are used in the same way. Embeddings
A trigram model meets a two-word context it has never seen in training. Smoothing

section: 16.10 Where this fits in the decision loop
text:
16.10 Where this fits in the decision loop


  A note-drafting language model in the decision loop
  A cycle: past clinical notes are the data; the language model is the model; it produces next-token probabilities and a suggested continuation, the information; the clinician accepts, edits or rejects the suggestion, which is the decision; the final note enters the record and becomes training data for the next model, so errors and biases that are accepted feed back into the data.
  
  
  Data
  past notes
  
  Model
  language model
  
  Information
  probable next words
  
  Decision
  accept, edit or reject
  
  Action and outcome
  the note enters the record, and the next corpus
  
  
  
  
  

A note-drafting model in the decision loop. The model supplies probable words, not checked facts; what the clinician accepts becomes tomorrow's training data.

A language model is a way of building the model step when the data are text: it learns, from past notes, a probability for every possible next token (Section 16.2, Section 16.3). The information it produces is a distribution over words, and a suggestion drawn from it by a decoding rule (Section 16.6); perplexity says how well the distribution fits held-out text (Section 16.5), not whether a given sentence is true. What can go wrong? A fixed window misses what was said earlier (Section 16.9), as with the wrong drug on Seán’s screen; skews in the corpus are absorbed by the embeddings and exaggerated by greedy decoding (Section 16.7, Section 16.6); fluent text can be false. And the loop closes on itself: accepted suggestions become the notes on which the next model is trained, so an error or a bias that nobody corrects is learned again, more strongly (Shumailov et al. 2024). Who stays in control? The clinician who reads every suggestion before it enters the record, and the team that decides on what text a model is trained, how it decodes, and how its outputs are monitored.

Run it here (training the neural model takes a few seconds in Python and a minute or two in R in the browser), or download it: ch16_lab.R · ch16_lab.py.

RPython























Two observations to take forward. First, after five passes with plain gradient descent the network clearly beats the smoothed bigram model on the test notes and roughly matches the best trigram model; the version used in the chapter, with more hidden units and the Adam optimiser, does better still. (R and Python draw different random numbers, so their results differ slightly.) title: 16  Predicting the next word: language models and embeddings
text:
16.12 Exercises

Counting by hand. Using the six notes of the gate, write the bigram probabilities \(\hat P(\cdot \mid \text{patient})\) and \(\hat P(\cdot \mid \texttt{<s>})\), and compute the probability of the note “patient reports pain .” (with </s>) under this tiny model.
Chain rule. Explain in two sentences why the chain rule (Equation 16.1) is exact, while a bigram model is an approximation. Which assumption does the bigram model add?
Smoothing. In the Lab, compute the add-\(\delta\) perplexity of the bigram model for \(\delta = 0.001\) and \(\delta = 0.0001\). Does it keep improving? What would happen with \(\delta = 0\), and why?
Perplexity as a branching factor. A model assigns probability \(1/4\) to every token of a test text. What are its cross-entropy and its perplexity? What if it assigns \(1/2\) to half of the tokens and \(1/8\) to the other half?
Temperature. In the temperature widget, choose “creatinine rising ,”. Why does the distribution barely change between \(\tau = 0.2\) and \(\tau = 1\), while “plan :” changes a lot?
Embeddings. In the embeddings explorer, find a word whose nearest neighbour belongs to a different category. Explain the neighbour using the contexts in which both words appear in the notes.
Bias. Suppose the Ward 7 autocomplete is retrained every month on the notes written that month, many of which were drafted with its suggestions. Describe what happens over time to the share of he after “the surgeon says” if suggestions are usually accepted. Propose two safeguards.
Code. Modify the Lab’s neural model to use a window of 1 token instead of 3. Compare its test perplexity with the bigram model’s. What does the comparison tell you?







Selected answers





1. After <s>: patient 5/6, no 1/6. After patient: reports 4/5, denies 1/5. After reports: pain 2/4. pain occurs four times, followed by “.” three times and by since once, so \(\hat P(. \mid \text{pain}) = 3/4\). After “.”: </s> every time. The probability of the note is \(5/6 \times 4/5 \times 2/4 \times 3/4 \times 1 = 0.25\).
4. Probability \(1/4\) everywhere: surprise 2 bits per token, cross-entropy 2 bits, perplexity \(2^2 = 4\). Half at \(1/2\) (1 bit) and half at \(1/8\) (3 bits): average surprise 2 bits, so the perplexity is again 4. Perplexity summarises the average surprise; different patterns of confidence can give the same value.
5. After “creatinine rising ,” the grammar always continues with kidney, so one logit is far larger than all the others; dividing by any temperature up to 1 leaves it dominant. After “plan :” five continuations are equally common, their logits are close, and temperature reshapes the distribution strongly.
7. Each month the training notes contain a slightly higher share of he, because greedy suggestions always propose he and are usually accepted; the model learns the higher share and proposes he even more firmly: a feedback loop that amplifies the original skew. Safeguards: exclude machine-drafted text (or text accepted without edits) from retraining; monitor the outputs for known skews; use decoding that does not complete pronouns or names; make editing easy and expected.
8. With a window of one token the network sees exactly what the bigram model sees, so it cannot do much better; any gain comes from smoother estimates for rare pairs, not from more context. The comparison isolates the contribution of the longer window.

title: 16  Predicting the next word: language models and embeddings
text:
16.13 Summary

A language model gives a probability to every possible next token given the text so far; it can score texts and, by repeatedly choosing a next token, generate them.
The chain rule writes the probability of any text exactly as a product of next-token probabilities; we work with sums of log-probabilities to avoid rounding to zero.
n-gram models estimate next-token probabilities by counting, using only the last \(n-1\) tokens. Counts become sparse very quickly, so they need smoothing to avoid zero probabilities.
Cross-entropy — the average surprise per token on held-out text — is both the training loss and the evaluation measure; perplexity, \(2^{H}\), is the effective number of choices. It is comparable only on the same text and tokenisation.
Softmax turns logits into probabilities; decoding turns probabilities into text. Temperature, top-\(k\) and top-\(p\) shape the distribution; low temperatures are repeatable but exaggerate the majority continuation. Generation involves chance, and fluent is not the same as true.
Embeddings replace one-hot symbols with learned dense vectors. By the distributional hypothesis, words used in similar contexts get similar vectors (skip-gram, GloVe); the geometry supports analogies and also absorbs the biases of the corpus.
A neural language model combines embeddings, a hidden layer and a softmax, trained by gradient descent on cross-entropy. Recurrent networks (and LSTMs, which ease the vanishing gradient) carry a hidden state beyond a fixed window, but still compress everything into one vector, read in order. That limitation motivates attention.

title: 17  Attention and the transformer
text:
How to use this chapter






Starting here?





This chapter builds directly on the two chapters before it and on the neural networks of Chapter 7. In a few lines:

Text is cut into tokens (words or pieces of words) drawn from a vocabulary \(\mathcal{V}\); the token at position \(t\) is written \(w_t\) (Chapter 15).
A language model gives a probability to a sequence of tokens. By the chain rule of probability, \(P(w_1, \dots, w_T) = \prod_{t=1}^{T} P(w_t \mid w_{<t})\), so the whole job reduces to predicting the next token from the ones before it. An n-gram model looks only at the last \(n-1\) tokens; a recurrent network (RNN) squeezes the whole past into one hidden vector (Chapter 16).
Each token is represented by an embedding, a learned vector \(\mathbf{e}_w\) of numbers in which similar words end up close together (Chapter 16).
The softmax turns a vector of scores \(z_1, \dots, z_C\) into probabilities that are positive and add up to 1, \(e^{z_c} / \sum_{c'} e^{z_{c'}}\) (Chapter 7); a language model uses it to give a probability to every possible next token, and it is trained by minimising the cross-entropy, the average of \(-\log P(\text{observed next token})\) (Chapter 16).
A neural network is built from layers of weighted sums followed by a nonlinear activation; its weights are learned by gradient descent, with gradients computed by backpropagation (Chapter 7). A model is a simplified representation built for a purpose (Definition 1.3), and it supplies information to a decision (Definition 1.4).

A two-minute refresher on vectors and matrices






A vector is a list of numbers, such as \(\mathbf{a} = (2, 0)\). The dot product of two vectors of the same length multiplies them entry by entry and adds up: \((2, 0) \cdot (1, 3) = 2 \times 1 + 0 \times 3 = 2\). It is large and positive when the two vectors point the same way, near zero when they are unrelated, and negative when they point in opposite directions.
A matrix is a table of numbers; \(\mathbf{X}\) with \(T\) rows and \(d\) columns is “\(T \times d\)”. Here each row is one token.
The matrix product \(\mathbf{A}\mathbf{B}\) is a table of dot products: entry \((t, s)\) is the dot product of row \(t\) of \(\mathbf{A}\) with column \(s\) of \(\mathbf{B}\). It needs the number of columns of \(\mathbf{A}\) to equal the number of rows of \(\mathbf{B}\): a \(T \times d\) matrix times a \(d \times d_k\) matrix gives a \(T \times d_k\) matrix.
The transpose \(\mathbf{B}^{\top}\) swaps rows and columns. So \(\mathbf{Q}\mathbf{K}^{\top}\) is the table of dot products between every row of \(\mathbf{Q}\) and every row of \(\mathbf{K}\).
In R, the matrix product is A %*% B and the transpose t(B); in Python (numpy) they are A @ B and B.T.

title: 17  Attention and the transformer
text:
17.1 Why looking back is hard
Every language model, from the simplest to the largest, estimates the same thing: the probability of the next token given the ones before it, \[
P(w_t \mid w_{<t}) = P(w_t \mid w_1, w_2, \dots, w_{t-1}) .
\qquad(17.1)\] The chain rule that leads to Equation 17.1 is an identity: it does not assume that words are independent, it simply writes the probability of a whole sentence as a product of next-token predictions (Chapter 16). What differs between models is not this objective but how they represent the context \(w_{<t}\) — how much of it they can see, and how they decide which parts matter.
In Seán’s note the decisive words, vancomycin and contrast, are far from the word being interpreted. Real clinical language is full of such long-range dependencies: a pronoun refers to a patient named sentences earlier; a negation such as “denies” changes the meaning of a symptom several words later; an instruction at the top of a letter governs everything below it. Earlier models handle them badly, in two ways (Jurafsky and Martin 2026).

A fixed window. An n-gram model keeps only the last \(n-1\) tokens, \(P(w_t \mid w_{<t}) \approx P(w_t \mid w_{t-n+1}, \dots, w_{t-1})\). Anything earlier is invisible. Widening the window does not rescue it: the number of possible contexts grows exponentially with \(n\), so most long contexts are never seen in training.
A bottleneck. A recurrent network reads one token at a time and carries a single hidden vector forward, \(\mathbf{h}_t = g(\mathbf{h}_{t-1}, \mathbf{e}_{w_{t-1}})\). In principle it can remember anything; in practice the whole past must squeeze into one vector of fixed length, and information from far back fades (Hochreiter and Schmidhuber 1997; Y. Bengio, Simard, and Frasconi 1994).







Figure 17.1: Attention keeps every earlier word available. When the model has to continue “The patient had many tests and now …”, it compares the current position with all earlier words and gives most weight to the informative one (“patient”), instead of relying on the nearest words or on a single compressed summary.



The code below rebuilds the toy example of the earlier edition of this book. Every sentence starts with “the patient” or “the trial”, continues with a random number of uninformative words, and ends with the word to be predicted: pain after a patient, events after a trial. The second word fully determines the last one, but it is buried at the start. For each window size \(k\), the code checks how often the decisive word is among the last \(k\) words before the target.

RPython























With a window of two words, the decisive word is never visible; with twelve it always is, but only because these sentences are short. The model fails not because the information is absent, but because its conditioning rule cannot reach it. Attention changes the rule: keep every earlier token available, and let the model compute, for each prediction, how much each one matters.

A trigram model (window of two words) reads Seán’s note and must judge the word after “passed very little …”. Why can it not use the fact that Aoife is on vancomycin?

Because “vancomycin” is a rare word that the model has never seen Rarity can be a problem, but here the issue would remain even for a common word. The trigram model only conditions on “very little”; anything earlier is outside its window, rare or not.
Because “vancomycin” lies outside the two-word window, so the model never conditions on it Correct. The information is in the note, but the model’s fixed conditioning rule cannot reach it. This is the structural problem attention solves.
Because n-gram models cannot use probabilities They are probability models: they estimate \(P(w_t \mid w_{t-2}, w_{t-1})\) by counting. The limit is which words they condition on, not whether they use probabilities.
Because the chain rule assumes that words are independent The chain rule is an identity that makes the dependence on all earlier words explicit. It is the n-gram approximation that throws most of that dependence away.

title: 17  Attention and the transformer
text:
17.2 Attention: a soft, learned look-up
Think of how Seán uses the drug chart. He has a question in mind (“is anything on this chart toxic to the kidneys?”). Each line of the chart has a label (the drug name) and content (dose, route, start date). He compares his question with every label, and reads the content of the lines that match. A database does the same with exact matches: one query, one matching key, one value returned.
Attention is a soft version of this look-up. Instead of returning the content of the single best match, it returns a weighted average of all the contents, with weights that grow with how well each label matches the question. The weights are positive and add up to 1, so they behave like probabilities: a share of attention given to each earlier token.

Definition 17.1 (Attention) Attention is an operation that builds a new representation for a position \(t\) as a weighted average of the representations of the positions it may look at, \[
\mathbf{c}_t = \sum_{s} \alpha_{ts}\, \mathbf{v}_s, \qquad \alpha_{ts} \ge 0, \quad \sum_{s} \alpha_{ts} = 1 ,
\qquad(17.2)\] where \(\mathbf{v}_s\) is the content (value) offered by position \(s\) and the attention weight \(\alpha_{ts}\) measures how relevant position \(s\) is to position \(t\). The weights are computed from the data themselves, separately for every position and every input. When the positions belong to the same sequence, the operation is called self-attention.

Two features make attention different from everything in Chapter 16. First, nothing is thrown away: every earlier token remains directly reachable, however far back it is. Second, the weights are not fixed by position (“the last two words”) but computed from the content: the same position can be ignored in one sentence and be decisive in the next.
The idea was introduced for machine translation. Bahdanau, Cho, and Bengio (2015) let a recurrent translation model, at each output word, look back over all the words of the source sentence and weight them — the model learned on its own to align each French word with the English words it translated. Vaswani et al. (2017) then asked whether recurrence was needed at all, and built a model in which attention does all the work of moving information between positions. They called it the transformer. The rest of this chapter takes it apart.

For the word “urine” in Seán’s note, a model gives the same attention weight to each of the 30 earlier tokens. What is \(\mathbf{c}_t\), the output of attention for “urine”?

The plain average of the 30 value vectors Correct. With equal weights \(\alpha_{ts} = 1/30\), Equation 17.2 is the ordinary mean. Attention is useful precisely when it learns unequal weights that pick out “vancomycin” and “contrast”.
The value vector of the most recent token That would be a weight of 1 on the last token and 0 on all others — a window of one word, not equal weights.
The sum of the 30 value vectors The weights add up to 1, not 30, so the result is an average, not a sum. Keeping the weights summing to 1 keeps the output on the same scale whatever the length of the text.
Nothing: attention weights must differ between tokens Equal weights are allowed; they are simply uninformative. An untrained model often starts close to this.

title: 17  Attention and the transformer
text:
17.3 Queries, keys and values
Where do the weights come from? Each token plays three roles at once, and the transformer gives it three different vectors, one for each role.

Definition 17.2 (Query, key and value) Each token vector \(\mathbf{x}_t\) entering an attention layer is multiplied by three learned matrices to give \[
\mathbf{q}_t = \mathbf{x}_t \mathbf{W}_Q, \qquad \mathbf{k}_t = \mathbf{x}_t \mathbf{W}_K, \qquad \mathbf{v}_t = \mathbf{x}_t \mathbf{W}_V .
\] The query \(\mathbf{q}_t\) describes what position \(t\) is looking for; the key \(\mathbf{k}_s\) describes what position \(s\) offers to be found by; the value \(\mathbf{v}_s\) is the content that position \(s\) passes on when it is attended to. Stacking the rows gives the matrices \(\mathbf{Q} = \mathbf{X}\mathbf{W}_Q\), \(\mathbf{K} = \mathbf{X}\mathbf{W}_K\) and \(\mathbf{V} = \mathbf{X}\mathbf{W}_V\).

The matrices \(\mathbf{W}_Q\), \(\mathbf{W}_K\) and \(\mathbf{W}_V\) are ordinary weights of a neural network, learned by gradient descent like those of Chapter 7. Nobody tells the model that “pain” should look for negations or that “denies” should advertise itself as one: the model discovers whatever queries and keys make its predictions better. Attention is therefore not a rule applied to text from outside — it is a learned neural computation.
The match between a query and a key is measured by their dot product, which is large when the two vectors point the same way. Dividing by \(\sqrt{d_k}\) and applying a softmax to each row turns the matches into weights, and the weights average the values. In matrix form this is the formula at the heart of every transformer (Vaswani et al. 2017): \[
\operatorname{Attention}(\mathbf{Q}, \mathbf{K}, \mathbf{V}) = \operatorname{softmax}\!\left( \frac{\mathbf{Q}\mathbf{K}^{\top}}{\sqrt{d_k}} \right) \mathbf{V} ,
\qquad(17.3)\] where the softmax is applied to each row separately. Row \(t\) of the result is \(\mathbf{c}_t\) of Equation 17.2, and row \(t\) of the softmax holds the weights \(\alpha_{t1}, \dots, \alpha_{tT}\). Figure 17.2 follows the computation step by step.

17.3.1 Why divide by \(\sqrt{d_k}\)?
The scaling is not decoration. A dot product adds up \(d_k\) products, so as the vectors get longer the scores spread out. If the entries of queries and keys are roughly independent with mean 0 and variance 1, the dot product has variance \(d_k\), so its typical size grows like \(\sqrt{d_k}\) (Vaswani et al. 2017). Large scores push the softmax to extremes: one token takes almost all the weight, the others almost none, and the gradients that training relies on become tiny. Dividing by \(\sqrt{d_k}\) brings the scores back to a spread of about 1 whatever the dimension. The simulation below draws random queries and keys and shows it (Table 17.1).

Three things to notice. First, the weights depend on the query: the same keys produce very different weights for a query that looks for negation and for one that looks for body sites. Second, the output is a blend of values, so “pain” can carry a negation signal it did not have before — its vector has been contextualised. Third, switch the scaling off and make the query long: the weights snap to almost 0 and 1. That is the saturation the \(\sqrt{d_k}\) protects against.
The same computation on a five-word sentence, with random vectors standing in for learned ones, is below. Run it line by line: each step is one box of Figure 17.2.

RPython























Because the vectors are random, the weights carry no linguistic meaning yet — “the” may attend mostly to “reports” for no good reason. Training is what turns \(\mathbf{W}_Q\), \(\mathbf{W}_K\) and \(\mathbf{W}_V\) into matrices whose weights make sense; Section 17.10 shows a trained example.

A colleague removes the division by \(\sqrt{d_k}\) from a transformer with \(d_k = 256\). What is the most likely consequence?

Nothing: the softmax gives the same weights whatever the scale of the scores The softmax is sensitive to scale. Multiplying all scores by 16 (which is \(\sqrt{256}\)) makes the largest one dominate far more. Try it in the widget by switching the scaling off.
The scores become very large, the softmax saturates on one token per row, and training becomes slow and unstable Correct. With \(d_k = 256\) the raw dot products have a spread of about 16 instead of 1 (Table 17.1). Near-0/1 weights give almost zero gradients, so the model struggles to learn which tokens matter.
The attention weights no longer add up to 1 The softmax always produces weights that add up to 1, whatever the scale of its inputs. What changes is how peaked they are.
The model can no longer attend to distant tokens Distance plays no role in the scores; every token is still reachable. The problem is numerical, not about reach.

title: 17  Attention and the transformer
section: 17.4 Masks: who may look at whom

title: 17  Attention and the transformer
text:
17.5 Many heads, many relationships
One attention operation produces one set of weights per token — one notion of relevance. But a clinical sentence carries several relationships at once. For “creatinine” in Seán’s note, one relevant link is to the drug (why is it being checked?), another to the patient (whose creatinine?), another to the time (since when?). Asking a single set of weights to capture all of them makes it a bottleneck.

Definition 17.4 (Multi-head attention) Multi-head attention runs \(h\) attention operations, called heads, side by side, each with its own projection matrices \(\mathbf{W}_Q^{(m)}, \mathbf{W}_K^{(m)}, \mathbf{W}_V^{(m)}\), so that each head can learn its own notion of relevance: \[
\text{head}_m = \operatorname{Attention}\big(\mathbf{X}\mathbf{W}_Q^{(m)},\, \mathbf{X}\mathbf{W}_K^{(m)},\, \mathbf{X}\mathbf{W}_V^{(m)}\big), \qquad m = 1, \dots, h .
\] The outputs of the heads are placed side by side (concatenated) and mixed by one more learned matrix \(\mathbf{W}_O\): \[
\operatorname{MHA}(\mathbf{X}) = \big[\text{head}_1, \dots, \text{head}_h\big]\, \mathbf{W}_O .
\qquad(17.5)\] Usually each head works with vectors of length \(d_k = d/h\), so the heads together cost about the same as one large head.

In trained models, heads do specialise. Studying BERT, Clark et al. (2019) found heads that attend to the previous or next word, heads that link a verb to its direct object, a determiner to its noun, or a pronoun to the noun it refers to — none of which anyone programmed. Specialisation is not guaranteed, though, and many heads have patterns that resist a simple description. The original transformer used \(h = 8\) heads with \(d = 512\) (Vaswani et al. 2017); BERT-base uses 12 heads with \(d = 768\) (Devlin et al. 2019).

A transformer has model dimension \(d = 512\). Its designers switch from 8 heads of size \(d_k = 64\) to 16 heads of size \(d_k = 32\). What happens to the number of weights in \(\mathbf{W}_Q\), \(\mathbf{W}_K\), \(\mathbf{W}_V\) and \(\mathbf{W}_O\) together?

It stays the same Correct. Each of the four matrices is still \(512 \times 512\) in total; the heads only split its columns into more, narrower pieces. More heads give more relevance patterns at no extra cost in weights.
It doubles, because there are twice as many heads Each head is half as wide, so the total is unchanged: \(16 \times 32 = 8 \times 64 = 512\) columns.
It halves, because each head is half as wide There are twice as many of them, so the halving is cancelled.
It depends on the length of the notes The weights do not depend on the number of tokens: the same matrices are applied to every position. The computation grows with length (Section 17.11), the number of weights does not.

title: 17  Attention and the transformer
text:
17.6 Word order: positional encodings
There is a surprising gap in everything so far. Look again at Equation 17.3: the scores compare vectors, and nothing in them says where a token is. Shuffle the rows of \(\mathbf{X}\) and the outputs are shuffled in the same way but otherwise unchanged. Attention treats its input as a set of tokens, not a sequence. Yet order carries meaning: “creatinine rose after vancomycin was started” and “vancomycin was started after creatinine rose” contain the same words and tell opposite clinical stories.

RPython
























Definition 17.5 (Positional encoding) A positional encoding is a vector \(\mathbf{p}_t\), one for each position \(t\), added to the token embedding before the first layer, so that every input vector carries both what the token is and where it is: \[
\mathbf{x}_t^{(0)} = \mathbf{e}_{w_t} + \mathbf{p}_t .
\] The encodings can be fixed functions of the position or learned like any other weight.

The original transformer used fixed waves of different frequencies: coordinate \(2r\) of \(\mathbf{p}_t\) is \(\sin(t / 10000^{2r/d})\) and coordinate \(2r+1\) is \(\cos(t / 10000^{2r/d})\), so each position gets a unique pattern and nearby positions get similar ones (Vaswani et al. 2017). BERT and the GPT models instead learn one vector per position (Devlin et al. 2019; Radford et al. 2019), which is also what the small model in Section 17.10 does. Many recent models encode relative position by rotating queries and keys by an angle that depends on the position, so that the score between two tokens depends on how far apart they are (Su et al. 2024).

A transformer without any positional information reads “creatinine rose after vancomycin was started” and “vancomycin was started after creatinine rose”. What can it tell about the two sentences?

It sees the difference, because attention compares every word with every other Attention compares contents. Without positions, both sentences give the same set of token vectors, and the outputs differ only by being listed in a different order.
Nothing that depends on order: to it they are the same bag of words Correct. Self-attention is blind to order (the code above shows the outputs are simply reordered). Adding a positional encoding to each token is what lets the model tell “before” from “after”.
It sees the difference only if it uses a causal mask A causal mask does let a generating model infer some order (each position sees a different number of tokens), but the standard design does not rely on it: positions are encoded explicitly.

title: 17  Attention and the transformer
text:
17.7 The transformer block
Attention moves information between tokens. On its own it is not yet a model. The transformer wraps it in a block with three more ingredients — a feed-forward network, residual connections and layer normalisation — and stacks many identical blocks.
The feed-forward network. After attention has mixed information across positions, each token’s vector goes, on its own, through a small neural network of the kind met in Chapter 7: a hidden layer, usually four times wider than \(d\), with a nonlinear activation \(g\), and back to width \(d\): \[
\operatorname{FFN}(\mathbf{x}) = g(\mathbf{x}\mathbf{W}_1 + \mathbf{b}_1)\,\mathbf{W}_2 + \mathbf{b}_2 .
\] The same weights are applied at every position. A useful slogan: attention decides where to look; the feed-forward network decides what to do with what was found. Without it, a stack of attention layers could only form weighted averages of value vectors. The activation \(g\) is usually ReLU or its smooth cousin GELU (Nair and Hinton 2010; Hendrycks and Gimpel 2016).

Definition 17.6 (Residual connection and layer normalisation) A residual connection adds a sublayer’s input to its output, \(\mathbf{x} + F(\mathbf{x})\), so the sublayer only has to learn a correction to the current representation; it also gives gradients a direct path through deep stacks (He et al. 2016). Layer normalisation rescales each token vector to mean 0 and standard deviation 1 across its \(d\) coordinates and then applies a learned gain \(\mathbf{g}\) and shift \(\mathbf{b}\), coordinate by coordinate: \(\operatorname{LN}(\mathbf{x}) = \mathbf{g} \odot (\mathbf{x} - \mu)/\sigma + \mathbf{b}\), where \(\mu\) and \(\sigma\) are the mean and standard deviation of the entries of \(\mathbf{x}\) and \(\odot\) is entry-by-entry multiplication (Ba, Kiros, and Hinton 2016). It keeps the numbers in a stable range as they pass through many layers.

Where exactly the normalisation goes matters, and two arrangements are in use. The original transformer normalised after adding the residual (post-LN): \(\mathbf{X}' = \operatorname{LN}(\mathbf{X} + \operatorname{MHA}(\mathbf{X}))\) (Vaswani et al. 2017). GPT-2 moved the normalisation to the input of each sublayer and added a final normalisation after the last block (Radford et al. 2019), and Xiong et al. (2020) showed why this pre-LN arrangement is easier to train: the residual path stays an untouched highway from input to output, gradients are well behaved from the start, and training needs less of the careful “warm-up” of the learning rate that post-LN requires. Most current models use pre-LN, and so does this chapter.

Definition 17.7 (Transformer block (pre-LN)) A transformer block takes a \(T \times d\) matrix of token vectors \(\mathbf{X}\) and returns a matrix \(\mathbf{Y}\) of the same shape: \[
\mathbf{X}' = \mathbf{X} + \operatorname{MHA}\big(\operatorname{LN}(\mathbf{X})\big), \qquad
\mathbf{Y} = \mathbf{X}' + \operatorname{FFN}\big(\operatorname{LN}(\mathbf{X}')\big) .
\qquad(17.6)\] A transformer stacks \(N\) such blocks, \(\mathbf{H}^{(l)} = \operatorname{Block}_l(\mathbf{H}^{(l-1)})\) for \(l = 1, \dots, N\), starting from \(\mathbf{H}^{(0)}\), the token embeddings plus positional encodings. In a text-generating model the attention in every block is causally masked.

Notice the invariant: every sublayer returns a \(T \times d\) matrix, so the residual additions are always defined and blocks can be stacked as deep as we like. Depth is used for repeated refinement. Studies of trained models suggest that lower layers tend to capture local, surface patterns and higher layers more abstract relationships, although the picture is far from neat (Clark et al. 2019).

Which part of the transformer does each job?

Lets the vector for “creatinine” pull in information from “vancomycin” twenty tokens earlier. Attention
Transforms each token’s vector on its own, through a hidden layer four times wider. Feed-forward network
Adds a sublayer’s input back to its output, so each layer only learns a correction. Residual connection
Rescales each token vector to mean 0 and standard deviation 1 before a sublayer. Layer normalisation
Lets the model know that “vancomycin” came before “creatinine”. Positional encoding
Stops a token from looking at the tokens that come after it. Causal mask


How big is one block? Count the weights. Each of \(\mathbf{W}_Q\), \(\mathbf{W}_K\), \(\mathbf{W}_V\) and \(\mathbf{W}_O\) is \(d \times d\) with a bias of length \(d\); the feed-forward network has a \(d \times d_{\text{ff}}\) matrix with \(d_{\text{ff}}\) biases and a \(d_{\text{ff}} \times d\) matrix with \(d\) biases; each of the two layer normalisations has a gain and a shift of length \(d\). As Exercise 17.1 shows, the feed-forward networks, not the attention, hold most of a transformer’s weights.

Count the weights of a block. The small transformer trained in Section 17.10 has \(d = 32\), \(h = 2\) heads and \(d_{\text{ff}} = 128\). The attention and layer-normalisation counts are written for you. title: 17  Attention and the transformer
section: 17.8 From vectors to the next word
text:
17.8 From vectors to the next word
After the last block, each position \(t\) holds a vector \(\mathbf{h}_t\) of length \(d\) that has gathered, through attention, whatever it needs from tokens \(1, \dots, t\). A language model must turn it into a probability for every token of the vocabulary. A linear layer gives one score (logit) per token, and the softmax of Chapter 16 turns scores into probabilities: \[
\mathbf{z}_t = \mathbf{h}_t \mathbf{E}^{\top}, \qquad
P(w_{t+1} = v \mid w_{\le t}) = \frac{e^{z_{t,v}}}{\sum_{u \in \mathcal{V}} e^{z_{t,u}}} .
\qquad(17.7)\] Here the output layer reuses the embedding matrix \(\mathbf{E}\), a common choice called weight tying (Press and Wolf 2017): the logit of token \(v\) is the dot product \(\mathbf{h}_t \cdot \mathbf{e}_v\), so the model predicts the tokens whose embeddings best match the current state, and it saves a \(d \times \lvert\mathcal{V}\rvert\) matrix of weights. Because of the causal mask, \(\mathbf{h}_t\) depends only on tokens up to \(t\), so Equation 17.7 is a genuine next-token prediction.
Training uses the same loss as in Chapter 16. Every position of every training text provides one prediction, and the model minimises the average cross-entropy, \[
\mathcal{L}_{\text{AR}} = -\frac{1}{T} \sum_{t=1}^{T} \log P(w_t \mid w_{<t}) ,
\qquad(17.8)\] that is, it maximises the likelihood of the text. No labels are needed — the next token is the label — which is why this is called self-supervised learning. Thanks to the mask, all \(T\) predictions of a text are computed in one parallel pass, which is a large part of why transformers train so much faster than recurrent networks (Vaswani et al. 2017).
Training and generation use the conditional probability differently. During training the model is always given the true previous tokens (this is called teacher forcing (Williams and Zipser 1989)). During generation it feeds on its own previous outputs: it predicts a distribution, picks a token (the most probable one, or a sample, as in Chapter 16), appends it, and repeats. A model can therefore do well on the training loss and still drift during long free-running generation, because one unlikely pick changes everything that follows (S. Bengio et al. 2015).
Putting the pieces together, the full path from text to prediction is: text → tokens → token identifiers → embeddings plus positions → \(N\) transformer blocks → final layer normalisation → logits → softmax → probability of the next token.

title: 17  Attention and the transformer
section: 17.9 Encoders, decoders and the two families
text:
17.9 Encoders, decoders and the two families
The original transformer was built for translation, with two stacks (Figure 17.4) (Vaswani et al. 2017). An encoder reads the whole source text with bidirectional self-attention and produces one contextual vector per token. A decoder generates the output one token at a time with causally masked self-attention, and in each block a third sublayer, cross-attention, takes its queries from the decoder and its keys and values from the encoder’s output, so that every generated word can look back at the source. A clinical example of the same design: an encoder reads Aoife’s discharge summary, and a decoder writes the instructions in plain language for her daughter, word by word, consulting the summary at every step.

Definition 17.8 (Encoder, decoder) A transformer encoder is a stack of blocks with bidirectional self-attention: every token can attend to every other, and the output is a contextual vector for each token. A transformer decoder is a stack of blocks with causally masked self-attention, used to generate text left to right. An encoder–decoder model connects them through cross-attention, in which queries come from the decoder and keys and values from the encoder.

Within two years, each half had become the basis of its own family, and the difference between them is precisely the mask and the training objective (Figure 17.5).
GPT: decoder only. The Generative Pre-trained Transformer keeps only the decoder stack, without cross-attention, and is trained on Equation 17.8 over large collections of text (Radford et al. 2018, 2019). Because its mask matches the chain rule, it defines a probability for any text and can generate. Given the prompt “The patient was admitted to”, it computes a distribution for the next token, picks one (“Ward”), appends it, and repeats: “The patient was admitted to Ward 7 with sepsis.” Each new token becomes context for the next, so generation is cumulative — and every pick shapes everything after it.
BERT: encoder only. Bidirectional Encoder Representations from Transformers keeps only the encoder and is trained to fill in blanks (Devlin et al. 2019). About 15 % of the tokens of each training text are selected; most of them are replaced by a special [MASK] token (some by a random token, some left unchanged), and the model must recover the originals using the words on both sides. The mask here corrupts the input, not the attention: attention stays fully bidirectional.

Definition 17.9 (Masked versus autoregressive language modelling) An autoregressive language model predicts each token from the tokens before it and is trained by minimising Equation 17.8; it defines a probability for whole texts and can generate. A masked language model hides a random set \(\mathcal{M}\) of positions and is trained to recover them from the rest of the text, \[
\mathcal{L}_{\text{MLM}} = -\sum_{t \in \mathcal{M}} \log P\big(w_t \mid \tilde{w}\big) ,
\qquad(17.9)\] where \(\tilde{w}\) is the corrupted text. It learns rich two-sided representations but does not define a left-to-right factorisation of the probability of a text, so it is not used to generate.

BERT’s strength is representation. A BERT model pretrained on general text can be fine-tuned with a small labelled set to classify notes (“does this note describe an adverse drug reaction?”) or to find the answer to a question inside a passage: given “The patient was admitted to the intensive care unit yesterday” and the question “Where was the patient admitted?”, it marks the span “the intensive care unit” (Rajpurkar et al. 2016; Devlin et al. 2019). Clinical and biomedical text is different enough from newspapers and web pages that domain-specific encoders help: BioBERT continued BERT’s pretraining on PubMed abstracts and full-text articles (Lee et al. 2020), ClinicalBERT on intensive-care notes (Alsentzer et al. 2019), and PubMedBERT was pretrained on biomedical text from scratch, with a vocabulary of its own (Gu et al. 2021). On Ward 7, a tool that flags drug-related kidney risk in notes is a classification task, a natural job for such an encoder; a tool that drafts the handover summary is a generation task, a job for a decoder. The large language models of Chapter 18 are decoders — GPT’s design, scaled up enormously.

The pharmacy team wants two tools: (A) one that labels each night note as “possible nephrotoxicity: yes/no”, and (B) one that drafts a morning summary of the night for each patient. Which pairing fits the two families best?

(A) a BERT-style encoder fine-tuned on labelled notes; (B) a GPT-style decoder Correct. Labelling a whole note benefits from two-sided context and a fixed-size representation, the strength of encoders; drafting text needs a model that generates left to right, which is what a causally masked decoder does.
(A) a GPT-style decoder; (B) a BERT-style encoder An encoder trained with masked language modelling does not define a left-to-right probability for text, so it is not used to generate summaries.
Either family for both: they are trained the same way They share the block, but not the mask or the objective (Table 17.2). That difference decides what each does well.
Neither: transformers cannot read clinical notes They can, and domain-specific encoders such as ClinicalBERT were built precisely for clinical text — though any tool must still be validated on local notes.

title: 17  Attention and the transformer
text:
17.10 A tiny transformer, trained
Everything so far used random or hand-picked numbers. To see what a trained transformer does, we trained a small one on Ward 7 medication notes. The notes were generated from templates (the script is scripts/precompute/ch17_tiny_transformer.py), for example:


  aoife was started on vancomycin on friday . tonight we check her creatinine
  priya was started on vancomycin on sunday . the team reviewed her and she sat in the chair and she ate some lunch and she walked to the window and her lines were changed . tonight we check her creatinine


In every note, the last word — the blood test to check tonight — is determined by the drug named at the start (vancomycin or gentamicin → creatinine, warfarin → INR, insulin → glucose, and so on), and the pronouns are determined by the patient’s name. A random number of everyday sentences sits in between, so the drug lies between 8 and 36 tokens before the last word (median 19). This is the “patient … pain” toy of Section 17.1, made clinical and harder.
The model is a decoder-only, pre-LN transformer exactly as in Figure 17.3, with \(N = 2\) blocks, \(h = 2\) heads, \(d = 32\), \(d_{\text{ff}} = 128\), learned positional encodings and weight tying: 28 960 weights in all, of which 12 704 per block (the number you computed in the mission). It was trained for 1500 steps of gradient descent on 6 000 notes, in one to a few minutes on a laptop CPU with PyTorch (Paszke et al. 2019), and tested on 1 000 new notes.
The result is stark. On the test notes the transformer predicts the last word correctly 100 % of the time. An n-gram predictor that sees only the last \(k\) words cannot do better than guessing the most common test (26 %) until its window is long enough to reach the drug — and long windows are rarely seen in training, so even with \(k = 16\) it reaches only 41 % (Figure 17.6).




ng = FileAttachment("data/precomputed/ch17/ngram_vs_tf.csv").csv({typed: true})
Plot.plot({
  height: 280, grid: true,
  x: {label: "n-gram window k (words)", type: "log", ticks: [1, 2, 4, 8, 16], tickFormat: d => d},
  y: {label: "accuracy on the last word", domain: [0, 1.05], tickFormat: ".0%"},
  marks: [
    Plot.line(ng.filter(d => d.model === "n-gram"), {x: "window", y: "acc_last_word", stroke: "#b35c00", strokeWidth: 2}),
    Plot.dot(ng.filter(d => d.model === "n-gram"), {x: "window", y: "acc_last_word", fill: "#b35c00", r: 4}),
    Plot.line(ng.filter(d => d.model === "n-gram"), {x: "window", y: "drug_visible", stroke: "currentColor", strokeDasharray: "4,4"}),
    Plot.ruleY(ng.filter(d => d.model === "transformer"), {y: "acc_last_word", stroke: "#1f6f8b", strokeWidth: 3}),
    Plot.text([[16, 0.97]], {text: ["transformer"], textAnchor: "end", fill: "#1f6f8b", fontSize: 12}),
    Plot.text([[16, 0.30]], {text: ["drug inside the window"], textAnchor: "end", fontSize: 11, dy: 12}),
    Plot.text([[1, 0.27]], {text: ["n-gram"], textAnchor: "start", fill: "#b35c00", fontSize: 12, dy: -10})
  ]
})

















Figure 17.6: Accuracy on the last word of the 1 000 test notes. The n-gram predictor sees only the last k words (dots); the dashed line shows how often the drug is inside that window. The transformer (solid line at the top) can attend to the whole note.



How does it do it? Attention weights can be read off the trained model. The widget shows them for five test notes, for each of the two blocks (layers) and each of the two heads.

Look inside a trained transformer. Each row is a position the model is processing; each column is a position it may look at (only earlier ones, because of the causal mask); darker means more attention. The bottom row is the position at which the model predicts the last word. Task: find a layer and head that, when predicting the last word, puts more than half of its attention on the drug.

att17 = FileAttachment("data/precomputed/ch17/attention.csv").csv({typed: true})
sent17 = FileAttachment("data/precomputed/ch17/sentences.csv").csv({typed: true})
sum17 = FileAttachment("data/precomputed/ch17/summary.json").json()
viewof hmS = Inputs.select(new Map([["Aoife · vancomycin", 1], ["Tomás · warfarin", 2], ["Priya · insulin", 3], ["Tomás · furosemide", 4], ["Aoife · heparin", 5]]), {label: "Note"})
viewof hmL = Inputs.radio([1, 2], {value: 2, label: "Layer (block)"})
viewof hmH = Inputs.radio([1, 2], {value: 2, label: "Head"})












































hmDrugs = ["vancomycin", "gentamicin", "furosemide", "warfarin", "insulin", "heparin", "digoxin", "morphine"]
hmTok = sent17.filter(d => d.sentence === hmS).sort((a, b) => a.pos - b.pos).map(d => d.token)
hmCells = att17.filter(d => d.sentence === hmS && d.layer === hmL && d.head === hmH)
hmLast = hmTok.length - 1
hmDrugPos = hmTok.findIndex(w => hmDrugs.includes(w))
hmOnDrug = (hmCells.find(d => d.query === hmLast && d.key === hmDrugPos) || {weight: 0}).weight
hmPred = sum17.example_predictions.find(d => d.sentence === hmS)
{
  const hit = hmOnDrug > 0.5;
  if (hit && window.aihs) window.aihs.complete("ch17-tryit-heatmap");
  return html`<p>Predicting the last word: the model's top choice is <strong>${hmPred.top[0][0]}</strong> (probability ${hmPred.top[0][1].toFixed(3)}).
  In layer ${hmL}, head ${hmH}, the bottom row puts <strong>${(100 * hmOnDrug).toFixed(0)} %</strong> of its attention on “${hmTok[hmDrugPos]}”.
  ${hit ? "✓ Found it: this head fetches the drug from far back." : ""}</p>`;
}
























































Plot.plot({
  width: Math.min(width, 760), height: Math.min(width, 760) * 0.85, marginLeft: 90, marginTop: 90, padding: 0.03,
  x: {domain: d3.range(hmTok.length), tickFormat: i => hmTok[i], tickRotate: -60, axis: "top", label: null},
  y: {domain: d3.range(hmTok.length), tickFormat: i => hmTok[i], label: null},
  color: {scheme: "blues", domain: [0, 1], legend: true, label: "attention weight"},
  marks: [
    Plot.cell(hmCells, {x: "key", y: "query", fill: "weight", title: d => `${hmTok[d.query]} → ${hmTok[d.key]}: ${d.weight.toFixed(2)}`}),
    Plot.frame({strokeOpacity: 0.2})
  ]
})










In every example note, head 1 of layer 1 puts between 55 % and 99 % of the last position’s attention on the drug, however many sentences lie in between. Nobody told it to: the head emerged because fetching the drug was the way to predict the last word. Explore the other heads too. Some concentrate on a single nearby word, others spread their attention more widely, and the heads of layer 2 put almost no weight on the drug at all — yet the prediction is right. They do not need to: after layer 1, the vector at the last position already carries the drug’s information, so layer 2 can work with nearby, already-contextualised vectors.
That last observation is a warning. It is tempting to read attention heatmaps as explanations — “the model flagged the note because it attended to vancomycin”. But attention weights show where information was gathered in one layer, not what the prediction depends on after the residual stream, the feed-forward networks and the other layers have done their work. Studies disagree on how much attention weights reveal: Jain and Wallace (2019) found that very different attention patterns can give the same predictions, and Wiegreffe and Pinter (2019) showed that, tested more carefully, attention can still carry useful but limited information. Treat heatmaps as clues, not proofs; Chapter 12 describes methods designed for explanation.

A vendor’s note-reading tool flags Aoife’s note and highlights “vancomycin” in dark red, saying: “the model’s attention shows that vancomycin drove the alert”. How should the AI committee read this?

As proof: attention weights are exactly the contributions of each word to the prediction They are not. Attention shows where one head gathered information in one layer; the prediction also depends on other heads, layers, residual connections and feed-forward networks. In our tiny model, layer 2 ignores the drug entirely and still predicts correctly.
As a plausible clue that needs checking, for instance by removing or replacing “vancomycin” and seeing whether the alert changes Correct. Attention can hint at what the model used, but evidence about what the prediction depends on comes from tests such as perturbing the input, and from the explanation methods of Chapter 12.
As meaningless: attention weights carry no information at all Too strong. In our trained model one head reliably fetches the drug. Attention is informative; it is just not a complete explanation.
As a sign of bias, because the model should attend equally to all words Equal attention would mean no selection at all (the first quick check). Unequal attention is the point of the mechanism.

title: 17  Attention and the transformer
section: 17.11 The price of attention, and its limits
text:
17.11 The price of attention, and its limits
Attention’s power has a cost. Every query is compared with every key, so a text of \(T\) tokens needs a \(T \times T\) table of scores in every head of every layer: computation and memory grow with \(T^2\). A note ten times longer costs a hundred times more attention. This is why models have a maximum context length, and why much research has gone into cheaper variants that attend to local windows, to a few selected positions, or to compressed summaries (Tay et al. 2022).
The architecture also has limits that no engineering removes. A transformer language model is trained to produce likely continuations, not verified ones. Fluent text that is wrong — an invented dose, a guideline that does not exist — follows directly from the objective in Equation 17.8, and is called hallucination (Ji et al. 2023). The model reproduces the patterns of its training text, including its gaps and biases. And text that looks like reasoning is not guaranteed to be sound reasoning. Chapter 18 returns to each of these when language models become clinical assistants.

title: 17  Attention and the transformer
section: 17.12 Where this fits in the decision loop
text:
17.12 Where this fits in the decision loop


  A note-reading transformer in the decision loop
  A cycle: nurses' free-text notes are the data; a transformer encoder is the model; it produces a flag of possible drug-related kidney risk with the words it relied on, the information; the pharmacist reviews the flag and the chart and decides whether to change a dose; the action and the outcome, including missed and false flags, are recorded and become new data.
  
  Data
  nursing notes
  
  Model
  transformer encoder
  
  Information
  flag: kidney risk?
  
  Decision
  pharmacist reviews
  
  Action and outcome
  dose change; log missed/false flags
  
  
  
  
  

A note-reading transformer in the decision loop. It turns free text into a flag; the pharmacist, not the attention map, decides.

Attention lets the model step reach information that sits anywhere in a text, which is what clinical notes demand: the reason a word matters is often many words away (Section 17.1, Section 17.2). The transformer turns that mechanism into a deep, trainable architecture (Section 17.7), and the choice of mask decides whether it reads text to produce information — a flag, a label, an extracted dose (BERT-style encoders) — or produces text itself (GPT-style decoders, Section 17.9). What can go wrong? A context window too short for the note (Section 17.11); a heatmap mistaken for an explanation (Section 17.10); fluent output that is not true; and, as in every chapter, a model never validated on local notes. Who stays in control? Seán, who reads the flag against the chart and the patient, and decides.

title: 17  Attention and the transformer
section: 17.13 Lab: a transformer block from scratch
text:
17.13 Lab: a transformer block from scratch
The Lab builds one pre-LN decoder block in base R and in numpy (R Core Team 2024; Harris et al. 2020), with random weights, on the sentence “the patient reports chest pain”: sinusoidal positional encodings, multi-head attention with a causal mask, the feed-forward network, residual connections and layer normalisation. It stacks two blocks, turns the output into next-token probabilities with weight tying, computes the cross-entropy, counts the weights, and finally reads the attention of the trained model of Section 17.10. Run it here, or download it: ch17_lab.R · ch17_lab.py.

RPython























Two observations to take forward. First, with random weights the cross-entropy is no better than that of a uniform guess over the vocabulary, and usually worse, because random weights make confident wrong guesses: the architecture alone knows nothing, and everything useful comes from training. Second, the trained model’s head puts most of the last position’s attention on “vancomycin”, many tokens back — the long-range look-up that an n-gram cannot make.

title: 17  Attention and the transformer
text:
17.14 Exercises

By hand. With \(\mathbf{q} = (1, 0)\) and keys \(\mathbf{k}_1 = (2, 0)\), \(\mathbf{k}_2 = (0, 2)\), \(d_k = 2\), compute the two scaled scores, the two attention weights and the output for values \(\mathbf{v}_1 = (1, 0)\), \(\mathbf{v}_2 = (0, 1)\). Check your answer with the widget of



Temperature in disguise. Dividing scores by \(\sqrt{d_k}\) before a softmax looks like the temperature of Chapter 16. Explain the similarity, and the difference in purpose.
Masks. Write the \(4 \times 4\) causal mask. Then write the mask for a batch where the fourth token is padding and no token may attend to it, in a bidirectional (BERT-style) model.
Order. Run the permutation code in Section 17.6, then add a different random vector to each row of X (a stand-in for positional encodings) and run it again. Is the output still simply reordered? Why?
Which family? For each task say whether you would start from an encoder, a decoder or an encoder–decoder: (a) extracting drug names and doses from ONCO-1 adverse-reaction reports;

answering free-text questions from patients about their HomeBeat watch; (c) translating a CellWorks batch record from Italian into English.

Inside the tiny model. In the heatmap widget, compare the note “Aoife · heparin” (no filler sentences) with “Priya · insulin” (three filler sentences). Does the head that fetches the drug behave differently? What does this say about the n-gram’s problem?
Explanation. Design a simple test, using only the trained tiny model’s inputs and outputs, that would show whether the prediction depends on the drug token, without looking at attention.
Code. Modify the Lab so that h <- 4 (R) or h = 4 (Python). Which shapes change, and does the number of weights in the block change?


Exercise 17.1 Where the weights are. GPT-2 small has \(d = 768\), \(d_{\text{ff}} = 3072\), 12 heads and \(N = 12\) blocks, a vocabulary of 50 257 tokens and 1 024 positions (Radford et al. 2019). Using the counting rule of the mission, compute the weights of one block, of the 12 blocks, and of the token and position embeddings (with weight tying). Which part is largest: attention, feed-forward networks or embeddings?







Selected answers





1. Raw dot products 2 and 0; scaled \(2/\sqrt{2} \approx 1.41\) and 0; weights \(e^{1.41}/(e^{1.41} + 1) \approx 0.80\) and \(0.20\); output \((0.80, 0.20)\).
2. Both divide scores by a number before the softmax, which flattens (large divisor) or sharpens (small divisor) the resulting distribution. The temperature is a choice at generation time that trades predictability for variety; the \(\sqrt{d_k}\) is a fixed design choice that keeps the scores on a stable scale whatever the dimension, so that training works.
3. Causal mask: zeros on and below the diagonal, \(-\infty\) above. Padding mask (bidirectional): zeros everywhere except column 4, which is \(-\infty\) in every row (the padding position itself needs no output; its row is usually ignored).
4. No. Once each row carries a vector that depends on its position, reordering the rows changes which position vector goes with which token, so the outputs change beyond a simple reordering. This is how positional encodings make the model sensitive to order.
5. (a) Encoder (extraction is understanding); (b) decoder (free-text generation); (c) encoder–decoder, the original translation design (a large decoder can also translate).
6. The head finds the drug in both cases; distance does not matter to attention. An n-gram with a small window would succeed only for the short note.
8. The head slices become narrower (\(d_k = 2\)) and there are four attention tables per block instead of two; the number of weights does not change.
Exercise Exercise 17.1. Per block: attention \(4(768^2 + 768) = 2\,362\,368\); feed-forward \(2 \times 768 \times 3072 + 3072 + 768 = 4\,722\,432\); layer norms \(4 \times 768 = 3\,072\); total \(7\,087\,872\). Twelve blocks: about 85.1 million. Embeddings: \(50\,257 \times 768 + 1\,024 \times 768 \approx 39.4\) million. With the final layer norm the total is about 124 million. The feed-forward networks hold about two-thirds of the block weights, and the token embeddings alone almost a third of the whole model.

title: 17  Attention and the transformer
text:
17.15 Summary

Every language model estimates \(P(w_t \mid w_{<t})\); models differ in how they represent the context. Fixed windows (n-grams) cannot reach far; recurrent networks squeeze the past into one vector.
Attention builds each token’s new vector as a weighted average of value vectors, with weights that are positive, add up to 1 and are computed from the content.
Each token gives a query, a key and a value through learned matrices; \(\operatorname{softmax}(\mathbf{Q}\mathbf{K}^{\top}/\sqrt{d_k})\mathbf{V}\). The \(\sqrt{d_k}\) keeps the softmax from saturating.
A causal mask (\(-\infty\) above the diagonal) stops tokens from seeing the future, matching the chain rule; bidirectional models use no causal mask.
Multi-head attention learns several relevance patterns in parallel at no extra cost in weights; positional encodings tell the order-blind attention where each token is.
A pre-LN transformer block adds attention and a feed-forward network to a residual stream, each after layer normalisation; blocks keep the \(T \times d\) shape and are stacked.
The output layer turns each final vector into logits and a softmax; training minimises the cross-entropy of the next token.
GPT (decoder, causal, autoregressive) generates text; BERT (encoder, bidirectional, masked LM) represents it; biomedical encoders adapt BERT to clinical text.
Attention costs grow with \(T^2\); attention maps are clues, not explanations; likely text is not verified text.

text: References

title: 18  From language model to clinical assistant
text:
How to use this chapter






Starting here?





This chapter puts together ideas from many earlier chapters. In brief:

Decisions and decision quality (Definition 1.4, Section 1.5). A decision chooses one alternative from a set \(\mathcal{A}\) on the basis of a state of knowledge \(\mathcal{K}\). Decision quality is a chain of six links — frame, alternatives, information, values, reasoning, commitment — and a decision is only as strong as its weakest link. In Chapter 1 the Ward 7 team decided that the kidney-protective bundle is worth starting when Aoife’s risk of acute kidney injury (AKI) is above 0.25.
Machines check consistency, not truth (Section 1.6). A system that produces plausible text has not checked it against the world.
Text as vectors (Chapter 15). A document becomes a vector of word weights; with TF-IDF, words that are frequent in a document but rare in the collection weigh most, and two documents are compared with the cosine of the angle between their vectors.
Language models (Chapter 16). A language model gives a probability to every possible next token \(w_t\) given the tokens before it, \(P(w_t \mid w_{<t})\); it is trained by minimising the cross-entropy of the real next tokens and generates text by sampling, with a temperature that controls how adventurous the sampling is. Embeddings are learned vectors in which words with similar meanings lie close together.
The transformer (Chapter 17). Attention lets every position look at every earlier position; a stack of transformer blocks with a causal mask, trained to predict the next token, is a decoder-only model of the GPT family.
Transfer learning (Chapter 7): a network trained on one large dataset is fine-tuned on a smaller one. Calibration (Chapter 5): a model is calibrated if, among the cases to which it gives 80 %, about 80 % are positive. Abstaining (Chapter 8): a model that knows how uncertain it is can refer hard cases to a person.
Reinforcement learning (Chapter 14): an agent follows a policy \(\pi\) and learns from rewards. Randomised trials (Chapter 13) are the strongest evidence that a treatment works.

title: 18  From language model to clinical assistant
section: 18.1 A model is not yet an assistant
text:
18.1 A model is not yet an assistant
Chapters 15 to 17 built a language model from the ground up: text became tokens and vectors, a model learned to give a probability to every possible next token, and the transformer made that model large and fast. Scaled up and trained on a large part of the written world, such a model can continue a sentence, summarise a document, answer a question or translate a paragraph, all by repeatedly computing \(P(w_t \mid w_{<t})\) and choosing a next token. Models of this kind are now called foundation models.

Definition 18.1 (Foundation model) A foundation model is a large model trained on broad data, usually by self-supervision at scale, that can be adapted to a wide range of downstream tasks (Bommasani et al. 2021). A large language model (LLM) is a foundation model for text; most current LLMs are decoder-only transformers (Chapter 17; Vaswani et al. (2017)) with billions of parameters.

A foundation model provides capability. It does not, by itself, provide what a ward needs: answers grounded in this hospital’s guidelines, exact arithmetic for a dose, a record of who asked what, a way to say “I don’t know”, and a person who checks before anything reaches a patient. Those come from the system built around the model (Figure 18.1): an interface that captures what the user wants, a workflow that decides the steps, access to external knowledge, tools, memory of the conversation, and monitoring.






Figure 18.1: From a foundation model to an application system. The model supplies general-purpose generation (text, summaries, answers, transformations); the system adds user intent, workflow orchestration, external knowledge, tools, memory and monitoring.



This distinction organises the whole chapter. A model predicts what is likely to come next; a system organises those predictions into behaviour that serves a purpose. Many of the failures that make headlines — fluent statements that are false, out-of-date facts, answers that cannot be checked — are not bugs in the transformer. They are what you should expect from a probabilistic text generator used without the structure around it (Thirunavukarasu et al. 2023). Seán’s assistant, as we will see, has a model at its heart; whether it is safe depends mostly on everything else.

18.2 How a foundation model is made
The model inside Seán’s assistant went through three stages of training (Figure 18.2). Each stage uses a different kind of data and changes the model’s behaviour in a different way.
