Figure 18.2: The three stages that turn a transformer into an assistant model.




18.2.1 Stage 1: pretraining

Definition 18.2 (Pretraining, pretraining corpus and scaling laws) Pretraining fits a language model to a very large pretraining corpus — web pages, books, scientific articles, code — by minimising the cross-entropy of the next token, exactly the objective of Chapter 16: \[
\mathcal{L}_{\text{pre}}(\theta) = -\sum_{t} \log P_\theta(w_t \mid w_{<t}) .
\qquad(18.1)\] Scaling laws are the empirical finding that this loss falls smoothly and predictably, as a power law, as the number of parameters, the amount of data and the computing budget grow (Kaplan et al. 2020; Hoffmann et al. 2022).

Nothing in Equation 18.1 mentions medicine, truth or helpfulness. The model is rewarded for predicting what text usually comes next. To predict the next word of a pharmacology textbook well it must pick up a great deal of pharmacology, which is why large models “know” so much (Brown et al. 2020). But it also learns whatever is common in its corpus, including outdated practice, errors and prejudice, and it learns nothing at all about what happened after its corpus was collected. A base model that has only been pretrained does not answer questions; it continues text. Ask it “What is the first-line vasopressor in septic shock?” and it may well reply with three more exam questions, because that is what often follows such a line on the web.


18.2.2 Stage 2: instruction tuning

Definition 18.3 (Instruction tuning) Instruction tuning (supervised fine-tuning) continues training a pretrained model on a collection of prompts \(x\) paired with good responses \(y\) written by people, minimising the cross-entropy of the response tokens given the prompt, \(-\sum_{t \in y} \log P_\theta(w_t \mid x, w_{<t})\) (Wei, Bosma, et al. 2022; Ouyang et al. 2022).

The objective is the same as before; only the data change. A few thousand examples of the form “instruction → helpful answer” are enough to turn a text continuer into a model that does what it is asked, because the capability was already there and only the format of the behaviour has to be learned. This is transfer learning (Chapter 7) applied to behaviour.


18.2.3 Stage 3: preference tuning
People find it easier to say which of two answers is better than to write the perfect answer. Preference tuning exploits this. Human raters see a prompt \(x\) and two responses \(y_A\) and \(y_B\) and say which they prefer. A reward model \(r(x, y)\) — itself a neural network — is trained so that preferred responses get higher scores, using the Bradley–Terry model of paired comparisons (Bradley and Terry 1952): \[
P(y_A \text{ preferred to } y_B \mid x) = \sigma\big(r(x, y_A) - r(x, y_B)\big),
\qquad(18.2)\] where \(\sigma\) is the logistic function of Chapter 5. The reward model is literally a logistic regression on the difference of two scores.
Then comes the step that gives the method its name. The language model is now seen as a policy \(\pi_\theta\) (Chapter 14): given a state (the prompt) it chooses actions (tokens) and, at the end of a response, receives a reward \(r(x, y)\). Reinforcement learning adjusts \(\theta\) to collect more reward, while a penalty keeps the new policy close to the instruction-tuned model \(\pi_{\text{ref}}\): \[
\max_\theta \;\; \mathbb{E}_{y \sim \pi_\theta(\cdot \mid x)}\big[r(x, y)\big] \;-\; \lambda\, \mathrm{KL}\big(\pi_\theta \,\|\, \pi_{\text{ref}}\big).
\qquad(18.3)\] The KL term (a measure of how different two probability distributions are (Kullback and Leibler 1951)) stops the model from drifting into strange text that happens to fool the reward model; \(\lambda\) sets how strongly.

Definition 18.4 (Preference tuning: RLHF and DPO) Reinforcement learning from human feedback (RLHF) trains a reward model on human comparisons of responses (Equation 18.2) and then optimises the language model, seen as a policy, to maximise that reward with a penalty for moving far from the starting model (Equation 18.3), usually with the PPO algorithm (Christiano et al. 2017; Schulman et al. 2017; Ouyang et al. 2022). Direct preference optimisation (DPO) reaches a similar result without a separate reward model or reinforcement learning, by fitting the policy directly to the comparisons with a logistic loss (Rafailov et al. 2023).

Preference tuning is why assistants are polite, structured and willing to say “consult a clinician”. It is also why they can be sycophantic and overconfident: raters tend to prefer answers that are fluent, complete and sure of themselves, and the model learns to give people what they reward (Sharma et al. 2024). Preference tuning shapes style and caution; it does not add knowledge the model lacked, and it does not make the model check facts.

The hospital’s guidelines were updated last month. Which training stage would teach the model the new guideline?

Pretraining, because it is where the model’s knowledge comes from Knowledge does come mainly from pretraining, but the corpus was collected before last month, and nobody re-pretrains a large model for one hospital’s guidelines.
Preference tuning, because raters would prefer answers that follow the new guideline Raters can only reward what the model already produces, and preference tuning shapes style and caution far more than facts. It is the wrong tool for injecting a specific document.
None of the three: the new guideline must be supplied to the system at the time of the question Correct. Up-to-date, local knowledge is best given to the model when it answers — by placing the relevant passages in the prompt. That is retrieval-augmented generation (Section 18.4).
Instruction tuning, because the guideline is a set of instructions Instruction tuning teaches the format of following instructions, from many examples. Training on one guideline would change the model slowly, unreliably and expensively, and would have to be repeated at every update.

title: 18  From language model to clinical assistant
text:
18.3 Prompting: steering without retraining
The simplest way to use a model is to give it a prompt and read the response. A prompt does not program the model in the classical sense: it defines no sequence of operations. It changes the context \(w_{<t}\) on which every next-token probability is computed, and so it reshapes the whole distribution from which the response is drawn. The same model behaves very differently depending on how the context is framed.

Definition 18.5 (Prompt, system prompt, few-shot and chain-of-thought prompting) A prompt is the text given to a language model as context for its response. Applications usually prepend a system prompt that the user does not see, setting the role, the rules and the format (“You are the Ward 7 guideline assistant. Answer only from the passages provided…”). Zero-shot prompting gives only the instruction; few-shot prompting adds a handful of worked examples of the task to the prompt (Brown et al. 2020); chain-of-thought prompting asks for, or demonstrates, intermediate reasoning steps before the answer (Wei, Wang, et al. 2022).

Take the request “Explain the role of TNF-alpha in inflammation.” With no further instruction the model produces a general explanation. “Explain the role of TNF-alpha in inflammation in three bullet points, for a first-year medical student” produces something shorter and simpler; “Summarise the role of TNF-alpha in inflammation using only mechanistic pathways” produces something denser. The task is the same; the framing moves the probability landscape. A few-shot prompt for Seán’s assistant might show two examples of a question, the guideline passage it rests on, and an answer that cites that passage, so that the model imitates the pattern.
Three facts about prompting matter in practice. First, outputs are sensitive to wording, to the order of the information and to the sampling temperature of Chapter 16: the same question asked twice can get two different answers, so any evaluation must use fixed prompts and repeated runs. Second, chain-of-thought text is not a window into how the answer was computed; it is more generated text, useful for checking but not guaranteed to be the real reason for the answer (Turpin et al. 2023). Third, a single prompt must carry both the task and the procedure, and as tasks grow it becomes fragile.
Prompt chaining addresses the third point by splitting a task into steps, each a separate call whose output feeds the next. Moving from explaining TNF-alpha to proposing a therapy, a chain might (1) produce a structured explanation of the pathway, (2) identify the points where the pathway could be blocked, (3) gather what is known about existing inhibitors and their clinical evidence, and (4) synthesise a proposal. Each intermediate output can be inspected, corrected or rejected, so an error can be located at the step where it arose instead of being buried in one opaque answer. Step 3, however, asks for facts — exactly what a language model on its own cannot guarantee. The next section shows how a system supplies them.

title: 18  From language model to clinical assistant
text:
18.5 Tools, agents and protocols
Some steps should not be done by a language model at all. Seán’s question needs Aoife’s creatinine clearance, which is arithmetic (Cockcroft and Gault 1976); a model that predicts digits one token at a time can get arithmetic wrong, while a calculator cannot. Other steps need data the model does not have: today’s laboratory results, the current formulary, a drug-interaction database.

Definition 18.7 (Tool use and agent) In tool use, the language model does not compute an answer itself but writes a structured request — “call creatinine_clearance with age 71, weight 68 kg, creatinine 1.4 mg/dL, female” — which the system executes with ordinary, deterministic software; the result is put back into the context and the model continues (Schick et al. 2023). An agent is a system in which the model also decides, while the task unfolds, which step to take next — whether to retrieve, call a tool, split the task or stop — usually alternating short reasoning steps with actions (Yao et al. 2023).

Returning to the TNF-alpha chain of Section 18.3: checking that TNF-alpha is a validated target, listing known inhibitors with their clinical status or estimating a pharmacokinetic property are jobs for curated databases and calculators. The model’s role changes from producing the answer to coordinating a process that combines generation with deterministic computation and external knowledge.
The difference between a fixed chain and an agent is how much freedom the system has (Figure 18.4). A chain always runs the same steps in the same order: predictable, easy to test, sometimes wasteful. An agent adapts: it may decide it already knows enough, or that it must retrieve, calculate or break the task into subtasks; it may draft a plan, carry it out and check its own work.






Figure 18.4: Chained versus agentic workflows. A chain runs fixed steps in a fixed order; an agent decides at run time whether to retrieve, call a tool or split the task.



Freedom has a price. Plans can be poor; agents take unnecessary steps, repeat work or wander; self-checking is unreliable when the same model generates and judges; and small errors accumulate over many steps. Every tool an agent can call is also an action it can take wrongly, or be tricked into taking by text it reads (prompt injection again). In a hospital the rule of thumb is simple: the more an agent can do — write to the record, send an order, contact a patient — the narrower its permissions, the more complete its logs and the more certainly a person approves each consequential action.
Many agents, and the protocols that connect them. Complex tasks are sometimes divided among several specialised agents — one retrieves, one analyses, one drafts, one verifies — like a small team. Two open protocols, both introduced recently, standardise the connections (Figure 18.5). The Model Context Protocol (MCP) defines how an agent discovers and uses external capabilities, which it groups as resources (data), tools (actions and computations) and prompts (reusable templates), so that one hospital connector to, say, the formulary can serve any MCP-compatible assistant (Model Context Protocol 2026). Agent-to-agent protocols (A2A) define how agents from different vendors describe their skills to each other, delegate tasks and exchange results (A2A Project 2026). Neither decides what a system should do: MCP standardises access, A2A standardises conversation, and orchestration remains a design choice — and a responsibility.






Figure 18.5: Two complementary standards. Left: through the Model Context Protocol (MCP), agents reach shared resources, tools and prompts. Right: with agent-to-agent communication (A2A), specialised agents exchange information and tasks directly.



Multi-agent designs pay off when a task really divides into distinct roles; for most clinical questions a single, well-tested chain with retrieval and one or two tools is easier to evaluate, monitor and trust.
Where such systems are used. The same pattern — a model inside a workflow with retrieval and tools — appears wherever generative AI is deployed: natural-language questions translated into database queries and literature searches (Figure 18.6), code assistants that read a repository and run its tests, assistants that answer staff questions from internal documents, drafting of marketing or patient-information material under review. In health and the life sciences the list includes literature assistance, summarisation of clinical notes, pharmacological information, extraction of structured data from reports and analysis of adverse-event narratives (Thirunavukarasu et al. 2023). In every case the value comes less from the model than from the system it sits in.






Figure 18.6: From a question to a grounded answer: the system translates a natural-language question into queries over structured data and searches over documents, then aggregates and synthesises the results.




In Seán’s assistant, which job should be given to a tool rather than left to the language model?

Rewording the guideline passage in plain English for a new nurse Rewording is what language models do well; the result still needs checking against the passage, but no tool is needed.
Computing Aoife’s creatinine clearance from her age, weight, sex and creatinine Correct. A formula should be computed by deterministic software that gives the same, exact answer every time. The model’s job is to recognise that the calculation is needed and pass the right inputs.
Deciding whether Aoife should start the kidney-protective bundle This is not a job for a tool, nor for the model alone: it is a clinical decision that weighs a risk against values (Chapter 1) and belongs to Emma and Seán.
Deciding which guideline passages are relevant That is the retriever’s job, which is a search component of the system — and the model then judges whether the passages actually answer the question.

title: 18  From language model to clinical assistant
text:
18.6 Fine-tuning, distillation or retrieval?
Sometimes a general model is not enough even with good prompts and retrieval: the outputs must follow a strict reporting format, use a specialty’s conventions, or run on a hospital server instead of a vendor’s cloud. Then the model itself can be adapted.

Definition 18.8 (Fine-tuning, LoRA and distillation) Fine-tuning continues training a pretrained model on data from the target task or domain, so that the desired behaviour is built into its weights (Chapter 7). Updating every weight is costly; parameter-efficient methods update a small number. LoRA (low-rank adaptation) freezes each large weight matrix \(\mathbf{W}_0\) and learns a low-rank correction, \(\mathbf{W} = \mathbf{W}_0 + \mathbf{B}\mathbf{A}\), where \(\mathbf{B}\) is \(d \times m\), \(\mathbf{A}\) is \(m \times d\) and the rank \(m\) is much smaller than \(d\) (Hu et al. 2022). Distillation trains a smaller student model to imitate the outputs of a larger teacher, keeping much of its behaviour at a fraction of the cost (Hinton, Vinyals, and Dean 2015).

The arithmetic of LoRA shows why it is popular. For one weight matrix with \(d =\) 4096, full fine-tuning updates \(d^2 =\) 16 777 216 numbers; LoRA with rank \(m =\) 8 updates \(2dm =\) 65 536, about 0.4 % as many. Adapters for several tasks can be stored side by side and swapped on the same base model.
Fine-tuning and distillation act on the model; prompting, retrieval and tools act on how the model is used at the moment of the question (Figure 18.7). Fine-tuning makes a model behave differently; distillation makes a model behave similarly under tighter constraints — smaller, faster, able to run on site, which also helps to keep patient data inside the hospital.






Figure 18.7: Different levers. Prompting, retrieval (RAG) and tool integration change the context and tools available at inference time; fine-tuning adapts a base model with domain data, and distillation transfers a teacher’s behaviour to a smaller student.






Table 18.1: Which lever for which need. In practice systems combine several.










Need
Best first lever
Why




Facts that change (guidelines, formulary, today’s results)
Retrieval
Updating a document is instant and auditable; answers can cite their source


A fixed output format or house style
Prompting, then fine-tuning
A few examples in the prompt often suffice; fine-tune if they do not

Fine-tuning
Patterns spread over thousands of examples are hard to fit in a prompt

Tools

A smaller model is cheaper and can stay inside the hospital






A common mistake is to fine-tune a model on guidelines to “teach it the facts”. Fine-tuning is a poor way of storing facts: the model may blend old and new versions, cannot say where an answer came from, and must be retrained at every update. Facts go in documents; behaviour goes in weights.

The pharmacy wants every answer in the same structure — recommendation, guideline source, monitoring, when to escalate — and has 3 000 examples of good answers written by pharmacists. Prompting with two examples gives the right structure only about two times in three. What is the most sensible next step?

Add the 3 000 examples to the retrieval collection Retrieval brings in facts relevant to the question; it is not designed to impose a format, and stuffing examples into the prompt crowds out the passages that carry the facts.
Fine-tune the model (for example with LoRA) on the 3 000 examples, and keep retrieval for the facts Correct. A consistent format learned from thousands of examples is exactly what fine-tuning does well; the facts still come from retrieval, so they stay current and citable.
Distil the model into a smaller one Distillation makes a model cheaper to run, not more consistent in format; a student imitates its teacher’s habits, inconsistency included.
Raise the sampling temperature so the model explores more structures The opposite: a higher temperature makes outputs more varied. Lower temperature can help a little; it will not teach a structure.

title: 18  From language model to clinical assistant
text:
18.8 Bias, privacy and regulation
A system that is accurate on average can still be unfair, can leak what it was told, and can be illegal to deploy. These questions shape the design from the start: whether to retrieve, whether to require citations, what to log, where the model runs and who checks the output.

18.8.1 Bias
A language model learns the associations in its pretraining corpus, including outdated and discriminatory ones. When four widely used models were asked medical questions in which race-based practices had been debunked — among them the race adjustment once built into equations for kidney function — they repeated the discarded practices in some answers (Omiye et al. 2023). Another study found that a general-purpose model produced differential diagnoses and clinical vignettes that stereotyped patients by race and gender (Zack et al. 2024). The remedies are those you met for predictive models: evaluate separately in the groups the system will serve (Chapter 5, Chapter 12), test deliberately with cases designed to expose bias, and keep the guideline — not the model’s associations — as the source of truth.


18.8.2 Privacy and data protection
Typing “Aoife Byrne, 71, sepsis, creatinine 1.4” into an assistant is processing personal health data. Under the European General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR), health data are a special category whose processing is prohibited unless one of a limited set of conditions applies, such as the provision of health care or scientific research with safeguards (European Parliament and Council of the European Union 2016, Article 9); processing likely to result in a high risk requires a data protection impact assessment (European Parliament and Council of the European Union 2016, Article 35); and people have the right not to be subject to decisions based solely on automated processing that significantly affect them (European Parliament and Council of the European Union 2016, Article 22). Pseudonymised data — names replaced by codes — are still personal data (European Parliament and Council of the European Union 2016, Recital 26). In practice this means: send the minimum necessary, prefer models that run inside the hospital or under a contract that forbids reuse of the data (another reason to distil), log access, and never use patient conversations to train a model without a lawful basis. Language models can also memorise and reproduce fragments of their training data (Carlini et al. 2021), so what goes into training can come out again.


18.8.3 Regulation: the AI Act and the medical device rules
Two European laws decide whether Seán’s assistant may be used at all, and on what terms.

Definition 18.11 (AI Act risk tiers) The European AI Act regulates AI systems according to the risk of their use (European Parliament and Council of the European Union 2024). Some practices are prohibited (Article 5). Systems are high-risk if they are, or are safety components of, products covered by the EU laws listed in Annex I — including the medical device regulations — that require assessment by an independent body (Article 6(1)), or if they are used in the areas listed in Annex III, such as emergency triage or access to essential services including health care (Article 6(2)). Some systems carry transparency obligations: people must be told that they are interacting with an AI system, and synthetic content must be marked (Article 50). Everything else is minimal risk. Providers of general-purpose AI models, such as the foundation models of this chapter, have separate obligations (Articles 51–55).

The informal name “limited risk” for the transparency tier is common, but it does not appear in the Act. High-risk systems must have a risk-management system, data governance, technical documentation, automatic logs, instructions that allow users to interpret the output, human oversight, and appropriate accuracy, robustness and cybersecurity (Articles 9–15); deployers such as a hospital must use them as instructed, assign competent people to oversee them and keep the logs (Article 26). The obligations apply in stages (Article 113): the prohibitions from February 2025, the rules for general-purpose AI models from August 2025 and most of the rest from August 2026. A 2026 amendment, the “Digital Omnibus on AI”, postponed the high-risk obligations to December 2027 for the areas of Annex III and to August 2028 for products such as medical devices (European Parliament and Council of the European Union 2026).

Definition 18.12 (Software as a medical device) Under the EU Medical Device Regulation (MDR), software is a medical device when its manufacturer intends it to be used for a medical purpose such as diagnosis, prevention, monitoring, prediction, prognosis or treatment of disease (European Parliament and Council of the European Union 2017, Article 2(1)); internationally this is called software as a medical device (IMDRF Software as a Medical Device (SaMD) Working Group 2013). Under classification Rule 11, software that provides information used to take decisions for diagnosis or therapy is at least class IIa, class IIb if such a decision could cause a serious deterioration of health, and class III if it could cause death or irreversible deterioration (European Parliament and Council of the European Union 2017, Annex VIII, Rule 11; Medical Device Coordination Group 2025).

What makes software a device is its intended purpose, not its technology. A general chatbot that is not marketed for a medical purpose is not a medical device. The same model, placed on the market as an assistant that recommends doses for individual patients, is one: under Rule 11 it is at least class IIa, which needs a notified body, which makes it a high-risk AI system under Article 6(1) of the AI Act. Figure 18.8: A simplified path through the risk tiers of the AI Act for a health-care system (European Parliament and Council of the European Union 2024, 2017). It is a teaching aid, not legal advice.




Classify five systems. For each system, choose the AI Act tier that applies first along the path of Figure 18.8. Feedback appears as you choose. Target: classify all five correctly.

The Ward 7 guideline assistant, sold to hospitals to recommend vancomycin doses for individual patients.
A chatbot on the hospital website that answers questions about visiting hours and parking.

  {s: "The Ward 7 guideline assistant, sold to hospitals to recommend vancomycin doses for individual patients.", a: "High risk",
   why: "It has a medical purpose (therapy decisions), so it is a medical device; under Rule 11 it is at least class IIa and needs a notified body, so Article 6(1) makes it high-risk."},
  {s: "A chatbot on the hospital website that answers questions about visiting hours and parking.", a: "Transparency obligations",

  {s: "Software that infers nurses' emotions from webcam video to assess their performance.", a: "Prohibited",
   why: "Emotion recognition in the workplace is prohibited by Article 5, except for medical or safety reasons; assessing performance is neither."},
  {s: "A filter that moves spam out of the hospital's email inboxes.", a: "Minimal risk",

]

  Inputs.radio(["Prohibited", "High risk", "Transparency obligations", "Minimal risk"], {label: `System ${i + 1}`})))
{

    const v = actAnswers[i];
    if (v == null) return `<li>${i + 1}. <em>not answered yet</em></li>`;
    return v === d.a ? `<li>${i + 1}. ✓ <strong>${d.a}</strong>. ${d.why}</li>`
                     : `<li>${i + 1}. ✗ Not ${v.toLowerCase()}. Follow the questions of the flowchart in order.</li>`;
  });

  if (allRight && window.aihs) window.aihs.complete("ch18-tryit-aiact");
  const div = document.createElement("div");

}

























Definition 18.13 (Human oversight) Human oversight means that a high-risk AI system is designed so that competent people can understand its capabilities and limitations, interpret its output correctly, remain aware of the tendency to over-rely on it, decide not to use it or override it, and stop it (European Parliament and Council of the European Union 2024, Article 14).

The tendency to over-rely has a name, automation bias: people working with a decision aid accept its suggestions even when they are wrong, and miss problems it does not flag (Goddard, Roudsari, and Wyatt 2012). The AI Act names it explicitly (European Parliament and Council of the European Union 2024, Article 14(4)(b)). Oversight that consists of a tired clinician clicking “accept” at 3 am is not oversight. It has to be designed: answers that show their sources, confidence that means something, disagreement that is easy to record, and workloads that leave time to check.
Operating the system. Because the behaviour of a language-model system depends on the model version, the prompts, the retrieval collection and the tools, all of them are versioned; every interaction is logged; the evaluation set is rerun before and after every change; errors and near misses are reported and reviewed; and there is a way to roll back. This operational discipline is sometimes called LLMOps. The World Health Organization’s guidance on large multimodal models in health sets out the same expectations for governments, developers and providers (World Health Organization 2024).

A start-up takes a general-purpose language model and sells it to hospitals as a tool that “suggests the most likely diagnosis from the admission notes”. What is the regulatory position?

It is not a medical device, because the underlying model is general-purpose What counts is the intended purpose of the product placed on the market, not the generality of the model inside it.
It is minimal risk, because a doctor always makes the final decision Human oversight is an obligation for high-risk systems, not a way out of the high-risk class.
It is a medical device (at least class IIa under Rule 11) and therefore a high-risk AI system under the AI Act Correct. Information used for diagnostic decisions puts it in class IIa or higher, which needs a notified body; Article 6(1) of the AI Act then makes it high-risk, with obligations for the start-up as provider and the hospitals as deployers.
It is prohibited, because AI may not make diagnoses in the EU Diagnostic AI is not prohibited; it is regulated. The prohibited practices of Article 5 are a short, specific list.

section: 18.9 From target to trial: a drug discovered with AI
text:
18.9 From target to trial: a drug discovered with AI
So far the language model has served a ward. Generative AI may have its largest effect elsewhere: in proposing scientific hypotheses — which protein to target, which molecule to make — that experiments then test. Chapter 1 promised a drug that went from AI-assisted design to a clinical trial. It is rentosertib, an inhibitor of the kinase TNIK, developed for idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis (IPF), a progressive scarring of the lungs with limited treatment options (Raghu et al. 2022; Ren et al. 2025; Xu et al. 2025).

18.9.1 AI and the scientific method
Science moves round a cycle: observation, hypothesis, test, refinement. The tests are expensive and slow, so the bottleneck has often been the supply of promising hypotheses: the space of possible targets and molecules is astronomically large and only a tiny part of it can be explored in the laboratory. In an AI-augmented cycle the structure stays the same, but computational models expand the hypothesis step — searching large spaces of targets and molecules and proposing candidates — while experiments remain the arbiter (Figure 18.9). AI does not replace the scientific method; it changes its operating conditions.






Figure 18.9: The classical scientific method relies on human intuition to generate hypotheses (left). In an AI-augmented cycle (right), models analyse data and suggest hypotheses, and testing still decides which survive.





18.9.2 A long and uncertain road
A new medicine passes through discovery, preclinical research, clinical trials, regulatory review and post-marketing safety monitoring (Figure 18.10). Most candidates fail: across therapeutic areas, only around one in seven development programmes that enter Phase I trials reaches approval (Wong, Siah, and Lo 2019). Even when the biological target is known, the road is long, as Table 18.2 shows.

about 12 years








18.9.3 Two different kinds of AI
The rentosertib programme used AI at two points, and they are different kinds of AI (Ren et al. 2025).
Target discovery is predictive. A target-discovery platform integrated omics data from fibrotic tissue, other biological evidence and the scientific literature, and ranked candidate proteins by their predicted role in fibrosis and their suitability as drug targets; TNIK came out near the top. This is supervised and unsupervised learning of the kind in Parts II and III of this book, and in spirit close to retrieval: the system aggregates and weighs evidence. The target still has to be validated experimentally (Figure 18.11).






flowchart TB
  TI[Target identification] --> HC[Have a compound<br/>with an effect]
  TI --> WC[Want a compound<br/>for a disease]
  HC --> TD[Target deconvolution]
  WC --> TDISC[Target discovery<br/>predictive AI ranks candidates]
  TD --> OT((One target))
  TDISC --> OT
  OT --> TV[Target validation<br/>experiments]




Figure 18.11: Two routes to one validated target. Starting from a compound with an effect, the target is found by deconvolution; starting from a disease with no compound yet, a target is discovered first. Either way the target must be validated.





Molecule design is generative. Once TNIK was chosen, a generative chemistry platform proposed new molecules expected to bind it, working on molecular graphs and sequences rather than words (Figure 18.12). The goal is not fluency but chemistry: candidates must be synthesisable, stable and active. An earlier demonstration of the approach had designed potent inhibitors of another kinase within weeks (Zhavoronkov et al. 2019). Each generated molecule is a hypothesis, and most are wrong.






Figure 18.12: Generative chemistry and candidate selection. Given a target, generative models propose a virtual library of molecules; predictive models and filters narrow it to a few compounds for testing.



Selection brings prediction back. From thousands of generated molecules, predictive models estimate binding to the target, toxicity (a strong binder predicted to damage the liver is dropped) and pharmacokinetics — absorption, distribution, metabolism and excretion — while rules of medicinal chemistry, such as limits on molecular weight and lipophilicity for oral drugs (Lipinski et al. 1997), remove poor candidates cheaply (Figure 18.13). A candidate must pass all criteria at once: a multi-objective problem in which a predictive model plays every role you have met in this book.






Figure 18.13: Candidate filtering: a large set of generated molecules is narrowed by predicted target binding, toxicity, pharmacokinetics and rule-based drug-likeness filters to a short list for testing.



Then the laboratory takes over. Selected molecules were synthesised and tested in cells and in animal models of lung fibrosis; pharmacokinetic and pharmacodynamic modelling linked dose to effect; and results fed back into the next round of design (Figure 18.14). Here the role of AI shifts from proposing to interpreting. The candidate then entered first-in-human studies to check safety and how the body handles the drug, before a Phase 2a trial in patients (Figure 18.15). The developers report that the whole route from target nomination to a preclinical candidate took about a year and a half (Ren et al. 2025), against the decades of Table 18.2 — though those decades also included discovering the biology itself.






Figure 18.14: From prediction to validation: in silico testing, in vitro studies, in vivo evaluation, and data analysis that feeds back into design.









Figure 18.15: Early clinical phases: Phase 0 (microdosing), Phase I (safety and dose) and Phase IIa (first signals of efficacy) take a candidate from computational design to testing in people.





18.9.4 Reading the Phase 2a trial
The Phase 2a trial randomised 71 patients with IPF to placebo or one of three doses of rentosertib for 12 weeks (Xu et al. 2025). Its primary endpoint was safety and tolerability. Adverse events were reported in 83.3 % of patients in the highest-dose arm (60 mg once daily) and 70.6 % with placebo. Lung function was an exploratory endpoint: forced vital capacity (FVC), the volume a patient can exhale after a full breath, changed by 98.4 mL on average in the 60 mg arm (95 % confidence interval 10.9 to 185.9 mL) and by −20.3 mL with placebo (−116.1 to 75.6 mL) (Xu et al. 2025).
How should Emma, or a regulator, read these numbers? You can do a rough check yourself with the tools of Chapters 2 and 13. Each interval is about \(\pm 1.96\) standard errors around its mean, so the standard errors are about 44.6 and 48.9 mL. If the two arms are independent, the difference of 118.7 mL has a standard error of about \(\sqrt{44.6^2 + 48.9^2} \approx\) 66.2 mL, and an approximate 95 % interval of −11.1 to 248.4 mL. This back-of-the-envelope calculation is not the trial’s own analysis, which used a different statistical model, but it makes the key point visible: with about 18 patients per arm for 12 weeks, the data are compatible with no effect as well as with a large one.
The appraisal, then, is the same as for any drug:

The design was right for its question. Randomisation and a placebo arm make the comparison fair (Chapter 13); a Phase 2a trial is meant to establish safety and look for a signal.
The safety result is reassuring but small. Seventy-one patients for 12 weeks cannot reveal rare or delayed harms.
The efficacy signal is a hypothesis, not a finding. It was exploratory, in small groups, over a short time, with intervals that overlap. Only a larger and longer confirmatory trial can tell whether rentosertib slows the decline of lung function in a way that matters to patients.
How the molecule was found does not change any of this. A molecule designed by a generative model is judged by exactly the same evidence as one found by a chemist.

AI can speed up discovery; it does not lower the evidence bar.

A news headline says: “AI-designed drug works in lung fibrosis trial.” Based on the Phase 2a trial, which statement is accurate?

The trial proved that rentosertib slows lung fibrosis Lung function was an exploratory endpoint in small groups over 12 weeks, with intervals compatible with no effect. That is a signal worth testing, not proof.
The trial showed an acceptable short-term safety profile and an encouraging, exploratory signal in lung function that needs confirmation Correct. Safety was the primary endpoint; the FVC difference is a hypothesis for a larger, longer trial to test.
Because AI designed the molecule, the usual trial phases can be shortened AI can shorten discovery; it does not change what counts as evidence that a drug is safe and effective in patients.
The trial shows nothing, because it was too small Small trials still tell us something: the drug was tolerated for 12 weeks and there is a signal worth pursuing. The mistake is to over-read them, not to read them at all.

section: 18.10 AI as a meta-player in the decision-quality chain
text:
18.10 AI as a meta-player in the decision-quality chain
Chapter 1 ended its discussion of decision quality with a promise. A decision is good if its six elements are good — an appropriate frame, creative and doable alternatives, meaningful and reliable information, clear values and trade-offs, logically correct reasoning, and commitment to action — and a decision is only as strong as its weakest link (Spetzler, Winter, and Meyer 2016). Decision quality is judged by how the decision was made, with the information available at the time, and not by the outcome, which also depends on luck (Howard 1988). Throughout this book models have served one link, information. Language-model systems can touch all six, which is what it means to call AI a meta-player: it can take part not only in supplying the information but in the process of deciding itself (figure below).



  The decision-quality chain with the role AI can play in each link
  The six interlocking links of decision quality. Link 3, information, and link 5, reasoning, are shaded dark: AI can strengthen them. Link 2, alternatives, is shaded light: AI can support it. Links 1 frame, 4 values and 6 commitment are not shaded: people lead, and AI can at most prompt them with questions.

The decision-quality chain of Chapter 1 (adapted from Spetzler, Winter, and Meyer 2016), with the role AI can play in each link today. Dark: AI can strengthen the link; light: AI can support it; unshaded: people lead and AI can at most prompt them.





Table 18.3: AI as a meta-player: what it can contribute to each link of decision quality, the main risk, and the safeguard.











Link
What an assistant can contribute (Ward 7)
Main risk
Safeguard




1. Frame
Ask which decision is really being made: “change the vancomycin” or “is the antibiotic plan still right for Aoife?”; by when; for whom
Adopting the user’s framing, or imposing a confident wrong one
The team states and owns the frame; the assistant asks, it does not set


2. Alternatives
Suggest options the team had not listed: a different beta-lactam, AUC-guided dosing, extended-interval dosing
Plausible but unavailable or unsafe options
Check every option against the formulary and guideline (retrieval, tools)


3. Information
Retrieve the guideline, compute the risk of AKI with a validated model, summarise the chart
Hallucination, miscalibration, missed passages
Grounding with citations, calibrated confidence, abstention, evaluation


4. Values
Explain trade-offs in plain language; help Aoife and her family say what matters to them
Suggesting values instead of eliciting them; nudging
Values come from the patient and clinicians; the threshold of Chapter 1 is theirs


5. Reasoning
Check calculations with tools; check consistency; flag anchoring and other biases (Tversky and Kahneman 1974)
Automation bias; the model’s own reasoning errors
Show the working; deterministic tools for arithmetic; a person verifies


6. Commitment
Remind the team of 12-hourly creatinine; check that the plan is carried out and documented
“The system said so”: responsibility diluted
A named person is responsible and recorded (DOC-1)






Here is how such a contribution might look in practice. Emma tells the assistant her plan and asks it to check the decision, not to make it.






Illustrative output C — a decision-quality check (invented)



Before you finalise the plan for Mrs Byrne, six questions: (1) Frame — is the decision about vancomycin only, or about the whole antibiotic regimen, given VAN-5? (2) Alternatives — have you considered an alternative beta-lactam? (3) Information — her current AKI risk estimate and the latest vancomycin level are not in the notes. (4) Values — has the trade-off between kidney protection and full antibiotic exposure been discussed with her or her family? (5) Reasoning — the creatinine clearance in the notes was computed with a creatinine from 36 hours ago. (6) Commitment — who will review the 12-hourly creatinine tonight?


Nothing in output C makes the decision. It asks questions that a careful senior colleague might ask (Spetzler, Winter, and Meyer 2016), and every one of them points back to people: the team frames, the patient’s values weigh, Emma and Seán decide and answer for it. That is the division of labour Chapter 1 proposed, now with the machinery to make it real: AI strengthens information and reasoning, supports the search for alternatives, and can prompt — but not own — framing, values and commitment. The rentosertib story fits the same chain: AI strengthened the alternatives (molecules) and the information (target ranking), while the decision to test the drug in patients, and later to approve it or not, rests on trial evidence, on the weighing of benefit against harm, and on people who commit to the decision.

Which link of the decision-quality chain should stay with people even when the assistant is excellent?

Information, because models can be wrong Information is precisely where models — and retrieval — strengthen the chain most, provided they are evaluated and grounded.
Reasoning, because only people can reason Checking calculations and consistency is something machines and tools do very well, and a second check reduces errors. People still verify, but this link is one AI can strengthen.
Values and trade-offs, because they belong to the patient and the clinicians Correct. An assistant can help people state their values clearly; it must not supply them. The bundle threshold of Chapter 1 came from how the team valued each consequence, and no model can know that.
Alternatives, because machines lack creativity Generating options is something generative models do well; the risk is options that are not feasible, which checking handles.

section: 18.11 Where this fits in the decision loop
text:
18.11 Where this fits in the decision loop


  The decision loop with a language-model assistant
  A cycle of five boxes: data feed a model; the model produces information; people combine the information with values to make a decision; the decision leads to actions and outcomes, which are recorded as new data. In this chapter the data are guidelines and the patient record, the model is a language model with retrieval and tools, the information is a grounded answer with citations, and the decision step includes human oversight.
  
  
  Data
  guidelines + record
  
  Model
  language model +
  retrieval + tools
  
  Information
  grounded answer, citations,
  confidence or "not covered"
  
  Decision
  values + human oversight
  
  Action and outcome
  logged, monitored, re-evaluated
  
  
  
  
  

The decision loop with a language-model assistant: the model box becomes a system, and the decision box keeps a person in charge.

Which decision does this support? Seán’s and Emma’s: how to adjust Aoife’s antibiotics, how closely to watch her kidneys, whether to start or continue the bundle. The assistant does not estimate a risk the way the models of Part II did; it finds and organises information — guideline passages, calculations, the relevant parts of the record — and it can help to check the decision itself. What can go wrong? It can invent claims in a confident voice, cite a passage that says something else, miss the passage that matters, mirror the biases of its training data, leak what it was told, and lull a tired team into accepting its suggestions. Who stays in control? The people who own the values and answer for the decision — supported by a system that shows its sources, says when it does not know, logs what it did, has been evaluated on local questions, and meets the legal requirements for its intended use. The loop is the same one Chapter 1 drew; the model box is now a whole system, and the human at the decision step matters more, not less.

18.12 Lab: a guideline assistant without the language model
The Lab builds every part of the assistant except the language model itself: the index, the retriever, the grounded prompt, a crude grounding check, the evaluation and the selective-answering curve, and ends with the rough appraisal of the rentosertib trial. Run it here, or download it and run it on your computer: ch18_lab.R · ch18_lab.py. The R code uses only base R (R Core Team 2025); the Python code uses NumPy and pandas (Harris et al. 2020; McKinney 2010).

RPython























Two observations to take forward. First, the crude grounding check flags the dialysis sentence and passes the other two — but it measures shared words, not meaning, so it would also pass a sentence that reverses a passage while reusing its words (“do stop vancomycin…”). Real systems use stronger checks, and still keep a person in the loop. Second, every number about the assistant came from an evaluation file, not from the assistant’s own description of itself: that habit is the most useful thing to take into any conversation with a vendor.

title: 18  From language model to clinical assistant
text:
18.13 Exercises

A system prompt. Write the system prompt for Seán’s assistant: its role, the rule to answer only from the passages and cite them, what to do when they do not cover the question, and what it must never do (for example, give a dose that is not in a passage). Which failure modes of Section 18.4 and Section 18.7 can a prompt not prevent?
Words and meanings. In the retrieval inspector, find two questions that a colleague might plausibly ask but that retrieve the wrong chunk because of different wording. Rewrite them so that they work. What does this suggest about dense embeddings, and about training staff?
Chunk size. Suppose AKI-3 and AKI-8 (two lists of drugs) were merged into one chunk, and all of the vancomycin guideline into another. What would happen to retrieval scores and to the length of the prompt? Give one advantage and one disadvantage of larger chunks.
Write your own hallucinations. Using only CEL-1 and CEL-2 (the CellWorks release procedure), write four claims about what should happen to batch CW-118 after its failed potency test: one supported, one contradicted, one unsupported, and one with a citation that does not support it. Swap with a colleague and classify each other’s claims.
Design an evaluation. Plan the local evaluation of the assistant before it is switched on for all staff: how many questions, from whom, which categories, the rubric, who grades, how you would handle disagreement, and what results would make you deploy it, restrict it or stop it.
Calibration. In the Lab, draw a reliability plot (stated confidence against proportion correct, in bins) for each configuration. Which configuration is overconfident, and by how much on average?
Classify. Where do these fall under the AI Act and the MDR, and why? (a) An app that lets people with IPF log their symptoms and shows general information about the disease; (b) a tool that drafts discharge letters from the notes for a doctor to edit; (c) a model that ranks patients on a waiting list for assessment for kidney transplantation. Note where you are unsure and what information would settle it.
Sample size. In the rough Phase 2a calculation, how many patients per arm would make the 95 % interval for the difference half as wide, if everything else stayed the same? Why would even that trial not be enough for approval?
Your own chain. Choose a decision from your own practice or studies. For each of the six links of decision quality, write one way an assistant could help and one way it could harm, and say who should own that link.







Selected answers





1. A prompt can ask for citations and abstention, but it cannot make the retriever find a passage it misses, guarantee that the model obeys (instructions are followed probabilistically), stop injected instructions hidden in documents, fix an outdated guideline, or check that a citation supports its claim. Those need retrieval tests, grounding checks, document governance and people.
3. A large chunk contains many topics, so its vector is diluted: scores for specific questions fall, and an irrelevant part of the chunk enters the prompt with the relevant one, making the prompt longer and the answer more likely to drift. Advantage: context is kept together (a list is not cut in the middle). Most systems use moderate chunks with a little overlap.
6. With the simulated data, the model alone states on average 31 % more confidence than its accuracy; with retrieval the gap is 0.4 %. The model alone is the overconfident one, and its reliability curve lies well below the diagonal.
7. (a) Probably not a medical device if it only records symptoms and gives general information without patient-specific recommendations; it may carry AI Act transparency obligations if it converses with users. (b) Usually considered an administrative tool rather than a medical device if it only drafts text that a doctor reviews and signs, but this depends on the intended purpose stated by the manufacturer — for example, if it also suggests diagnoses or treatments, Rule 11 applies. (c) Likely high-risk: prioritising access to a health-care service can fall under Annex III, and if it informs clinical decisions it may also be a medical device. In each case the intended purpose is the information that settles it.
8. The standard error falls with the square root of the sample size, so halving the interval needs four times as many patients, about 72 per arm. Approval needs more than a narrower interval on a surrogate measure at 12 weeks: evidence over a longer period, on outcomes that matter to patients, with enough people to detect less common harms, usually in a confirmatory Phase III trial.

title: 18  From language model to clinical assistant
text:
18.14 Summary

A foundation model supplies capability; a system — interface, workflow, retrieval, tools, memory, monitoring and people — turns it into an assistant. Most safety properties belong to the system.
Models are made in three stages: pretraining on next-token prediction (governed by scaling laws), instruction tuning on prompt–response pairs, and preference tuning (RLHF, which treats the model as a policy rewarded by a model of human comparisons, or DPO). Preference tuning shapes style and caution, not knowledge.
Prompts steer a model without changing it; outputs are sensitive to wording and sampling. Chaining splits a task into checkable steps.
Retrieval-augmented generation supplies current, local, citable facts at the moment of the question. The retriever always returns something, can miss what matters, and depends on wording.
Tools do exact computation; agents decide their own next step, which adds flexibility and risk. MCP and A2A standardise connections, not judgement.
Fine-tuning (often with LoRA) changes behaviour and format; distillation makes models smaller; facts belong in documents, behaviour in weights.
Evaluate locally, with a rubric, out-of-scope questions, enough questions for useful confidence intervals, and repeated runs after every change. Benchmarks are not deployment evidence.
Hallucinations contradict the source or cannot be verified from it, including invented and misattributed citations. Calibrated confidence allows selective answering.
Bias, privacy (GDPR) and regulation (AI Act risk tiers; MDR Rule 11 for software with a medical purpose; human oversight against automation bias) shape the design from the start.
In drug discovery, AI ranked targets (predictive) and designed molecules (generative); the resulting drug still had to pass randomised trials. AI can speed up discovery; it does not lower the evidence bar.
AI can be a meta-player in the decision-quality chain: strengthening information and reasoning, supporting alternatives, prompting — but not owning — framing, values and commitment.

title: 19  Generative models beyond text
text:
How to use this chapter






Starting here?





This chapter borrows a few ideas from earlier ones:

A model is a simplified representation of reality; a statistical model writes \(y = f(\mathbf{x}) + \varepsilon\) (Definition 1.3). Each row of a dataset is an instance with features \(\mathbf{x}_i\) (Definition 1.7). Chapter 1 sorted learning into supervised, unsupervised, reinforcement and generative (Section 1.6.2), and contrasted predictive with generative AI (Section 1.6).
A probability distribution describes how likely each value of a random variable is; the normal distribution is the bell curve, and Bayes’ theorem links \(P(y \mid \mathbf{x})\) with \(P(\mathbf{x} \mid y)\) (Chapter 2).
Models are trained on one set of data and judged on data they never saw; a model that is too flexible overfits, and can memorise its training examples (Section 1.8, Definition 1.8).
A neural network is a stack of layers of weighted sums and activations, trained by gradient descent on a loss; PneumoniaMNIST is the collection of paediatric chest X-rays, 28 × 28 pixels, used there (Chapter 7).
Multiple imputation fills each missing value several times with draws from a model of the data (Chapter 9). Standardising a variable puts it on a scale of standard deviations, and a low-dimensional representation \(\mathbf{z}_i\) summarises a row in a few numbers (Chapter 10).

title: 19  Generative models beyond text
section: 19.1 Two questions a model can answer
text:
19.1 Two questions a model can answer
Every model you have met since Chapter 3 answers one kind of question: given what I see about this patient, what is the outcome? Logistic regression gives Priya’s probability of acute kidney injury; a convolutional network gives the probability that an X-ray shows pneumonia. In the language of Chapter 2, these models estimate a conditional distribution, \(P(y \mid \mathbf{x})\): the outcome, given the features. They draw a boundary between outcomes, and they are called discriminative.
A second kind of model asks a different question: what do the data themselves look like? It learns the distribution of the features, \(p(\mathbf{x})\) — or of features and outcome together, \(p(\mathbf{x}, y)\) — well enough to draw new examples from it. Chapter 1 called this generative modelling (Section 1.6.2) and placed generative AI beside predictive AI (Section 1.6).

Definition 19.1 (Generative and discriminative models) A discriminative model learns the distribution of an outcome given the features, \(P(y \mid \mathbf{x})\), and is used to predict or classify. A generative model learns the distribution of the data, \(p(\mathbf{x})\) or \(p(\mathbf{x}, y)\), and can therefore sample from it: produce new examples that resemble the training data without copying them.

The two are linked by Bayes’ theorem. A generative model of \(p(\mathbf{x} \mid y)\) and \(P(y)\) can be turned into a classifier, \(P(y \mid \mathbf{x}) \propto p(\mathbf{x} \mid y)\,P(y)\); the reverse is not true, because a discriminative model never learns what \(\mathbf{x}\) looks like. Learning the whole distribution is a harder task than drawing a boundary: with plenty of data, discriminative classifiers usually reach lower error, while generative ones can do better when data are scarce (Ng and Jordan 2001). You have already met generative models in this book without the name. The Gaussian mixture of Chapter 11 describes each cluster of patients as a cloud from which new patients could be drawn. Multiple imputation in Chapter 9 generates plausible values for Lena’s missing nights — the trap in the gate.
And there is a larger one. Every running example in this book is synthetic. The 1 250 Ward 7 patients, the ONCO-1 trial, HomeBeat and CellWorks were all produced by short scripts that the author wrote by hand (listed in the data appendix): draw an age, then a severity that depends on age, then a creatinine change that depends on both, plus noise. Each script is a generative model, written from knowledge instead of learned from data. This chapter is about learning such models from data, when the data are too rich — 784 pixels of an X-ray, nine interlocking signals of a smartwatch, the atoms of a molecule — to write the recipe by hand.
The simplest learned generative model is one you can build in a line. Chapter 2 described resting heart rate in HomeBeat with a normal distribution; estimate its mean and standard deviation, and rnorm() produces as many new heart rates as you like. The difficulty starts when several variables must be generated together: a frail, inflamed 75-year-old should get a high heart rate and a low heart-rate variability and a low activity index. For an X-ray the “variables” are 784 pixels whose values depend on each other in intricate ways — ribs are continuous, lungs are symmetric, the heart sits on the left. The rest of the chapter shows four ways of learning such joint distributions, three with neural networks and one with plain statistics.

Which of these models is generative?

A logistic regression that estimates the probability of a deterioration event from HomeBeat signals It estimates \(P(y \mid \mathbf{x})\): the outcome given the signals. It cannot produce a new participant.
A model of the joint distribution of age, heart rate, heart-rate variability and activity that can produce new, realistic participants Correct. It learns \(p(\mathbf{x})\) and can sample from it. That is exactly what the HomeBeat statistician needs for synthetic data.
The convolutional network of Chapter 7 that flags pneumonia A classifier: it maps an image to \(P(\text{pneumonia} \mid \text{image})\). It has learned features of X-rays, but not how to produce one.
A random forest that predicts potency of CellWorks batches A regression model of the outcome given process factors: discriminative.

title: 19  Generative models beyond text
text:
19.2 Latent variables and autoencoders
Look at how HomeBeat was simulated. Each participant first receives an age, a frailty and a level of baseline inflammation; the smartwatch signals — resting heart rate, heart-rate variability, skin temperature, activity — are then generated from those few hidden quantities, plus noise (sim_homebeat.R). If frailty and inflammation had not been recorded, they would still be there, shaping every signal from behind the scenes. Such hidden causes are called latent variables.

Definition 19.2 (Latent variable) A latent variable is a quantity that is not observed directly but helps to explain, or to generate, the variables that are. A latent-variable model generates an example in two steps: draw a short code \(\mathbf{z}\) from a simple distribution, then turn \(\mathbf{z}\) into an example \(\mathbf{x}\).

Clinicians reason with latent variables all the time — “frailty”, “physiological reserve”, “disease activity” are not measured by any single number, but they summarise many. The cluster membership of Chapter 11 is a latent variable too. For an X-ray, nobody knows what the right latent variables are. The idea of the methods below is to let a neural network discover them.

19.2.1 The autoencoder
An autoencoder is a neural network trained to copy its input to its output through a narrow passage (Hinton and Salakhutdinov 2006). The first half, the encoder, squeezes the 784 pixels of an X-ray into a few numbers \(\mathbf{z}\) — in this chapter, just two. The second half, the decoder, tries to rebuild the 784 pixels from those two numbers. The network is trained, by gradient descent as in Chapter 7, to make the reconstruction \(\hat{\mathbf{x}}\) as close as possible to the input \(\mathbf{x}\). No labels are needed: the image is its own target.

Definition 19.3 (Autoencoder) An autoencoder is a neural network made of an encoder, which maps an example \(\mathbf{x}\) to a short code \(\mathbf{z}\) (the bottleneck or latent space), and a decoder, which maps the code back to a reconstruction \(\hat{\mathbf{x}}\). It is trained to minimise a reconstruction error between \(\mathbf{x}\) and \(\hat{\mathbf{x}}\).

Because two numbers cannot store 784, the network is forced to keep only what matters most for rebuilding most images — overall brightness, the size and shape of the lung fields, the contrast between lungs and mediastinum. In this sense an autoencoder is a learned, non-linear version of the dimension reduction of Chapter 10: an autoencoder with no activation functions and a squared reconstruction error finds the same low-dimensional subspace as principal component analysis (Baldi and Hornik 1989).
Is a trained autoencoder a generative model? Half of one. The decoder can turn any pair of numbers into an image, so we could pick a point in the latent space and decode it. But which point? A plain autoencoder places its codes wherever is convenient for reconstruction — in our trained autoencoder the test images have codes centred near (−1.51, −0.77), in an irregular cloud, with empty regions in between. Nothing tells us where the decoder has learned to produce realistic images and where it produces nonsense. To generate, we need a latent space with a known shape from which to draw codes. That is what the variational autoencoder adds.

An autoencoder with a 2-number bottleneck is trained on 4 708 chest X-rays. What does it need as training data?

Only the images: each image is both the input and the target Correct. The network learns to reconstruct its input, so no diagnosis or other label is needed. This makes autoencoders unsupervised (or self-supervised) learners.
The images and their diagnosis (normal or pneumonia) The diagnosis is never used. Later in the chapter you will see that the codes partly separate the two diagnoses anyway, without having been told them.
The images and two numbers per image chosen by a radiologist Nobody chooses the codes: the encoder learns them. That is the point of a latent variable — it is discovered, not measured.

title: 19  Generative models beyond text
19  Generative models beyond text
text:
19.4 Generative adversarial networks
In 2014 Goodfellow et al. (2014) proposed a completely different way to train a generator: set it against an opponent. A generative adversarial network (GAN) has two neural networks (Figure 19.3).

The generator \(G\) takes random noise \(\mathbf{z}\) and turns it into a fake example \(G(\mathbf{z})\), say an X-ray.
The discriminator \(D\) receives an example — sometimes a real X-ray, sometimes a fake one — and outputs the probability \(D(\mathbf{x})\) that it is real. It is simply a classifier, like the networks of Chapters 5 and 7: a discriminative model working for a generative one.

The two are trained in alternation. The discriminator learns to tell real from fake; the generator learns, through the discriminator’s gradients, to produce fakes the discriminator accepts. The original paper compares them to counterfeiters and the police: each improves because the other does. In symbols, they play the game
\[
\min_G \max_D \; \mathbb{E}_{\mathbf{x} \sim \text{data}}\big[\log D(\mathbf{x})\big] + \mathbb{E}_{\mathbf{z}}\big[\log\big(1 - D(G(\mathbf{z}))\big)\big] .
\qquad(19.4)\]
The discriminator wants \(D\) close to 1 on real images and close to 0 on fakes, which makes the expression large; the generator wants its fakes to score high, which makes it small. The first term is exactly the log-likelihood of a logistic classifier (Chapter 5). If both players reach the best they can do, the generator’s distribution equals the data distribution and the discriminator can only guess, \(D = \tfrac12\) everywhere (Goodfellow et al. 2014).

Definition 19.5 (Generative adversarial network) A generative adversarial network (GAN) consists of a generator \(G\), which maps random noise \(\mathbf{z}\) to synthetic examples, and a discriminator \(D\), a classifier that estimates the probability that an example is real. They are trained in alternation, \(D\) to separate real from synthetic examples and \(G\) to make \(D\) classify its examples as real (Equation 19.4).

GANs produce strikingly sharp images — no averaging blur, because a blurry fake is easy for the discriminator to catch. In medicine they have been used, for example, to synthesise liver-lesion images that improved a CT classifier trained on a small dataset (Frid-Adar et al. 2018). But the game is hard to train. If the discriminator becomes too good, its gradients vanish and the generator stops learning; if the two keep chasing each other, training oscillates instead of settling (Salimans et al. 2016; Arjovsky, Chintala, and Bottou 2017).
The best-known failure is mode collapse. A mode is a peak of the data distribution — a kind of example, such as normal X-rays of toddlers, or pneumonia X-rays with dense consolidation. A generator that has found one kind of fake the discriminator accepts can keep producing variations of it and ignore the others. Every individual image looks perfect; the collection is far too narrow. For a synthetic training set this is dangerous precisely because it is invisible image by image: a collapsed generator of chest X-rays might never produce a pleural effusion, or a child with a central line, and a classifier trained on its output would never learn them. Variants of the GAN loss reduce the problem (Arjovsky, Chintala, and Bottou 2017), and the only reliable defence is to measure diversity across many samples, as we do in Section 19.6.

A GAN trained on chest X-rays from four hospitals produces images that radiologists cannot tell from real ones. Looking at 1 000 samples, you notice they all resemble the adult-sized, upright films of one hospital. What is the most likely problem?

Overfitting: the generator has memorised individual training images Memorisation is a real risk (Section 19.6), but here the samples are varied images of one kind, not copies of particular images.
Mode collapse: the generator covers only part of the data distribution Correct. Each sample is convincing, but whole kinds of images — the other hospitals, other positions, other ages — are missing. Fidelity looks perfect; diversity has collapsed.
The discriminator is too weak A weak discriminator would let poor-quality fakes through. Here quality is high; it is the variety that is missing.

title: 19  Generative models beyond text
19  Generative models beyond text
text:
19.6 Synthetic data in health
Back to HomeBeat. What the statistician proposes has a name.

Definition 19.7 (Synthetic data) Synthetic data are data produced by a generative model — learned from real data, written from expert knowledge, or both — rather than measured on real people or objects. They are meant to reproduce chosen properties of the real data, for a stated purpose, without being a record of any real individual.

Synthetic data are used in health for several purposes (Chen et al. 2021; Jordon et al. 2022): sharing data that could not otherwise leave an institution, as HomeBeat hopes; augmenting a small training set or a rare class, as Emma’s vendor proposes; testing software and pipelines on realistic records before real ones are touched — the Synthea project generates complete, fictional electronic health records from models of disease progression for exactly this purpose (Walonoski et al. 2018); simulating scenarios that have not happened; and teaching — this book’s datasets are synthetic for that reason.
Whatever the purpose, three properties must be checked (Alaa et al. 2022; Jordon et al. 2022):

Definition 19.8 (Fidelity, diversity and privacy) Fidelity: synthetic records look like real ones — individually plausible, with the right distributions and the right relationships between variables. Diversity (or coverage): the synthetic data cover the whole range of the real data, including rare kinds of records, not just the most typical ones. Privacy: the synthetic data do not reveal information about the real individuals used to train the generator — in particular, they do not contain copies or near-copies of real records. A fourth property, utility, asks whether an analysis done on synthetic data gives the same answer as on real data.

The three pull against each other. The highest fidelity is achieved by copying the real data, which destroys privacy; the safest data are random noise, which have no fidelity. Every generator sits somewhere on that trade-off, and only measurement tells you where.

19.6.1 A generator you can write in ten lines: the Gaussian copula
For a table like HomeBeat, a neural network is not the only option. A classic statistical generator, the Gaussian copula, separates a joint distribution into its marginals — the distribution of each variable on its own — and its dependence — how the variables move together (Sklar 1959; Nelsen 2006). It is a standard baseline in synthetic-data software (Patki, Wedge, and Veeramachaneni 2016). The recipe:

For each variable, replace every value by its rank, scaled to lie between 0 and 1, and convert it to a normal score with the normal quantile function (qnorm in R). Each column now looks standard normal, whatever its original shape.
Compute the correlation matrix of the normal scores. This captures the dependence.
Draw as many new rows as you like from a multivariate normal distribution with that correlation.
Convert each new column back through the normal distribution function (pnorm) to a number between 0 and 1, and read off the matching quantile of the real variable. The new values have the real marginal distributions, and the real correlations, approximately.

You will write it yourself in the Lab. We fitted it, and three other generators, to the 400 training participants of the book’s fixed HomeBeat split (data/splits/homebeat_split.csv, the same split as in Chapter 8), keeping its 100 test participants aside, never used by any generator (script). Each generator produced 400 synthetic participants with all nine variables:

Independent columns — each variable resampled on its own. Perfect marginals, no relationships: a deliberately bad baseline.
Gaussian copula — the recipe above.
Tabular VAE — a small VAE (four latent dimensions) on the standardised table, the tabular cousin of the X-ray network (L. Xu et al. 2019).
Copy and jitter — real participants copied with 2 % noise added. It looks perfect. It is the memorising generator that every privacy check exists to catch.



19.6.2 How to judge synthetic data
Each column of Table 19.2 answers one question.

Marginals. For each variable, the largest gap between the cumulative distributions of real and synthetic values (the Kolmogorov–Smirnov statistic (Massey 1951)), averaged over the nine variables: 0 means identical distributions.
Correlation gap. The average absolute difference between the real and synthetic correlation matrices. Fidelity of relationships.
Precision and recall. For each real participant, draw a small ball reaching to their fifth nearest real neighbour (on standardised variables). Precision is the share of synthetic records that fall inside some real ball — are the fakes realistic? Recall does the reverse with balls around synthetic records — is every kind of real participant represented? These are fidelity and diversity, measured on whole records (Kynkäänniemi et al. 2019).
Utility. Fit a linear regression of the stress score on the other signals using the synthetic data, then measure its error (RMSE) on the 100 real held-out participants: train on synthetic, test on real (Esteban, Hyland, and Rätsch 2017).
Privacy: distance to the closest record (DCR). For each synthetic record, the distance to the nearest real training participant. The yardstick is how close a new real person — one of the 100 held out — typically comes to a training participant. A synthetic record much closer than that is suspicious; too close counts records nearer than the closest 5 % of held-out people.

Read the table row by row, and notice how each generator fails differently.

Independent columns wins on marginals and fails everything that involves more than one variable. In the real data, resting heart rate and heart-rate variability have a correlation of −0.77; here it is 0.01. Only 24 % of its records are realistic as whole records (a 25-year-old with the frailty of a 90-year-old), and a regression trained on it predicts real stress scores with an error of 20.1 instead of 6.2.
The Gaussian copula keeps marginals and relationships (correlation −0.78), gives a regression as good as one trained on real data (6.19), and its records are no closer to real participants than new real people are: median DCR 0.98 against 0.95, with 6.5 % too close against the 5 % expected by chance. Its weak spot is the binary deterioration event: a Gaussian copula is designed for continuous variables (Nelsen 2006), and the correlation between the event and age falls from 0.41 in the real data to 0.06 — look at the event row of the heatmap in the widget below. Discrete variables need extra care.
The tabular VAE keeps the relationships at least as well (correlation gap 0.059) and passes the privacy check, but its marginals are worse (0.109) and so is its utility (6.58). It handles the binary event better than the copula (correlation with age 0.38). With 400 rows a neural network has little to learn from, and a simple statistical model is hard to beat.
Copy and jitter is the best or nearly the best on every fidelity column — and every one of its records sits right next to a real participant (median DCR 0.06). Released, it would hand over the trial’s participants, Lena included, with a thin coat of paint.

The holdout row is a reminder that small samples are noisy: 100 real people differ from 400 real people by more, on marginals, than the synthetic datasets do. Judge synthetic data against what real data of the same size would show.

hbLabels = new Map([["Age (years)", "age"], ["Baseline inflammation", "baseline_inflammation"], ["Frailty index", "frailty"],
  ["Resting heart rate (bpm)", "resting_hr"], ["Heart-rate variability (ms)", "hrv"], ["Skin temperature (°C)", "skin_temp"],
  ["Activity index", "activity_index"], ["Stress score", "stress_score"], ["Deterioration event (0/1)", "event_occurred"]])
hbDcr = {
  const tr = hbs.filter(d => d.source === "real_train");
  const mu = hbVars.map(v => d3.mean(tr, d => d[v])), sd = hbVars.map(v => d3.deviation(tr, d => d[v]));
  const z = d => hbVars.map((v, j) => (d[v] - mu[j]) / sd[j]);
  const T = tr.map(z);
  const nearest = d => { const q = z(d); let best = Infinity; for (const t of T) { let s = 0; for (let j = 0; j < q.length; j++) s += (q[j] - t[j]) ** 2; if (s < best) best = s; } return Math.sqrt(best); };
  const out = {};
  for (const src of ["real_holdout", "independent", "copula", "vae", "copy"]) out[src] = hbs.filter(d => d.source === src).map(nearest);
  out.threshold = d3.quantile(out.real_holdout, 0.05);
  return out;
}

19.6.3 Synthetic is not the same as anonymous
The copy-and-jitter generator is a caricature, but real generators can memorise too. A flexible model trained too long on too few records — exactly the overfitting of Definition 1.8 — can reproduce individual training examples, and outliers are the most exposed: the one 98-year-old in a trial, the patient with a rare combination of conditions. Researchers have recovered near-exact copies of individual training images from large diffusion models (Carlini et al. 2023), and attacks on synthetic tables can often infer whether a particular person’s record was in the training data (membership inference) (Stadler, Oprisanu, and Troncoso 2022). A distance check like the one in the widget catches crude copying; it does not prove that nothing can be learned about anyone.
The rigorous answer is differential privacy: a mathematical guarantee that the generator’s output would be almost the same whether or not any one person’s record had been used, achieved by adding carefully calibrated noise during training (Dwork and Roth 2014). It comes at a cost in fidelity, largest for small datasets and rare subgroups — the trade-off again, now with a dial.
The law follows the same logic. Under the GDPR, information that no longer relates to an identifiable person is outside its scope, but data that could be linked back to someone remain personal data (European Parliament and Council of the European Union 2016, Recital 26). Training a generator on patient records is itself processing personal data, and whether its output is anonymous is a question to be assessed and documented, not assumed (Jordon et al. 2022).

Yes: no record belongs to a real person Exact matches are only the crudest leak. Near-copies, and the ability to infer whether someone was in the training data, are not excluded by “no exact matches”.
Not automatically: near-copies and membership inference must be checked, and formal guarantees need methods such as differential privacy Correct. Synthetic data reduce risk; they do not remove it by definition. Distance checks, attack tests or differential privacy — and a documented assessment — are what justify calling them anonymous.
No: synthetic data derived from patients can never be shared Many organisations do share synthetic data, after assessing the risk. The point is that the assessment is needed, not that sharing is impossible.
