title: 19  Generative models beyond text
text:
19.7 Molecules
Generative models are not limited to images and tables. One of their most consequential uses is in drug discovery, where the “data” are molecules. The number of small molecules that could plausibly be drugs has been estimated at around \(10^{60}\) (Bohacek, McMartin, and Guida 1996) — far more than could ever be made or tested. Chemists have always explored this space with intuition and analogy; a generative model can propose candidates at a scale no team can match.
A molecule can be written as a string — in the SMILES notation, aspirin is CC(=O)OC1=CC=CC=C1C(=O)O (Weininger 1988) — or as a graph of atoms joined by bonds. Both can be modelled with the tools of this chapter. A VAE trained on SMILES strings maps molecules into a continuous latent space, where moving smoothly changes the molecule and properties such as solubility can be optimised by searching the space (Gómez-Bombarelli et al. 2018) — the latent walk you took with X-rays, with molecules instead. Generative models combined with reinforcement learning (Chapter 14) have designed kinase inhibitors that were synthesised and shown to be active within weeks (Zhavoronkov et al. 2019), and diffusion models now design new protein structures and binders that have been confirmed experimentally (Watson et al. 2023).

model

Figure 19.5: Generative chemistry: the model widens the search; filters, experiments and trials narrow it.



What a generative model produces is a hypothesis, not a drug. Most generated molecules cannot be made, would not reach their target, or would be toxic. So generation is always followed by filtering (Figure 19.5): rules of thumb such as Lipinski’s rule of five for oral drugs — molecular weight up to 500, few hydrogen-bond donors and acceptors, moderate fat-solubility (Lipinski et al. 1997) — and predictive models of binding, toxicity and pharmacokinetics. Here the complementarity of Chapter 1 becomes literal: the generative model proposes, discriminative models screen, and experiments decide.
Chapter 18 follows one such molecule all the way. Rentosertib, an inhibitor of the protein kinase TNIK for idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis, combined a target found with predictive models and a molecule designed with generative chemistry (Ren et al. 2025). It then had to clear the same hurdles as any other drug: laboratory and animal studies, and a randomised, placebo-controlled phase 2a trial in 71 patients over 12 weeks whose primary endpoint was safety (Z. Xu et al. 2025). The generative model shortened the path to the first patient. It did not shorten the evidence: AI can speed up discovery; it does not lower the bar.

A generative model proposes 50 000 molecules predicted to bind a target protein strongly. What is the right way to think of them?

As 50 000 drug candidates ready for animal studies Almost all will fail on synthesis, safety, absorption or real (not predicted) binding. They are not yet candidates in the pharmacological sense.
As hypotheses to be filtered by rules, predictive models and experiments, of which very few may survive Correct. Generation widens the search; it does not replace the evidence. Each surviving molecule still needs laboratory, animal and clinical testing, as rentosertib did.
As unreliable, because a model cannot propose molecules no chemist has imagined Proposing molecules nobody has imagined is precisely the point. The issue is not novelty but verification.

title: 19  Generative models beyond text
text:
19.8 Limits and governance
Generated data and images are persuasive, which is exactly why they need rules. Five risks recur.

Hallucinated features. A generator produces what is plausible, not what is true — the same warning Chapter 1 gave for language models. When image-to-image networks were trained on scans in which tumours were over- or under-represented, they learned to add or remove tumour-like features in the images they produced (Cohen, Luck, and Honari 2018). A synthetic or “enhanced” image must never be read as a measurement of the patient.
Bias, reproduced and amplified. A generator learns the population it was trained on. Groups that are rare in the training data are generated rarely and poorly, and mode collapse can make them vanish altogether. Augmenting a training set with synthetic data from a biased generator adds more of the same bias.
Weak evaluation. There is no single number for “good synthetic data”. Popular image scores, such as the Fréchet Inception Distance (Heusel et al. 2017), compare features from a network trained on everyday photographs, which may not capture what matters in an X-ray. Clinical review of samples, task-specific utility tests and privacy tests are all needed.
Feedback loops. Models trained on data produced by earlier models gradually lose the tails of the real distribution — rare cases first — a degradation called model collapse (Shumailov et al. 2024). As generated content spreads, keeping track of which data are real matters more, not less.
Validation on synthetic data. A model can be developed with the help of synthetic data, but its performance must be established on real data from the population where it will be used (Chapters 3 and 7). Testing a model on data from the same generator that helped to train it tells you how well it learned the generator, not the patients.

The regulatory frame is forming around the same points. The EU AI Act requires providers of systems that generate synthetic images, audio, video or text to mark the output in a machine-readable way, so that it can be detected as artificially generated (European Parliament and Council of the European Union 2024, Article 50(2)); data protection law applies to the real records used to train a generator (Section 19.6). In practice, the questions in Table 19.3 belong in the documentation of any synthetic dataset, alongside the code and seed that produced it — the same reproducibility that Chapter 1 asked of every analysis.



Table 19.3: Questions to answer before releasing or using a synthetic dataset.









Question
Why it matters




What is the synthetic data for, and who will use it?
Fidelity, diversity and privacy needs differ between teaching, software testing, sharing and training a model.


Which real data trained the generator, and under what legal basis?
Training a generator is processing personal data.


How were fidelity and diversity measured, and against what reference?
Marginals alone hide broken relationships and missing subgroups.


How was privacy tested (distances, attacks, differential privacy)?
Synthetic is not automatically anonymous.


Is the data labelled as synthetic wherever it travels?
To prevent it from being mistaken for real evidence, or used to validate models.


Will any clinical decision rest on it?
Performance claims need real data from the target population.







A start-up trains a pneumonia classifier on real X-rays plus 20 000 GAN-generated ones, and reports an AUC of 0.97 on a test set of 5 000 further GAN-generated X-rays. What should Emma’s committee conclude?

The classifier is excellent: 0.97 on 5 000 images is a large, reliable test Large, but drawn from the generator, not from children. It measures how well the classifier learned the GAN’s version of pneumonia.
Synthetic X-rays should never have been used for training Augmenting training data with synthetic images can help, especially for rare classes. The problem is the test, not the training.
Nothing yet about real patients: performance must be measured on real X-rays from the population where the tool will be used Correct. Synthetic data can help to develop a model; only real, representative data can validate it — ideally external and prospective, as Chapter 7 argued.

title: 19  Generative models beyond text
section: 19.9 Where this fits in the decision loop
text:
19.9 Where this fits in the decision loop


  The decision loop
  A cycle of five boxes: data feed a model; the model produces information; people combine the information with values to make a decision; the decision leads to actions and outcomes, which are recorded as new data. In this chapter the model box holds a generative model, which produces new examples and candidate alternatives, and a dashed arrow from the model back to the data box marks synthetic data that must be labelled and kept apart from real data.
  
  
  Data
  real, kept apart
  
  Model
  generative: learns what
  the data look like
  
  Information
  new examples,
  candidate alternatives
  
  Decision
  + values, human in the loop
  
  Action and outcome
  recorded as new data
  
  
  
  
  
  
  synthetic data, labelled

The decision loop. Generative models feed the loop at two points: they widen the set of alternatives, and they produce data that must stay labelled as synthetic.

Chapter 1 described models as the source of information for link 3 of the decision-quality chain. Generative models work elsewhere too. When they propose molecules, protocols or scenarios, they strengthen link 2, creative alternatives — a set of options larger than any team would have thought of, to be narrowed by evidence. When they produce synthetic data, they act on the Data box itself: they can make data available that could not otherwise be shared, but they can also quietly replace observation with imitation. Two things therefore stay human. Deciding what generated content is for, and whether its fidelity, diversity and privacy are good enough for that purpose, is a value judgement. And every decision about a patient must ultimately rest on evidence from real patients — rentosertib’s trial, not its design software; the X-ray tool’s external validation, not its synthetic test set.

title: 19  Generative models beyond text
text:
19.10 Lab: generating and auditing
The Lab gathers the chapter’s code in one place: sampling with the reparameterisation trick and the KL formula, the forward diffusion process on an X-ray, and a Gaussian copula written from scratch for HomeBeat, with fidelity and privacy checks. Run it here, or download it and run it on your computer: ch19_lab.R · ch19_lab.py. The R code uses base R (R Core Team 2025); the Python code uses NumPy, pandas, SciPy and Matplotlib (Harris et al. 2020; McKinney 2010; Virtanen et al. 2020; Hunter 2007). The neural networks were trained beforehand with PyTorch (Paszke et al. 2019).

RPython























Two observations to take forward. First, ten lines of statistics produce synthetic HomeBeat participants whose relationships, utility and privacy are comparable with those of the neural generator in Table 19.2: for a small table, the simplest generator that passes the checks is often the right one. Second, every check needed real data — the 400 participants to compare with and the 100 held out to set the yardstick. Synthetic data are audited against reality, never instead of it.

title: 19  Generative models beyond text
text:
19.11 Exercises

Discriminative or generative? For each running example (Ward 7, ONCO-1, HomeBeat, CellWorks), write one discriminative and one generative question, and say who would use the answer.
The KL term by hand. Using Equation 19.2, compute the KL penalty for \((\mu, \sigma) = (0, 1)\), \((1, 1)\), \((0, 0.5)\) and \((0, 2)\). Which change of the encoder is penalised more: moving the code one unit from the origin, or halving its standard deviation?
Latent walks. In the latent-space widget, keep \(z_2 = 0\) and move \(z_1\) from −2.5 to 2.5. Describe what changes in the image. Then do the same for \(z_2\). Why should you be careful before calling one of these directions “the pneumonia direction”?
Noise schedule. Modify the Lab so that \(\beta_t\) rises from 0.0001 to 0.04 instead of 0.02. At which step do signal and noise now carry equal variance? What would that mean for a network learning the reverse process?
Copula without correlation. In the Lab, replace the correlation matrix R by the identity matrix (diag(length(vars)) in R, np.eye(len(vars_)) in Python). Which generator of Table 19.2 have you rebuilt? Check the correlation gap and the utility.
Privacy against fidelity. In the Lab, make a “copy and jitter” generator — sample real rows and add noise equal to a fraction \(k\) of each standard deviation — for \(k\) = 0.02, 0.2, 0.5 and 1. Plot the share of records that are too close and the correlation gap against \(k\). Where would you set \(k\), and who should decide?
A release note. Write the documentation for a synthetic HomeBeat dataset made with the Gaussian copula, answering each question of Table 19.3 in one or two sentences.







Selected answers





2. \((0, 1)\): 0. \((1, 1)\): 0.5. \((0, 0.5)\): \(\tfrac12(0.25 - \log 0.25 - 1) \approx 0.32\). \((0, 2)\): \(\tfrac12(4 - \log 4 - 1) \approx 0.81\). Moving the code one unit from the origin costs 0.5, more than halving its standard deviation (about 0.32); widening the cloud to \(\sigma = 2\) costs the most of the three changes.
3. Along \(z_1\) the image mostly changes in the clarity of the lung fields; along \(z_2\), mainly in brightness, contrast and exposure. The codes of the two diagnoses differ on average, but the network was never told the diagnoses: a direction that separates them may reflect disease, or the way images were acquired (exposure, positioning, equipment). Only a study with known acquisition details could tell the two apart — the shortcut-learning warning of Chapter 7.
4. With \(\beta_t\) up to 0.04, \(\bar\alpha_t\) falls about twice as fast and reaches 0.5 near step 185 (instead of 260). The image is destroyed earlier, so fewer of the 1 000 steps are spent on fine detail; the reverse network gets fewer gentle steps to learn from, and samples tend to lose detail. The schedule is a design choice with consequences.
5. The independent-columns generator: with an identity matrix the normal scores are drawn independently, so the marginals are kept and every relationship is lost. The correlation gap jumps to about the value in the table, and the utility collapses.
6. As \(k\) grows, the share of records that are too close falls and the correlation gap grows (noise weakens relationships). There is no value at which the generator becomes as good as the copula: adding noise to real records trades privacy for fidelity record by record, while a generative model learns the distribution and samples new records from it. Where to stop is a judgement about acceptable risk for a stated use, to be made with the data protection officer and, ideally, participant representatives — not by the analyst alone.

title: 19  Generative models beyond text
text:
19.12 Summary

Discriminative models learn \(P(y \mid \mathbf{x})\) and predict; generative models learn \(p(\mathbf{x})\) or \(p(\mathbf{x}, y)\) and can produce new examples. Every running example of this book was produced by a hand-written generative model.
Latent variables are hidden quantities that generate what we observe. An autoencoder compresses examples into a short code and reconstructs them; a VAE makes the code a distribution, pulls it towards \(\mathcal{N}(\mathbf{0}, \mathbf{I})\) with a KL penalty, and trains through the reparameterisation trick \(z = \mu + \sigma\varepsilon\), so that random codes decode to plausible examples. Its samples tend to be blurry.
A GAN trains a generator against a discriminator; it gives sharp samples but is unstable and prone to mode collapse.
A diffusion model destroys examples with a fixed forward noising process, \(\mathbf{x}_t = \sqrt{\bar\alpha_t}\mathbf{x}_0 + \sqrt{1-\bar\alpha_t}\mathbf{\varepsilon}\), and learns to reverse it by predicting the noise; it gives sharp, diverse samples at the cost of slow generation.
Synthetic data must be judged on fidelity, diversity, privacy and utility, all measured against real data. A simple Gaussian copula can be an excellent generator for small tables; a generator that copies real records looks perfect and protects nobody. Synthetic is not automatically anonymous.
In drug discovery, generated molecules are hypotheses, filtered by rules, predictive models and experiments; rentosertib shows that AI can shorten discovery but not the evidence.
Generated content can hallucinate, reproduce bias, degrade through feedback loops and mislead if used for validation. It must be labelled, documented and kept apart from real data.

title: Appendix A — Setting up R, Python, Git and GitHub
text:
A.1 A first taste of code
Everything in this book runs in your browser, so you can start without installing anything. Sooner or later, though, you will want to run the Labs on your own computer, work with your own data and keep your projects safe and shareable. This appendix sets up the four tools that make that possible: R, Python, Git and GitHub. Follow the parts you need; each one ends with a check that it worked.
Why bother? Chapter 1 argued that results only count when someone else can reproduce them (Section 1.11). Code is how we tell the computer exactly what to do, and version control is how we keep track of every change to that code, recover from mistakes and work with other people without overwriting each other’s work. In health research and regulation, that traceability is not a luxury: it is part of the evidence.
Code is a list of instructions written in a language the computer understands. The example below creates five heart-rate readings, computes their average, prints a message and builds a small table. Run it in either language.

A.2 Install R and an editor

R. Download and install the latest version for your system from CRAN, https://cran.r-project.org (R Core Team 2024).
An editor. Install RStudio Desktop (https://posit.co/download/rstudio-desktop/) or Positron (https://positron.posit.co), both free. RStudio also includes Quarto, the tool used to build this book.
The packages used in the Labs. Open RStudio and run, once:
install.packages(c("tidyverse", "glmnet", "rpart", "ranger", "mice", "knitr", "rmarkdown"))

The packages are the tidyverse (Wickham et al. 2019), glmnet (Friedman, Hastie, and Tibshirani 2010), rpart (Therneau and Atkinson 2023), ranger (Wright and Ziegler 2017), mice (Buuren and Groothuis-Oudshoorn 2011), knitr (Xie 2015) and rmarkdown (Xie, Allaire, and Grolemund 2018).
Check: in the RStudio console, R.version.string prints your R version, and library(glmnet) runs without an error.

title: Appendix A — Setting up R, Python, Git and GitHub
text:
A.3 Install Python
There are two common routes; choose one.

Anaconda or Miniconda (https://www.anaconda.com/download) installs Python together with the conda package manager. Many universities and hospitals already use it.
python.org (https://www.python.org/downloads/) installs plain Python, which you then extend with pip.

Create a separate environment for the book, so that its packages do not clash with others:
# with conda
conda create -n aihs python=3.12 pandas numpy scikit-learn matplotlib jupyter
conda activate aihs

# or with plain Python
python3 -m venv aihs
source aihs/bin/activate          # on Windows: aihs\Scripts\activate
pip install pandas numpy scikit-learn matplotlib jupyter
You can write Python in VS Code (https://code.visualstudio.com), Positron, JupyterLab, or in RStudio itself.
Python is maintained by the Python Software Foundation (Python Software Foundation 2025); the packages are pandas (McKinney 2010), NumPy (Harris et al. 2020), scikit-learn (Pedregosa et al. 2011) and Matplotlib (Hunter 2007).
Check: python -c "import pandas, sklearn; print('ok')" prints ok.

title: Appendix A — Setting up R, Python, Git and GitHub
section: A.4 Git and GitHub: what they are
text:
A.4 Git and GitHub: what they are
Git is a version control system (Chacon and Straub 2014): it records snapshots of a project’s files over time. Each snapshot is a commit, with a short message saying what changed and why. With Git you can compare versions, go back to an earlier one, and work on an idea in a separate branch without disturbing the main version.
Git works on your own computer. GitHub (and similar services such as GitLab or Bitbucket) keeps a copy of the project online, a remote repository, which gives you a backup, a public or private place to share your work, and tools to collaborate: other people can propose changes through a pull request, which you review before accepting.


  The everyday Git and GitHub cycle
  Files in the working folder are staged with git add, recorded in the local repository with git commit, sent to GitHub with git push, and brought back from GitHub with git pull.
  
  
  Your files
  working folder
  
  Staging area
  changes chosen
  
  Local repository
  history of commits
  
  GitHub
  remote copy
  
  
  
  
  add
  commit
  push
  pull

The everyday cycle: choose changes (add), record them (commit), share them (push), and fetch other people's changes (pull).







Health data never go to GitHub



Repositories hold code, documentation and, at most, simulated or fully anonymised data. Never commit patient-identifiable data, even to a private repository: list data folders in a .gitignore file so Git ignores them, and follow your institution’s data-protection rules (in Europe, the GDPR (European Parliament and Council of the European Union 2016)). All datasets in this book are simulated precisely so that they can be shared.

title: Appendix A — Setting up R, Python, Git and GitHub
section: A.5 Set up Git and GitHub, step by step
text:
A.5 Set up Git and GitHub, step by step

A.5.1 1. Create a GitHub account
Go to https://github.com, sign up with a short, professional username (it becomes part of your project addresses) and turn on two-factor authentication under Settings → Password and authentication.


A.5.2 2. Install Git
Check whether Git is already installed by typing in a terminal (the Terminal tab in RStudio works):
git --version
If it is not:

macOS: xcode-select --install (or, with Homebrew, brew install git).
Windows: download it from https://git-scm.com/download/win, or run winget install --id Git.Git -e --source winget.
Linux (Debian/Ubuntu): sudo apt update && sudo apt install -y git.



A.5.3 3. Tell Git who you are (once)
git config --global user.name  "Your Name"
git config --global user.email "you@example.com"   # the e-mail of your GitHub account
git config --global init.defaultBranch main


A.5.4 4. Let your computer talk to GitHub
GitHub does not accept your account password from Git; it uses a personal access token. The easiest way to create and store one is from R:
install.packages(c("usethis", "gitcreds"))
usethis::create_github_token()   # opens GitHub in the browser; create the token and copy it
gitcreds::gitcreds_set()         # paste the token when asked
If Git ever asks for a “password” in the terminal, paste the token, not your GitHub password. (Advanced users may prefer SSH keys: ssh-keygen -t ed25519 -C "you@example.com", then add the contents of the .pub file under Settings → SSH and GPG keys on GitHub.)


A.5.5 5. Turn on Git in RStudio
Tools → Global Options → Git/SVN: check that RStudio found Git and tick Enable version control interface. Restart RStudio. A Git tab now appears in projects that use Git.


A.5.6 6. Start a project under version control
From RStudio: File → New Project → New Directory, tick Create a git repository. Then, in the console, usethis::use_github() (Wickham et al. 2023) creates the matching repository on GitHub and connects the two.
From the terminal:
cd my-project
git init
git add .
git commit -m "First version"
git branch -M main
git remote add origin https://github.com/<your-username>/my-project.git
git push -u origin main
Check: your files appear at https://github.com/<your-username>/my-project.

title: Appendix A — Setting up R, Python, Git and GitHub
text:
A.6 The daily routine
git pull                         # 1. bring in changes made elsewhere
# ... edit, run, check ...
git add analysis.R               # 2. choose what to record
git commit -m "Add baseline model for Ward 7"   # 3. record it, with a meaningful message
git push                         # 4. share it
In RStudio the same four steps are buttons in the Git tab: Pull, tick the files, Commit, Push. Commit small, coherent changes often, and write messages that your future self will understand (“Fix leakage: drop post-treatment tumour size”, not “changes”).

Which command does each job?

Record the chosen changes in the project’s history, with a message. git commit
Bring a colleague’s latest changes from GitHub into your copy. git pull
Send your recorded changes to GitHub. git push
Choose which modified files will go into the next snapshot. git add

title: Appendix A — Setting up R, Python, Git and GitHub
text:
A.7 When things go wrong







Problem
What to do




git: command not found (macOS)
Run xcode-select --install, or brew install git.


RStudio does not see Git
Set the path to Git in Tools → Global Options → Git/SVN, then restart RStudio.


Asked for a password on git push
Paste your personal access token; if it expired, run gitcreds::gitcreds_set() (Csárdi 2022) again.


“Divergent branches” when pulling
Choose a strategy once: git config --global pull.rebase false (merge).


Committed with the wrong e-mail
Fix the setting with git config --global user.email ..., then git commit --amend --reset-author.


A data file was committed by mistake
Do not just delete it in a new commit: it stays in the history. Ask your institution’s IT or data-protection officer for help before pushing.

title: Appendix A — Setting up R, Python, Git and GitHub
text:
A.8 A minimal portfolio
Every craft has its workbench. For anyone working with data, a small set of well-kept GitHub repositories is the simplest portfolio: each with a short README that says what the project answers, how to run it and where the data come from; code that runs from raw data to results; a fixed random seed; and a record of package versions (for example with renv (Ushey and Wickham 2023) in R or a requirements.txt file in Python). The Labs of this book are a good place to start: put each one in a repository, change it, and let the history show what you learned.

B.1 Example 1 · Ward 7 ICU: acute kidney injury
All tabular datasets are simulated. They imitate the structure of real clinical and manufacturing data but describe no real person, batch or hospital. Each one comes with the R or Python script that generated it (fixed random seed, so you get exactly the same file), and you are free to download and reuse it. The tables below are in chapter order.
The full ONCO-1 trial (10 000 patients × 2 000 genes, about 140 MB) is too large for the browser; run sim_onco1.R on your computer to regenerate it.
One row per ICU patient, from four ICU sites. B.6 Imaging data · Paediatric chest X-rays (PneumoniaMNIST)
Unlike the four running examples, these are real, de-identified images, released publicly for research and teaching. The chest X-rays were collected from children aged one to five at a hospital in Guangzhou, China, and labelled by expert physicians (Kermany et al. 2018); they are also distributed on Kaggle (Mooney 2018). text:
B.8 Chapter 10 · Dermato-ATT and the Digital Trial
Dermato-ATT simulates 200 people with psoriasis starting an anti-IL-17 (Griffiths et al. 2021) biologic, with 1 850 baseline measurements: 2 clinical scores (PASI_baseline, DLQI) (Fredriksson and Pettersson 1978; Finlay and Khan 1994), 18 blood cytokines, 30 exposome variables (NO2, PM10, UV_index, temperature, humidity, expo_6 … expo_30), 1 500 genes and 300 microbiome features (ASV_1 … ASV_300), and the outcome Outcome_PASI12, the change in PASI after 12 weeks. The browser file keeps every clinical, cytokine and exposome column, the first 100 genes and the first 50 microbiome features; run sim_dermato_att.R to regenerate the full table. The four hidden factors that generate the blocks (latent_G1, latent_G2, latent_M1, latent_M2) are in dermato_latent.csv; gene and microbe names are labels, and no named pathway is simulated.
The Digital Trial dataset simulates 500 participants with four cytokines, four wearable summaries, three clinical variables, a response delta_score and a responder label. Its features are functions of points drawn on two geometric shapes, a helix (350 participants) and a Swiss roll (150); digital_trial_truth.csv gives each participant’s shape, position along it and coordinates X1–X3. Chapter 10 keeps this file hidden until it has shown the t-SNE and UMAP maps (Maaten and Hinton 2008; McInnes, Healy, and Melville 2018).

B.12 Chapter 13 · Ward 7, extended, and ONCO-1 in routine practice
Ward 7, extended (ward7_dag.csv) is a separate simulated ward (identifiers X7_0001 … X7_1250, not the patients of icu_aki.csv). It follows the same generating rules as Ward 7 (re-implemented in ward7_scm.R) and adds three recorded variables whose causal role is known (Hernán and Robins 2020). The total effect of protocol adherence is −0.28 mg/dL per unit, as in Ward 7 (direct −0.18, about −0.10 through nephrotoxic drugs).

ONCO-1 in routine practice (onco1_routine.csv) is an observational twin of the ONCO-1 trial. Instead of a coin, oncologists “chose”: each trial patient was kept with a probability that depends on the arm and on age, tumour grade, performance status and gene_05 (offered chemotherapy more often when younger, fitter, with a higher-grade tumour or low gene_05). The kept patients have a known propensity score (Rosenbaum and Rubin 1983) and the trial’s covariate distribution, so the trial’s difference in means is a fair benchmark. Columns: patient_id, chemo (1 = chemotherapy; 252 of 509 patients), patient_age, tumor_grade, performance_score, gene_05, dose_intensity and the outcome response_percent, as in onco1.csv. The true propensity score is not saved: in real life nobody knows it.

text:
B.13 Chapter 15 · Synthetic clinical text
Every sentence is invented from templates by sim_ch15_text.py; no real note, report or medicine leaflet was used or copied. clinical_notes.csv has one row per document: doc_id; source (ward7_discharge, 450 discharge summaries; ward7_tonight, the admission notes written tonight for Aoife, Tomás and Priya, which reveal no outcome; onco1_ae, 400 adverse-event notes; leaflet, 34 patient-leaflet sentences); patient_id (a simulated Ward 7 or ONCO-1 patient, so each note inherits the book-wide split in data/splits/); set (train, test, tonight or none); adr (1 if the note reports a suspected adverse drug reaction (Edwards and Aronson 2000), 0 if not, empty for leaflets and tonight’s notes); drug (the suspected drug, unclear for borderline notes labelled 1); and text. Each note is built from a symptom, an attribution (to a drug, to something else, or unclear) and an action, so the same words occur in notes with and without a reaction; notes with an unclear attribution are labelled 1 or 0 at random, which imitates disagreement between reviewers. Discharge summaries quote the patient’s simulated baseline and 48-hour creatinine from icu_aki.csv; ONCO-1 notes quote the tumour sizes and performance status from onco1.csv. negation_sentences.csv lists short sentences with a finding, a gold label negated (1 = denied or absent) and the pattern each one illustrates (simple trigger, long list, termination, pseudo-negation, post-negation, hard) (Chapman et al. 2001).

title: Appendix B — Data used in this book
text:
B.14 Chapter 16 · Ward 7 short notes
ward7_notes.csv contains 8 000 short notes generated from a small template grammar, so the corpus describes no real person and its regularities are known by construction. Columns: note_id (N0001 … N8000), set (train, 7 147 notes; test, 853 notes) and text. Tokens are lower-case words and the punctuation marks , . : separated by single spaces, so splitting on spaces recovers them. The grammar plants the regularities that Chapter 16 uncovers: drugs of the same class appear in similar contexts; each laboratory marker goes with one organ and one specialty; staff roles are followed by “she” or “he” with deliberately unequal frequencies (a bias the embeddings inherit (Caliskan, Bryson, and Narayanan 2017)); “meropenem” never follows “started”; and some notes name the drug started and, a clause or two later, ask to check the level of that same drug (a long-range dependence).

title: Appendix C — Glossary
text:
Each term links to the chapter, and where possible to the definition, in which it is introduced. Terms are listed alphabetically; the short meanings are reminders, and the chapter gives the full definition.



Term
Short meaning
Defined in




Accuracy
Proportion of instances classified correctly
Ch. 5


Activation function (ReLU)
Turns a neuron’s weighted sum into its output: step, sigmoid or the rectified linear unit \(\max(0, z)\)
Ch. 7


Adjusted Rand index (ARI)
Agreement between two partitions over all pairs of instances, corrected for chance; 1 = identical
Ch. 11


Agent and environment
Whatever chooses the actions, and everything it acts on but cannot fully control
Ch. 14


AI Act risk tiers
The EU classification of AI uses: prohibited, high-risk, transparency obligations, minimal risk
Ch. 18


Artificial intelligence (AI)
Systems that perform tasks that would require cognition if done by humans
Ch. 1


Artificial neuron (perceptron)
Multiplies its inputs by weights, adds a bias and passes the sum through an activation function
Ch. 7


Attention
Builds a new representation for a position as a weighted average of the positions it may look at; the weights \(\alpha_{ts}\) sum to 1
Ch. 17


Autoencoder
An encoder that compresses an example to a short code and a decoder that reconstructs it
Ch. 19


Automation bias
The tendency to over-rely on an automated system’s output
Ch. 18


Average treatment effect (ATE, CATE)
\(\mathbb{E}[Y(1)] - \mathbb{E}[Y(0)]\) in a population; the CATE is the same contrast within a subgroup
Ch. 13


Backdoor criterion
A set of variables suffices for adjustment if it blocks every backdoor path and contains no descendant of the treatment
Ch. 13


Backpropagation
Computes the gradient of the loss for every weight by applying the chain rule from the output back to the input
Ch. 7


Bag of words
Describes a document by how often each vocabulary word occurs, ignoring order; stacked, the vectors form a document-term matrix
Ch. 15


Bagging
Fits one model per bootstrap sample and averages their predictions (bootstrap aggregating)
Ch. 6


Baseline model
The simplest sensible prediction (the training mean, or current practice) that any model must beat
Ch. 3


Batch and epoch
The subset of instances used for one gradient step, and one complete pass through the training set
Ch. 7


Bayes’ theorem
Rule that updates a prior probability with evidence: posterior ∝ likelihood × prior
Ch. 2


Bayesian additive regression trees (BART)
A sum of small trees with priors favouring shallow trees, fitted by MCMC; gives predictions with uncertainty
Ch. 8


Bayesian regression
A regression whose coefficients receive priors; the result is their joint posterior rather than single estimates
Ch. 8


Benchmark and real-world evaluation
A fixed public test set, versus testing the whole system on the tasks, documents and users where it will be deployed
Ch. 18


Bias (of a model)
Systematic error from assumptions that are too rigid; leads to underfitting
Ch. 1


Bootstrap sample
\(n\) instances drawn at random with replacement from a dataset of \(n\)
Ch. 6


Byte-pair encoding (BPE)
Builds a subword vocabulary by repeatedly merging the most frequent pair of adjacent symbols
Ch. 15


Calibration
Agreement between predicted probabilities and observed frequencies
Ch. 5


Causal mask
Stops each position from attending to later positions, so a model can generate text left to right
Ch. 17


Centroid and medoid
The mean of a cluster’s members (a synthetic point), and the member closest on average to all the others (a real one)
Ch. 11


Chain rule of probability
The probability of a sequence is the product of each token’s probability given the previous ones
Ch. 16


Classification
Supervised learning with a categorical outcome
Ch. 1


Classification threshold
Probability \(t\) above which a case is classified as positive; a choice of use, not a property of the model
Ch. 5


Cluster and clustering
A group of instances more similar to one another than to others; clustering finds such groups without labels
Ch. 11


Coefficient (regression)
Expected difference in the outcome per unit of a predictor, other predictors held fixed; an association, not necessarily an effect
Ch. 4


Coefficient of determination (\(R^2\))
One minus the ratio of the model’s squared error to that of a baseline predicting the mean
Ch. 3


Coefficient path
Each coefficient of a regularised model drawn as a function of \(\lambda\)
Ch. 4


Collider
A variable caused by two others on a path; adjusting or selecting on it creates a spurious association
Ch. 13


Collinearity
One feature can be written, exactly or nearly, as a weighted sum of others; the features carry overlapping information
Ch. 10


Complete-case analysis
Keeps only the rows in which every variable used is observed (listwise deletion)
Ch. 9


Confidence interval
A range computed so that, over many repetitions of the study, 95 % of such ranges would contain the true value
Ch. 4


Confounder
A common cause of a treatment (exposure) and an outcome; it opens a backdoor path
Ch. 13


Confusion matrix
Cross-table of predicted and actual classes: true and false positives, false and true negatives
Ch. 5


Conjugate prior
A prior that gives a posterior of the same family (beta prior with a yes/no likelihood)
Ch. 8


Convolution
Slides a small filter of learned weights across an image, producing a feature map
Ch. 7


Convolutional neural network (CNN)
Stacks convolution, activation and pooling blocks, followed by fully connected layers
Ch. 7


Cosine similarity
Cosine of the angle between two vectors; for documents, 0 = no word in common, 1 = same proportions
Ch. 15


Cost-complexity pruning
Cuts back a tree by charging a price \(c_p\) for every leaf
Ch. 6


Counterfactual
A statement about what would have happened under an intervention that did not take place
Ch. 13


Counterfactual explanation
A small change in the inputs that would change the model’s output in a specified way; describes the model, not the patient
Ch. 12


Credible interval
An interval containing 95 % of the posterior probability: given model, priors and data, the parameter lies inside with 95 % probability
Ch. 8


Cross-entropy
Average surprise when outcomes from \(P\) are predicted with a model \(Q\); the training loss of language models
Ch. 16


Cross-validation
Repeatedly holding out part of the training data to estimate performance
Ch. 1


Curse of dimensionality
As dimensions grow, data become sparse and distances concentrate, so neighbourhood methods need far more data
Ch. 10


Data
Recorded representations of facts, observations or measurements
Ch. 1


DBSCAN
Density-based clustering: grows clusters from core points with at least minPts neighbours within radius \(r\); other points are noise
Ch. 11


Decision
Choice of one alternative from a set, given a state of knowledge
Ch. 1


Decision basis
Explicit alternatives, consequences, preferences and uncertainties of a decision
Ch. 1


Decision threshold
Probability at which two alternatives have equal expected value
Ch. 1


Decision tree
Predicts by a sequence of yes/no questions on the features, from the root node to a leaf
Ch. 6


Decoding (temperature, top-k, top-p)
Turning next-token probabilities into text: greedy choice or sampling, reshaped by temperature \(\tau\) and top-\(k\)/top-\(p\)
Ch. 16


Design matrix
Matrix with one row per instance and one column per coefficient, with 0/1 dummy columns for categories
Ch. 4


Differential privacy
A mathematical guarantee that the output changes little whether or not any one person’s data were used
Ch. 19


Diffusion model
Learns to reverse a process that gradually adds noise; generates by denoising pure noise step by step
Ch. 19


Dimension (high-dimensional data)
The number of features \(p\); data are high-dimensional when \(p\) is large relative to \(n\)
Ch. 10


Directed acyclic graph (DAG)
A diagram of causal assumptions: arrows for direct effects, no cycles; missing arrows are the strongest assumptions
Ch. 13


Distance
A rule turning two feature vectors into a non-negative number (Euclidean, Manhattan, cosine, Mahalanobis)
Ch. 10


Distributional hypothesis
Words that occur in similar contexts tend to have similar meanings
Ch. 16


Dynamic treatment regime
A sequence of decision rules mapping a patient’s history at each decision point to a treatment
Ch. 14


Early stopping and dropout
Keep the weights with the lowest validation loss; randomly switch off neurons during training. Both reduce overfitting
Ch. 7


Elastic net
A mixture of the lasso and ridge penalties, with mixing parameter \(\alpha\) from 0 (ridge) to 1 (lasso)
Ch. 4


Embedding
A dense vector of \(d\) learned numbers representing a token, a row of the embedding matrix
Ch. 16


Encoder and decoder
Stacks with bidirectional attention (contextual vectors) or causally masked attention (generation); joined by cross-attention
Ch. 17


Entropy
Expected surprise of a random variable, in bits; 0 when the outcome is certain
Ch. 2


Expectation and variance
Long-run average of a random variable, and the average squared distance from it (its square root is the standard deviation)
Ch. 2


Expected loss
Average loss of an action, each loss weighted by the probability of the state that produces it; choose the smallest
Ch. 2


Expected value
Average score of an alternative, weighting consequences by their probabilities
Ch. 1


Experimental data
Data generated when the investigator assigns exposures by design
Ch. 1


Explainability
Methods that build a separate, simpler description of a model’s behaviour
Ch. 12


Explained variance (scree plot)
Share of the total variance carried by each component, shown in order in a scree plot
Ch. 10


Exploration and exploitation
Trying uncertain actions to learn about them, versus choosing the action that looks best now
Ch. 14


Feature
A column (variable) of a dataset
Ch. 1


Fidelity, diversity and privacy (of synthetic data)
Synthetic records look real, cover the whole range of the real data, and reveal nothing about the individuals used for training
Ch. 19


Fine-tuning (LoRA, distillation)
Further training on target-task data; LoRA learns a small low-rank correction, distillation trains a small model to imitate a large one
Ch. 18


Foundation model (LLM)
A large model trained on broad data that can be adapted to many tasks; a large language model is one for text
Ch. 18


Gaussian mixture model (GMM)
Assumes each instance comes from one of \(K\) normal components chosen with probabilities \(\omega_k\)
Ch. 11


Generalisation
Good performance of a model on new, unseen data
Ch. 1


Generative adversarial network (GAN)
A generator that makes synthetic examples and a discriminator that tries to tell them from real ones, trained against each other
Ch. 19


Generative and discriminative models
Learning the distribution of the data, so new examples can be sampled, versus learning the outcome given the features
Ch. 19


Generative modelling
Learning the data distribution to create new, realistic examples
Ch. 1


Global and local explanations
Describe a model’s behaviour over a population, or one prediction for one individual
Ch. 12


Gradient boosting
Builds a model in rounds, each small tree fitted to the current residuals and added with a learning rate
Ch. 6


Gradient descent
Minimises a loss by repeatedly moving every weight a small step against its gradient
Ch. 7


H statistic
Share of the joint effect of two features not explained by their separate effects (Friedman–Popescu)
Ch. 12


Hallucination
Fluent, plausible content not supported by the source or the facts, including invented references
Ch. 18


Hierarchical clustering (dendrogram)
Repeatedly merges the two closest clusters; the merges form a tree, cut at a height to give a partition
Ch. 11


Human oversight
Designing a high-risk system so that competent people can understand, override and stop it
Ch. 18


Hyperparameter
A setting that controls how a model is learned, chosen on data not used for fitting (tuning)
Ch. 3


Impurity (Gini index)
How mixed the outcomes in a node are: within-node variance, Gini index or entropy; splits are chosen to reduce it
Ch. 6


Instance
A row of a dataset (a patient, a batch…)
Ch. 1


Instruction tuning
Further training on prompts paired with good responses written by people
Ch. 18


Internal validation index (silhouette)
Scores a partition from the data alone by balancing compactness and separation of the clusters
Ch. 11


Interpretability
A person can understand how a model works from its structure (a short equation, a small tree)
Ch. 12


Intervention
Setting a variable to a chosen value instead of letting it take its own value
Ch. 13


Inverse probability weighting (IPW)
Weights each patient by the inverse of the probability of the treatment received, creating a pseudo-population without confounding
Ch. 13


\(k\)-means
Alternates assigning each instance to the nearest centroid and moving centroids to the mean of their members
Ch. 11


\(k\)-nearest neighbours (\(k\)NN)
Predicts a new instance by averaging (or voting among) the \(k\) closest training instances
Ch. 3


Kullback–Leibler divergence
Cross-entropy minus entropy; zero only when the model equals the true distribution
Ch. 16


Label
The known value of the outcome for an instance
Ch. 1


Language model
A probability distribution over token sequences, given by next-token probabilities \(P_\theta(w_t \mid w_{<t})\)
Ch. 16


Lasso
Regularisation with the sum of absolute coefficients (L1 penalty); sets some coefficients exactly to zero
Ch. 4


Latent variable
An unobserved quantity that helps explain or generate the observed variables
Ch. 19


Leakage
Information unavailable at prediction time, or from the evaluation data, reaching the model during development; gives optimistic performance
Ch. 3


Learning rate
Step size \(\eta\) that scales each update in boosting and in gradient descent
Ch. 6


Leverage and Cook’s distance
How far an instance’s predictors lie from the others, and how much removing it would change the fit
Ch. 4


Likelihood
Probability of the observed data viewed as a function of the parameter; not the probability that the parameter is true
Ch. 2


Linear regression
Outcome written as an intercept plus a weighted sum of predictors plus error; linear in the coefficients
Ch. 4


Logistic (sigmoid) function
\(\sigma(z) = 1/(1+e^{-z})\), an S-shaped curve that turns any number into a probability
Ch. 5


Logistic regression
Models the probability of a binary outcome as \(\sigma(\beta_0 + \beta_1 x_1 + \dots)\): linear on the log-odds scale
Ch. 5


Loss function
The penalty \(\mathcal{L}(y, \hat y)\) for predicting \(\hat y\) when the truth is \(y\); fitting minimises its average
Ch. 3


Machine learning (ML)
AI that learns from data instead of explicit rules
Ch. 1


Markov chain Monte Carlo (MCMC)
Produces chains of draws whose distribution approaches the posterior; checked with trace plots, R-hat and effective sample size
Ch. 8


Markov decision process (MDP)
States, actions, transition probabilities and rewards, with the next state depending only on the current state and action
Ch. 14


Masked and autoregressive language modelling
Recovering hidden tokens from the rest of the text (BERT), versus predicting each token from the ones before (GPT)
Ch. 17


Matching
Pairs treated patients with similar untreated ones and compares outcomes within pairs; usually estimates the effect in the treated
Ch. 13


Maximum likelihood estimate (MLE)
The parameter value with the highest likelihood, \(\hat\theta\)
Ch. 2


Mean absolute error (MAE)
Average absolute distance between predictions and observed outcomes
Ch. 1


Mean squared error (MSE) and RMSE
Average squared prediction error, and its square root in the units of the outcome
Ch. 3


Mediator
A variable on the causal path from treatment to outcome; adjusting for it removes part of the effect
Ch. 13


MICE (chained equations)
Imputes several incomplete variables by cycling through them, each predicted from all the others
Ch. 9


Missing at random (MAR)
Given the observed data, the probability of a gap no longer depends on the unobserved values
Ch. 9


Missing completely at random (MCAR)
The probability of a gap depends on nothing in the data
Ch. 9


Missing not at random (MNAR)
The probability of a gap depends on the unobserved values themselves, even given the observed data
Ch. 9


Missing value
A value that was meant to be recorded but was not; the indicator \(R_{ij}\) records whether it was observed
Ch. 9


Mode collapse
A generator that produces only a few kinds of examples, missing much of the variety of the real data
Ch. 19


Model
A simplified, purpose-built representation of reality
Ch. 1


Model-agnostic and model-specific methods
Methods that only query a model’s predictions, versus methods that use its internal structure
Ch. 12


Multi-armed bandit
A repeated choice among actions with unknown mean rewards, with no state carrying over between rounds
Ch. 14


Multi-head attention
Several attention operations (heads) side by side, each with its own projections, their outputs concatenated
Ch. 17


Multilayer perceptron (MLP)
Neurons arranged in layers, each hidden layer applying weights and an activation to the previous layer’s output
Ch. 7


Multiple imputation
Creates \(M\) completed datasets with random draws for the gaps, analyses each and pools the results
Ch. 9


n-gram model
Assumes the next token depends only on the previous \(n-1\) tokens; probabilities estimated by counting
Ch. 16


Natural language processing (NLP)
The discipline that makes computers analyse and produce human language
Ch. 15


Negation detection
Deciding whether a mentioned finding is affirmed or negated, using trigger phrases and their scope
Ch. 15


Nested cross-validation
An outer cross-validation that estimates performance and an inner one that tunes hyperparameters, so tuning is included in the estimate
Ch. 3


Net benefit and decision curve
True positives minus false positives weighted by the threshold odds; plotted against the threshold, it shows whether a model is worth using
Ch. 5


Observational data
Data recorded as things happen, without intervention
Ch. 1


Odds and log-odds
\(p/(1-p)\), how many times more likely an event is than not; its logarithm is the logit
Ch. 5


Odds ratio (OR)
Ratio of the odds in two groups; in logistic regression \(e^{\beta_j}\) per unit of \(x_j\)
Ch. 5


One-standard-error rule
Choose the largest \(\lambda\) whose cross-validated error is within one standard error of the minimum
Ch. 4


Ordinary least squares (OLS)
Estimates the coefficients that make the residual sum of squares as small as possible
Ch. 4


Out-of-bag (OOB) error
Error of predictions made by the trees that did not see each instance; a nearly free estimate of test error
Ch. 6


Outcome
The feature we want to predict or explain (response, target)
Ch. 1


Overfitting
Following the noise of the training data; good training, poor test performance
Ch. 1


p-value
Probability of an estimate at least as far from zero as observed if the true value were zero and the assumptions held
Ch. 4


Partial dependence and ICE curves
How one patient’s prediction (ICE) or the average prediction (PDP) changes when one feature is varied
Ch. 12


Permutation importance
Average increase in error when one feature’s column is shuffled
Ch. 12


Perplexity
Two raised to the cross-entropy in bits: the effective number of equally likely choices at each step
Ch. 16


Policy
A rule for choosing actions from states, \(\pi(a \mid s)\)
Ch. 14


Pooling
Shrinks a feature map by summarising small blocks (maximum or average)
Ch. 7


Positional encoding
A vector added to each token embedding so the model knows where the token is
Ch. 17


Posterior predictive distribution
Distribution of a future outcome, averaging the model’s predictions over the whole posterior
Ch. 8


Potential outcomes
The outcomes a patient would have under each treatment, \(Y(1)\) and \(Y(0)\); only one is ever observed
Ch. 13


Precision, recall and F1
Positive predictive value, sensitivity, and their harmonic mean
Ch. 5


Precision–recall curve
Precision against recall over all thresholds; informative when positives are rare
Ch. 5


Prediction versus causation
A model that predicts well need not tell us what would happen if we intervened
Ch. 1


Predictive mean matching (PMM)
Imputes by copying the observed value of a participant whose prediction is close; imputed values always occur in the data
Ch. 9


Predictive values (PPV, NPV)
Probability of having the condition after a positive test, and of not having it after a negative one
Ch. 2


Predictor
A feature used to make a prediction (input)
Ch. 1


Preference tuning (RLHF, DPO)
Training a model on human comparisons of responses, through a reward model and reinforcement learning or directly
Ch. 18


Pretraining
Fitting a language model to a very large corpus by minimising next-token cross-entropy
Ch. 18


Prevalence
Proportion of the population tested that has the condition; for one patient, the prior probability
Ch. 2


Principal component analysis (PCA)
Replaces correlated features by uncorrelated weighted sums ordered by the variance they carry
Ch. 10


Prior and posterior distribution
What is assumed about a parameter before the data, and what is known after: posterior ∝ likelihood × prior
Ch. 8


Prior and posterior probability
Probability of an event before and after seeing the evidence
Ch. 2


Probability distribution
The values a random variable can take and how probable each is; for a continuous variable, a density whose area gives probabilities
Ch. 2


Prompt
The text given to a language model as context; may include a system prompt, worked examples (few-shot) or a request to reason step by step
Ch. 18


Propensity score
A patient’s probability of receiving the treatment given covariates, \(e(\mathbf{x})\)
Ch. 13


Q-learning
Learns action values from experience by moving each estimate towards reward plus discounted best next value
Ch. 14


Query, key and value
Three learned projections of each token: what it looks for, what it offers to be found by, and the content it passes on
Ch. 17


Random forest
Bagged deep trees that consider only a random subset of \(m_{\text{try}}\) features at each split
Ch. 6


Random variable
A quantity whose value is not known in advance and is described by probabilities
Ch. 2


Randomisation
Assigning treatment by chance, so treated and untreated groups are exchangeable for measured and unmeasured characteristics
Ch. 13


Recurrent neural network (RNN)
Reads a sequence token by token, updating a hidden state with the same weights at every position
Ch. 16


Regression
Supervised learning with a numerical outcome
Ch. 1


Regular expression
A compact language for describing text patterns to find, extract or replace
Ch. 15


Regularisation (shrinkage)
Fitting with a penalty on the size of the coefficients, of strength \(\lambda\); adds bias, reduces variance
Ch. 4


Reinforcement learning
Learning a policy for acting from rewards over time
Ch. 1


Reparameterisation trick
Writing a random code as \(\mathbf{\mu} + \mathbf{\sigma} \odot \mathbf{\varepsilon}\) so gradients can flow through the sampling step
Ch. 19


Reproducibility
Others can rerun the analysis and obtain the same results
Ch. 1


Residual
Observed minus predicted outcome, \(e_i = y_i - \hat y_i\)
Ch. 4


Residual connection and layer normalisation
Adding a sublayer’s input to its output; rescaling each token vector to mean 0 and standard deviation 1
Ch. 17


Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG)
A retriever finds the chunks most similar to a question, which are put into the prompt so the answer can be grounded in them
Ch. 18


Return and discount factor
The discounted sum of future rewards, \(G_t\); the discount factor \(\gamma\) sets how much later rewards count
Ch. 14


Review queue
Two thresholds on a classifier’s probability: clear below one, act above the other, send the rest to a person
Ch. 15


Reward hacking
An agent maximising a misspecified reward in ways its designers did not intend
Ch. 14


Ridge regression
Regularisation with the sum of squared coefficients (L2 penalty); shrinks all coefficients
Ch. 4


ROC curve and AUC
Sensitivity against 1 − specificity over all thresholds; the area under it is the probability that a case is ranked above a non-case
Ch. 5


Rubin’s rules
Pool multiply imputed results: average the estimates; add within- and between-imputation variance
Ch. 9


Scores and loadings
An instance’s coordinates on the components, and how strongly each feature relates to each component
Ch. 10


Sensitivity analysis (δ-adjustment)
Repeats an analysis under different assumptions, for example shifting imputed values by \(\delta\), to see whether the conclusion holds
Ch. 9


Sensitivity and specificity
Proportion of people with the condition who test positive, and of people without it who test negative
Ch. 2


Shapley value
A feature’s marginal contribution to one prediction, averaged over all orders in which features could be added
Ch. 12


Shortcut learning
Good performance obtained from features associated with the outcome but not its cause (a marker, a scanner); fails when the association changes
Ch. 7


Single imputation
Fills every gap once (mean, median, a prediction) and analyses the table as if fully observed
Ch. 9


Skip-gram (word2vec)
Learns embeddings by predicting the words within a small window around each word
Ch. 16


Smoothing
Adjusts count-based probabilities so no possible token has probability zero (add-\(\delta\))
Ch. 16


Soft assignment
Posterior probability that an instance belongs to each component, instead of a single label
Ch. 11


Softmax
Turns a vector of scores into probabilities that add up to 1; the multi-class version of the logistic function
Ch. 7


Software as a medical device
Software intended by its manufacturer for a medical purpose such as diagnosis, prediction or treatment
Ch. 18


Stacking
A meta-model learns to combine the out-of-fold predictions of several base models
Ch. 6


Standardisation
Subtracting a feature’s mean and dividing by its standard deviation, so units no longer matter
Ch. 10


State, action and reward
What the agent observes at time \(t\), what it does, and the number that scores the consequence
Ch. 14


Statistical model
\(y = f(\mathbf{x}) + \varepsilon\): systematic part plus error
Ch. 1


String and character encoding
An ordered sequence of characters, and the mapping of characters to numbers and bytes (Unicode, UTF-8)
Ch. 15


Supervised learning
Learning a mapping from features to a known outcome
Ch. 1


Synthetic data
Data produced by a generative model rather than measured, meant to reproduce chosen properties of real data
Ch. 19


t-SNE
A nonlinear map that keeps neighbours together; distances between far-apart groups are not meaningful
Ch. 10


Tensor
An array of numbers with any number of axes; its shape lists the length of each axis
Ch. 7


Test set
Data kept aside to estimate performance on new cases
Ch. 1


Text classifier
A supervised model that maps a document vector to a probability for each class
Ch. 15


TF-IDF
Term frequency times inverse document frequency: weights words that are frequent in a document but rare in the collection
Ch. 15


Thompson sampling
Chooses each action with the posterior probability that it is the best, by drawing from each arm’s posterior
Ch. 14


Token and vocabulary
The unit a text is cut into (word, subword, character, byte), and the set of distinct tokens a system knows
Ch. 15


Tool use and agent (LLM)
The model writes requests executed by ordinary software; an agent also decides which steps and tools to use
Ch. 18


Training set
Data used to fit a model
Ch. 1


Transfer learning
Reusing a network trained on a large dataset as the starting point for a new task
Ch. 7


Transformer block
Multi-head attention and a feed-forward network, each with layer normalisation and a residual connection; a transformer stacks \(N\) blocks
Ch. 17


UMAP
Builds a nearest-neighbour graph and lays it out in few dimensions; settings n_neighbors and min_dist
Ch. 10


Unsupervised learning
Finding structure in data without an outcome
Ch. 1


Validation set
Data used to compare candidate models or settings and choose among them, before the test set is opened
Ch. 3


Value function
Expected return from a state, \(V^\pi(s)\), or from taking an action in a state, \(Q^\pi(s,a)\), under a policy
Ch. 14


Value of information
How much better a decision is expected to become if an uncertainty is resolved before deciding
Ch. 2


Value-suppressing uncertainty palette (VSUP)
A colour scale that merges shades as uncertainty grows, so only reliable values stand out
Ch. 12


Vanishing gradient and LSTM
Gradients shrink over many steps back in time; the LSTM adds a memory cell with gates to keep information longer
Ch. 16


Variance (of a model)
Sensitivity of a model to its particular training set
Ch. 1


Variational autoencoder (VAE)
An autoencoder whose code is sampled from a normal distribution, with a KL penalty that makes the code space suitable for sampling
Ch. 19


Weakly informative prior
A prior that only rules out implausible values
Ch. 8

title: Appendix D — Notation
text:
D.1 Symbols used throughout the book
One symbol per idea, throughout the book. Vectors are bold lower-case (\(\mathbf{x}\)), matrices bold upper-case (\(\mathbf{X}\)), estimates carry a hat (\(\hat f\)). The first table lists the symbols used everywhere; the next ones list, chapter by chapter, the symbols each chapter adds (each chapter also opens with its own “notation at a glance” box). A few letters unavoidably carry more than one meaning, because the literature of each field uses them; the last table lists them, with the chapter where each meaning applies.

a parameter; here mostly the probability of AKI

Symbol
Meaning
Introduced

impurity of a node \(S\), impurity reduction of a split

title: Appendix D — Notation
section: D.3 Symbols with more than one meaning
text:
D.3 Symbols with more than one meaning
When a letter appears below, its meaning is always the one of the chapter you are reading; each chapter’s notation box says so.







Symbol
Meanings (chapter)




\(p\)
number of predictors (Ch. 1, 10); probability of an event and its estimate \(\hat p\) (Ch. 5, 15)


\(\pi\)
prevalence or prior probability of disease (Ch. 2); policy \(\pi(a \mid s)\) (Ch. 14) and language model seen as a policy \(\pi_\theta\) (Ch. 18)


\(\sigma\)
standard deviation (Ch. 2, 8; of a VAE code, Ch. 19); logistic (sigmoid) function \(\sigma(z)\) (Ch. 5, 7, 16)


\(\mu\)
mean of a normal distribution (Ch. 2); centroid \(\mathbf{\mu}_k\) (Ch. 11); mean reward \(\mu_k\) of a bandit arm (Ch. 14); mean of a VAE code \(\mathbf{\mu}\) (Ch. 19)


\(V\)
number of cross-validation folds (Ch. 1, 3); within-, between- and total variance \(V_W\), \(V_B\), \(V_T\) (Ch. 9); value of a state \(V^\pi(s)\) (Ch. 14); value matrix \(\mathbf{V}\) (Ch. 17)


\(Q\)
action value \(Q^\pi(s, a)\) (Ch. 14); model distribution \(Q\) in the cross-entropy (Ch. 16); query matrix \(\mathbf{Q}\) (Ch. 17)


\(K\), \(k\)
\(K\): number of clusters (Ch. 11), number of bandit arms (Ch. 14), key matrix \(\mathbf{K}\) (Ch. 17); \(k\): neighbours in \(k\)NN (Ch. 3), top-\(k\) sampling (Ch. 16), chunks retrieved (Ch. 18)


\(T\), \(t\)
\(T\): a tree with \(\lvert T\rvert\) leaves (Ch. 6), sequence length (Ch. 17), number of diffusion steps (Ch. 19); \(t\): decision or classification threshold (Ch. 2, 5; \(t_{\text{low}}\), \(t_{\text{high}}\) in Ch. 15), time step or position (Ch. 14, 16, 17, 19)


\(\varepsilon\), \(\epsilon\)
\(\varepsilon\): error term (Ch. 1, 4), standard normal noise injected by a VAE or a diffusion model (Ch. 19); \(\epsilon\): exploration rate of \(\epsilon\)-greedy (Ch. 14)


\(\alpha\)
elastic-net mixing parameter (Ch. 4); attention weight \(\alpha_{ts}\) (Ch. 17); share of signal left after \(t\) diffusion steps, \(\bar\alpha_t\) (Ch. 19)


\(\beta\)
regression coefficients \(\beta_j\) (Ch. 4 onwards); noise added at diffusion step \(t\), \(\beta_t\) (Ch. 19)


\(\delta\)
shift of imputed values in a sensitivity analysis (Ch. 9); pseudo-count of add-\(\delta\) smoothing (Ch. 16)


\(\tau\)
conditional average treatment effect \(\tau(\mathbf{x})\) (Ch. 13); sampling temperature (Ch. 16)


\(H\), \(h\)
\(H\): entropy (Ch. 2, 16), interaction strength \(H_{jk}\) (Ch. 12); \(h\): leverage \(h_{ii}\) (Ch. 4), number of attention heads (Ch. 17); bold \(\mathbf{h}\): hidden layer or state (Ch. 7, 16)


\(M\), \(m\)
\(M\): number of imputations (Ch. 9), mask matrix \(\mathbf{M}\) (Ch. 17); \(m\): number of trees in BART (Ch. 8), index of a principal component (Ch. 10), of a shuffle (Ch. 12) or of a completed dataset (Ch. 9), rank of a LoRA update (Ch. 18)


\(N\)
the \(k\) nearest training instances \(N_k(\mathbf{x})\) (Ch. 3); number of shuffles \(N_s\) (Ch. 12); number of tokens in a sequence (Ch. 16); number of stacked transformer blocks (Ch. 17)


\(L\), \(\mathcal{L}\)
likelihood \(L(\theta)\) (Ch. 2); a confounder or set of confounders \(L\) (Ch. 13); loss \(\mathcal{L}\) (Ch. 3, 7, 12)


\(G\), \(g\)
\(G\): number of classes (Ch. 6), return \(G_t\) (Ch. 14), generator of a GAN (Ch. 19); \(g\): activation function (Ch. 7), cluster label \(g_i\) (Ch. 11), layer-normalisation gain \(\mathbf{g}\) (Ch. 17)


\(D\)
an event such as a disease (Ch. 2); Cook’s distance \(D_i\) (Ch. 4); the data table \(\mathbf{D}\) (Ch. 9); a dataset \(D\) (Ch. 12); discriminator of a GAN (Ch. 19)


\(R\), \(r\)
\(R^2\) (Ch. 3); leaf regions \(R_m\) (Ch. 6); missingness indicator \(R_{ij}\) (Ch. 9); R-hat \(\widehat{R}\) (Ch. 8); \(r\): DBSCAN radius (Ch. 11), reward \(r_{t+1}\) or \(r(x, y)\) (Ch. 14, 18)


\(e\)
prediction error or residual \(e_i\) (Ch. 3, 4); propensity score \(e(\mathbf{x})\) (Ch. 13); embedding \(\mathbf{e}_w\) (Ch. 16, 17)


\(w\)
weight of a neuron \(w_j\) (Ch. 7); inverse-probability weight \(w_i\) (Ch. 13); token \(w_t\) (Ch. 15–18)


\(z\)
linear predictor or weighted sum (Ch. 5, 7); principal-component scores \(\mathbf{z}_i\) (Ch. 10); logits \(\mathbf{z}\), \(\mathbf{z}_t\) (Ch. 16, 17); latent code \(\mathbf{z}\) (Ch. 19)


\(d\)
distance \(d(\mathbf{x}_i, \mathbf{x}_{i'})\) (Ch. 10); embedding or model dimension (Ch. 16, 17), with \(d_k\) and \(d_{\text{ff}}\) (Ch. 17); chunk vector \(\mathbf{d}_j\) (Ch. 18)


\(S\), \(s\)
\(S\): a node of a tree (Ch. 6), number of posterior draws (Ch. 8), a set of features (Ch. 12); \(\mathbf{S}\): covariance matrix (Ch. 10); \(s\): index of a posterior draw (Ch. 8), silhouette \(s(i)\) (Ch. 11), state \(s_t\) (Ch. 14), key position (Ch. 17)


\(C\)
losses \(C_{\text{FP}}\), \(C_{\text{FN}}\) (Ch. 2, 5) and review cost \(C_{\text{R}}\) (Ch. 15); cluster \(C_k\) (Ch. 11); complement of a feature set, \(\mathbf{x}_C\) (Ch. 12)


\(A\), \(\mathcal{A}\)
set of alternatives or actions \(\mathcal{A}\) (Ch. 1, 14); treatment or exposure \(A\) (Ch. 13); LoRA matrix \(\mathbf{A}\) (Ch. 18)


\(B\), \(\mathbf{b}\)
\(B\): number of bootstrap samples or trees (Ch. 6); LoRA matrix \(\mathbf{B}\) (Ch. 18); \(b\), \(\mathbf{b}\): bias of a neuron or layer (Ch. 7), layer-normalisation shift (Ch. 17); \(\text{Beta}(a, b)\) prior counts (Ch. 8)


\(n\)
number of instances (Ch. 1), including documents in a collection (Ch. 15); the \(n\) of an \(n\)-gram, unrelated (Ch. 16)
